A one-off lifts the level once and stops. A growth rate lifts it again next year, off the new higher base, forever. In budget terms: a one-time saving versus a run-rate saving.

The reason anyone cares is that the one-off almost always looks bigger when you compare them, and almost always loses.

Proposal A: output jumps 5% once, permanently. By year 17, still 5% ahead.

Proposal B: the growth rate rises from 2.0% to 2.3% — three tenths of a point. By year 17 it has caught A, by year 40 it is 12.5% ahead, and it never stops pulling away.

Opposite verdicts depending on when you look. The only thing that changed is whether the gain repeats — and the crossover sits at year 17, which is why a government facing an election and a pension fund facing 2070 rank these two differently and both are right.

So the test on any growth claim: does it move the level or the rate? Tax rebates, a one-time investment, a commodity windfall move the level. Tooling, training, competition, infrastructure move the rate.

Productivity is just the name for the rate — output per hour worked, the one input that repeats. And the rule of 70 gives you the crossover fast: 70 divided by the growth rate is the doubling time, which tells you whether your horizon is long enough for a rate change to have paid off yet.

Inflation: how the CPI is built, and why 2% is the target

Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level. Two words in that sentence need unpacking. Sustained rules out one-off jumps in a single price: petrol rising after a hurricane is not inflation, it is one price moving. General means the average across the things people buy, so inflation is a statement about money rather than about any particular product. And because it describes money, it can be read from the other direction with no change of meaning: prices rising by 5% and each dollar buying 5% less are the same event described twice.

To measure it you need a price level, and a price level is built as an index. An index is a single number that stands for the average price of a whole collection of things, set to 100 in some chosen base period so that only its movement carries meaning: 100 in the base year and 106 four years later says prices are 6% higher than they were, and nothing else. Inflation is then the rate of change of that index, normally quoted either month over month or against the same month a year earlier. The most famous such index is the CPI, the Consumer Price Index.

The construction is simple in concept and enormous in execution. The Bureau of Labor Statistics first defines a basket: a fixed list of the goods and services a typical urban household actually buys, from rent and eggs to haircuts and car insurance. It then sends staff out to collect roughly 80,000 individual prices every month from shops, landlords and service providers, so that it is pricing the same items in the same places over time. Finally it combines those price changes into one number using weights taken from surveys of how households really spend their money — shelter gets about a third of the weight, food about 13%, energy about 7%.

The combining step is the part worth being explicit about, because it drives everything else in this subsection. In words: multiply each item's price change by the share of a household budget that item represents, then add those products up. That is a weighted average, and it is the reason a price change matters in proportion to how much of your money it touches rather than how dramatic it looks. Shelter at a third of the budget moves the index more than petrol at 3% of the budget does, even when the petrol price move is several times larger.

Your edge

CPI is literally a weighted average — a dot product of budget-share weights and price changes. Two consequences fall out of the math. First, your personal inflation rate differs from the headline whenever your budget weights differ (renters in hot cities live a higher inflation rate than the index). Second, big-weight items dominate: a 5% move in shelter moves the index more than a 20% move in gasoline.

Worked example: a mini-CPI

Say the basket is 35% rent, 15% food, 5% gasoline, 45% everything else. This year rent rises 5%, food 2%, gas 20%, everything else 1%. Inflation = 0.35×5 + 0.15×2 + 0.05×20 + 0.45×1 = 1.75 + 0.30 + 1.00 + 0.45 = 3.5%. Note the 20% gas spike — the thing everyone sees on street signs — contributes only 1 point.

Two of the components in that basket behave differently from the rest. Food and energy prices are set in global markets that respond to weather, harvests, wars and shipping disruptions, so they can jump 20% and give it all back within a year. Because they swing hard in both directions, a month in which they spike tells you very little about where prices are heading next. Analysts therefore track a second version alongside the headline: core inflation, which is the same index with food and energy removed.

Dropping them is not an attempt to make the number look better — over a decade the two versions converge, since the spikes cancel out. It is an attempt to see the persistent part, the inflation embedded in rents, wages and services that keeps going once it starts. The working rule is that headline inflation is what households actually experience and pay, while core inflation is what predicts next year better, so policymakers watch core when deciding and everyone quotes headline when arguing.

Where does inflation come from in the first place? There are three standard explanations, they describe genuinely different mechanisms, and real episodes almost always mix them.

The first is demand-pull. Total spending grows faster than the economy's ability to produce. Every business finds more buyers than it can serve, so instead of expanding output — which takes time, staff and equipment it does not have — it raises prices, because raising prices is instant and it can still sell everything it makes. Repeat that across the whole economy and the price level rises. The United States in 2021 is the textbook case: stimulus payments and accumulated savings hit a reopening economy whose supply chains and workforces had not come back yet.

The second is cost-push. Nothing happens to demand at all; instead the cost of an input that everything else depends on jumps, and firms pass it forward to protect their margins. Energy is the classic input because it enters the cost of almost every good, directly through manufacturing and indirectly through transporting it. When the 1973 oil embargo quadrupled crude prices, the cost of producing and moving nearly everything rose at once, and prices followed even though no one was spending more.

The third is monetary. If the quantity of money in an economy grows persistently faster than the quantity of goods that money can buy, then sooner or later there is more money chasing each unit of output and prices adjust upward to absorb it. Milton Friedman's line that inflation is "always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon" is the strong form of this claim, and it is contested for ordinary inflation of a few percent, where the link between money growth and prices is loose and slow. It becomes exactly and undeniably true in every hyperinflation, where a government printing money at speed is unmistakably the cause.

Given all that, why do the Fed, the ECB and nearly every other modern central bank aim for about 2% inflation instead of zero? Deliberately planning to make money lose value each year sounds perverse until you look at the four reasons, which are all about what happens near the bottom.

The first is measurement. A price index compares a fixed basket over time, but products improve and people substitute. When this year's laptop is faster than last year's at the same price, that is a price cut in everything but name, and statisticians only partly manage to capture it; when beef gets expensive and shoppers switch to chicken, a fixed basket keeps pricing the beef. Both biases push measured inflation above true inflation, by an estimated half to one point, so a measured 2% is probably nearer 1% in reality.

The second is distance from the edge. Inflation is not steered precisely; policy affects it with lags of a year or more, and shocks arrive uninvited. Aiming at zero means that an ordinary miss on the low side lands you in deflation, which the next paragraph explains is far harder to escape than an overshoot. Two percent is a buffer chosen to keep normal errors from crossing zero.

The third concerns wages. Employers rarely cut anyone's stated pay: workers react so badly to a smaller number on the payslip that firms would rather lay people off than reduce salaries. But an economy constantly needs some workers to become relatively cheaper — a declining industry has to shed cost somehow. With 2% general inflation, a firm can simply freeze pay for a year and the real cost of that worker falls 2% without anyone's stated salary going down. At zero inflation, that adjustment is only available through outright cuts or redundancies.

The fourth is about the central bank's own ammunition. What actually influences borrowing and investment is the real interest rate, meaning the stated rate minus inflation: borrowing at 3% while prices rise 5% costs you −2% in real terms, because you repay in money worth less than what you borrowed. A central bank cannot push the stated rate far below zero, since people can always hold cash at 0%. So the lowest real rate it can engineer is roughly minus the inflation rate. At 2% inflation it can drive real rates to about −2% in a slump; at 0% inflation the floor is 0% and it is out of room exactly when it needs room most. That constraint, and what banks do when they hit it, is the subject of Section 4 (Central Banks).

Which leaves the question of why falling prices are a problem at all. Cheaper things sound like good news, and for one product they are. As a general, sustained condition they set off two mechanisms that feed each other.

The first works through spending. If prices are reliably falling, waiting is profitable: the car costs less next quarter, so buy it then. Enough people postpone and firms find demand has dropped, so they cut prices further to shift stock and cut staff to cut costs, which reduces incomes, which postpones more spending. The expectation of falling prices is what makes it self-reinforcing — each round of cuts confirms that waiting was right.

The second works through debt, and it is the more dangerous of the two. Loans are written in fixed money amounts: a $300,000 mortgage stays $300,000 no matter what prices do. If wages and prices fall 3%, the borrower has 3% less income to service a debt that has not shrunk at all, so the real weight of every mortgage and business loan rises each year without anyone borrowing another cent. Households and firms respond by cutting spending to pay debt down, which lowers demand further, which lowers prices further, and the burden rises again. Japan lived in a mild version of this from the 1990s into the 2000s, with prices roughly flat or drifting down and growth stalled for two decades. That experience is why central banks are far more frightened of 0% than of 3%.

Inflation time machine

Set an average inflation rate and watch what it quietly does to cash. Try the presets — especially the third one.

Your cash will buy what this buys today$41.20
Needed then to match your amount today$242.73
Purchasing power halves every23 yrs

At 3% average inflation, in 30 years your $100.00 buys what $41.20 buys today. To match it, you would need $242.73.

It is worth pushing the presets to feel where the compounding bites. At the 2% target, $100 held as cash still buys about $55 of today's goods after thirty years — a slow leak you can plan around. At the 7% the United States averaged across the 1970s, the same $100 falls to roughly $13 of buying power over thirty years, which is most of a lifetime's savings erased without a single bad investment decision. This is the precise sense in which "cash is safe" is only true over short horizons: cash cannot fall in nominal value, and that is exactly what makes it certain to fall in real value. Sections 7 (Equities) and 8 (Fixed Income) are largely about what people hold instead.

And then there's hyperinflation — conventionally, inflation above 50% per month. In Weimar Germany in 1923, prices doubled roughly every three to four days at the peak; workers were paid twice daily and sprinted to spend wages before evening, and banknotes were cheaper than firewood. Zimbabwe in November 2008 hit an estimated 79 billion percent per month — prices doubling roughly every day — until the country simply abandoned its own currency. The mechanism is always the same: a government that can't tax or borrow prints money to pay its bills, everyone races to swap cash for anything real, and money stops doing its job (recall the three functions of money from Section 1 — hyperinflation kills all three). The "Argentina-style 50%" preset above is annual, not monthly — and even that halves your purchasing power every 1.7 years.

Real world: your inflation is not the CPI

The CPI is a weighted average for a statistical average household — a household that does not exist. Because it is a dot product, your personal rate is the same formula with your weights, and it can differ by several points. During the 2021–23 US episode the components moved wildly apart:

Component CPI weight Peak 12-month move
Shelter (rent + owners' equivalent rent) ≈ 34% +8% (2023, lagging market rents by a year)
Used cars & trucks ≈ 3% +45% (mid-2021), then negative
Gasoline ≈ 3.5% +60% (June 2022), then −20%
Food at home ≈ 8% +13% (Aug 2022)
Medical care services ≈ 6.5% +5%, then briefly negative on an insurance-accounting quirk

A 25-year-old renting in a city, driving a used car to work, spends far more than 34% + 3% + 3.5% of income on the three fastest-rising lines — their lived inflation ran well above the headline. A retired homeowner with a paid-off house and low mileage experienced much less. Both were told inflation was 9%.

Try this as a weekend project: export a year of your bank transactions, bucket them into CPI categories, normalise to shares, and dot them with the published category indices from the BLS. You will have built a personal CPI in about forty lines of pandas — and you will understand basket construction better than most people who quote the number.

Make it click

Inflation answers one question: how much less will a fixed sum of money buy by the time you spend it?

Which makes every price you fix in advance a bet. You lock a number today; inflation decides what it is worth later. Fix below the inflation that arrives and you win. Fix above it and you lose.

The reason anyone cares is that this happens silently, in contracts nobody files as financial.

Three-year supply deal priced off 2% expected inflation. Inflation arrives at 6% → by year three you pay about 12% below the real market rate. Your supplier ate it.

Same deal, same clause. Inflation arrives at 0% → you are locked into rises nobody else is paying, out of your own margin.

Same contract, opposite outcome. The only thing that changed is the inflation rate that turned up.

So choose your index by purpose. Forecast on core, which drops food and energy because they spike and fall back. Pay on headline, because a cost-of-living rise has to cover what people actually buy. Swap them and you either underpay staff through an energy spike, or bake that spike into a three-year baseline.

The rest follows. CPI is a weighted average of a basket, so your rate differs whenever your spending does. The 2% target is a promise about the number everyone indexes to. And deflation is the same bet inverted: falling prices make every fixed debt heavier, which is why borrowers fear it and lenders do not.

Unemployment: one number, many stories

The third headline number is the unemployment rate, and the thing to understand about it is what sits underneath the division line. It is not the share of the population without a job. It is the share of the labor force that is jobless and actively looking, where the labor force means people who are either working or actively looking. In the United States that is established by a monthly survey of about 60,000 households, which asks whether the person did any paid work last week and, if not, whether they took a specific step to find work in the past four weeks.

Both of those conditions exclude real people. Retirees, full-time students, stay-at-home parents and anyone who has stopped searching are not counted as unemployed, because they are not in the labor force at all — they are neither in the numerator nor the denominator. That is defensible: a seventy-year-old who has retired is not evidence of a weak job market. But it has a consequence that matters enormously in practice, which is that people can move between "unemployed" and "not in the labor force" without any job being created or destroyed.

Work it through with round numbers. Imagine 100 working-age adults: 60 have jobs, 4 are jobless and searching, and 36 are out of the labor force entirely. The labor force is 60 + 4 = 64, so the unemployment rate is 4 ÷ 64 = 6.25%.

Now let two of those four searchers give up. They have not found work; they have concluded there is no point applying and stopped. Employment is unchanged at 60. But the labor force falls to 62 because two people left it, and the count of unemployed falls to 2, so the rate is now 2 ÷ 62 = 3.2%. The headline has almost halved while not one additional person is working, and the underlying situation is slightly worse, not better. This is not a hypothetical quirk: discouraged workers leaving the labor force is a normal feature of long downturns, and it flatters the headline exactly when conditions are grimmest.

Common pitfall

Never read the unemployment rate alone. Always check the labor-force participation rate next to it — if unemployment fell but participation fell too, discouraged workers may be doing the "improving." Broader measures like U-6 (which adds discouraged workers and part-timers who want full-time work) often tell a darker story than the headline U-3 rate.

Economists also sort unemployment by cause, because the three causes call for completely different responses and mistaking one for another produces bad policy. Frictional unemployment is people in transit between jobs — a data scientist who resigned on Friday and starts interviewing on Monday. The jobs exist and the skills match; the only thing missing is time for the search. It needs nothing more than better information and faster matching.

Structural unemployment is a mismatch of skills or geography. There are vacancies, but not ones this person can do, or not within commuting distance — coal miners in a region whose new employers are data centres. Extra spending will not fix it, because the constraint is not a shortage of demand; retraining, housing and relocation are what move the number, and they take years. Cyclical unemployment is the recession kind: demand falls across the entire economy at once, so layoffs sweep through industries that have nothing to do with each other and the vacancies genuinely are not there. This is the type that monetary and fiscal policy are designed to attack, and the only one they can attack quickly.

Because the frictional and structural kinds never go away, zero unemployment is neither achievable nor something to aim for. An economy where nobody was ever between jobs would be one where nobody ever left a bad match for a better one, and that churn — people quitting, searching and re-matching — is how workers and employers find each other in the first place. The rate that remains when there is no recession, just normal churn, is called the natural rate, and in the United States it is usually put at somewhere between 4% and 5%.

It matters because the natural rate marks the point where the economy's two problems swap places. Push unemployment below it and employers who want staff must bid them away from other employers, so wages rise faster than productivity, costs rise, and firms pass that into prices — the labour market becomes an inflation engine. Let unemployment sit above it and the opposite waste occurs: people who want to work and could be producing are not, and that output is gone permanently. The Fed is legally required to weigh both sides at once, an obligation known as the dual mandate, which is where Section 4 begins.

Worked example: unemployment falls, nobody gets a job

Take an economy of 100 million working-age adults. Run two consecutive months in which employment does not change at all.

Month 1 Month 2
Employed 60.0M 60.0M
Unemployed (searching) 4.0M 3.0M
Labor force 64.0M 63.0M
Unemployment rate 6.25% 4.76%
Participation rate 64.0% 63.0%

The headline rate improved by 1.5 percentage points because one million people stopped looking. Employment is identical. Any analyst reading only the first number writes the wrong note.

The fix is to read three series together: the unemployment rate (U-3), the participation rate, and the employment-to-population ratio — the last of which cannot be gamed by people leaving the labor force. The BLS also publishes U-6, which adds discouraged workers and people working part-time who want full-time hours; it typically runs about 3–4 points above U-3, and the gap between them widens when the labor market is softer than the headline admits.

Make it click

The unemployment rate answers one question: of the people who want a job, what share cannot find one?

Note what that leaves out. The denominator is not everyone — it is only people working or actively looking. Stop looking and you leave the denominator entirely, and the rate improves. So a falling rate means one of two opposite things, and the rate alone cannot tell you which.

It matters because this is true of every ratio you report, not just this one.

Cost per active user falls from $4.00 to $3.20. Total cost fell $400k → $320k, users steady at 100,000. You saved $80,000.

Cost per active user falls from $4.00 to $3.20. Cost held at $400k; "active" was redefined and users went 100,000 → 125,000. You saved nothing.

Same 20% improvement, opposite reality. The only thing that changed is whether the numerator fell or the denominator grew.

So the check is two questions: which line actually moved, and is there a version of this metric whose denominator cannot walk away? Unemployment has one — the employment-to-population ratio, where the denominator is everybody. Read it next to the headline and the ambiguity disappears.

The remaining terms sit on that. U-3 is the headline rate, U-6 the wider one that counts discouraged and part-time workers. Frictional, structural and cyclical are causes rather than measures, and the split matters because only cyclical unemployment responds to the interest rate lever in the next chapter.

Business cycles: the economy's heartbeat

Plot real GDP over fifty years and you see two things at once: a line climbing steadily upward, and a wobble around it. The upward climb is the growth story above — productivity compounding. The wobble is the business cycle, and it has a standard vocabulary. Activity rises through an expansion until it reaches a peak, then contracts through a recession down to a trough, after which recovery begins the next expansion.

Why an economy should oscillate at all rather than grow smoothly comes down to two ingredients. First, shocks keep arriving — an oil embargo, a housing bust, a pandemic, a burst of over-optimistic investment. Second, and more importantly, the economy amplifies them instead of absorbing them. A firm facing weaker sales cuts staff; those workers cut their own spending, which weakens some other firm's sales. Banks that took losses tighten lending, so even healthy firms cannot borrow. Businesses run down inventories rather than reorder, so factory output falls by more than final demand did. Each of those loops turns a shock into something broader and longer than the shock itself, and the same loops run in reverse on the way up.

What the cycle is not is periodic. It recurs, but never on a schedule: post-1945 US expansions have run anywhere from one year to more than a decade, averaging about five years, with recessions averaging around ten months. Anyone selling you a fixed-length cycle clock — an eighteen-year property cycle, a seven-year crash rhythm — is selling astrology dressed up in a chart.

Who decides that a recession officially happened? You may have heard the rule that two consecutive quarters of falling GDP make a recession. That is a piece of journalistic shorthand, not the definition. In the United States the call is made by the National Bureau of Economic Research, a private research body whose Business Cycle Dating Committee identifies peaks and troughs using a dashboard of monthly series — payroll employment, real household income, industrial production, real consumer spending — on the grounds that a recession is a broad decline across the economy, not a number on one series.

The practical catch is timing. The committee only declares once the evidence is unambiguous, and being unambiguous takes revisions and months of confirming data, so the announcement always comes long after the event. The 2020 recession ended in April 2020; the committee said so in July 2021, fifteen months later. By the time a recession is official, asset prices have already reflected it, recovered from it, or both. Anything you want to act on has to come from the data as it arrives, not from the label.

Which is why analysts care so much about when a series turns relative to the economy as a whole. Data gets sorted into three families by timing, and the reason each behaves as it does is mechanical rather than mysterious.

Leading indicators turn months before the economy: building permits, new factory orders, stock prices, weekly jobless claims, the yield curve. They lead because each one measures a decision taken now about activity that happens later. A permit is pulled months before construction starts; an order is placed before anything is manufactured; a claim for unemployment benefit is filed the week someone is let go, long before that shows up in quarterly output. Coincident indicators — payroll employment, industrial production — move with the economy and effectively define where it currently is.

Lagging indicators turn only after the fact and confirm rather than predict. The unemployment rate is the important example, and it is worth knowing why it lags: firms facing a downturn first cut hours and hiring, and firms seeing a recovery first restore hours and only later commit to new permanent staff. Hiring is expensive and hard to reverse, so employers wait until they are convinced. The result is that unemployment often keeps rising for months after a recovery has actually begun — which is exactly when the political pressure to do something about a recession that is already over peaks.

One leading indicator gets more attention than all the others, and it needs its own explanation because it is not obvious why it should work. The yield curve is simply the interest rate the government pays to borrow, plotted against how long it is borrowing for: 3 months, 2 years, 10 years, 30 years. Its normal shape slopes upward, because lending for longer means more time for inflation or events to go wrong, and lenders want compensation for that.

A long rate is best understood as the market's average expectation of short rates over that whole period, plus a bit extra for the risk of being locked in. So when the curve inverts — when the 2-year rate rises above the 10-year — investors are collectively saying they expect short-term rates to be lower in the future than they are now. Central banks cut rates for one main reason, which is a weakening economy. So an inverted curve is the bond market pricing in an expectation that the central bank will be forced to cut, which means it is pricing in an expectation of trouble.

The historical record is genuinely striking: an inversion has preceded every US recession of the past six decades, typically by six to twenty-four months, with essentially one clear false alarm in the mid-1960s. It is also a record with a small sample and a large caveat — the long, deep inversion of 2022 to 2024 was not followed by a recession on anything like the usual schedule, which is a live argument rather than a settled one. Why the signal works mechanically, and why quantitative easing may have weakened it, is a story for Section 8 (Fixed Income).

Real world: the yield curve's actual record

The 10-year-minus-2-year (or 10-year-minus-3-month) Treasury spread going negative has preceded every US recession since the 1950s, with roughly one false positive (1966). It is the most respected leading indicator in markets — and the least useful for timing.

Inversion began Recession began Lead time
Aug 1978 Jan 1980 17 months
Sep 1980 Jul 1981 10 months
Dec 1988 Jul 1990 19 months
Feb 2000 Mar 2001 13 months
Dec 2005 Dec 2007 24 months
Aug 2019 Feb 2020 6 months (pandemic)
Jul 2022 — longest inversion on record, no promptly dated recession

Three analyst lessons. One: lead times of 6 to 24 months make it unusable as a trading trigger — a fund that sold equities on the 2005 signal missed two years of gains. Two: a signal with roughly eight independent observations cannot be backtested to any useful confidence, no matter how clean the chart looks. Three: the 2022 episode is a live reminder that the mechanism can change — the curve inverted partly because inflation was expected to fall, not only because growth was expected to.

Make it click

A leading indicator answers one question: is a downturn more likely than it was last month?

Notice it does not answer "when." The yield curve has inverted before every US recession in sixty years, but the gap between the signal and the recession has run anywhere from 6 to 24 months. A signal with that much timing error is worth acting on as a probability and worthless as a date.

The reason anyone cares is that those two readings produce opposite instructions from the same data.

Read as a date: the curve inverts in December 2005, so freeze hiring and defer capex now. The recession arrives December 2007 — you spent two years shrinking while competitors grew.

Read as a probability: same December 2005 signal, so write the downside plan, agree what gets cut and in what order, draw the credit line while terms are good — and change nothing until payrolls actually turn.

Same signal, same accuracy, opposite outcomes. The only thing that changed is whether it triggered action or triggered preparation.

So the rule is to match your response to the signal's timing error. Wide error, you prepare. Narrow error, you act.

That is what the three families of indicator are for. Leading ones — permits, jobless claims, the curve — shift the probability. Coincident ones — payrolls, industrial production — are your trigger. Lagging ones — unemployment, CPI — only confirm, which is why the official recession call took fifteen months and is never a plan.

AD–AS: one mental model for every shock

You now have the three dashboard numbers — output, prices, jobs — and no way of relating them to each other. What is missing is a framework that takes an event and tells you which of the three should move and in which direction. That framework is aggregate demand and aggregate supply, and it is deliberately built to look like the supply-and-demand cross from Section 2, with the whole economy substituted for the single market. Total real output sits on the horizontal axis where quantity used to be, and the overall price level sits on the vertical axis where the price of one good used to be.

Aggregate demand is total spending on domestic output — the same C + I + G + NX from the start of this section, now plotted against the price level. It slopes downward, meaning more is bought when the general price level is lower, and the reason is not the microeconomic one. In a single market you buy less beef when beef is expensive because you switch to chicken; here there is nothing to switch to, since every price is moving together. The reasons are that a lower price level makes the money and savings people already hold go further, that it tends to come with lower interest rates which makes borrowing to buy houses and equipment cheaper, and that it makes the country's goods cheaper relative to foreign ones, so exports rise and imports fall.

Aggregate supply is the total output producers are willing to make at each price level, and in the short run it slopes upward for a specifically human reason: wages and many contract prices are sticky. Pay is renegotiated once a year, supply contracts are signed for eighteen months, menus are reprinted seasonally. So when selling prices rise, costs do not immediately follow, each unit sold is briefly more profitable, and firms respond by producing more and hiring more.

That stickiness is temporary, and this is the key to the whole framework. As contracts come up for renewal, workers notice their pay buys less and negotiate it back, and suppliers reprice. Once costs have caught up with prices, the extra profitability is gone and firms cut production back to what their actual capacity justifies. So in the long run aggregate supply is a vertical line at the economy's potential output — the amount determined by the workforce, the capital stock and the productivity fundamentals discussed earlier. Demand decides how much of that potential is being used this year; productivity decides where the line itself sits.

With those two curves in place, any macroeconomic event becomes a two-part question with a testable answer. First, does the event change how much people want to buy, or how much it costs to produce? That tells you whether demand or supply moved. Second, does it increase or decrease that thing? That tells you which direction the curve shifted. The prediction then falls out of the geometry: a demand curve shifting right raises both output and prices, a demand curve shifting left lowers both, a supply curve shifting left lowers output while raising prices, and a supply curve shifting right raises output while lowering prices. The useful part is that the two cases leave different fingerprints — demand shocks move output and prices in the same direction, supply shocks move them in opposite directions — so you can work backwards from the data to the cause.

Shock Curve Output Prices
Stimulus checks, tax cuts, rate cuts AD shifts right ↑ ↑
Oil spike, supply-chain breakdown, war AS shifts left ↓ ↑
Financial crisis, confidence collapse AD shifts left ↓ ↓
Pandemic lockdown Both shift left at once ↓↓ mixed

Real world: 2020–2022 in one framework

The pandemic hit both curves: AS left (factories and services shut) and AD left (spending froze) — output cratered while prices barely moved at first. Then 2021 reversed the demand side violently: trillions in stimulus plus reopening shifted AD hard right while AS was still crippled by supply chains and, in 2022, an energy shock. Demand up plus supply down is the textbook recipe for the inflation surge to ~9% — and the model also explains why it faded as supply chains healed and the Fed leaned on demand.

The supply-shock case is the one that causes real trouble, and it earned its own word in the 1970s: stagflation, stagnation and inflation at the same time. The trouble is not that it feels bad but that it leaves the central bank with no clean move. Raising rates to fight the inflation reduces demand and deepens the slump; cutting rates to support output adds demand to an economy that is already short of supply and entrenches the inflation. One instrument cannot fix two problems that point in opposite directions.

It also broke the era's favourite empirical relationship, the Phillips curve. Through the 1960s, US data traced a tidy inverse trade-off: years with low unemployment came with higher inflation and years with high unemployment came with lower inflation, which fits neatly if you assume every shock is a demand shock moving along a fixed supply curve. Policymakers began treating the relationship as a menu they could order from — accept a bit more inflation, buy a bit less unemployment. Then the 1973 oil shock pushed aggregate supply left, and the dots left the curve entirely: high inflation and high unemployment together, which the menu said could not happen. What had actually been discovered was that the curve only describes an economy being hit by demand shocks.

Deep dive: why the Phillips curve broke — expectations

Milton Friedman and Edmund Phelps predicted the breakdown before it happened, in 1968. Their argument: the trade-off only works while workers are fooled. Run the economy hot and inflation rises; workers eventually notice, demand raises to match, firms' cost advantage evaporates, and unemployment drifts back to its natural rate — but now with permanently higher inflation baked in. Formally, the expectations-augmented version is:

π = πe − b × (u − u*) + supply shocks
π = inflation · πe = expected inflation · u = unemployment · u* = natural rate · b > 0

The policy punchline: the curve is only a usable trade-off when expectations (πe) stay anchored. That is why modern central banks talk obsessively about "anchored expectations" and why they react so aggressively when surveys and market-implied inflation forecasts start drifting — once πe moves, you're fighting the 1970s again. The bond-market gauges of πe live in Section 8.

Worked example: diagnose six headlines in ten seconds each

The whole payoff of AD–AS is that it turns news into a two-question drill: which curve moved, and which way? Cover the right-hand columns and try it.

Headline Curve Output Prices
OPEC+ cuts production; crude jumps 20% AS left Down Up
Congress passes a $1.9tn spending package AD right Up Up
Fed raises rates 75bp AD left Down Down
Ports unclog; shipping rates fall 80% AS right Up Down
Immigration expands the labor force AS right (and AD right) Up Ambiguous
Housing crash wipes out household wealth AD left Down Down

The diagnostic value is in the sign pattern, not the magnitude. If output and prices move together, you are looking at a demand shock and the central bank's job is easy — one lever fixes both. If they move in opposite directions, it is a supply shock and the central bank is trapped: fighting the inflation deepens the slump, and cushioning the slump entrenches the inflation. That is the entire policy dilemma of 1973, 1979, and 2022 in one sentence.

Make it click

AD–AS answers one question: when something hits the economy, will the central bank be able to help?

You read it off the signs. If output and prices move the same way, it was demand — one lever fixes both, and the bank will pull it. If they move opposite ways, it was supply — every lever fixes one and worsens the other, so the bank is stuck.

This matters because the same fall in your revenue is survivable in one case and not the other.

2008 — output and prices both fall. Rates cut to zero. Your revenue drops 3%, your input costs ease, your borrowing gets cheaper. Cheap money bridges the gap.

2022 — output weakens while prices rise. Your revenue drops the same 3%, but input costs jump about 9% and the policy rate goes from near zero to 5.3%. Revenue, costs and financing all move against you at once.

Same 3% revenue fall, opposite survivability. The only thing that changed is whether prices fell with output or rose against it.

So you can call it off the first two data releases, months before anyone names the recession — and phase your contingency accordingly: short and supported, or long with no rescue coming.

Stagflation is just the name for the second case. Sticky wages are why the supply curve slopes up at all — pay is renegotiated slowly, so rising prices are briefly profitable. And the Phillips curve broke because it assumed only demand shocks existed, which stopped being true in 1973.

Reading macro data like an analyst

There is one more thing to know about macro data, and textbooks tend to skip it. In markets these numbers are not background reading; they are scheduled events that reprice trillions of dollars within seconds of being published. Understanding how that repricing works changes what the numbers mean to you.

The mechanic to grasp is that the market has already made its own forecast before the release. Ahead of every major statistic, news organisations survey dozens of professional economists and publish the average of their forecasts as the consensus estimate. Traders have positioned for that number: if everyone expects payrolls of +200,000, then bonds and equities are already trading at prices that assume +200,000. When the release arrives, the part everyone expected changes nothing, because it was bought and sold days ago. Only the gap between what arrived and what was expected is new information, so only that gap moves prices.

This is why market reactions look perverse if you read only the level. A jobs report showing weak hiring can send stocks up, provided the hiring was less weak than economists had forecast. An inflation print of 3.1% — high by any standard — can leave prices unchanged if 3.1% was exactly what everyone penciled in. The general principle, that prices already contain everything known and public, is the subject of Section 17 (Market Efficiency).

Release Cadence Why markets care
CPI Monthly, 8:30 a.m. ET Sets expectations for Fed rate moves; bonds, stocks, and FX reprice within seconds of a surprise.
Jobs report (payrolls + unemployment + wages) First Friday, monthly The single most-watched release; nonfarm payrolls is the headline number of the month.
PCE price index Monthly The Fed's preferred inflation gauge — less famous than CPI, more important to policymakers.
GDP (advance estimate) Quarterly, revised twice Backward-looking, so usually less explosive — unless it surprises on growth direction.
FOMC rate decision 8 meetings/year The policy response itself — the star of Section 4.
ISM manufacturing PMI 1st business day, monthly Survey-based and early — one of the first reads on each month's cycle momentum.
Initial jobless claims Weekly, Thursday The most timely labor signal; noisy, so watch the 4-week average.

Two habits follow from that, and both are worth adopting permanently. The first is to never look at a macro number without immediately asking "versus what?". A payrolls print of +180,000 carries no information on its own. If consensus was +200,000 it is a miss and the market reads it as weakness; if consensus was +150,000 it is a beat and the same print reads as strength. The number is only half a fact until you attach the expectation to it.

The second is to know which regime you are in, because the market's interpretation of good news is not fixed. In an ordinary expansion, strong employment is straightforwardly good for shares: more people earning means more spending and higher profits. But when the central bank is fighting inflation, strong employment means it will keep rates high for longer, which lowers the present value of every future profit — and the same strong report sends shares down. That is the well-known "good news is bad news" regime, and it is not investors being irrational. It is the same report being fed into a different question: in one regime the binding worry is recession, in the other it is inflation.

Your edge

If you build models on macro data, respect two data-engineering realities. Releases get revised — payrolls are routinely restated by tens of thousands of jobs over the following two months — so backtesting on today's cleaned-up series quietly leaks the future. Serious quant shops use point-in-time ("vintage") datasets that store what was known on each date. And engineer features from surprises (actual minus consensus), not levels: the level was already priced.

Worked example: the number moves nothing, the surprise moves everything

CPI is released at 8:30 a.m. Eastern. Economists' consensus is +0.2% for the month, 3.1% year-over-year. Three scenarios, same release:

Print Surprise 2-year yield S&P 500 Dollar
+0.2% / 3.1% In line ≈ unchanged ≈ unchanged ≈ unchanged
+0.4% / 3.4% Hot +15 to +25 bp −1% to −2% Stronger
+0.0% / 2.8% Cool −15 to −25 bp +1% to +2% Weaker

Inflation was high in all three rows. Markets barely blinked in the first, because 3.1% was already in the price. The transmission chain is worth memorising: surprise → expected path of the policy rate → short-term bond yields → the discount rate on every future cash flow → equity prices and the currency. Every one of those arrows is a present-value calculation from Section 1.

Two practical consequences for anyone modelling this. First, your feature is actual − consensus, never actual; consensus is published (Bloomberg, Reuters surveys) and you must join it in. Second, the reaction function itself shifts: in 2021 strong payrolls lifted stocks (growth is good), while in 2022 strong payrolls sank them (growth means more hikes). A model trained across that boundary without a regime variable will learn the average of two opposite behaviours.

Make it click

A data release answers one question: was the news better or worse than what was already expected?

Not better or worse in absolute terms — better or worse than consensus, the published average of economists' forecasts. Prices already contain consensus before the number lands, so only the gap between actual and consensus moves anything. Beat it and markets react as though the news were good, however grim the level.

The reason anyone cares is that the same number can be a rally or a selloff.

Payrolls come in at +180,000, consensus was +150,000. A beat. Yields rise, rate-cut bets get pushed back.

Payrolls come in at +180,000, consensus was +200,000. A miss. Yields fall, rate-cut bets get pulled forward.

Identical jobs number, opposite market reaction. The only thing that changed is the number people were already expecting.

Which tells you where forecasting effort pays. If a consensus exists and is free, your own forecast is only worth the gap between it and consensus — and for CPI, payrolls and GDP, dozens of paid economists make that gap very hard to earn. For your own input costs, your regional wage pressure, what your suppliers are about to pass through, no consensus exists. Same hours, real return.

Two habits carry over. Store the surprise, actual minus consensus, not the level. And use point-in-time data: payrolls get restated by tens of thousands over the following two months, so scoring an old forecast against today's revised series marks you against an answer sheet that was rewritten afterwards.

Check your understanding

1. Nominal GDP grew 6% last year while the GDP deflator rose 4%. Real growth was roughly…

Real growth ≈ nominal growth minus inflation: exactly 1.06 ÷ 1.04 − 1 ≈ 1.9%, or 2% with the quick subtraction shortcut. Always strip out prices before calling something "growth."

2. Why do most central banks target about 2% inflation rather than 0%?

Zero leaves no safety margin: a small shock tips you into deflation, where falling prices raise real debt burdens and reward waiting instead of spending. A 2% cushion also absorbs the slight upward bias in measured inflation and greases nominal wage adjustment.

3. The unemployment rate falls from 6.3% to 5.8%. Which scenario is consistent with a weaker economy?

The rate only counts people actively looking. If searchers give up, they exit the labor force and the rate falls even though nobody found a job — which is why analysts read the participation rate alongside the headline number.

4. An inverted yield curve is best described as a ___ indicator.

Inversion has preceded every US recession of the past six decades, typically by 6–24 months — the definition of a leading indicator. Lagging indicators like the unemployment rate only confirm turns after the fact.

5. An oil price spike hits the economy. In the AD–AS framework, this…

Oil is an input cost, so it moves the supply curve — leftward, since production gets more expensive at every price level. That pushes output and prices in opposite directions, the signature of a supply shock and of the 1970s.

Key takeaways

  • GDP = C + I + G + NX measures production, with US consumption ~68% of the total. Use real (inflation-adjusted) and per-capita versions for growth and living standards — and remember GDP ignores unpaid work, the environment, and distribution.
  • Growth compounds: 1.5% vs 3% per year turns identical countries into a 2.4× income gap within one lifetime. Long-run growth per person comes almost entirely from productivity.
  • Inflation is a weighted average of basket price changes (CPI). Central banks target ~2% as a buffer against the self-reinforcing deflation trap. Compounding cuts hard: at the 1970s' ~7%, $100 keeps only ~$13 of purchasing power over 30 years.
  • Hyperinflation (>50% per month) is always a fiscal-printing story — Weimar 1923 and Zimbabwe 2008 destroyed their currencies within months.
  • The unemployment rate counts only active job-seekers: read it with labor-force participation, and remember some (frictional) unemployment is healthy churn.
  • Business cycles are recurring but not periodic. Leading indicators (yield curve, permits, claims) turn before the peak; lagging ones (unemployment, CPI) only confirm. NBER dates recessions long after the fact.
  • AD–AS is the diagnostic: demand shocks move output and prices together; supply shocks split them apart (stagflation). It explains 2020–22 in one picture.
  • Markets price the consensus in advance — data moves markets only by surprising, and revisions mean serious analysis needs point-in-time data.

Part I · Economic Foundations

4. Central Banks and Monetary Policy

One committee of twelve people in Washington sets a single interest rate, and within months it moves your mortgage, your savings yield, the stock market, and the value of the dollar. By the end of this section you'll understand how that machine works — and be able to read a Fed headline the way a trader does.

What a central bank is (and is not)

A central bank is a bank whose customers are other banks and the government. You cannot open an account at the Federal Reserve. Commercial banks can, and the balances they hold there are called reserves: electronic money that exists only inside the central bank's ledger and can only be held by institutions with an account there.

Reserves exist because payments between banks have to settle somewhere. When you pay $500 to someone who banks elsewhere, your bank does not physically send anything; it owes the other bank $500. Multiply that by millions of payments a day in both directions and the banks end each day owing each other net amounts, which they settle by moving reserves between their accounts at the central bank. Because every bank has an account at the same institution, a payment between any two of them is a single entry in one ledger. That is the plumbing role, and it is the foundation for everything else the central bank does.

On top of the plumbing sit three more jobs. It issues the physical currency, so the notes in your wallet are literally its liabilities. It supervises banks, checking that they hold enough capital and are not taking risks that would leave depositors exposed. It acts as lender of last resort, meaning that when a fundamentally sound bank cannot borrow because everyone is panicking, the central bank lends to it so the panic does not spread. And the job markets watch obsessively is monetary policy: setting the price of that overnight money in order to steer inflation and employment across the whole economy.

America's central bank is the Federal Reserve, created in 1913, and its structure is strange on purpose. There is a seven-member Board of Governors in Washington, appointed by the President and confirmed by the Senate, and twelve regional Federal Reserve Banks — New York, Chicago, San Francisco and so on — each with its own president and its own research staff. The split was the price of getting the institution created at all: a country deeply suspicious of concentrated financial power in either Washington or New York would only accept a central bank whose power was divided between the capital and the regions.

Interest-rate decisions are made by the FOMC, the Federal Open Market Committee, which has twelve votes: the seven governors, the president of the New York Fed permanently, and four of the remaining eleven regional presidents on an annual rotation. New York votes every year because the Fed's market operations are executed there. The committee meets eight times a year on a published schedule. One structural detail does real work: governors serve staggered fourteen-year terms, longer than any president can serve, and cannot be removed over a policy disagreement. That is what makes the independence discussed below more than a stated intention.

Congress gave the Fed a dual mandate written into law: stable prices and maximum employment. Neither phrase means anything operationally until it is turned into a number, so the Fed has interpreted stable prices as inflation of about 2% a year, measured by the PCE price index rather than the CPI. PCE covers a wider set of spending, including healthcare paid for on someone's behalf by an insurer or the government, and it updates its weights as people substitute between goods, which is why it usually runs a few tenths cooler than CPI. Maximum employment is deliberately left without a number, because the highest sustainable level of employment moves over time with demographics and the structure of the labour market.

The two halves of the mandate frequently point in opposite directions, and it is worth being precise about why. The Fed's only real instrument is the cost of borrowing. To reduce inflation it raises that cost so that households buy fewer houses and cars and firms fund fewer projects; less spending means firms face weaker demand, and weaker demand means fewer people hired and some laid off. Reducing inflation therefore runs through the labour market by design — the loosening of the job market is not a side effect, it is the mechanism. So whenever inflation is above target and employment is below it, the committee cannot serve both goals at once and has to decide how much of one to trade for the other, in real time, using data that is weeks old and will be revised.

Which raises the question of why central banks are made independent — free to set rates without needing political approval. The argument is not that officials are wiser than elected politicians. It is about a specific timing problem.

Cheap money produces its pleasant effects quickly and its unpleasant ones slowly. Cut rates and within a year borrowing rises, hiring rises and the economy feels strong; the inflation that follows takes a year or two more to show up, and taming it takes a recession. An official facing an election in eighteen months therefore has a standing incentive to cut now and leave the bill for a successor. The damage is not merely that they might do it once. It is that everyone can see the incentive. Firms setting prices and unions negotiating wages will assume the promise to hold inflation at 2% will be abandoned when it becomes inconvenient, so they build higher inflation into their own decisions, which makes higher inflation actually happen. A promise that everyone expects to be broken cannot anchor anything.

Independence is what makes the promise credible: if the person setting rates cannot be removed for setting them where the mandate requires, the threat behind the incentive disappears. The cautionary case is the early 1970s, when Fed chair Arthur Burns kept policy loose under sustained pressure from President Nixon ahead of the 1972 election. The inflation that followed took a decade to extinguish, and the cure was Paul Volcker's Fed pushing rates towards 20% and accepting the deep recession that came with it. The cross-country evidence points the same way: countries whose central banks are legally insulated from their governments have lower and steadier inflation, at no cost in growth. Independence is not institutional decoration; it is the thing that makes a 2% target believable.

The same design appears everywhere, with local variations that tell you something about each country's history. The European Central Bank sets policy for the twenty countries using the euro, and it has a single mandate rather than a dual one — price stability comes first by treaty, and supporting growth and employment is explicitly secondary. That hierarchy is a German condition for giving up the Deutschmark, rooted in the country's own inflation history. Decisions are made by a Governing Council instead of an FOMC.

The Bank of England, founded in 1694 and the oldest of them, targets 2% inflation through its Monetary Policy Committee, and works under an unusual rule of accountability: if inflation misses the target by more than a percentage point in either direction, the governor must write a public letter to the Chancellor explaining why and what will be done about it. The Bank of Japan spent three decades on the opposite problem from everyone else — prices that would not rise — and as a result invented most of the unconventional toolkit that the rest of the world later borrowed, including quantitative easing in 2001 and negative policy rates in 2016, which it finally abandoned in 2024. Different acronyms, different mandates, the same machine underneath.

Key idea

A central bank doesn't set "the" interest rate on your loans directly. It sets one overnight rate at the very base of the system, and lets arbitrage and expectations propagate it outward — like changing a root constant that every other rate in the economy is computed from.

Real world: what independence is actually worth

Independence sounds like constitutional trivia until you watch it removed. Two natural experiments, run 40 years apart:

Volcker's Fed, 1979–83 — independence used. US inflation hit 14.8% in March 1980. Paul Volcker pushed the fed funds rate to about 20%, the highest in US history. The medicine worked and it hurt: unemployment peaked at 10.8% in late 1982, farmers drove tractors to Washington to blockade the Fed's building, and Congress drafted impeachment bills. Inflation fell to roughly 3% by 1983 and stayed low for a generation. No elected official could have survived making that choice.

Turkey, 2019–23 — independence removed. The president, holding the unorthodox view that high rates cause inflation, fired three central bank governors in under two years and had the policy rate cut from 19% to 8.5% while inflation was accelerating. Official inflation peaked at 85.5% in October 2022 (independent estimates put it far higher), and the lira fell from about 8 to the dollar in early 2021 to beyond 27 by mid-2023. In mid-2023 the policy reversed and rates were hiked to 50%.

That asymmetry is the whole argument: a politician's horizon is the next election, and the cost of inflation control always arrives before the benefit. Independence is a commitment device — a way to make a promise your future self cannot break.

Make it click

A central bank answers one question for you: when inflation and jobs pull in opposite directions, which one will it protect?

The mandate tells you, in three cases out of four. Inflation high and unemployment low — no conflict, expect rate rises. Inflation low and unemployment high — no conflict, expect cuts. Both bad at once, and the mandate gives no answer at all; that is when rate forecasting gets hard.

It matters because a mandate only binds if the person holding it cannot be removed for obeying it.

US, 1979 — inflation at 14.8%, and the chair cannot be fired for the cure. Rates go to 20%, unemployment hits 10.8%, Congress drafts impeachment bills, and inflation is back near 3% by 1983.

Turkey, 2019 — inflation accelerating, and the president can fire the governor. Three are removed in two years, rates are cut from 19% to 8.5%, and inflation peaks above 85%.

Same problem, opposite outcome. The only thing that changed is whether the person setting rates could be removed for setting them.

So before you trust a published inflation target, check that one fact. Where the governor is protected, treat the target as a plan. Where they are not, treat it as a preference and plan for worse.

Everything else here follows from that. Reserves are the accounts banks hold at the central bank, which is why it is a bank for banks and you cannot open an account. And the fourteen-year terms, twelve regional banks and rotating votes are all machinery built to make that firing question answer "no."

How banks create money (yes, really)

Now to the fact that surprises almost everyone who hears it: most of the money in an economy is not created by the government printing it. It is created by ordinary commercial banks making loans.

Start with what counts as money. Notes and coins are a small fraction of it; the overwhelming majority of what people spend is deposits — numbers in bank accounts, moved by card, transfer or direct debit. A deposit is money in every practical sense, because you can buy things with it. So the question "where does money come from?" is mostly the question "where do deposits come from?", and the answer is not that someone carried cash into a branch.

When a bank approves your $900 loan, it does not go and fetch $900 of somebody else's savings. It makes two entries at once: it records a $900 asset, your promise to repay, and it credits your account with $900, a $900 liability it now owes you. That second entry is a new deposit that did not exist a moment earlier, and you can immediately spend it. The bank did not move money; it created a matching pair of promises. When people say loans create deposits rather than deposits funding loans, this is the entire content of the claim. And the reverse is equally true — repay the loan and both entries vanish, which is why paying down debt across an economy actually shrinks the money supply.

What keeps this from being infinite is fractional-reserve banking: a bank keeps only a fraction of its deposits available and puts the rest to work, so it must be able to hand over reserves whenever a customer moves money elsewhere. The textbook treatment turns that fraction into a loop, and the loop is worth walking through slowly even though the next callout will explain why it is not literally how a modern banking system works.

Suppose banks keep 10% of every deposit as reserves. You deposit $1,000. Your bank keeps $100 and lends $900 to someone else. That borrower spends the $900, and whoever receives it deposits it at their own bank, which keeps $90 and lends $810. That $810 gets spent, deposited, and $729 of it gets lent. Each round is 90% of the round before, so the deposits created form the series $1,000 + $900 + $810 + $729 and onwards — the same geometric series that drives compounding in Section 1, running in the opposite direction.

A geometric series where each term is a fixed fraction of the last has a finite total, and the rule in words is: the total amount of deposits the system can support equals the original deposit divided by the fraction each bank must keep back. Keeping back a tenth means the system supports ten times the original; keeping back a fifth would support five times. That divisor is called the money multiplier:

Total deposits = Initial deposit × 1reserve ratio = $1,000 × 10.10 = $10,000
The 1/reserve-ratio factor is the money multiplier — here 10×, so $1,000 of base money supports up to $10,000 of deposits ($9,000 newly created)

Common pitfall: the multiplier is a teaching device

The clean 1/reserve-ratio story is a useful mental model, not a literal description of 2020s banking. The US cut reserve requirements to zero in March 2020, and banks today are limited by capital rules, risk appetite, and whether profitable borrowers exist — not by a reserve count. In the real world causality mostly runs backwards: banks find creditworthy borrowers first, create the deposits, and obtain reserves afterwards. Keep the multiplier as intuition for how banking amplifies base money; don't use it to forecast.

Money creation has a mirror image, and it is the reason banking is structurally fragile rather than merely risky. A bank promises that your deposit is available the moment you want it, while the money is committed to loans that will not be repaid for years — a thirty-year mortgage cannot be called back this afternoon. Borrowing on demand and lending long is called a maturity mismatch, and it is not a flaw a better-run bank could avoid. It is the service banks provide: savers want instant access, borrowers want long commitments, and the bank stands in between absorbing the difference.

The consequence is that no bank, however sound, can pay everyone at once. And that turns depositor belief into a self-fulfilling force. If you think a bank may fail, the rational move is to withdraw immediately, because the people who withdraw early get paid in full and the ones who wait may not. Everyone reasons the same way, so everyone withdraws, so the bank must sell its loans and bonds urgently into a market that knows it is a forced seller and pays accordingly. Those fire-sale losses can turn a solvent bank into an insolvent one, which means the fear produced exactly the failure it predicted. That is a bank run, and the important feature is that it does not require the bank to have done anything wrong. It only requires enough people to believe others will run.

Two defences exist, and each attacks a different link in that chain. The first is deposit insurance: in the United States the FDIC guarantees up to $250,000 per depositor per bank, so an insured depositor is paid in full whether they run or not. Removing the advantage of being early removes the reason to run at all, which is why the guarantee works mostly by never being needed. The second is the central bank as lender of last resort. The classic formulation, from Walter Bagehot in 1873, is to lend freely, against good collateral, at a penalty rate: a bank that is solvent but temporarily short of cash can borrow rather than dump assets, while the penalty rate and the collateral requirement stop the facility from becoming a subsidy for banks that are genuinely broke.

Neither defence is complete, and March 2023 showed exactly where the gap is. Silicon Valley Bank's depositors were mostly startups and venture funds holding balances far above the $250,000 cap, so insurance protected almost none of the money and every one of them had a reason to move first. They also shared investors, group chats and social media, so the coordination that used to take days of queuing outside a branch took hours: $42 billion was requested in a single day, by app. The underlying cause of that failure was an interest-rate bet gone wrong, which gets a full autopsy in Section 16 (Risk Management); the wider structure of the banking system is Section 6.

Worked example: watch a loan create a deposit

Forget the multiplier for a moment and just do the bookkeeping. A bank approves your $200,000 mortgage. Here is what physically happens:

Bank's balance sheet Before After
Assets — reserves at the Fed $50M $50M
Assets — loans outstanding $400M $400.2M
Liabilities — customer deposits $420M $420.2M
Equity $30M $30M

The bank typed two numbers. It created a $200,000 asset (your promise to pay) and a $200,000 liability (the deposit in your account) in the same keystroke. No existing depositor's balance went down. Reserves did not move at signing. The money supply just grew by $200,000 out of nothing but a contract.

Reserves only matter at the next step: when you pay the seller and they bank elsewhere, this bank must settle by shipping reserves to the seller's bank. So reserves constrain a bank's ability to lose deposits, not its ability to originate loans. What actually limits lending is capital (equity per unit of risky asset — see Section 6), profitable demand for loans, and the bank's own risk appetite.

The loop also runs backwards. When you make your final payment, the loan asset and the deposit both vanish and that $200,000 of money is destroyed. In a credit contraction — 2009, say — repayments exceed originations across the system and the money supply shrinks without anyone deciding to shrink it.

Make it click

Bank lending answers one question: where does the money you borrow actually come from?

Not from someone else's savings. The bank types your loan into its assets and the matching deposit into its liabilities in the same keystroke. The money is new. Which means lending is not limited by a pile of cash sitting somewhere — it is limited by whether the bank judges you good for it.

The reason anyone cares is that judgements change with the weather, and cash in a vault would not.

February 2020, uncommitted facility: the paperwork says "subject to lender approval at drawdown." You ask for $20m in March. It is a request. Declined.

February 2020, committed facility: you have been paying about 35 basis points a year for the privilege. You ask for $20m in March. It is an obligation the bank already booked. Funded.

Same company, same numbers, same month, opposite answer. The only thing that changed is whether the promise was made before conditions turned or after.

So price the promise, not the paperwork. A committed line costs real money in every year you don't draw it, and is worth all of it in the year you do. An uncommitted line is free because it is worth nothing under stress.

The rest of the vocabulary follows. Maturity mismatch is borrowing short and lending long, which is why a bank cannot survive everyone asking at once — that is a bank run, and deposit insurance exists to stop small depositors starting one. Repayment destroys money exactly as lending created it, which is why credit contractions feed themselves.

The policy rate: what the Fed actually sets

When financial news says "the Fed raised rates," exactly one rate is meant: the federal funds rate, what banks charge each other to borrow reserves overnight without collateral. It exists because the day's payments never balance perfectly. Some banks end the day with more reserves than they need and others end short, and rather than leave the imbalance sitting there, the long ones lend to the short ones until morning.

That makes it the shortest and safest loan in the economy — one night, to a regulated bank, in the safest asset there is — which is why every other interest rate is built on top of it. Anything longer, riskier or less liquid has to offer more than overnight money does, or nobody would hold it. Move the base and the whole stack above it moves.

Two details of the vocabulary matter for reading headlines. The FOMC does not announce one number; it announces a target range, such as 4.25%–4.50%, and then uses its tools to keep the rate actually traded in the market inside that band. And moves are quoted in basis points, each one hundredth of a percentage point, so a "25 basis point hike" raises the range by a quarter of a point. The unit exists because in fixed income a hundredth of a percent on a large balance is real money, and saying "point two five percent" out loud invites errors.

How does a committee make a market rate land where it wants? The answer changed completely in 2008, and both versions are worth understanding because the old one is still how people describe it.

The original method was open market operations. Reserves have a price like anything else, set by supply and demand. The Fed controlled the supply: buying Treasury securities from banks paid for them with newly created reserves, so reserves became more plentiful and their overnight price fell; selling securities drained reserves and pushed the price up. Because reserves were kept deliberately scarce, small daily adjustments were enough to move the rate, and the New York trading desk did precisely that every morning.

That mechanism stopped working after 2008 for a straightforward reason. Quantitative easing flooded the system with reserves — trillions rather than tens of billions — and when a resource is superabundant, adding or removing a few billion of it changes nothing about its price. So the Fed switched to what is called an ample-reserves or floor system: instead of manipulating how many reserves exist, it simply announces what it will pay for them and lets that set the market. Two administered rates do the work.

The first is IORB, Interest on Reserve Balances: the Fed pays banks interest on reserves left sitting in their accounts. The consequence is an arbitrage argument with no moving parts. If the Fed pays 4.40% for reserves that require no effort and carry no risk, no bank will lend those same reserves to another bank overnight at 4.20%, because doing nothing pays more. IORB therefore becomes a floor under the whole overnight market, enforced not by intervention but by the fact that every bank has a better alternative.

The second exists because that argument only binds institutions that have a Fed account. Money-market funds — which hold enormous amounts of cash and are not banks — cannot earn IORB, so on its own the floor would leak: they would lend below it because they have nowhere better to go. The ON RRP facility, the Overnight Reverse Repurchase, closes that gap by letting non-banks park cash at the Fed overnight at a set rate, giving them a risk-free alternative too. Between the two rates, essentially everyone with cash to lend overnight has an outside option, and the market rate has nowhere to go but the narrow band between them.

There is a ceiling as well as a floor. The discount window lets a bank borrow directly from the Fed against collateral at a rate a little above the target range, so no bank needs to pay far above that to borrow elsewhere. The practical result of the whole arrangement is that the Fed sets its rate by announcement rather than by daily trading: change the two administered numbers and the entire overnight market follows within a day, with no fine-tuning required.

Your edge

Think of IORB as a risk-free max() bound in an optimization: no rational lender accepts less than the guaranteed alternative. The entire floor system is one arbitrage constraint, enforced by trillions of self-interested dollars — a distributed system with no central scheduler that still converges every night.

Real world: the trillion dollars that walked out of banks

In 2022–23 the Fed raised the policy rate from 0–0.25% to 5.25–5.50%. Watch what each rate did in response — the differences are the whole lesson in how transmission actually works:

Rate Early 2022 Mid 2023 Pass-through
Fed policy rate 0.08% 5.33% —
3-month T-bill 0.05% 5.4% ≈ 100%
Money market funds 0.02% 5.0% ≈ 95%
Large-bank savings account 0.01% 0.42% (average) ≈ 8%
Credit card APR (average) 16.4% 21.5% ≈ 97%

Banks passed the hike through to borrowers almost fully and to savers barely at all — the industry calls that gap deposit beta, and a low one is pure profit. Savers eventually noticed: money market fund assets climbed from roughly $4.6 trillion to over $6 trillion, one of the largest voluntary migrations of cash in financial history.

Two consequences you can trace. For a household, the difference between 0.42% and 5.0% on $50,000 of savings is $2,290 a year for about ten minutes of paperwork. For the banking system, the outflow drained the cheap funding that regional banks had lent long against — which is one of the threads that pulled Silicon Valley Bank apart in March 2023.

Make it click

The policy rate answers one question: what does completely safe, overnight money earn right now?

Everything else is priced off that floor. The central bank sets it by offering to pay that rate itself, so nobody lends to anyone else for less. But the floor only reaches you if you go and stand on it — your bank is under no obligation to pass it on, and mostly doesn't.

The reason anyone cares is the size of the gap between the rate that exists and the rate you are getting.

$50m left in the operating account through 2022–23. Banks passed on about 8% of the rise, so it paid 0.42%. You earn $210,000.

$50m swept into T-bills over the same period, at 5.3%. You earn $2.65m — and take less credit risk, since deposits above $250,000 are unsecured claims on a bank.

Same cash, same period, $2.4m apart. The only thing that changed is whether somebody had written a sweep policy.

The asymmetry is the rule worth budgeting on: what you owe reprices almost fully, what you are owed barely moves. Credit cards passed through 97%, T-bills 100%, savings accounts 8%. So model floating debt at full pass-through and cash income at nearly none, unless someone is actively moving the money.

Deposit beta is the name for the share your bank hands on — a low one is their profit. Basis points are hundredths of a percent, so 25bp is a quarter point. And IORB and the ON RRP are simply the two windows where the central bank pays that floor rate: one for banks, one for money funds.

Transmission: one rate moves everything (slowly)

Everything so far concerns a rate on overnight loans between banks, which on its own is irrelevant to almost everyone. Its power comes from transmission: the set of connections through which a change in that one rate propagates into what you pay on a mortgage, whether a factory gets built, what shares are worth and what a dollar buys abroad. There are five channels worth knowing, they operate at very different speeds, and they do not all point the same way at the same time.

Consumer borrowing is the fastest channel, though it splits in two. Banks price loans off what funding costs them, so anything indexed to short-term rates moves almost immediately. The prime rate, which sets credit cards and many small-business loans, sits mechanically at the fed funds rate plus three percentage points, so a hike passes through in days — credit-card rates averaged over 21% at the 2023 peak.

Mortgages work differently, and the difference confuses people constantly. A thirty-year mortgage is not priced off the overnight rate at all; it is priced off long-term Treasury yields, because that is the horizon of the money being lent (see Section 8). What links it back to Fed policy is expectations: long yields reflect where markets think short rates will average over the coming decade, so when the Fed signals a sustained tightening, long yields rise even on days the Fed does nothing. In 2022, mortgage rates went from under 3% to around 7% within a year.

That difference is larger than it sounds because a mortgage payment is not proportional to the rate. On a $400,000 loan, monthly payments run about $1,633 at 2.75% and about $2,528 at 6.5% — a 55% jump in the payment from a rate that did not quite quadruple, and roughly $322,000 more paid over the life of the loan. At that point buyers who qualified stop qualifying, sales fall, builders stop breaking ground, and construction employment falls. A single overnight rate has reached into the job market through the housing market.

Business investment is the second channel. A company approves a project when the return it expects beats the cost of the money needed to fund it, a comparison formalised in Section 14.
