Raising rates raises that hurdle, and the projects that fail it first are the marginal ones — the additional data centre, the factory expansion with a thin margin, the startup that was not quite profitable. Nothing dramatic happens to good projects; the effect is entirely at the boundary, which is why it takes time to show up in the data.

Asset prices are the third, and this channel is pure arithmetic. A share or a bond is worth the cash it will produce in future, discounted back to today at some rate — the machinery from Section 1 and Section 13. Raise the discount rate and every one of those future amounts is worth less now, so prices fall without anything changing about the businesses themselves. The effect is largest where the cash is furthest away, which is why 2022 hit fast-growing technology companies — whose value sits mostly in profits expected in the 2030s — far harder than it hit utilities earning cash today.

The exchange rate is the fourth. Higher US interest rates make dollar deposits and Treasury bonds more attractive to investors everywhere, so money flows in, and buying dollars to invest bids the dollar up (Section 10). A stronger dollar makes imported goods cheaper in dollar terms, which pushes inflation down directly, and makes American exports more expensive abroad, which reduces demand for them. Rate policy reaches inflation through this route noticeably faster than through the labour market.

Expectations are the fifth and least visible, and they may matter most. If firms and workers genuinely believe the central bank will return inflation to 2%, they set next year's prices and wage demands as though inflation will be 2% — and because prices and wages are what inflation is made of, the belief substantially delivers the outcome. This is why central bankers spend so much effort on communication, and why a loss of credibility is expensive: once people stop believing the target, the bank has to produce the same result using interest rates alone, which means a much deeper slowdown.

Now the feature that makes this genuinely hard rather than merely complicated: the lag. Milton Friedman's description was that monetary policy operates with "long and variable lags," and the usual estimate is twelve to eighteen months before a rate change has fully worked through into inflation and employment. The reason is visible in the channels above. Credit-card rates move in days, mortgage rates in weeks, but a household only feels the mortgage when it moves house, a firm only cancels the project at its next investment review, and the workers not hired for that project show up in employment data months after that.

The consequence is that today's inflation reading is largely the result of decisions taken more than a year ago, so a committee that waits for inflation to visibly break before stopping will have tightened for a year past the point of enough. And the same lag runs in reverse: cutting rates during a downturn does not rescue the current quarter, it helps the one after next. Policy therefore has to be set against a forecast of where the economy will be in a year, using data describing where it was three months ago — which is why central banks are wrong in public, at scale, on a recurring basis.

Key idea: why the Fed acts on forecasts

Put the lag together with the mandate and you get the defining constraint of the job. If a policymaker responds to the inflation number in front of them, they are responding to conditions that existed a year ago, and their response will land a year from now on conditions nobody has seen yet. Doing that consistently produces exactly the wrong pattern: still tightening while the economy is already slowing, still easing while it is already overheating, and turning a mild cycle into a larger one.

The only workable alternative is to set policy against a forecast — to act on where inflation and employment are expected to be in twelve to eighteen months, and to stop tightening before the current data says you should. That is why FOMC statements read as though they are about the future rather than the present, and why the committee's projections attract as much attention as its decisions. It also guarantees a permanent public cost: forecasts are wrong regularly, so a central bank doing its job correctly will systematically appear to be acting too early or too late, and will be criticised for both.

Monetary policy simulator

Drag the policy rate and watch it ripple through a mortgage, your savings, business borrowing, and the dollar — or jump to a historical moment with the presets.

30-yr mortgage rate (policy + 2.5)5.50%
Monthly payment, $400k loan$2,271/mo
High-yield savings on $10k2.50% · $250/yr
Business loan (prime rate)6.00%
US dollar◆ near neutral
Inflation pressure◆ roughly balanced
Jobs & hiring◆ roughly balanced

Around 2.5–3% is many economists’ guess at the neutral rate — the setting that neither stimulates nor restrains the economy. Nobody can observe it directly; the Fed steers toward it like a driver aiming at a line seen only in the rearview mirror.

Inflation and jobs arrows show the direction of pressure, which takes 12–18 months to fully arrive. Simplifications: mortgages actually price off 10-year Treasury yields plus a spread; the savings figure assumes a high-yield account paying policy minus 0.5 points (big banks often pay far less); prime = policy + 3 points is the real US convention.

Worked example: check the widget's math

Set the slider to 4.00%. The mortgage rate becomes 4.00 + 2.50 = 6.50%. Monthly rate r = 0.065 ÷ 12 = 0.005417, n = 360 payments, so payment = 400,000 × r × (1+r)360 ÷ ((1+r)360 − 1) = $2,528 a month. Same formula as Section 1's annuity math — monetary policy is just the time value of money with a committee attached.

Worked example: what a rate cycle did to one homebuyer

Transmission is abstract until you price it. Take a household that can afford $2,500 a month for principal and interest on a 30-year fixed mortgage — the same household, the same budget, three different years.

Period Mortgage rate Loan $2,500/mo buys
January 2021 (peak QE) 2.65% $620,000
2021 average 3.00% $593,000
Late 2023 7.00% $376,000

The buyer's income did not change. Their purchasing power fell about 37% in two years. Read it the other way and it is worse: the payment on a fixed $400,000 loan went from $1,686 to $2,661 — up 58%.

This is also the cleanest demonstration of the lock-in effect. A family holding a 3% mortgage cannot move without repricing to 7%, so they do not list the house. Existing-home supply collapses, prices stay high despite brutal affordability, and the rate hike that was supposed to cool housing partly freezes it instead. One overnight rate, two opposing effects — this is why the Fed cannot predict its own transmission precisely.

Make it click

Transmission answers one question: how long after a rate change do you actually feel it?

Longer than you would guess, and it varies by channel. The prime rate moves in days, so credit cards and floating business loans reprice almost immediately. Mortgages take weeks. Hiring, investment and defaults take 12 to 18 months. So the pain from a hike peaks well after the hike does.

This is what decides which quarter you put the contingency in.

Budget the squeeze for the quarter rates peak — say Q3 2023 — then ease off. Demand and defaults bottom out in late 2024, by which point you have already released the contingency.

Budget the squeeze for the year after the peak, while headlines are announcing relief and the central bank is cutting. The contingency is still standing when it is needed.

Same rate path, opposite preparedness. The only thing that changed is which quarter you assumed the damage lands in.

The lag runs both ways, which catches people twice: a cut will not rescue this quarter either. Anything justified on an expected cut needs its own bridge for a year.

That is all "long and variable lags" means, and it is why the Fed acts on forecasts rather than current readings. The channels are just the routes it travels: borrowing costs, investment hurdles, asset prices, the dollar, and expectations — of which expectations is the fastest, because believing a hike is coming is enough to change behaviour before it lands.

QE and QT: policy by balance sheet

In December 2008 the Fed ran out of its normal instrument. It had cut the fed funds rate to effectively zero and the economy was still contracting, which left it with a target it could not lower any further. The obstacle is called the zero lower bound, and its cause is physical: banknotes pay 0% and can be stored, so if a central bank tried to impose a meaningfully negative rate, holders would convert deposits into cash and hold that instead. In practice rates can go a little below zero, because storing and insuring billions in notes costs something, but not far.

So the Fed changed which price it was targeting. Instead of setting the cost of overnight money, it went directly after the cost of long-term money — the ten-year and thirty-year rates that actually determine mortgages and corporate borrowing — by intervening in those markets itself.

The instrument is quantitative easing, or QE: the central bank buys very large quantities of long-term government bonds and mortgage-backed securities, and pays for them with reserves it creates for the purpose. It works through three separate mechanisms, and keeping them apart is what makes the arguments about QE intelligible.

The first is the direct effect on price. Bonds trade in a market, and a buyer arriving with hundreds of billions of dollars pushes prices up. The step that people new to finance find counterintuitive is what a higher bond price does to the interest rate: a bond pays a fixed number of dollars each year, so if you pay more for that same fixed stream, your return on the money you paid is lower. Price and yield move in opposite directions by definition, a relationship developed properly in Section 8. Pushing bond prices up is therefore the same act as pushing long-term interest rates down, and mortgages and corporate loans are priced off those rates even when the overnight rate is stuck at zero.

The second is portfolio rebalancing. The investors who sold their government bonds to the Fed now hold cash and still need somewhere to put it, and the safe asset they used to own has become expensive. So they buy the next thing along — corporate bonds, then equities — which raises those prices too and lowers the cost of raising money for companies. The third is signalling: a central bank committing to buy bonds for the next year is telling everyone it does not intend to raise short rates during that year, and since long-term rates are built out of expected short rates, that statement moves them by itself.

The reverse gear is quantitative tightening, or QT, and it is deliberately undramatic. Rather than selling its holdings into the market, the Fed simply stops replacing them: when a bond it owns matures and the Treasury repays it, the Fed does not use the proceeds to buy another one. The reserves that were created to buy that bond are extinguished when it is repaid, so the balance sheet shrinks passively, month by month, at a pace set by the maturity schedule rather than by trading.

The passivity is a deliberate choice, and 2013 is why. That May, Fed chair Ben Bernanke merely mentioned that the pace of bond purchases might slow at some future point. He announced no sale and no rate change, but markets reassessed the expected path of policy immediately: ten-year Treasury yields rose more than a percentage point over the following months and emerging markets saw sharp capital outflows. The episode is remembered as the "taper tantrum," and its lesson is that a balance sheet this large cannot be adjusted abruptly without moving the prices of everything priced off it.

The scale involved deserves a moment. Before 2008 the Fed held under $1 trillion of assets, most of it short-term Treasury bills, and its balance sheet was an operational detail nobody outside the plumbing discussed. Three successive rounds of QE took it to roughly $4.5 trillion by 2014. Then came COVID: at the peak in 2020 the Fed was buying $120 billion of bonds a month — more each month than its entire pre-crisis holdings of some securities — and the balance sheet approached $9 trillion in 2022 before QT began reducing it. Something that had been a technical footnote became one of the largest single positions in global financial markets, which is why the composition of that portfolio is now itself a subject of analysis.

Common pitfall: "QE is just printing money, so hyperinflation is coming"

QE creates bank reserves, not wallets full of cash — reserves sit inside the banking system and don't buy groceries. A decade of massive QE (2009–2019) coincided with inflation stubbornly below 2%. The 2021–2022 inflation burst had QE in the mix, but alongside pandemic supply-chain chaos and trillions in direct fiscal transfers (Section 5) — checks that, unlike reserves, really did land in spendable accounts. Be suspicious of one-variable explanations of inflation.

Deep dive: September 2019, when QT broke the plumbing

The first QT experiment ended with a bang. By September 2019 the Fed had drained reserves from about $2.8 trillion to $1.4 trillion — and discovered, live, that "ample" had quietly become "scarce." On September 17, the repo rate (overnight lending against Treasury collateral) spiked from about 2% to nearly 10% intraday as banks ran short of spare cash on a corporate-tax-payment day. The fed funds rate broke above its target range — the one thing the system is built to prevent.

The Fed responded within hours, injecting tens of billions through repo operations and soon resuming asset purchases to rebuild the reserve buffer. The lesson analysts took away: nobody, including the Fed, knows exactly where the minimum comfortable level of reserves sits — so QT is always a game of approaching an invisible cliff slowly. When you hear "reserves are getting scarce" in 2020s Fed coverage, this episode is the ghost in the room.

Real world: QE at full scale, twice

The Fed, March 2020. Within three weeks the Fed announced unlimited Treasury and mortgage-bond purchases, then settled into a run rate of $80 billion of Treasuries and $40 billion of mortgage-backed securities per month. The balance sheet went from $4.2 trillion in February 2020 to $8.9 trillion by April 2022. Downstream: 30-year mortgage rates hit an all-time low of 2.65% in January 2021, US corporate bond issuance set records, and the S&P 500 more than doubled off its March 2020 low. Bond buying by a central bank is, mechanically, a bid for duration — and every other asset gets repriced off the yield it displaces.

The Bank of Japan, 2013–present. Japan ran the experiment to its logical end. The BOJ now owns roughly half of all outstanding Japanese government bonds and, through ETF purchases, became the single largest owner of Japanese equities. Under yield curve control it committed to pinning the 10-year JGB yield rather than merely nudging it — promising to buy unlimited amounts at a target price. When markets tested that promise in 2022, the BOJ bought so aggressively that the JGB market went days with almost no trades in benchmark bonds.

The takeaway for an analyst is a market-structure one. When the largest buyer is a price-insensitive institution with an unlimited balance sheet, the yield stops being a clean signal about growth and inflation. Any model that reads a QE-era yield as pure market expectation is reading a partly-administered price.

Make it click

Quantitative easing answers one question: what can a central bank do once the overnight rate is already at zero?

It buys long-term government bonds and pays with newly created reserves. More buyers push bond prices up, and a bond's price and its yield move in opposite directions — pay more for the same fixed payments and your return is lower. So long-term borrowing gets cheaper, which is what mortgages and corporate debt are priced off. QT is the same machine reversed.

The reason anyone cares is that people assume this is money printing and that inflation has to follow. Sometimes it does. The difference is where the money lands.

2009–2019: roughly $3.5tn of bond buying. Inflation ran below the 2% target for most of a decade.

2020–2021: bond buying again, but alongside trillions in direct payments to households. Inflation reached about 9%.

Same tool, opposite inflation. The only thing that changed is whether the new money stayed as reserves inside the banking system or landed in accounts people could spend from.

So when you see a central bank expanding its balance sheet, the question to ask is not how big but who receives it.

The rest of the vocabulary sits on that. Reserves are bank money that cannot buy groceries. The zero lower bound is the floor the policy rate hit in 2008, because nobody lends at negative rates while cash exists. And the taper tantrum is what happens when buying is merely expected to slow — yields jumped on the announcement, long before a single bond was sold.

Reading the Fed like a market participant

Eight times a year the FOMC meets for two days and publishes a statement at 2:00 p.m. Eastern, with the chair's press conference at 2:30. Those ninety minutes are as close as financial markets get to a scheduled earthquake, and the sequence is worth knowing because each piece answers a different question.

The statement is short and deliberately formulaic, which is what makes it informative: because the wording changes little between meetings, the parts that do change stand out. Minutes containing the discussion behind the vote follow three weeks later. Four of the eight meetings — March, June, September and December — also carry the Summary of Economic Projections, in which officials publish their forecasts for growth, unemployment and inflation, along with the dot plot. The dot plot is a scatter chart on which each of the nineteen officials anonymously marks where they think the policy rate should sit at the end of each of the next few years. The median dot becomes the headline — "the Fed projects two cuts next year" — though it is worth remembering what it actually is: nineteen individual opinions about a future that none of them controls, not a commitment.

Because the committee is nineteen people with different weightings of the same mandate, Fed-watchers classify them. Hawks lean toward higher rates, on the view that letting inflation persist is the costlier error; doves lean toward lower rates, on the view that unnecessary unemployment is. The labels are not about ideology so much as about which half of the dual mandate someone reaches for when the two conflict.

Tracking that balance is a real job on trading desks, for a specific structural reason: the four rotating regional presidents change every January, so the same nineteen opinions can produce a different set of twelve votes from one year to the next. A committee whose voting membership has just shifted toward hawks may behave differently in March than the same committee did in November, without anybody changing their mind.

All of which raises the obvious question: why do markets convulse over a single adjective in a statement? The answer is that the current rate is almost irrelevant compared with the expected path of rates.

A ten-year Treasury yield is essentially the market's average expectation of the overnight rate over the next ten years, plus a small premium. A mortgage rate is built on that. A share price is the value today of profits arriving over decades, discounted at rates derived from the same expectations. So what determines all of them is not what the rate is tonight but what people believe the rate will average over years. Tonight's decision is usually already priced; the revision to the expected path is the news.

Central banks exploit this deliberately, through forward guidance — telling markets what they intend to do later in order to move long rates now, without touching the current rate at all. It is a genuine policy instrument, and it is the reason committee language is engineered word by word. When a statement drops "patient," or the chair says "some time" where he previously said "considerable time," traders are not doing literary criticism; they are updating a probability distribution over the next two years of policy, and every asset priced off that distribution reprices in seconds. The market's own estimate of those probabilities is directly observable in fed funds futures, which is what a headline such as "markets price a 78% chance of a March cut" is quoting (futures themselves are Section 9).

Your edge

Traders literally run a diff on the FOMC statement — news wires publish red-lined versions minutes after release, word-level changes highlighted like a pull request. With your background you could build that pipeline in an afternoon: scrape the statements, diff the token streams, timestamp the changes against tick data. That's an event study, and it's a standard quant research pattern you'll meet again in Section 18.

For any Fed event, then, there is a sensible order in which to read what comes out, and it follows how much new information each piece carries. The rate decision itself comes first and usually matters least, because futures prices told you days ago what it would be. Next comes the statement compared against the previous one — the changed phrases are where the committee signals a shift, and the unchanged ones are noise. If it is a projections meeting, the dot plot follows: what matters is not the level of the median dot but how far it moved since the last one, since the move is the information. The press conference comes last and is the most dangerous, because it is the only unscripted part; a chair answering an unexpected question can move markets further than the decision did.

The general rule underneath that ordering is one you have now met three times in two sections. If the Fed does precisely what markets expected and says nothing that changes the expected path, prices barely move, however large the action. It is the surprise, not the action, that reprices anything — a principle Section 17 makes precise.

Real world: one word, trillions repriced

In January 2015 the Swiss National Bank abandoned its currency cap with no warning at all; the franc moved ~20% against the euro in minutes and several brokers went insolvent. That's the extreme case of why central banks now telegraph moves — and why, when a Fed chair merely hints ("we're not even thinking about thinking about raising rates" — Jerome Powell, 2020), it is front-page financial news.

Worked example: pricing the Fed's next move yourself

You do not have to guess what the market expects — it is quoted. CME fed funds futures settle at 100 − the average daily fed funds rate for the contract month, so the implied rate is just 100 minus the price.

Contract Price Implied rate Cuts from 4.33% (25bp each)
Current effective rate — 4.33% —
March 95.83 4.17% 0.6
June 96.17 3.83% 2.0
December 96.75 3.25% 4.3

Read the March row as a probability: the market prices 0.6 of a 25bp cut, so roughly a 60% chance the Fed cuts in March and 40% it holds (this is the arithmetic behind the CME FedWatch tool everyone quotes). By December it prices about 108bp of easing.

Now do the thing that actually earns money: compare that curve with the FOMC's own dot plot from the quarterly Summary of Economic Projections. In late 2021 the dots showed three hikes for 2022 while futures priced fewer; the market was wrong and repriced violently. In late 2023 the market priced six cuts for 2024 while the dots showed three; the market was wrong again. The gap between what the committee says it will do and what the curve says it will do is a tradable, measurable, weekly quantity — and building that spread series is an excellent portfolio project.

Make it click

Fed watching answers one question: what do rates do next, and does the market already know?

You can read it off a price rather than guessing. Fed funds futures settle at 100 minus the average rate for that month, so 100 minus the price is the expected rate. A March contract at 95.83 implies 4.17%; against a current 4.33% that is 0.6 of a quarter-point cut — read as a 60% chance of one.

The reason anyone cares is that the decision itself usually moves nothing. The gap between the decision and what was priced moves everything.

Fed holds rates. Market had priced a hold. Yields barely move, the press conference is the only news.

Fed holds rates. Market had priced a cut at 80%. Yields jump, equities fall, the dollar strengthens — on a decision to do nothing.

Identical action, opposite market reaction. The only thing that changed is what was already expected.

So before any Fed meeting, look up the priced probability first. It costs nothing and it tells you whether you are exposed to the decision or only to the surprise.

The remaining terms are all about that expected path. Forward guidance is the Fed talking about future rates in order to move today's long-term rates. The dot plot is each official's own forecast of where rates should sit — a snapshot, not a promise. Hawks weight inflation, doves weight employment. And when the dots and the futures curve disagree, one of them is about to reprice.

Check your understanding

1. The Fed's dual mandate consists of which two goals?

Congress assigned the Fed price stability (interpreted as ~2% PCE inflation) and maximum employment. The dollar, stocks, and specific loan rates are affected by policy but are not mandate targets.

2. When a commercial bank makes a new loan, what happens to the money supply?

Loans create deposits: the bank credits the borrower's account with new money that didn't exist before. This is how most money in the economy comes into being.

3. How does the Fed keep the federal funds rate inside its target range today?

In the modern ample-reserves "floor system," the Fed pays interest on reserves (IORB) and offers the ON RRP facility to non-banks; arbitrage keeps the market rate pinned near those administered rates. Reserve requirements are zero, and daily fine-tuning OMO is history.

4. The Fed hikes rates by a surprise 100 basis points. Which reaction is most likely, all else equal?

Higher US yields attract foreign capital (stronger dollar) and make existing lower-coupon bonds less attractive (prices fall as yields rise). The inflation effect is real but takes 12–18 months, not a month.

5. What does the dot plot show?

Each of the 19 officials anonymously marks where they think rates should be at future year-ends; the median is quoted as "the Fed's projection." It's a forecast snapshot, not a promise — and market-implied odds come from fed funds futures instead.

Key takeaways

  • A central bank is the bank for banks and the government; the Fed's FOMC sets policy under a dual mandate of ~2% inflation (PCE) and maximum employment, and its independence is what makes the inflation target credible.
  • Most money is created by commercial banks when loans create deposits; the money multiplier (1 ÷ reserve ratio) is useful intuition, but modern banks are constrained by capital and loan demand, not reserve counts.
  • Bank runs are self-fulfilling panics born of maturity mismatch; deposit insurance (FDIC, $250k) and the lender of last resort exist to prevent them — SVB 2023 showed the app-era version.
  • The federal funds rate is an overnight bank-to-bank rate steered through a floor system: IORB for banks, ON RRP for money funds, with rates quoted in basis points (25 bp = 0.25%).
  • Transmission runs through mortgages, credit cards (prime = policy + 3), business hurdle rates, asset prices, and the dollar — with a 12–18 month lag that forces the Fed to steer by forecast.
  • QE buys long-term bonds with new reserves to push long yields down when the policy rate hits zero; QT lets them run off. It is not literal money-printing into wallets, and its inflation effect is contested.
  • Markets trade the expected path of rates, not the current level — so statement wording, dot plots, and press-conference phrasing move prices more than the decision itself.

Part I · Economic Foundations

5. Fiscal Policy, Government Debt and Global Trade

Central banks steer the economy by setting the price of money; governments steer it by taxing, spending and borrowing — and every country does all of this while trading with everyone else. By the end of this section you'll be able to judge whether a national debt is sustainable, explain why trade isn't a scoreboard, and read a headline about tariffs or a falling currency without flinching.

The government's other lever: taxing and spending

Fiscal policy is the other lever on total demand, and it belongs to elected politicians rather than to the central bank of Section 4. The central bank changes the price of borrowing and then waits for millions of private decisions to respond. A government changes spending and taxes directly: it builds a bridge, cuts a payroll tax, or mails cheques to households.

That difference in mechanism produces a difference in speed and in precision. A rate cut only works if banks pass it on and if somebody wants to borrow, which in a bad enough recession they may not — you can make credit cheap and still find no takers. Government spending does not need anyone's cooperation: the money is in specific hands on a known date, and it can be aimed at particular people, regions or industries in a way an interest rate cannot. The cost of that directness is that it has to pass through a legislature, which is where most of its problems come from.

Part of fiscal policy happens with no vote at all, and that part is more important than it sounds. Automatic stabilizers are features of the existing tax and benefit system that push against the cycle by themselves. In a recession, incomes fall, so income and payroll tax bills fall with them — a household whose earnings drop keeps a larger share of what it still earns — while unemployment insurance and food assistance payments rise as more people qualify. Nobody legislates any of this. The deficit widens on its own, in the same quarter the downturn happens, and the extra money supports spending exactly where incomes fell. In a boom the same machinery runs in reverse, taking more tax and paying out less benefit, which cools things without anyone deciding to.

Discretionary stimulus is the other kind: a specific new law, such as the 2009 Recovery Act or the 2020 CARES Act. It can be far larger than the stabilizers and can be aimed anywhere, but it must clear three delays that the automatic kind skips entirely. There is a recognition delay, because the data confirming a recession has begun arrives months late and gets revised. There is a legislative delay, because a bill has to be drafted, negotiated and passed. And there is an implementation delay, because infrastructure money in particular cannot be spent until projects are designed, tendered and permitted. Add them up and stimulus intended for a downturn routinely arrives during the recovery, when it does less good and more harm.

Key idea: why the timing problem is structural

The contrast between those two kinds of fiscal policy is not that one is well designed and the other badly designed. It is that they respond to different triggers. A stabilizer is triggered by the event itself — the moment someone's income falls, their tax falls — so its timing is automatically correct and its size is automatically proportional to how bad things are. Discretionary stimulus is triggered by a decision about the event, and the decision depends on evidence, agreement and administrative capacity, none of which arrive quickly.

That is why the two tools are argued about differently. A debate about stabilizers is a debate about how generous the system should be in general, settled long before any recession. A debate about stimulus is a debate about something that has to be got right under time pressure with incomplete information, and the honest critique of discretionary fiscal policy is not that spending does not work — it is that a package legislated in month nine of a downturn may land in month twenty-four, by which point it is adding demand to an economy that no longer needs it.

How much extra economic activity does a dollar of government spending produce? More than a dollar, in principle, because the dollar does not stop moving when it is first spent. The fiscal multiplier is the name for that knock-on total.

Follow the chain. The government pays contractors $100 billion to build roads. That is $100 billion of income to construction firms and their workers, who spend part of it on rent, restaurants and cars. The restaurant owners and car dealers now have extra income, and they in turn spend part of theirs. Each round is smaller than the last, because nobody spends every extra dollar they receive. The fraction that does get spent is the marginal propensity to consume, and if it is 0.6 then each round is 60% of the round before.

Stated in words, the rule is: total spending generated equals the original amount divided by the fraction of each dollar that is not passed on. With 60 cents of every dollar spent again, 40 cents drops out each round, so the total is the original divided by 0.4 — two and a half times the original. Written as the series, that is 100 × (1 + 0.6 + 0.36 + …) = 100 ÷ (1 − 0.6) = $250 billion. It is the same geometric series as the banking multiplier in Section 4, and the same recursion as expected visits in a Markov chain.

Real-world estimates come in far below 2.5, and — this is the important part — they disagree with each other for structural reasons rather than because the econometrics is sloppy. Three things shrink the number, and how much they shrink it depends on the state of the economy at the time.

The first is leakage. Each round loses more than just saving: part of the income is taken in tax, and part is spent on imports, which becomes income for producers in another country. Only what is spent domestically and after-tax continues the chain, so the effective fraction passed on is considerably below the headline propensity to consume.

The second is capacity. The multiplier story quietly assumes there are idle workers and unused machines waiting to meet the extra demand. If the economy is already running at full capacity, the extra spending cannot call forth extra output, so it bids up the prices of the output that already exists. You get inflation rather than construction.

The third is the central bank's reaction, and it is the one people most often forget. If the Fed judges that fiscal stimulus will push inflation above target, it raises rates in response, deliberately subtracting private demand to offset the public demand being added. In that case the multiplier is not just reduced, it is actively driven toward zero by policy.

This is why empirical estimates cluster between roughly 0.5 and 1.5, and why the highest ones come from deep recessions with rates already at zero — where there is spare capacity to use, little private investment to displace, and a central bank that wants the stimulus rather than wanting to offset it. When two economists quote different multipliers, they are usually not disagreeing about arithmetic; they are assuming different states of the world, and the right question is which one.

Real world: multipliers, measured

Multipliers are not one number — they depend on who receives the money and what else is happening. The CBO and academic estimates cluster like this:

Policy Typical multiplier Why
Unemployment benefits 0.9 – 1.9 Goes to people who spend nearly all of it immediately.
Infrastructure / direct purchases 0.5 – 2.5 Government buys real output directly; slow to start.
Aid to state and local governments 0.7 – 1.8 Prevents layoffs that would otherwise happen.
Broad tax cuts to lower earners 0.6 – 1.5 High marginal propensity to consume.
Tax cuts to high earners / corporations 0.2 – 0.6 Much of it is saved or buys existing assets.

Two conditions swamp the policy choice. Slack: in 2009, with unemployment near 10%, extra spending pulled idle workers and factories into use, so multipliers ran high. In 2021, with unemployment falling fast and supply chains jammed, the same dollars met a wall — output could not respond, so more of the impulse came out as prices. That difference is a large part of why the 2021 stimulus is argued about and the 2009 one is not.

The central bank's reaction: if the Fed offsets fiscal stimulus by hiking rates, the effective multiplier collapses toward zero. Fiscal and monetary policy are not additive levers — they are two players who can cooperate or cancel each other out.

Make it click

Fiscal policy answers one question: if the government spends a dollar, how much total spending does that dollar create?

More than a dollar, if recipients spend most of what they get — their spending is someone else's income, which gets partly spent again. Take the fraction spent each round and the total is the original divided by one minus that fraction: at 60 cents in the dollar, $100bn becomes $250bn. That is the ceiling, not the estimate. Real measurements land between 0.5 and 1.5.

The reason anyone cares is that the same package is worth five times as much in one year as another, and you can check which in advance.

$100bn in 2009: unemployment near 10%, factories idle, rates already at zero. Nothing to crowd out and no offsetting hike → roughly $150bn of activity.

$100bn into a full-employment economy: the central bank raises rates to hold inflation at target, cancelling the demand it just received → closer to $30bn, and mostly higher prices.

Same $100bn, opposite result. The only thing that changed is whether there was spare capacity and whether the central bank let it through.

So whenever someone quotes a multiplier, ask which state of the world they assumed. It is the assumption, not the arithmetic, that is doing the work.

Two terms left. Automatic stabilisers are the part that needs no vote: in a downturn tax receipts fall and benefit payments rise by themselves, so the deficit widens before anyone legislates. And the marginal propensity to consume is just that fraction spent each round — the higher it is, the bigger the multiplier.

Deficit vs debt: a flow and a stock

Two words get used interchangeably in public discussion and mean completely different things. The budget deficit is the gap between what a government spends and what it collects in a single year. The national debt is the total it owes, which is every past deficit added together and never paid off.

The distinction is the one between a flow and a stock, and if you have written code it is the distinction between the delta computed in one iteration and the accumulator variable that survives the loop. In calculus terms the deficit is the derivative and the debt is the integral. The practical consequence is that the two can move in opposite directions without any contradiction: a government can cut its deficit every single year and still watch the debt rise, because as long as the deficit is positive at all, something is being added to the pile. The debt only falls when the government runs a surplus — which is rare — or when the economy underneath it grows faster than the pile does, which is the subject of the r-versus-g subsection below.

Raw dollar figures are close to meaningless on their own. "Thirty-six trillion dollars of debt" is a number without a denominator, in the same way that a latency of 500 milliseconds tells you nothing until you know what workload produced it. What makes a debt heavy or light is the income available to service it.

So the standard measure is the debt-to-GDP ratio: the total owed divided by one year of the entire economy's output (Section 3). A household owing $360,000 is in serious trouble on a $40,000 income and entirely comfortable on $900,000, and the same logic scales up. Judged that way, US federal debt sits around 120% of GDP in the mid-2020s on the gross measure, Japan carries roughly 240%, and Germany about 63%. Note that Japan, with twice America's ratio, borrows at far lower interest rates than many countries with much smaller ratios — proof that the level by itself does not determine whether a debt is a problem. What matters is the interest rate on it and the growth rate beneath it.

It is also worth asking who is actually owed this money, because the popular picture — a country in hock to foreign rivals — is mostly wrong. US federal debt exists as Treasury securities, tradable bonds that anyone can buy and that you will meet properly in Section 8 (Fixed Income). They are held by American pension funds, insurers, banks, mutual funds and households, by US government trust funds such as Social Security, by the Federal Reserve itself, and by foreign investors. The approximate breakdown:

Holder of US federal debt Rough share (mid-2020s) What that means
US government accounts (Social Security trust fund, etc.) ~20% One arm of the government owes another
Federal Reserve ~12% Bought during QE (Section 4); interest largely flows back to the Treasury
US private investors — funds, banks, pensions, insurers, households ~43% Americans' own savings, parked in the safe asset
Foreign investors (Japan, China, UK among the largest) ~25% The mirror image of trade flows — see the balance of payments below

So the claim that "we owe it to ourselves" is about three-quarters true for the United States. That does not make the debt costless, and it is worth being clear about what the remaining cost is. Interest payments are a transfer from taxpayers in general to bondholders in particular, and bondholders are on average wealthier than taxpayers, so servicing the debt redistributes upward. Interest also has to be funded out of the same budget as everything else, so a rising interest bill crowds out other spending inside the government's own accounts. But this is a distributional and budgetary problem rather than a solvency problem, which is a different kind of problem from owing money to creditors abroad who can decline to roll it over.

Worked example: read the actual US budget

Abstractions about "spending" dissolve the moment you see the line items. Approximate US federal fiscal year 2024, in trillions:

Line $tn % of outlays
Social Security 1.46 22%
Medicare (net) 0.87 13%
Defense 0.87 13%
Net interest on the debt 0.88 13%
Medicaid 0.62 9%
Veterans, income security, everything else 2.05 30%
Total outlays 6.75 100%
Total revenue 4.92 —
Deficit 1.83 ≈ 6.4% of GDP

Three things jump out. One: in 2024 net interest passed defense spending for the first time in decades — that is the r-vs-g arithmetic of the next subsection arriving as a budget line. Two: Social Security, Medicare, Medicaid and interest are roughly 57% of outlays and are not voted on annually; the annual appropriations fight covers a minority of the budget. Three: a 6.4% deficit while unemployment was near 4% is historically unusual — deficits that size normally appear in recessions.

Now scale it to something you can feel. Divide by roughly 131 million US households: about $51,500 of federal spending, $37,500 of federal taxes, and $14,000 of borrowing per household per year, with roughly $6,700 of that spending going to interest.

Make it click

Deficit and debt answer one question: when someone says the national debt is rising, should you care?

Two numbers get mixed up. The deficit is this year's shortfall — a per-year flow. The debt is every past deficit added together — a running total. Any deficit at all adds to the total, which is why "we halved the deficit" and "the debt keeps growing" are both true at the same time.

The reason anyone cares is that neither number means anything alone. What matters is debt measured against the income available to service it. And that ratio can fall while the debt itself rises.

Debt $30tn, GDP $25tn — a 120% ratio. Borrow 3% more while GDP grows 5% → $30.9tn against $26.25tn. Ratio falls to 117.7%.

Same 3% more borrowing, but GDP grows 1% → $30.9tn against $25.25tn. Ratio climbs to 122.4%.

Identical borrowing, opposite trajectory. The only thing that changed is how fast the economy grew underneath it.

So the question is never "how much debt," it is "debt against what, growing how fast" — which the next section turns into an equation.

Two more terms. About three quarters of US federal debt is held by Americans or by other arms of government, so the interest mostly moves money between citizens rather than out of the country. And net interest is the line worth watching, because it is the only large budget item nobody votes on.

Can a government go broke?

The answer turns entirely on one question: what currency is the debt written in? Nothing else about the size or the ratio matters as much.

A government that borrows in its own currency — the United States, Japan, the United Kingdom — has promised to deliver something it alone is allowed to create. It can always produce the dollars, yen or pounds required to make a payment, so a technical sovereign default on that debt is a decision or a political accident, never an arithmetic necessity. The United States has come close twice through debt-ceiling standoffs, in which Congress authorised the spending and then separately refused to authorise the borrowing to fund it — a self-inflicted default risk with no economic cause at all.

A government that has borrowed in someone else's currency is in a completely different position, because it has promised something it cannot make. Argentina's repeated defaults have been on dollar-denominated debt: it can print pesos all day and that does not produce a single dollar. Greece discovered in 2010 that membership of the euro puts a country in the same category — Athens uses the euro but cannot issue it, so for the purposes of default risk the euro was effectively a foreign currency, and its private creditors eventually accepted a write-down of more than half of what they were owed. Whenever you assess a country's debt, find out its currency composition before you look at anything else.

"Can always print" is not the same as "can safely print," and the difference is where the real constraint lives. Paying for a deficit with newly created money rather than by borrowing from savers is called monetization, and it is not free money — it is a tax collected without a vote. The government acquires real goods and services with the new money, and the resulting inflation reduces the purchasing power of every unit of currency that anyone already held. Economists call that revenue seigniorage, and its burden falls on whoever holds cash and fixed-rate savings, which tends to mean people without access to inflation-protected assets.

Inflation also works on the existing debt directly, and this is the part that makes it tempting. A bond promising to pay $1,000 in 2035 promises a fixed number of dollars, so higher inflation between now and then shrinks what those dollars are worth without any payment being missed. The debt is reduced in real terms while every contract is honoured in nominal terms.

What stops governments doing this routinely is that lenders can see it coming. Push inflation hard and buyers of new bonds demand much higher interest rates to compensate for the expected erosion, which raises the cost of all future borrowing; push further and they refuse to lend in your currency at all, at which point you are back to borrowing in dollars and have lost the very advantage you were exploiting. Meanwhile the economy bears the costs from Section 3: price signals stop carrying information, savings are destroyed, and planning horizons collapse. Weimar Germany and Venezuela after 2018 are what the valve looks like jammed fully open.

There is a quieter cost that shows up long before any inflation crisis. Crowding out is the argument that a government borrowing heavily is competing for the same pool of savings that companies borrow from. More total demand for those savings means a higher price for them — a higher interest rate — and at a higher interest rate some private projects no longer clear their hurdle. The concrete image is a factory that does not get built because the savings that would have funded it bought Treasury bonds instead.

Whether this actually happens depends on whether savings are scarce, and that depends on where the economy is in the cycle. At full employment, workers, materials and savings are all genuinely limited, so anything the government uses is unavailable to someone else and the crowding-out argument is strong. In a deep recession, savings sit idle because firms are not investing at any interest rate, so government borrowing absorbs resources that nobody else was going to use and displaces very little. This is the same disagreement as the multiplier debate above, seen from the other side, which is why neither argument is ever settled in general — both are correct in different states of the world.

Real world: markets discipline even money-printers

In September 2022 the UK — an own-currency borrower — announced large unfunded tax cuts. Within days, 30-year government bond yields jumped by more than a full percentage point, the pound slumped, and pension funds hit margin spirals severe enough that the Bank of England intervened. The prime minister was gone within weeks. No default, no arithmetic crisis — just the bond market repricing fiscal credibility in real time. Own-currency status buys patience, not immunity.

Real world: four sovereigns, four outcomes

Country Debt in… What happened
Japan Own currency (yen) Debt above 250% of GDP — the highest in the developed world — and 10-year yields spent a decade near zero. No default, no crisis. It borrows in money it issues.
Greece, 2010–12 Euro — cannot print Adopting the euro was, in effect, borrowing in a foreign currency. Yields hit 30%+, the 2012 restructuring wrote down about €200bn (the largest sovereign default in history), GDP fell ~25%.
Argentina US dollars Nine sovereign defaults since independence, including roughly $95bn in 2001 and a restructuring in 2020. Dollar debt cannot be inflated away — it must be earned or refinanced.
Sri Lanka, 2022 US dollars Ran out of FX reserves, defaulted on external debt for the first time in its history, and suffered fuel and medicine shortages — a currency problem that became a physical one.

The dividing line is not how much debt but whose money it is promised in. The moment a government owes something it cannot create, its solvency depends on earning foreign exchange — and that is a hard budget constraint identical to a company's. This distinction, called original sin in the literature, explains most emerging-market crises of the last fifty years.

Make it click

Sovereign default answers one question: can a government actually run out of money?

Only if it owes something it cannot create. A government borrowing in its own currency can always produce more of it, so default is a choice rather than an arithmetic outcome. A government borrowing in someone else's currency must earn or refinance it, exactly like a company.

This matters because the debt level tells you almost nothing on its own. The currency it is written in tells you nearly everything.

Japan: debt above 250% of GDP, the highest in the developed world, borrowed in yen it issues. Ten-year yields sat near zero for a decade. No default.

Greece 2010: debt around 130% of GDP — half Japan's — but in euros Athens cannot print. Yields passed 30% and the restructuring wrote off roughly €200bn.

Half the debt, catastrophically worse outcome. The only thing that changed is whether the borrower can create what it owes.

So when you read a sovereign debt headline, find the currency before you react to the percentage. The literature calls borrowing in someone else's money "original sin," and it explains most emerging-market crises of the past fifty years.

Two limits on that comfort. Printing to cover deficits is called monetisation, and it pays the bill through inflation instead — a tax on everyone holding the currency. And own-currency status buys patience, not immunity: in 2022 the UK announced unfunded tax cuts, bond yields jumped more than a point in days, and the policy was reversed within a month. No default, just the bond market repricing credibility.

Debt sustainability: the r vs g race

Everything about debt sustainability comes down to a race between two compounding processes, and there is one equation that describes it. Before the symbols, here is what it says in words.

A country's debt ratio is debt divided by GDP, so it can change for two separate reasons: the top of the fraction grows, or the bottom of the fraction grows. The top grows because interest accrues on debt that already exists — last year's debt multiplied by one plus the interest rate. The bottom grows because the economy produces more and prices rise — last year's GDP multiplied by one plus the nominal growth rate. So the existing debt ratio gets multiplied each year by the interest factor divided by the growth factor, which shrinks it whenever growth outpaces interest and expands it whenever interest outpaces growth. On top of that, whatever the government overspends this year before counting interest gets added to the pile. That last quantity — spending minus revenue, excluding interest — is called the primary deficit, and it is separated out precisely because it is the part the government controls this year, whereas the interest bill is inherited.

Writing d for the debt-to-GDP ratio, r for the average nominal interest rate paid on the debt and g for the nominal growth rate of GDP, that sentence becomes:

dt+1 = dt × 1 + r1 + g + primary deficit
d = debt ÷ GDP · r = avg nominal interest rate on debt · g = nominal GDP growth · primary deficit as % of GDP

Read the equation as a ratio of two compounding processes. The numerator of the debt ratio compounds at r, because that is what unpaid interest does. The denominator compounds at g, and note that g is nominal growth, so it includes inflation: an economy growing 2% in real terms with 3% inflation has a nominal GDP growing at about 5%, and all five points work on the denominator.

If g is larger than r, the multiplying factor is less than one and the existing debt ratio falls a little every year on its own, with no policy effort whatsoever. That built-in shrinkage means a government can run a permanent moderate primary deficit and still not spiral: each year's new borrowing adds to the ratio while the growth term subtracts from it, and the two settle at a finite plateau rather than climbing without limit.

If r is larger than g, the factor exceeds one and the arithmetic reverses. The debt ratio now grows by itself even if the government spends not one cent beyond its revenue, because interest is compounding faster than the income available to pay it. Stabilising the ratio then requires running a primary surplus — taxing more than you spend before interest, every year — just to stand still. That is a far harder political task than doing nothing, which is why the sign of r minus g matters more to a country's fiscal outlook than the level of its debt does.

Worked example: a 30-year trajectory

Start at debt = 100% of GDP, with r = 2%, g = 6% (say 3.5% real growth + 2.5% inflation), and a primary deficit of 1% of GDP, forever. Year 1: 100 × (1.02 ÷ 1.06) + 1 = 97.2%. Year 2: 97.2 × 0.9623 + 1 = 94.6%. After 10 years: 76.5%. After 30: 49.7% — half the starting ratio, despite never once balancing the budget. The path is gliding toward a plateau of 1 ÷ (1 − 0.9623) = 26.5%. Growth did all the work.

This is precisely how the United States disposed of its Second World War debt, and the mechanism is worth knowing because it is so often described incorrectly. Federal debt held by the public stood near 106% of GDP in 1946 and was down to about 23% by 1974. Washington did not pay it off: primary budgets over that stretch were only roughly balanced, and the nominal dollar value of the debt actually rose. What happened is that nominal GDP grew around 7% a year — strong real growth plus steady inflation — while the average interest rate paid on the debt stayed near 2% to 3%. Every year, the denominator ran away from the numerator.

The low interest rate was not an accident either. Through much of that period the US practised financial repression: caps on deposit rates, regulations requiring banks and insurers to hold government bonds, and limited alternatives for ordinary savers, all of which kept a captive audience buying low-yielding debt. Savers paid for the war debt through returns below inflation, quietly, over three decades.

The opposite configuration is a grind, and Italy is the standing example. Through most of the 1990s and 2000s Italy ran primary surpluses — genuinely spending less than it collected before interest — and its debt ratio barely moved, because r exceeded g and interest refilled the tub as fast as austerity drained it. That is the trap in austerity: cutting spending also reduces g, so a programme aimed at the numerator can damage the denominator enough to leave the ratio unchanged or higher.

The simulator below runs that equation forward for thirty years so you can watch the two compounding processes race. Start with the presets, then move r and g one tenth of a point at a time near the point where they are equal. What you are looking for is the knife-edge: on one side of it a permanent deficit converges to a stable plateau, and on the other side the same deficit produces a ratio that climbs without ever settling. The distance between those two worlds is much smaller than the drama of the outcomes suggests.

Debt dynamics simulator

Drag r, g and the primary deficit and watch 30 years of debt/GDP unfold — start with the presets, then try to build your own doom loop.

Debt/GDP in year 30—
Change vs today—
Long-run plateau—

Deep dive: deriving the debt equation

Let D be debt in dollars, Y nominal GDP, and PD the primary deficit in dollars. Each year the debt grows by interest plus new borrowing: Dt+1 = Dt(1 + r) + PD. GDP grows as Yt+1 = Yt(1 + g). Divide the first equation by the second and write d = D ÷ Y, pd = PD ÷ Y:

dt+1 = dt × 1 + r1 + g + pd1 + g
The simulator drops the (1+g) under pd — a <0.5% approximation at realistic rates.

This is a linear recurrence dt+1 = a·dt + b with a = (1+r)/(1+g). From any discrete-systems course: it converges to the fixed point b ÷ (1 − a) when |a| < 1 (that is, g > r) and diverges when a > 1 (r > g). The whole sustainability debate is a fight about one eigenvalue.

Worked example: rating four countries on r − g

You can screen sovereign risk on a napkin. Take the average interest rate a government pays, subtract nominal GDP growth, and check the primary balance. Approximate mid-2020s figures:

Country r g (nominal) r − g Primary balance Verdict
United States 3.3% 4.5% −1.2% −3.5% Denominator helps, but the deficit overwhelms it — ratio rises.
Japan 0.9% 2.5% −1.6% −2.0% Very cheap debt; ratio drifts sideways despite huge stock.
Italy 3.5% 3.0% +0.5% +0.5% r > g — needs a permanent surplus just to stand still.
Emerging market, dollar debt 8.0% 6.0% +2.0% −1.0% Compounding against you and still borrowing. Danger.

Run the recurrence one step for Italy at d = 135%: 135 × (1.035 ÷ 1.030) − 0.5 = 135.7 − 0.5 = 135.2%. A half-point primary surplus barely offsets the interest drag. Now give it the US's −3.5% primary balance: 135.7 + 3.5 = 139.2%, and it compounds from there. That single line of arithmetic is what a sovereign credit analyst is paid to iterate, with scenarios on r and g.

The uncomfortable implication: r − g is not a policy choice. It is set by global rates and demographics. A country can control only the primary balance — which is why fiscal debates are ultimately about a number most voters have never heard of.

Make it click

Debt sustainability answers one question: is this debt shrinking on its own, or does someone have to do something about it?

Compare two rates. Interest makes the debt grow; economic growth makes the income behind it grow. If growth is faster, the burden shrinks every year by itself, even while the government keeps borrowing. If interest is faster, only a surplus holds the line.

This is what decides whether austerity is necessary or pointless, and the two cases look identical from the debt number alone.

US after 1946: debt 106% of GDP. Interest around 2%, nominal growth around 7%. Budgets never balanced — and by 1974 the ratio was 23%. Growth did all of it.

Italy in the 1990s and 2000s: ran primary surpluses year after year, genuinely painful ones. Interest above growth meant the ratio barely moved.

One country never balanced its budget and escaped; the other ran surpluses for two decades and stood still. The only thing that changed is which of the two rates was larger.

So the test on any debt story is: compare the average interest rate on the debt against nominal GDP growth. If growth wins, the deficit debate is smaller than it sounds.

The primary deficit is the gap before interest — the part policy actually controls, since interest is set by markets and growth by the economy. And financial repression is the historical thumb on the scale: rules that kept savers in low-yielding government bonds, which held the interest rate down artificially.

Trade: why it isn't zero-sum

Switch from one government's books to the relationships between countries. The deepest result in trade economics is comparative advantage, and it is genuinely counterintuitive: two countries both gain from trading even when one of them is better at producing everything.

The reason the result surprises people is that they are thinking about absolute advantage — who can make a thing with fewer hours — when what actually determines the gains is opportunity cost, the idea from Section 2: what you must give up to make one more of something. A country's hours are finite, so every hour spent making shirts is an hour not spent making chips. Being the best in the world at making shirts is irrelevant if those same hours would have produced something even more valuable. The question is never "can we make this?" but "what do we lose by making this instead of the alternative?" — and the answer can differ between two countries even when one is faster at both.

Numbers make it concrete. Two countries, Acadia and Bolandia, each with 120 labour-hours, both making chips and shirts. Acadia needs 2 hours per chip and 3 hours per shirt. Bolandia needs 8 hours per chip and 4 per shirt. Acadia is faster at both — it has the absolute advantage in each good — so the intuitive conclusion is that it should make everything itself and Bolandia has nothing to offer.

Now compute what each chip actually costs, in shirts. For Acadia, a chip takes 2 hours and a shirt takes 3, so making one more chip means giving up two-thirds of a shirt. For Bolandia, a chip takes 8 hours and a shirt takes 4, so a chip costs it two whole shirts. Chips are three times as expensive for Bolandia in the only sense that matters — what has to be sacrificed to get one. Turn it around and the same fact reads the other way: a shirt costs Acadia one and a half chips but costs Bolandia only half a chip. Acadia should make chips and Bolandia should make shirts, even though Acadia is faster at both.

Check that this actually creates something. Under autarky, meaning each country supplies itself and splits its hours evenly, Acadia makes 30 chips and 20 shirts, Bolandia makes 7.5 chips and 15 shirts, and the world total is 37.5 chips and 35 shirts. Now reallocate the identical 240 hours according to opportunity cost — Acadia mostly on chips, Bolandia entirely on shirts — and world output rises to 45 chips and 40 shirts. No new technology, no extra worker, no longer hours. The same inputs produced more because they were assigned better.

Trade is what distributes that extra output. Suppose they exchange 10 chips for 12 shirts. Acadia ends up consuming 35 chips and 22 shirts, against 30 and 20 when it did everything itself. Bolandia ends up with 10 chips and 18 shirts, against 7.5 and 15. Both countries consume more of both goods than either could produce alone. Any exchange rate between two-thirds of a shirt per chip and two shirts per chip leaves both better off, because that range sits between the two countries' opportunity costs; the particular price within the range decides how the gains are split, but not whether there are gains. This is an assignment problem with a strictly better solution available, not a contest with a winner and a loser.

If the logic is that clean, why is trade politically explosive? Because the gains and the losses land on completely different people, in completely different concentrations.

The gains are real but diffuse: every consumer in Acadia pays a little less for shirts, spread across millions of people who will never attribute their slightly cheaper clothing to trade policy. The losses are concentrated and visible: the shirt factory in one Acadian town closes, and its workers do not costlessly turn into chip designers. They have specific skills, a mortgage in a town whose main employer just left, and no obvious path into the industry that is expanding somewhere else. The economics that says the country is better off in aggregate is describing a sum in which one group's large loss is outweighed by many small gains — which is true, and is no comfort whatsoever to the group.

The evidence supports both halves. The "China shock" research on US regions most exposed to Chinese import competition after 2000 found deep and persistent damage to local employment and wages, lasting well over a decade rather than resolving in a few years as standard models had assumed. Trade expanded the total and created identifiable losers who were not compensated. An honest argument about trade policy is therefore about transition support and who bears the adjustment, not about denying either half of the result.

The standard policy response is a tariff, a tax on imported goods and the classic instrument of protectionism. The question that decides whether a tariff does what its supporters expect is incidence: not who hands over the money, but whose income actually falls.

Legally, the answer is unambiguous — the foreign exporter writes no cheque to US customs. The importing company does, when the goods arrive. The economic question is what happens next: does the importer absorb the tax by accepting a thinner margin, does the exporter cut its price to keep the sale, or does the importer raise the shelf price and pass it to customers? Studies of the 2018–19 US tariffs found the answer was overwhelmingly the third: prices of the affected goods in the United States rose by close to the full amount of the tariff, meaning American buyers bore almost all of it.

Follow the money through the whole system and there are four effects, not one. Consumers pay more. Domestic producers who compete with the imports gain, because they can now charge more too. The government collects the tariff revenue. And two slices of value disappear entirely, benefiting nobody: the extra resources burned producing domestically at a higher cost than the world price, and the purchases that simply do not happen because the artificial markup put buyers off. Those two slices are deadweight loss. The often-quoted illustration is the 2018 washing-machine tariff, which preserved American manufacturing jobs at an estimated consumer cost of roughly $800,000 per job per year — a real transfer to real workers, at a price that would have funded those same jobs many times over by simpler means.

Real world: who paid the 2018–19 tariffs

The 2018–19 US-China trade conflict is the best-measured tariff experiment in modern history, because economists could watch import prices at the dock in near real time. The findings were remarkably consistent across independent teams:

  • Pass-through was essentially complete. Prices of tariffed goods at the US border rose by close to the full tariff. Chinese exporters did not cut their prices to absorb it — so the tax was paid by US importers and, downstream, US buyers.
  • The bill was roughly $50bn a year in higher costs to US firms and consumers, or on the order of $400 per household per year, with a deadweight loss component of several billion — value destroyed rather than transferred.
  • The washing machine case is the cleanest. After the 2018 washer tariff, US washing machine prices rose about 12% — and dryer prices rose by a similar amount, though dryers were never tariffed, because retailers price them as a pair. Roughly 1,800 manufacturing jobs were created at an estimated consumer cost of around $815,000 per job.
  • Retaliation is targeted at politics, not economics. China's counter-tariffs concentrated on soybeans and other farm goods from politically pivotal states. The US then paid farmers roughly $28bn in compensation — taxpayers funding both sides of the same policy.

None of this says tariffs are never justified — national security, infant industries and bargaining leverage are real arguments. It says the cost is concrete, measurable, and lands mostly at home. Whenever you read "we charged them a tariff," mentally substitute "we taxed our own importers."

Make it click

Trade theory answers one question: if another country makes everything more cheaply than you, is there any reason to trade with them?

Yes, because "better at" is the wrong test. What matters is what each side gives up. Every hour Acadia spends on shirts is an hour not spent on chips, where its advantage is much bigger — so Acadia should make chips and buy shirts, even though it could make shirts faster too. Whoever sacrifices less should make the thing.

The reason anyone cares is that the gains spread thinly across everyone and the losses land on a few people, so the same policy can be scored as a success or a disaster.

The 2018 washing machine tariff, counted in jobs: about 1,800 US manufacturing jobs created. A win.

The same tariff, counted in cost: washer prices up about 12%, at roughly $815,000 of consumer cost per job per year. A loss.

Same policy, opposite verdict. The only thing that changed is whether you counted the concentrated benefit or the diffuse cost.

So when a tariff is announced, ask who actually writes the cheque. Measurements of 2018–19 found pass-through was near complete: import prices rose by close to the full tariff, so American importers and buyers paid it.

Comparative advantage is the name for that opportunity-cost test. Absolute advantage — just being faster — is what it replaces. And deadweight loss is the part that reaches nobody: output made at higher cost than necessary, plus the purchases that simply stopped.

The balance of payments: a forced mirror

Every transaction a country has with the outside world is recorded in its balance of payments, and the thing to know about it is that it is double-entry bookkeeping applied at national scale. Every entry has an offsetting entry, which means the accounts contain an identity you can lean on the way a physicist leans on conservation of energy.

It has two main halves. The current account records flows of goods and services plus income earned across borders — what a country sells abroad, what it buys, and the interest and dividends flowing each way. The capital account, formally the financial account, records purchases of assets: bonds, shares, property, whole companies. Because every payment for a good is matched by a movement of money that must end up held as some asset, the two halves are mirror images by construction, and sum to zero. A country with a deficit on one side necessarily runs a surplus of the same size on the other. This is not an empirical finding that might one day fail; it is what the accounting requires.

Follow a single import and the identity stops being abstract. An American buys a $1,000 machine from a manufacturer in Osaka. The dollars leave the American's account and end up with the Japanese exporter, who now holds $1,000. Those dollars are of no use in Japan — Japanese wages, taxes and suppliers are paid in yen — so they have to come back to the United States as a purchase of something American.

There are exactly two possibilities. Either the money buys American goods and services, in which case exports rise and the trade deficit closes by $1,000. Or it buys American assets: Treasury bonds, Apple shares, an apartment block in Cleveland, a stake in a company. If the exporter sells the dollars to someone else rather than spending them, that only moves the question along — whoever ends up holding them faces the same two choices. So a trade deficit is not money vanishing abroad. It is precisely matched, dollar for dollar, by foreigners acquiring claims on the country.

That gives you the second reading of the same identity, and it is the one professionals use. A country running a current-account deficit is consuming and investing more than it produces, and foreigners are financing the difference. Rearranged once more: a current-account deficit is exactly equal to the gap between what a country invests domestically and what it saves. A country that invests heavily and saves little must import the difference in capital, and importing capital is the same event as running a trade deficit. This is why the trade balance responds to savings behaviour and budget deficits at least as much as to tariffs.

Common pitfall: reading the deficit as a scoreboard

A trade deficit is not "losing at trade," and a surplus is not winning — Germany ran huge surpluses through a decade of stagnant wages, while the US ran huge deficits through its strongest growth runs. The deficit is an accounting mirror of savings and investment choices, and its twin is foreigners' eagerness to hold US assets. Judge it by what the borrowed resources bought: productive investment is a very different story from consumption.

The American case has one additional feature that most countries do not have. The dollar is the world's reserve currency: central banks hold their reserves in it, commodities are priced in it, and cross-border contracts between two countries that are neither American are routinely denominated in it. That creates enormous, structural demand for safe dollar assets, and the safest dollar asset is a Treasury bond.

Run that through the identity and the consequence follows automatically. A permanent global appetite for US assets is a permanent capital inflow, and a permanent capital inflow must be mirrored by a permanent current-account deficit. The United States runs a structural trade deficit in part because the world wants to hold its bonds — the two are the same fact recorded on opposite pages, and it loops back to the table of who owns the debt earlier in this section.

Worked example: what a trade deficit buys the seller

Follow the mirror concretely for one year of a simplified US–Japan relationship. The US imports $1,000 of goods and exports $700.

Account US Japan
Current account (goods & services) −$300 +$300
Financial account (net asset purchases) +$300 −$300
Sum 0 0

Japan ends the year holding $300 of US dollars, and dollars are only useful for buying dollar things: Treasuries, corporate bonds, shares, farmland, an office tower in Dallas. So the trade deficit is the capital inflow — the same event described from two sides of the ledger, exactly as debits equal credits.

In actual magnitudes: foreign investors hold roughly $8 trillion of US Treasury securities, Japan and China being the largest official holders at roughly $1.1 trillion and $0.8 trillion. The US net international investment position is around −$20 trillion — the world owns far more of America than America owns of the world.

And here is the twist that confuses people: despite that deeply negative position, the US has usually earned positive net investment income. Foreigners buy safe, low-yield US assets (Treasuries); Americans buy risky, high-yield foreign assets (factories, equity stakes). Being the world's banker means borrowing cheaply and lending dearly — the "exorbitant privilege" a French finance minister complained about in the 1960s.

Make it click

The balance of payments answers one question: when a country buys more than it sells, where do the dollars go?

They come back, because dollars are only good for buying dollar things. An American buys a $1,000 machine from Osaka; the Japanese seller now holds $1,000 that is useless in Japan. They can buy American goods with it — which would cancel the trade gap — or buy American assets: Treasuries, shares, property. So a trade deficit is the same event as a capital inflow, counted from the other side. The two accounts have to sum to zero.

The reason anyone cares is that "trade deficit" gets read as losing, and the record does not support it.

Germany, 2010s: large, sustained trade surpluses — alongside a decade of stagnant real wages.

US, same period: large, sustained trade deficits — alongside its strongest growth run in the developed world.

Opposite balances, and the surplus country had the worse decade. The only thing the balance told you was whether the country saved more than it invested.

So the useful question is not the sign of the deficit but what the borrowed resources bought. Financing productive investment is a very different story from financing consumption, and the headline number cannot tell them apart.

Two terms left. The current account is trade in goods, services and income; the financial account is who bought which assets. And reserve currency status is why the US case is extreme — the world wants safe dollar assets, that demand is a permanent capital inflow, and its mirror image is a permanent trade deficit.

Exchange rates: floating, pegged, and the Big Mac test

An exchange rate is nothing more exotic than a price: the price of one currency stated in another, such as 150 yen per dollar. It is set in the largest market in the world, where over $7 trillion changes hands daily, which matters because a market that size cannot be pushed around for long by anyone who is not a government.

Countries choose between two regimes for that price. Under a floating exchange rate — the dollar, euro, yen and pound — nobody sets the rate; it moves continuously with whoever wants to buy and sell. Under a currency peg — the Hong Kong dollar, the Gulf currencies — the central bank promises a fixed rate and makes that promise real by standing ready to trade at it, selling its foreign-currency reserves to buy its own currency whenever markets push the other way.

A peg buys predictability, which is valuable for a small trading economy, and it costs monetary independence: defending the rate means matching the anchor country's interest rates whether or not they suit your own economy. It also has a specific failure mode. Because defending a peg means spending finite reserves, speculators can work out roughly when those reserves will run out, and betting against a currency that can only fall is close to a one-way trade. When the defence is abandoned, the rate does not drift — it snaps, in a devaluation. Britain in 1992 and Thailand in 1997 are the standard examples, and in both cases the currency had been visibly misaligned for months before the break.
