What moves a floating currency? Four forces do most of the work, and they operate on different time horizons, which is why they can point in opposite directions at once.

Interest-rate differences dominate day to day. If US rates rise above Japan's, holding dollars pays more than holding yen, so investors move money into dollar deposits and bonds — and because they must buy dollars to do it, the dollar rises. This is the direct link from the central-bank decisions of Section 4 into the currency market, and it is why an unexpected rate hike moves the exchange rate within seconds.

Inflation differences dominate over years. A currency losing 30% of its domestic purchasing power annually cannot hold its value against one losing 2%, because anyone holding it is watching their wealth evaporate and will eventually swap into something stabler. Sustained inflation gaps show up as sustained currency depreciation.

Trade and investment flows act as the slow structural pull. Persistent foreign demand for a country's exports, or for its assets, means persistent demand for its currency to pay for them, and that supports the rate over long periods.

Risk appetite overrides everything else during a crisis. When markets panic, money moves into dollars, yen and Swiss francs — the safe haven currencies — regardless of interest rates or trade balances. This produces results that look absurd on paper: in 2008, a crisis that began in American housing finance caused the dollar to rise, because a panic sends money toward the deepest and most liquid market available, and that market is the American one.

Over the very long run there is an anchor underneath all that movement, and it is called purchasing power parity, or PPP. The reasoning is an arbitrage argument: if an identical good costs much less in one country than another once you convert the currencies, somebody can buy it where it is cheap, sell it where it is dear, and take the difference. The buying and selling required to do that pushes the two prices together, and the exchange rate along with them. So over time, exchange rates should drift toward the level that makes the same basket of goods cost the same everywhere.

The Economist's Big Mac index is a deliberately unserious application of a serious idea, and it works because a Big Mac is a standardised basket of tradable ingredients, local labour and local rent, assembled to the same specification worldwide. Suppose one costs $5.80 in the United States and ¥480 in Japan. The exchange rate implied by burger parity is 480 ÷ 5.80, about 83 yen per dollar. If the market rate is actually 150 yen per dollar, then measured against burgers the yen is roughly 45% below its parity value.

Do not expect the gap to close next quarter. Most of what people buy is not shippable — you cannot import a haircut, a flat or a school place — so the arbitrage argument only bites on the tradable part of the basket, and deviations from parity persist for years or decades. What the index is genuinely useful for is flagging extremes: a currency 60% away from parity is telling you something, even if it will not tell you when.

Key idea: closing Part I — the four macro levers

You now hold the full demand-management toolkit. Monetary policy (Section 4) works through the price of money: policy rates and the central bank's balance sheet. Fiscal policy works through the government's budget: taxes and spending. Markets referee both in real time — the bond market prices fiscal credibility into yields (Section 8), the currency market prices the policy mix (Section 10), and equities price the growth consequences (Section 7). When both levers push the same way, expect regime-sized moves: 2021's floored rates plus trillions of stimulus fed the inflation that Section 4's tightening then had to break. Every macro headline you'll ever read is some combination of these four dials — and Part II begins with the machine that transmits them: the financial system.

Your edge: macro data is free and clean

Everything in this section is public, well-curated time series: FRED (fred.stlouisfed.org) has debt-to-GDP, deficits and interest costs; the BEA publishes the full balance of payments; the BIS posts effective exchange rates. Rebuilding Figure 5.4's quadrants from raw FRED series, or backtesting the r-vs-g recurrence against actual US history, is an afternoon in pandas — and exactly the kind of portfolio piece that shows a hiring manager you can connect an equation to a dataset.

Worked example: the Big Mac test and the carry trade

PPP, the burger version. A Big Mac cost about $5.69 in the US and ¥450 in Japan in early 2024. Implied exchange rate: 450 ÷ 5.69 = 79 yen per dollar. The market rate was about 148. By this crude test the yen was roughly 47% undervalued.

The index is a joke with a serious core — burgers include local rent and wages, which do not arbitrage across borders — but it is directionally informative over decades, and it makes the key point: PPP is a long-run anchor and a terrible short-run forecast.

The carry trade, the reason the yen was there. Suppose you borrow ¥100,000,000 at 0.1%, convert at 148, and buy US T-bills at 5.3%.

Step Amount
Borrow yen at 0.1% for a year ¥100,000,000
Convert at ¥148/$ $675,676
Earn 5.3% on T-bills $711,487
Owe back (principal + 0.1%) ¥100,100,000
Convert back at ¥148 — profit ≈ ¥5,199,000 (+5.2%)

A 5.2% return with no market view — as long as the exchange rate holds. If the yen strengthens to 140 your dollars buy back fewer yen and the entire profit is gone; at 132 you lose about 6%. And leverage of 5–10× is normal in this trade, so a 5% currency move becomes a 25–50% loss.

This is not hypothetical. In early August 2024, an unexpected Bank of Japan hike plus weak US data strengthened the yen sharply in days; carry positions unwound at once, and Japan's Nikkei fell 12.4% in a single session — its worst day since 1987. Carry trades earn a small premium most of the time and lose enormously, all at once, occasionally. That shape — "picking up nickels in front of a steamroller" — recurs across finance, and you will meet it again in Section 16.

Make it click

Exchange rates answer one question: if you can borrow at 0.1% in one country and lend at 5.3% in another, why isn't that free money?

Because you change currencies twice, and the rate can move in between. Borrow yen, convert to dollars, buy Treasury bills, convert back to repay. The interest gap is yours only if the exchange rate stands still; if the yen strengthens, your dollars buy back fewer yen than you owe.

It matters because this trade pays reliably and small, then loses violently and all at once.

Rate holds at ¥148: borrow ¥100m at 0.1%, earn 5.3% on T-bills, convert back → about +5.2% for taking no view on anything.

Yen strengthens to ¥132: identical trade, identical interest earned → about −6%. At the 5–10× leverage normal in this trade, that is a 30–60% loss.

Same position, same interest income, opposite outcome. The only thing that changed is the exchange rate on the way back.

That is not hypothetical. In August 2024 an unexpected Bank of Japan hike strengthened the yen in days, carry positions unwound at once, and the Nikkei fell 12.4% in a single session — its worst day since 1987.

Purchasing power parity is the long-run anchor: the same goods should cost the same everywhere once converted, which is what the Big Mac index measures. It is a reasonable guide over decades and a terrible one over months. A peg is a promise to hold the rate fixed, defended with reserves — and it holds until the reserves run out.

Check your understanding

1. Which of these is a stock rather than a flow?

The debt is the accumulated total — the integral. Deficits, growth and interest payments are all per-period flows that feed into it.

2. A country has debt at 100% of GDP, pays r = 3% on it, grows nominally at g = 5%, and runs a primary balance of exactly zero. Over time its debt ratio will…

With a zero primary balance, the ratio is multiplied by (1.03 ÷ 1.05) ≈ 0.981 each year. Growth outruns interest, so the ratio melts — the post-WW2 US mechanism.

3. Acadia produces both chips and shirts more efficiently than Bolandia. Why does Acadia still gain from trading with it?

Comparative advantage runs on opportunity cost, not absolute efficiency. Every hour Acadia spends on shirts is an hour not spent on chips, where its edge is far bigger — so it pays to buy shirts from Bolandia.

4. The US runs a $900 billion trade deficit this year. Which statement must also be true?

The balance of payments is double-entry: a current-account deficit is mirrored, dollar for dollar, by a capital-account surplus. The dollars spent on imports return as purchases of Treasuries, stocks and property.

5. Studies of the 2018–19 US tariffs found that the cost was borne mostly by…

Pass-through was close to complete: US import prices rose by roughly the tariff amount. That's incidence — the legal payer and the economic payer are different questions, and revenue never offsets the deadweight loss.

Key takeaways

  • Fiscal policy moves demand directly through taxes and spending; automatic stabilizers act instantly, discretionary stimulus is powerful but slow, and the multiplier depends on slack, leakages and the central bank's reaction.
  • Deficit is the flow, debt is the stock — and only debt-to-GDP, not raw dollars, tells you whether the burden is heavy.
  • An own-currency sovereign can't be forced into arithmetic default, but inflation is the escape valve and markets can still repunish fiscal recklessness through yields and the currency.
  • Debt sustainability hinges on r vs g: when growth exceeds the interest rate, even permanent modest deficits plateau; when r > g, only primary surpluses prevent a doom loop — the post-WW2 US grew out of 106% debt/GDP without ever repaying it.
  • Comparative advantage makes trade positive-sum even against a country that's better at everything, but the gains are diffuse while the losses are concentrated on specific workers and towns.
  • Tariff incidence usually lands on domestic consumers, with part of the loss pure deadweight — value destroyed rather than transferred.
  • The balance of payments is double-entry bookkeeping: a trade deficit is exactly matched by foreigners accumulating claims, so it reflects savings-versus-investment choices, not "losing."
  • Exchange rates respond to rate differentials, inflation gaps, trade flows and risk appetite; purchasing power parity — Big Mac included — anchors them only over long horizons.

Part II · Financial Markets & Instruments

6. The Financial System: A Guided Tour

Before you study stocks, bonds, or derivatives, you need the map: who the players are, what each one does, and what actually happens in the seconds after you tap Buy. This section is your orientation tour — by the end you will be able to place any headline, job posting, or trade confirmation on the map, and you will have run your own orders through a live order book.

The core job: routing money from savers to users

Strip away the towers and the vocabulary and the financial system does one job. Some people have more money than they currently need — a household saving for retirement, a company between investment projects, a country running a surplus. Other people can do something productive with money they do not have: a firm that could build a factory, a government that could build a road, a household that could buy a home decades before it could pay cash for one. The system's entire purpose is to move purchasing power from the first group to the second.

Nothing moves for free, so the second group hands something back: a security or a contractual promise — a share, a bond, a loan agreement. Every one of those instruments is the same kind of object underneath: a claim on money that will arrive later. The differences between them, which occupy the next several sections, are differences in what triggers the payment, how certain it is, who gets paid first if something goes wrong, and how easily the claim can be sold to somebody else.

There are exactly two routes that money can take from saver to user, and every institution in this section sits on one of them.

In direct finance you buy the claim yourself in a market. You purchase Apple shares or a Treasury bond, and you hold the claim in your own name; when it pays, it pays you. You have chosen the borrower, you carry the consequences of that choice, and nobody stands between you and the outcome.

In indirect finance you hand your money to an intermediary and it decides who gets funded. Your current account is the clearest example: the bank pools your deposit with millions of others and lends the pool out as mortgages and business loans. You have no idea who those borrowers are, and that is the point — your claim is against the bank, not against them. If a borrower defaults, the bank absorbs it and still owes you your balance in full. You have exchanged the upside of picking well for the certainty of not having to pick at all.

That raises an obvious question. If a market can match savers with borrowers directly, why does anyone use an intermediary that takes a cut for standing in the middle? There are three answers, and each corresponds to a real problem the market route leaves you holding — all three connected to the market failures from Section 2 (Microeconomics).

Information. Lending is the textbook case of information asymmetry: the borrower knows their own finances, plans and intentions, and you know almost nothing. Working out whether a particular small business will repay a five-year loan means examining its accounts, understanding its market and verifying its collateral, which takes expertise and days of work. That cost is fixed regardless of loan size, so for the $1,000 you were thinking of lending it is wildly uneconomic.

A bank makes the same investigation pay by doing it at scale. It employs credit analysts full time, sees the applicant's actual cash flows through their accounts, and spreads the fixed cost of building that assessment capability across thousands of loans. It is the same economics as training one model and serving millions of queries from it: the expensive part happens once and the marginal application is cheap. What you are buying from the bank is not the loan, it is the assessment.

Maturity transformation. Savers and borrowers want incompatible things from the same money. You want your savings available on demand, because you do not know when the boiler will break. A homebuyer wants the money for thirty years, because that is how long it takes to repay from a salary. No single contract satisfies both, so left alone the two would simply not trade.

A bank resolves it by performing maturity transformation: it borrows short, from you, and lends long, to the homebuyer. The bet it is making is statistical rather than reckless — on any given day, some depositors withdraw and others deposit, and with enough independent depositors the net flow is small and predictable. That works exactly as long as depositors behave independently. The failure mode is that they stop behaving independently the moment they get frightened, which is the bank run from Section 4 and much of Section 17 (Crises). The usefulness and the fragility are the same feature seen from two sides.

Diversification. With $1,000 you can fund a slice of one borrower, and your outcome is then binary: they repay or they do not. A fund with $10 billion holds thousands of loans or hundreds of companies, so a single default moves its return by a fraction of a percent. Pooling money buys small savers a diversification they could not construct on their own.

It is worth being precise about what diversification does and does not do, because the point recurs throughout this book. It does not raise the average outcome — the expected return on a thousand loans is the same as on one. It reduces the variance around that average, because independent failures partially cancel instead of compounding. And it only works to the extent the failures really are independent: in a recession, borrowers default together, which is precisely when diversification delivers least. The statistics of this are the heart of Section 15 (Portfolio Theory).

Key idea: what an intermediary actually sells

Notice that all three reasons describe the same commercial transaction from different angles. In each case the saver has a problem — not knowing who is creditworthy, needing money back sooner than the borrower can return it, being too small to spread risk — and the intermediary takes that problem onto its own balance sheet in exchange for a margin. What a bank sells is not money. It is assessment, liquidity and risk-pooling, priced as the gap between what it pays you and what it charges the borrower.

That framing tells you where to look when something goes wrong. Every one of those three services can fail, and each fails in a characteristic way: the assessment can be wrong, which produces bad loans; the liquidity promise can be called all at once, which produces a run; and the risk pooling can turn out to be pooling correlated risks rather than independent ones, which produces a solvency crisis. Nearly every financial failure in this book is one of those three, and the question worth asking about any new institution is which of the three it is taking on and what happens when that one breaks.

Worked example: your $10,000, four routes

The abstraction becomes concrete the moment you follow one saver's money. Same $10,000, four channels, four completely different risk positions:

Route Where it ends up What you hold Who eats the loss
Bank savings account The bank's mortgage book A fixed claim on the bank The bank's equity, then the FDIC (to $250k)
Government money market fund T-bills and repo Fund shares priced near $1.00 You — but the assets are the safest in existence
Corporate bond ETF Loans to ~1,000 companies A diversified slice of credit risk You, directly and immediately in the price
Private credit fund Loans to a few dozen mid-sized firms An illiquid partnership interest You, and you may not find out for a year

The routes differ on exactly three dimensions, and they are the three you should ask about any product for the rest of your life: who bears the credit loss, how fast you can get out, and who is marking the price. The bank route converts your risk into someone else's problem in exchange for a low return. The fund routes hand you the risk directly in exchange for a higher expected one. There is no fourth option where you get both.

Make it click

The financial system answers one question: when you hand over money, who takes the loss if the borrower doesn't pay?

There are only two arrangements. Direct — you buy the claim yourself, and the loss is yours immediately, visible in the price. Indirect — you give the money to a bank or fund, which lends it on and stands between you and the borrower. Someone else absorbs the first loss, and charges you for it in return you don't receive.

The reason anyone cares is that identical lending can be safe or risky to you depending only on the wrapper around it.

$10,000 in a savings account. The bank's mortgage borrower defaults → the bank's equity absorbs it, then deposit insurance. You still have $10,000.

$10,000 in a corporate bond fund lending to similar borrowers. One defaults → the fund's price marks down that day. You have $9,700.

Same credit risk underneath, opposite exposure. The only thing that changed is whether anyone stood between you and the borrower.

So three questions settle any financial product: who bears the credit loss, how fast can you get out, and who sets the price you are shown. Nothing gives you the buffer and the higher return at once — the gap between them is what the buffer costs.

Maturity transformation is the trick that makes banks useful and fragile at the same time: your money is withdrawable today, the mortgage it funded runs thirty years. It works right up until everyone asks at once.

The cast, mapped

Financial writing assumes you already know who everyone is, and the vocabulary is the main barrier for the first year. The table below is the full cast in one place; read it once now and treat it as a lookup while you work through the rest of Part II.

It is organised around a single distinction that makes the list far easier to hold in your head. Every institution here is doing one of three things. Some are channels for money — they take money in from savers at one end and put it to work at the other, which is what banks, funds and insurers do. Some are service providers to those channels — they do not route money themselves but sell something the channels need, such as execution, advice, ratings or audits. And some are infrastructure — the exchanges, clearing houses and depositories that everyone else runs on top of. When you meet an unfamiliar firm, placing it in one of those three categories tells you most of what you need to know about how it earns money and what it is exposed to.

Player What it does How it makes money
Commercial bank Takes deposits, makes loans, runs payments (JPMorgan Chase's retail arm, Bank of America) Interest spread: charge borrowers more than it pays depositors
Investment bank Helps firms issue stocks/bonds, advises on M&A, trades (Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley) Fees on deals and underwriting; trading revenue
Asset manager Runs mutual funds, index funds, ETFs for the public (BlackRock, Vanguard, Fidelity) Management fee: a % of assets per year
Hedge fund Flexible, often leveraged strategies for institutions and the wealthy (Citadel, Bridgewater) Classically “2 and 20”: 2% of assets + 20% of profits
Private equity / VC PE buys whole companies to restructure; VC funds startups (Blackstone, KKR; Sequoia, a16z) Fees plus a share of exit profits (“carry”)
Pension fund Invests retirement savings over decades (CalPERS) Not-for-profit for members; managers earn fees
Insurer Collects premiums, invests the pool (“float”), pays claims (Allianz, MetLife) Underwriting margin + investment returns on the float
Sovereign wealth fund Invests a nation's surplus (Norway's $1.7T oil fund, Singapore's GIC) Returns accrue to the state
Exchange Runs the marketplace and publishes prices (NYSE, Nasdaq, CME) Trading fees, listing fees, and — increasingly — selling market data
Broker Routes customer orders to venues (Schwab, Interactive Brokers, Robinhood) Commissions, interest on cash, payment for order flow
Market maker Quotes two-sided prices all day so you can always trade (Citadel Securities, Jane Street) Earns the bid–ask spread, many thousands of times a day
Custodian Safekeeps assets, tracks ownership records (BNY, State Street) Small fees on enormous asset piles
Rating agency Grades bond issuers' default risk (Moody's, S&P, Fitch) — see Section 8 Issuers pay to be rated (a conflict worth remembering)
Data vendor Sells prices, news, analytics (Bloomberg, Refinitiv, FactSet) Subscriptions — a Bloomberg Terminal runs ~$30k/year

Real world: scale

BlackRock alone manages over $11 trillion — more than the GDP of every country except the US and China. When you hear “institutional investors,” picture a handful of asset managers, pension funds, and sovereign funds that collectively own most of the stock market. Retail investors — individuals like you — are the minority of volume in most markets.

Real world: who actually owns a big American company

Pull the ownership page of almost any S&P 500 company and you will see roughly the same faces at the top:

Holder Typical stake Why they are there
Vanguard 8 – 9% Index funds — bought because the company is in the index, not because anyone liked it
BlackRock 6 – 8% Same, plus active mandates
State Street 3 – 5% Same
Pensions, endowments, insurers 20 – 30% Long-horizon liabilities to fund
Active managers, hedge funds 20 – 30% Trying to beat the index
Retail investors direct 10 – 20% You, your brokerage account, your 401(k)

The "Big Three" index managers together typically hold about 20% of a large US company — and they vote those shares at every annual meeting. That is a genuinely new feature of capitalism: the largest shareholders of most public companies are institutions that are legally required not to have an opinion on whether the business is any good. Whether that is a governance problem is one of the live debates in the field, and it is a good interview topic.

Make it click

Every financial firm answers one question about itself: how does it get paid — and what does that make it want?

Three payment models cover almost everyone. A percentage of assets held, which rewards gathering and keeping money. A fee per transaction, which rewards activity. Or a spread, the gap between the buying and selling price, which rewards volume. Find the model and you have found the incentive.

This matters because the same recommendation means different things from differently-paid people.

Adviser paid 1% of assets a year. You ask about moving $500,000 out to repay a mortgage. Their revenue falls $5,000 a year if you do.

Adviser paid a flat $3,000 for the review. Same question, same $500,000, same answer either way — their revenue does not move.

Same advice sought, opposite pressure on the person giving it. The only thing that changed is what their fee is calculated on.

So read the fee before the advice. This is not about dishonesty — it is that incentives shape which options get raised at all, and the option that costs the adviser money tends not to come up.

The cast then sorts into three groups. Firms that hold other people's money are channels: banks, asset managers, pension funds, insurers. Firms paid per deal or per trade are services: investment banks, brokers, market makers. Firms running the marketplace itself are infrastructure: exchanges, custodians. And a rating agency is worth singling out — the issuer being rated pays for the rating, which is a conflict that has mattered before.

The referees: who regulates what

Section 2 introduced market failures — information asymmetry, externalities, monopoly power — as the situations where a free market does not produce a good outcome on its own. Financial regulation is best understood as the institutional response to precisely those three, and reading it that way turns a list of agencies into something with a logic.

Securities regulation attacks information asymmetry. If a company can sell shares while knowing things about its finances that buyers do not, buyers must assume the worst, and good companies get priced as though they were bad ones. Mandatory disclosure — audited accounts, quarterly filings, a prospectus for every new issue — is the fix. Bank capital regulation attacks an externality. When a bank fails it damages people who never chose to deal with it: other banks it owed money to, businesses that lose access to credit, taxpayers who fund the rescue. That spillover is systemic risk, and capital requirements force a bank to hold enough of its own money at stake that the cost of its mistakes lands on it first. Market-structure and antitrust rules attack concentration, since exchanges and clearing houses are natural near-monopolies that everyone is obliged to use.

In the United States, each regulator owns one slice of that job:

Regulator Watches Exists because…
SEC Securities markets: stocks, bonds, funds, disclosure Investors can't verify claims themselves — so issuers must publish audited truth (see Section 11)
Federal Reserve Banks' safety, plus monetary policy (Section 4) Bank failures cascade; someone must be lender of last resort
FDIC Insures bank deposits up to $250,000 per depositor, per bank Deposit insurance stops bank runs before they start
FINRA Brokers and their salespeople (industry-funded self-regulator) Front-line policing of the people who touch retail money
CFTC Derivatives and commodities futures (Section 9) Leverage in derivatives can blow holes in the real economy
FCA (UK) / ESMA (EU) Rough overseas equivalents of the SEC + FINRA Same failures, different jurisdictions

The pattern worth noticing in that table is that nobody sees the whole picture. A single bank holding company can answer to the Federal Reserve for its balance sheet, the SEC for its brokerage arm, the CFTC for its swaps desk and the FDIC for its insured deposits — four supervisors, each with a complete view of one part and no view of the rest.

That fragmentation is not merely untidy; it creates a predictable incentive. If the same economic activity can be structured to fall under a lighter set of rules, some of it will be, and the practice has a name: regulatory arbitrage. Mortgage lending migrating from regulated banks to lightly supervised originators before 2008 is the canonical case, and the same plot recurs through crisis post-mortems. The practical lesson for an analyst is that when risk seems to have disappeared from a regulated sector, the first question is whether it disappeared or simply moved to where nobody publishes statistics about it.

Real world: which referee showed up, and which one was missing

Event Who acted The gap it exposed
Madoff, 2008 SEC (after the fact) The SEC received detailed tip-offs from Harry Markopolos from 1999 onward and did not act. Disclosure regimes need someone who reads the disclosures.
AIG, 2008 Fed + Treasury ($182bn) AIG's derivatives unit was an insurance company writing bank-style risk, supervised by neither a bank regulator nor a securities one.
LIBOR rigging, 2012–15 FCA, CFTC, DOJ — roughly $9bn of fines A rate underpinning hundreds of trillions of contracts was set by a daily survey with no regulator and no transaction data behind it.
Archegos, 2021 Nobody, until $10bn was lost A family office was exempt from most registration, so no regulator (and no single bank) could see its total leverage across prime brokers.
FTX, 2022 DOJ criminal prosecution Crypto exchanges combined the roles of exchange, broker, clearing house and custodian — a combination illegal in every regulated market, and unregulated here.
SVB, 2023 Fed supervision, FDIC resolution Interest-rate risk in the held-to-maturity book was visible in filings and not treated as urgent. The Fed's own post-mortem said so.

The pattern to internalise: financial crises rarely happen where regulation is strict. They happen in the seams — between agencies, between countries, and between the legal categories a new business model does not fit. When you hear of a fast-growing activity that "isn't really a bank," look for the seam.

Make it click

Financial regulation answers one question: who is checking that this firm can do what it promises?

The answer is assigned by legal category, not by activity. Securities go to the SEC, bank safety to the Fed, deposits to the FDIC, derivatives to the CFTC. Which means the question has a gap in it: if a business does something that looks like banking but is not legally a bank, no one owns it. Risk drifts toward whichever category is watched least.

The reason anyone cares is that this is where losses actually happen — not in the regulated middle, but at the edges.

A hedge fund's leverage is visible to its prime brokers and to the SEC. It gets margined and monitored.

Archegos ran the same strategies as a family office, which was exempt from most registration. No regulator and no single bank could see the total position. Banks lost about $10bn.

Same trades, same leverage, opposite oversight. The only thing that changed was the legal wrapper the money sat in.

So the practical test on any fast-growing financial product: name the regulator. If the answer is "it's not technically a bank" or "it's structured as a technology company," you have found the seam, and the seam is where the last several crises came from.

Regulatory arbitrage is the name for deliberately choosing the wrapper with the lightest supervision. And systemic risk is why any of this is public business at all — a failing bank damages people who never banked there, which is a cost the bank had no reason to price.

Buy side vs sell side: the industry's two halves

Practitioners divide the entire industry into two halves, and the division is worth learning early because it structures every job posting, every conference and every conversation you will have in the sector.

The buy side manages money that belongs to somebody else: asset managers, hedge funds, pension funds, private equity and venture capital, insurers, sovereign wealth funds. Its product is investment performance, its customers are the people whose savings it invests, and it is paid a percentage of the money it looks after. The name comes from the fact that it is the buyer of everything the other half produces — research, execution, new issues.

The sell side sells services to the money: investment banks, brokers, market makers and research departments. Its products are execution of trades, creation of new securities, advice on transactions and analysis of companies. Its customers are the buy side, and it is paid in fees, commissions and spreads. When a bank publishes a report on a company, the report is not a favour to the public; it is a service delivered to institutional clients whose trading business the bank wants.

The economics of the two halves are genuinely different, and the difference predicts most of their behaviour. Buy-side revenue scales with assets under management: a fund charging 0.5% a year on $50 billion collects $250 million whether markets rise, fall or barely open. That revenue is smooth, arrives regardless of activity, and grows automatically as the assets grow.

Sell-side revenue scales with activity: deals completed, trades executed, spreads captured on volume. When markets are quiet and companies are not raising money, that revenue simply does not appear. This is why sell-side headcount expands and contracts with deal cycles while large asset managers grind steadily along, and why the two halves react differently to the same market conditions — a volatile quarter is a good quarter for a trading desk and an anxious one for a fund whose investors are watching their balances fall.

The career geography follows from that. The sell side hires analysts into three broad functions: investment banking, which builds the financial models behind mergers and share issues and is known for its hours; sales and trading, which prices and executes transactions for clients; and research, which covers companies in depth using the accounting and valuation skills of Sections 12–13.

The buy side hires portfolio managers who decide what to own, research analysts who investigate individual investments, and — increasingly since the 2010s — quantitative researchers and data scientists who build systematic signals from data rather than analysing companies one at a time (Section 18). The traditional path runs from the sell side to the buy side after two or three years, because the sell side trains people at scale and the buy side prefers to hire people already trained. Section 20 (Career Roadmap) maps the routes in detail.

Your edge

Data roles now live on both sides: market makers and hedge funds run some of the most demanding ML and low-latency engineering anywhere, while banks and asset managers hire heavily for risk analytics, surveillance, and client data. When you read a posting, first ask: buy side or sell side? That single bit tells you the business model, the pace, and how your work gets monetized.

Worked example: the economics of four finance jobs

Job postings make more sense once you can see the revenue that pays for the seat. Rough but realistic economics:

Firm Revenue model Annual revenue Staff Revenue per head
Index fund manager, $500bn AUM 0.04% fee $200M 300 $0.7M
Active equity manager, $10bn AUM 0.50% fee $50M 40 $1.3M
Hedge fund, $2bn AUM, +15% gross 2% + 20% of $300M $100M 25 $4.0M
M&A team, one $1bn deal 1.2% success fee $12M 6 (6 months) $2.0M per deal

Four consequences you can predict from the table alone. Index managers must be ruthlessly automated — $0.7M per head cannot support armies of analysts, which is precisely why they hire engineers rather than stock pickers. Active managers live and die on AUM, so their worst year is one of outflows, not one of losses. Hedge funds have violently variable revenue — that $100M becomes $40M in a flat year — which is why compensation is bonus-heavy and teams are small. Bankers earn nothing until a deal closes, which explains both the hours and the industry's brutal cyclicality.

For your own search: the buy side pays you to be right; the sell side pays you to be useful. Data and quant roles now sit on both sides, but the highest-leverage seats for someone with your background are where revenue per head is high and headcount is small — which is exactly where a reproducible pipeline replaces five people with spreadsheets.

Make it click

Buy side and sell side answer one question about any finance job: does this firm get paid for being right, or for being useful?

The buy side manages money and charges a percentage of it, so its revenue depends on performance and on assets staying put. The sell side provides execution, research and deals, and charges per transaction, so its revenue depends on activity. One is paid for outcomes, the other for volume.

The reason anyone cares is that it predicts the shape of the job before you read a word about responsibilities.

Asset manager, $50bn at 0.5%: $250m of revenue arriving whether markets rise or fall. Steady headcount, bad year means outflows.

M&A team: nothing until a deal closes, then $12m on a $1bn transaction. Same market conditions, revenue swings to zero when deals stop.

Same industry, opposite revenue stability. The only thing that changed is whether the fee is charged on a stock of money or on an event.

So when you see a posting, work out revenue per head. High revenue and small teams means automation and leverage, and it is where someone who can build a reproducible pipeline replaces five people with spreadsheets. Low revenue per head means the firm needs volume, and your work will be judged on throughput.

That also explains the hiring cycles: sell-side headcount booms and crashes with deal flow, while large asset managers grind along, which is why the same CV gets very different responses in different years.

Primary vs secondary markets: issuance and trading

Every security lives two separate lives, and confusing them is one of the most common misunderstandings in finance.

It is born in the primary market, where the issuer creates it and sells it, and the cash goes to the issuer. This is the only moment at which the company or government actually receives funding. It then spends the rest of its existence in the secondary market, changing hands between investors who buy it from each other.

The consequence catches people out constantly. When Apple stock trades $10 billion in a day, not one cent of that reaches Apple. The money moves from investors who bought to investors who sold, exactly as buying a used car sends money to the previous owner rather than to the manufacturer. Apple received its money once, at issuance, years ago. What the share price does afterwards matters to the company for other reasons — it affects what employees' stock is worth, what an acquisition would cost, and whether raising new money later is cheap or expensive — but a rising share price does not put cash in the business.

The headline primary-market event is the IPO, the first time a private company sells shares to the public. The company hires investment banks to run the process, a service called underwriting, and the word is precise: in a traditional deal the banks do not merely introduce buyers, they buy the shares from the company themselves and resell them. That means they, not the company, carry the risk that demand is weaker than expected — which is what the fee, typically around 7% for a US IPO, is paying for.

The work runs in a set order. The banks value the business and agree a price range. They prepare the prospectus, the legal disclosure document filed with the SEC that sets out the business, its audited financials and an unusually candid list of everything that could go wrong — these are free to read at sec.gov/edgar and are the single best primary source on any company about to list. They then run a roadshow, presenting to institutional investors and collecting indications of how much each would buy at what price, which is how demand is discovered before a price is fixed. Finally the price is set, the shares are allocated, and trading begins.

Bond issuance follows the same logic but is faster and far more routine. A large company with an established credit rating can announce a bond in the morning, take orders through the day and raise several billion by the afternoon, several times a year — closer to calling a familiar API than to the months-long production of an IPO (Section 8).

Worked example: IPO economics

A company sells 10 million new shares at $20: gross proceeds $200 million. The underwriters' fee (the gross spread) is a typical 7%, or $14 million, so the company nets $186 million. If the stock closes its first day at $26, that 30% “pop” means the company arguably left 10M × $6 = $60 million on the table — money captured by the investors who got IPO allocations instead of by the firm. Underpricing is one of the best-documented puzzles in finance.

If issuers receive nothing from secondary trading, why does the secondary market matter? Two reasons, and both are load-bearing.

The first is that secondary liquidity is what makes the primary market possible at all. Ask yourself whether you would lend money to a government for thirty years if the only way to get it back were to wait thirty years. Almost nobody would, and those who did would demand a much higher interest rate for locking their money away. Because a Treasury bond can be sold in seconds at a known price, buying one is a thirty-year loan you can exit on Tuesday, and lenders accept a far lower rate for it. The issuer's cost of borrowing is set by the ease with which its lenders can leave.

The second is that secondary prices do the economy's allocation work. Continuous trading produces a continuously updated valuation of every listed company, which determines how cheaply each can raise new money, which decides where new capital goes. A firm the market values highly can issue shares on good terms and expand; one it values poorly cannot. That is the price-signal mechanism from Section 2, running at millisecond resolution across thousands of companies at once. How equities and their exchanges work in detail is Section 7.

Common pitfall

“I bought shares, so I gave the company money.” Only in the primary market. Buying AAPL on the secondary market sends your money to whoever sold you the shares — the company was paid once, at issuance, possibly decades ago.

Real world: three IPOs that show the whole range

  • Airbnb, December 2020 — the underpricing extreme. Priced at $68, the stock opened at $146 and closed its first day near $145, up about 113%. Airbnb raised roughly $3.5bn; had it priced at where the stock actually traded, it would have raised something like twice that. That gap is called "money left on the table," and whether it is a failure of underwriting or the price of a stable shareholder base is a genuine argument in the field.
  • Facebook, May 2012 — the overpricing extreme. Priced at $38 with enormous retail demand; Nasdaq's systems failed for hours on opening day; the stock fell below $18 within four months. Institutional buyers had been told of reduced revenue forecasts that retail buyers had not seen. It recovered enormously later — but the IPO itself transferred value from buyers to sellers.
  • Spotify, April 2018 — skipping the ritual. Spotify did a direct listing: no new shares, no underwriters buying the book, no lockup in the traditional form. It raised zero — it did not need money, it needed liquidity for existing holders. Slack and Coinbase later did the same.

Notice what the three have in common: the IPO price is a negotiated price, not a market one. Only the second day onward is the market talking. This is why "the IPO popped 100%" is a statement about the bankers' pricing, not about the company.

Make it click

Primary and secondary markets answer one question: when you buy a share, does the company get your money?

Once, and only once. A security is sold by the issuer in the primary market, and that is the only time the company receives cash. Every trade afterwards is in the secondary market, between investors, and the company gets nothing. Apple can trade $10bn in a day without a cent reaching Apple.

This matters because the two markets set prices by completely different processes.

Airbnb's IPO price, December 2020: $68. Negotiated between the company and its bankers, based on demand they canvassed.

Airbnb's price at the close of its first trading day: about $145. Set by open bidding among everyone who wanted in.

Same company, same week, more than double the price. The only thing that changed is whether the price was negotiated or discovered.

So "the IPO popped 113%" is a statement about the bankers' pricing, not about the business — and that gap, roughly $3.5bn here, was value that went to allocated investors rather than to the company.

Underwriting is the banks' job of valuing, marketing and buying the shares to resell, and the gross spread is their fee, typically around 7%. A direct listing skips it: existing shares simply start trading, raising no new money — useful when a company needs liquidity for its shareholders rather than cash for itself. And the secondary market matters to issuers even though they earn nothing from it, because nobody buys a thirty-year bond at issue without knowing they can sell it on Tuesday.

Market microstructure: inside the order book

Now zoom all the way in, to the data structure sitting at the centre of every modern market: the order book. There is no trading floor and no negotiation. There are two sorted lists.

One side holds the bids: every outstanding offer to buy, ordered from the highest price down, so the top of the list is the most anyone is currently willing to pay. The other holds the asks: every outstanding offer to sell, ordered from the lowest price up, so the top is the least anyone will currently accept. They are two priority queues pointed at each other.

Two numbers describe the state of that book and they are the two numbers that determine what trading costs you. The bid–ask spread is the gap between the best bid and the best ask — buy at the ask and sell immediately at the bid and you lose exactly that gap, which makes it the price of transacting right now. The depth is how much quantity is resting at each price level, which determines how far the price moves when a large order arrives. A tight spread with thin depth is cheap for small trades and expensive for big ones.

You interact with that book through two order types, and the choice between them is a choice about which risk you would rather carry.

A market order says: fill me now, at whatever prices are available. It walks down the opposite side of the book consuming resting orders, starting with the best price and continuing into worse ones until it is filled. You are guaranteed to trade; you are not guaranteed the price, and if the book is thin the average price you get can be materially worse than the one you saw.

A limit order says: fill me only at this price or better. If someone is already offering that price, you trade immediately. If not, your order joins the book and waits, becoming part of the depth that somebody else's market order will consume. You are guaranteed the price; you are not guaranteed to trade at all, and while you wait the market can move away from you.

Matching follows price-time priority: the best price is served first, and among orders at the same price the one that arrived earliest fills first. It is a stable sort with two keys, simple enough to implement in an afternoon, and the fact that it runs at nanosecond scale on hardware costing millions is the entire reason the speed race described below exists.

Worked example: walking the book

Using Figure 6.6's book, send a market buy for 1,000 shares. You lift 200 @ $100.05, then 400 @ $100.10, then 300 @ $100.15, then 100 @ $100.20. Average fill = (200×100.05 + 400×100.10 + 300×100.15 + 100×100.20) ÷ 1,000 = $100,115 ÷ 1,000 = $100.115 — 6.5¢ per share worse than the best ask, a $65 cost known as slippage. Your own order moved the market: that's price impact, and it's why large investors slice big orders into thousands of small ones.

Who keeps those queues populated? If everyone only traded when they happened to want to, the book would be nearly empty most of the time and anyone in a hurry would get a terrible price. Market makers exist to prevent that. A market maker posts a bid and an ask simultaneously and continuously — offering to buy at $99.95 and sell at $100.05 all day — so that anybody arriving with an order finds someone on the other side.

Their revenue is the spread: buy at the bid, sell at the ask, repeat thousands of times. Their risk is inventory. Between buying and selling they own the stock, and if the price moves against them in that interval the loss can exceed many spreads. That is why spreads widen when markets are volatile or news is imminent — the compensation has to rise with the risk of being caught holding something that is repricing.

Most market making is now done by HFT firms whose advantage is speed: servers co-located in the exchange's own data centre, microwave links between Chicago and New Jersey that beat fibre by milliseconds, market data parsed in hardware. Speed matters because a quote is a standing offer, and the market maker who updates last is the one who gets traded against at a stale price.

The verdict on all this is genuinely mixed and worth holding as two facts rather than one opinion. Spreads on liquid US stocks fell from around 12 cents in the 1990s to roughly a cent today, and that saving is collected by every investor on every trade. At the same time, a large part of the spending on speed is spent winning a race against other market makers rather than producing anything a saver benefits from, and the resulting system has failure modes of its own. Section 17 returns to this, including the 2010 Flash Crash.

Key idea

The spread is the price of immediacy. Market orders pay it; limit orders earn it (in exchange for execution risk — the market may run away without filling you). Every execution strategy in existence is a tradeoff along this line.

Order book simulator

Send orders into a live book. Try the default (market buy, 600 shares) and check the average fill — then send a 2,000-share market order and watch it walk the book.

Last price$100.00
Bid–ask spread$0.10
Avg fill price—
Price impact—

Book seeded: 5 bid levels, 5 ask levels around $100. Submit an order to begin.

Three scenarios are worth running deliberately, because each teaches something different about what an order actually does.

Start with the default market buy of 600 shares. It fills 200 at $100.05 and the remaining 400 at $100.10, for an average of $100.0833. The price you saw quoted was $100.05, so a third of a cent per share has quietly disappeared — that gap between the quoted price and the average price you achieved is called slippage, and it is a cost nobody invoices you for.

Now send a limit buy of 500 at $100.05. Two hundred shares are available at that price and fill immediately; the other 300 have nowhere to go, so they rest in the book as the new best bid. Look at what that does to the spread: it narrows to $0.05, because your order is now the best price anyone can sell to. You have stopped consuming liquidity and started providing it, and the exchange will typically pay you a small rebate for doing so.

Finally, send repeated 2,000-share market buys and watch the ask side disappear level by level while the last traded price climbs. Nothing has changed about the company; the price moved because your demand exhausted the supply resting at each level. That is price impact, and it is why a fund moving $50 million cannot simply press Buy. Execution algorithms exist entirely to spread an order across time and venues so that this does not happen.

Worked example: what the spread really costs, retail and institutional

Trading costs feel invisible because nobody sends an invoice. Price them explicitly and behaviour changes.

Case 1 — a retail investor in a liquid stock. You buy 100 shares of a $150 stock quoted $149.99 / $150.01. The half-spread is $0.01, so a round trip costs about $2 on $15,000 — 1.3 basis points. Genuinely negligible. Trade it 200 times a year and it is 2.7% — not negligible at all. Cost per trade is small; cost per strategy depends on turnover.

Case 2 — the same investor in a thin small cap. A $5 stock quoted $4.90 / $5.10 has a 4% spread. Buying and selling 100 shares costs $20 on $500 exposure. The stock must rise 4% before you break even. Most of the "unlucky" returns in illiquid names are just this.

Case 3 — a fund buying $50 million. Suppose the stock trades $100 with a 4bp spread and 2 million shares a day of volume. Your 500,000 shares are 25% of a day's volume, so you cannot simply lift the offer — you would walk the book several cents up. Realistic total cost:

Component Cost (bp) Dollars
Half spread paid on each child order 2 $10,000
Market impact (your own buying moves the price) 35 $175,000
Commission 1 $5,000
Implementation shortfall 38 $190,000

A strategy that backtests at +50bp per trade is a +12bp strategy in production, and a losing one after fees. This gap between paper and live returns is where most quant strategies die — and modelling it is an entire well-paid specialty called transaction cost analysis. If you want a portfolio project that gets attention, build one.

Make it click

Market microstructure answers one question: when you place a trade, what price do you actually get?

Not the price on the screen — that is the best price for a small amount. Orders sit stacked at rising prices and a large one eats through them upward, so your average fill is worse than the quote. That gap is slippage, and it grows with your size relative to what is resting.

It matters because a strategy can be profitable on paper and lossmaking in practice on this alone.

Buy 200 shares with 200 offered at $100.05 → you pay $100.05. The quoted price was the real price.

Buy 1,000 shares from the same book → you take $100.05, then $100.10, then $100.15, then $100.20. Average $100.115, or $65 of cost that didn't exist at 200 shares.

Same stock, same second, same quoted price, and one trade cost nothing extra while the other paid up. The only thing that changed is size relative to what was resting.

So the number that matters is your order as a share of daily volume. A fund buying 25% of a day's volume can expect around 35 basis points of impact — enough to turn a strategy that backtests at +50bp per trade into roughly +12bp live, and a loser after fees.

A market order takes whatever is there and pays the spread. A limit order names a price and waits, earning the spread but risking no fill. Market makers are the firms posting both sides all day to collect that spread. And the spread itself is simply the price of trading right now instead of waiting.

A trade, end to end

You tap Buy on your phone and a confirmation appears almost instantly. What actually happened between those two moments involves several institutions you have never heard of, operating on three quite different timescales, and the reason the process is elaborate is that at each stage somebody has to be protected from somebody else not paying.

Milliseconds — routing and execution. Your broker's systems check the order is valid and that you have the money, then decide where to send it. It might go to a public exchange, but most retail orders go instead to a wholesale market maker who has paid your broker for the right to receive them, an arrangement called payment for order flow. The venue's matching engine crosses your order against the resting book according to the priority rules above, and the confirmation reaches your phone before your thumb has left the screen. From this instant the economics are yours: if the price moves in the next second, the gain or loss is on your account, even though nothing has legally been transferred yet.

Hours — clearing. Overnight, a clearing house — for US equities, the NSCC — takes over the trade. It performs novation, which means it legally replaces your single trade with two: you against the clearing house, and the clearing house against the seller. Neither side ever has to trust or even identify the other, because both now face the same well-capitalised institution. That is the entire reason you can buy from an anonymous stranger without checking whether they are good for it.

The clearing house also performs netting. A broker that bought 5 million shares of a stock and sold 4.9 million during the day does not settle ten million share movements; it settles the net 100,000. Across the whole market this routinely removes around 98% of the obligations that would otherwise have to move, which reduces both the operational load and the amount of money exposed at any moment. It is the same compression any data engineer would apply to a log of offsetting transactions, with the difference that here it is also the main defence against a settlement failure cascading.

One day — settlement and custody. On T+1, meaning the business day after the trade — the US standard since May 2024 — settlement occurs: cash and securities actually change hands at the Depository Trust Company, the central depository where nearly all US securities exist as electronic entries rather than certificates. Your broker's custodian records you as the beneficial owner, which in practice means the shares are held in the broker's name on your behalf.

The point of the entire apparatus is to compress counterparty risk — the risk that the party on the other side simply fails to deliver — into as short a window as possible. Every hour between agreeing a trade and completing it is an hour during which somebody can go bankrupt while owing you something, which is exactly what happened at scale in 2008. The shortening of that window from five days in the 1990s to one day now, and the arguments about going to same-day settlement, are all about the same trade-off: less time exposed, against less time to find the money and the securities.

Real world: January 2021

When meme-stock volumes exploded, the clearing house demanded billions more in collateral (margin) from brokers to cover the two-day settlement gap that then existed. Several brokers restricted buying in GME because they literally couldn't post the deposit fast enough. The invisible plumbing became front-page news — and the episode accelerated the US move from T+2 to T+1.

Deep dive: where your “free” retail order really goes

Most US retail brokers charge zero commission because of payment for order flow (PFOF): wholesale market makers like Citadel Securities pay the broker a fraction of a cent per share to execute your order internally rather than send it to an exchange. Why pay for it? Retail orders are “uninformed” in the statistical sense — a random retail buy predicts nothing about the next price move, so making markets against retail is safer than quoting on an exchange where sharper counterparties lurk. Wholesalers typically fill retail slightly inside the public quote (price improvement of a fraction of a cent), and brokers must report execution quality. Critics argue the improvement is measured against a quote the wholesalers themselves help set, and that the conflict — your broker is paid by your counterparty — deserves more scrutiny; the EU banned PFOF outright from 2026. Either way, “free” means the spread, not the commission, is where the money moves.

What flows through this machinery is the subject of the next four sections: equities, bonds, derivatives, and currencies, commodities & alternatives. Each is a different kind of claim on future money, and each one travels the same route you have just traced — issued in a primary market, priced in an order book, guaranteed by a clearing house, and recorded at a depository.

Worked example: why settlement dates are not paperwork

You sell $20,000 of stock on Monday to pay a bill on Tuesday. Here is what the calendar actually allows:

When What is true
Monday, 10:31 a.m. (T) Trade executed. You no longer own the shares. You do not yet own the cash.
Monday night NSCC novates and nets your trade against everyone else's. Roughly 98% of obligations cancel out.
Tuesday (T+1) Settlement. Shares move at DTC, cash lands. Now it is legally yours.
Tuesday or Wednesday ACH withdrawal to your bank clears. Many brokers hold it a further day or two.

Two practical consequences. For you: "I have the money" is false for one to three days, and buying with unsettled proceeds in a cash account can trigger a good-faith violation. For the system: every day between trade and settlement is a day someone can fail, which is why the clearing house demands collateral — and why the US moved from T+2 to T+1 in May 2024, cutting NSCC's required clearing fund by roughly 30%.

That change created a new seam, which is exactly the kind of thing an analyst gets paid to notice: US equities now settle in one day while standard spot FX still settles in two. A European fund buying US shares must fund dollars before its currency trade settles — so it either pre-funds, borrows overnight, or trades FX in a shorter, more expensive window. A plumbing change in one market became a daily funding cost in another.

Make it click

Settlement answers one question: you sold on Monday — when is the money actually yours?

Not Monday. The trade executes in milliseconds and you stop owning the shares immediately, but cash and shares only change hands the next business day. That gap is settlement, currently one day in US equities. Between execution and settlement you have neither the shares nor the money, and someone could still fail to deliver.

The reason anyone cares is that the gap is where obligations pile up and someone has to post collateral against them.

Normal volumes: the clearing house nets everyone's trades against each other, cancelling roughly 98% of obligations. Collateral required from a broker is modest.

January 2021, meme-stock volumes: same one-day gap, but position sizes exploded. Collateral demands ran to billions, and several brokers restricted buying because they could not post it in time.

Same settlement system, opposite outcome for customers. The only thing that changed is how large and one-sided the unsettled positions got.

So if you are timing a payment against a sale, count business days and add the broker's own transfer delay — "I have the money" is false for one to three days, and spending unsettled proceeds can breach your account terms.

Clearing is the step in between: the clearing house inserts itself as the counterparty to both sides, so neither has to trust the other. Netting is the cancelling-out that shrinks obligations by 98%. And custody is who holds the record that the shares are yours — which is the only reason a broker failing does not mean your shares vanish.

Check your understanding

1. A bank funds 30-year mortgages using deposits customers can withdraw at any time. This is called…

Borrowing short (deposits) to lend long (mortgages) is maturity transformation — a core service of banks, and the reason bank runs are possible when everyone demands their short-term money at once.

2. A hedge fund analyst and an investment-bank M&A analyst are, respectively…

Hedge funds manage money (buy side); investment banks sell services — deals, underwriting, execution — to the money (sell side).

3. The book shows asks of 200 shares at $100.05 and 400 at $100.10. A market buy for 600 shares fills at an average of…

(200 × 100.05 + 400 × 100.10) ÷ 600 = 60,050 ÷ 600 = $100.0833. It's a size-weighted average, not a simple midpoint — the extra 3.3¢ over the best ask is slippage.

4. You buy 100 shares of AAPL through your broker today. Who receives your money?

Secondary-market trades move money between investors. Apple was paid once — in the primary market, when the shares were originally issued.

5. What does a clearing house (CCP) fundamentally do?

Through novation the CCP guarantees both legs of every trade, and through netting it shrinks what actually has to move at settlement. Central custody is the depository's job (the DTC), not the clearing house's.

Key takeaways

  • The financial system routes money from savers to users of capital via two channels: direct finance (markets) and indirect finance (intermediaries such as banks and funds).
  • Intermediaries exist to solve information asymmetry, perform maturity transformation, and provide diversification — services no individual saver can replicate alone.
  • Buy side manages money and earns fees on assets; sell side sells execution, research, and new issues, and earns on activity. Every finance job sits on one side or the other.
  • Regulators map to market failures: the SEC forces disclosure, the Fed and FDIC contain systemic risk and bank runs, FINRA polices brokers, the CFTC covers derivatives.
  • Issuers get paid only in the primary market (IPOs, bond issues, via underwriters); the secondary market prices those claims continuously and gives them liquidity.
  • The order book is two price-time priority queues; the bid–ask spread is the price of immediacy, and big market orders walk the book, paying slippage.
  • A trade executes in milliseconds but settles at T+1: clearing houses net trades and guarantee both sides, then cash and securities swap at the depository, with custodians keeping the records.

Part II · Financial Markets & Instruments

7. Equities: The Stock Market

Stocks are the asset class most people mean when they say "the market," and they're where most long-run wealth in public markets has been created — and occasionally vaporized. By the end of this section you'll know exactly what a share is, where equity returns actually come from, how indices are built, and how to read a stock quote like an analyst instead of a tourist.

What a share actually is

A share of stock is a fractional ownership claim on a corporation. Not a claim on any particular asset — you cannot walk into a factory and demand your share of a lathe — but a proportional claim on the whole thing: every factory, every patent, every brand, and every dollar of profit the business earns from now until it ceases to exist. If a company has issued 1 billion shares and you hold 100 of them, you own 0.00001% of all of that.

Equity is the formal word for that ownership interest, and the definition is worth stating precisely because it explains everything that follows: equity is what remains of a company's assets after every debt has been paid. It is a subtraction, not a fixed quantity. That single fact is why equity returns are large and why they are dangerous.

Two legal features turn that claim into the specific bargain investors are actually taking.

The first is that shareholders are the residual claimants. There is a fixed order in which a company's cash is distributed: employees' wages, suppliers' invoices, taxes, interest to lenders, and repayment of principal all come before shareholders receive anything. Shareholders are last in that queue and are entitled to whatever is left, which may be an enormous amount or may be nothing at all. Being last is why equity is riskier than debt — and it is also why equity captures the upside, because once everyone ahead of you has been paid their fixed amounts, every additional dollar of profit belongs entirely to the residual claimant.

The second is limited liability, which caps your loss at what you paid. If the company collapses owing billions, your shares go to zero and the creditors cannot pursue your house or your salary. This is a deliberate legal invention rather than a natural fact, and it is what made public stock markets possible: without it, buying a small stake in a company you do not control would expose you to unlimited liability for decisions you had no part in, and nobody sensible would do it. The combination — losses floored at your investment, gains uncapped — is the asymmetry that defines the asset class.

Why would a company sell pieces of itself rather than keep them? Because growth requires money before it produces money, and equity is the only funding that never has to be repaid.

Compare the two ways of raising it. Borrowing creates a fixed obligation: the interest is due whether or not the year went well, and missing it can put the company into bankruptcy regardless of how good the underlying business is. Selling equity creates no obligation at all. If the year is bad, shareholders simply receive nothing and the company continues. The founder with a good idea and no capital who sells 30% to investors ends up owning 70% of a company that exists, rather than 100% of one that never got built.

The price of that flexibility is permanent and proportional. Equity investors have accepted the risk of the bad years, so they are entitled to a share of every good year, forever — not a fixed sum, but a percentage. A lender who has been repaid is gone; a shareholder never is. That is the trade every company makes when it chooses one form of financing over the other, and it is the subject of Section 14.

Key idea: the order in which money is paid out

The single structure that explains most of what happens to a company's investors is the order in which claims are paid. Secured lenders are paid first, from the specific assets pledged to them. Then other lenders, in a contractual ranking of their own. Then preferred shareholders, who hold a hybrid instrument with a fixed entitlement. Ordinary shareholders are paid last, out of whatever survives. This ordering is fixed in advance by contract and law, and it holds in good years and bad.

In a normal year the ordering is invisible, because there is enough to pay everybody and the interesting question is how much profit is left over. In a failure it becomes the only thing that matters, and it is brutally mechanical: each level is paid in full before the next receives a cent, so a shortfall does not spread proportionally across investors. It stops at whichever level the money runs out, and everyone below that line receives nothing. A bondholder recovering 60 cents and a shareholder recovering zero is the normal outcome, not an unlucky one.

Keep this ordering in mind through the rest of Part II, because it is what distinguishes the instruments from each other. A bond, a preferred share and an ordinary share can all be claims on the identical business, generating identical cash. What separates them is position in this queue — and position in the queue determines both how safe the instrument is and how much of the upside it can capture.

Real world: "residual claimant" is not a metaphor

The capital stack is an abstraction right up until a company fails, at which point it is a payout table.

Case Bondholders got Shareholders got
Lehman Brothers, 2008 Roughly 20–35 cents on the dollar, after years of litigation Zero
General Motors, 2009 Unsecured bondholders received equity in the new GM Old GM shares cancelled — zero
Enron, 2001 Partial recovery through the estate Zero — including employees whose 401(k)s held company stock
Hertz, 2020–21 Paid in full, with interest Roughly $8 per share — a genuine rarity

Hertz is the exception that proves the rule. It filed for bankruptcy in 2020, retail investors piled into the "worthless" stock, and then used-car prices exploded — the fleet turned out to be worth far more than anyone had assumed, so there was money left after every creditor was paid. Equity holders got a real recovery. In the overwhelming majority of bankruptcies there is nothing left, which is exactly what "last in line" means.

The flip side is why anyone accepts that deal: a bondholder's best possible outcome is being repaid in full, while a shareholder's upside is unbounded. Limited liability caps your loss at what you invested; the residual claim leaves your gain uncapped. Every equity investment is that trade.

Market cap, share classes, and dilution

The headline size of a public company is its market capitalization, usually shortened to market cap: the share price multiplied by the number of shares in existence. It is what the market currently says the entire ownership of the business is worth.

This makes the first myth in equity investing worth killing immediately. A $50 stock with 4 billion shares is a $200 billion company. A $500 stock with 20 million shares is a $10 billion company — twenty times smaller, at ten times the price per share. The share price on its own tells you nothing about the size of a business or whether it is expensive, because the number of shares is an arbitrary decision the company made at some point in its history. The company chose how many slices to cut the pizza into; the price per slice reflects that choice as much as it reflects the pizza. Only price multiplied by share count says anything about the whole.

Analysts sort companies by that measure into large-cap (above roughly $10 billion), mid-cap ($2–10 billion), and small-cap (below about $2 billion). The buckets are not arbitrary snobbery; size correlates with three things that change how a stock behaves.

Larger companies are usually more diversified across products and geographies, so a single bad quarter in one division does less damage. They are more liquid, meaning you can buy or sell a meaningful position without moving the price against yourself — which matters enormously to a fund and not at all to someone buying $2,000. And they attract far more analyst coverage, so more people are examining the same public information, which makes genuinely mispriced large-caps rarer than mispriced small ones. That last point is why investors hunting for an edge tend to look down the size scale, and why doing so also exposes them to the first two problems.

Not every share in a company carries the same rights. Companies can create multiple share classes that differ in how many votes each share carries, while carrying identical economic entitlements to profits.

Alphabet is the standard illustration. Its Class A shares, ticker GOOGL, carry one vote each. Class C, ticker GOOG, carry no votes at all. The founders hold Class B shares carrying ten votes each and not traded publicly. The arrangement lets the founders sell most of the economic ownership of the company while retaining voting control of it, and Meta and many other technology firms use the same structure.

What this means in practice is that owning the stock and having any influence over the company are separate things. If a dual-class founder makes an acquisition shareholders dislike, or pays himself extravagantly, or refuses to sell the company at a good price, the ordinary shareholders have no mechanism to object — there is no vote they can win. That is not necessarily bad; insulating management from short-term pressure is a real argument, and some of these companies have performed extremely well. But it should be priced, and when you see "dual-class" the correct translation is that the founders answer to essentially no one.

Your ownership percentage is not fixed either, and this is the quietest way shareholders lose money. When a company issues new shares — to raise cash, to pay employees in stock, or to fund an acquisition — the number of claims on the same business rises, so each existing claim becomes a smaller fraction of it. That is dilution.

Work through the arithmetic. You own 100,000 shares of a firm with 1 million outstanding, so you own 10%. The company issues 250,000 new shares. You still hold exactly 100,000 shares — nothing was taken from you and no transaction appeared on your statement — but there are now 1,250,000 shares, so your stake is 100,000 ÷ 1,250,000, or 8%. Your claim on every future dollar of profit has fallen by a fifth.

Dilution is not automatically bad, and this is where judgement comes in. If the company raised $250 million and used it to build something that adds more than $250 million of value, then a smaller share of a larger business is worth more than a larger share of the old one, and everyone gains. The case that should worry you is the one where nothing is raised at all: stock-based compensation that quietly grows the share count by 2–3% a year transfers ownership from you to employees without any cash arriving and without appearing as an expense in the headline profit figures many companies emphasise. Spotting it in the filings is a skill developed in Section 11 (Financial Statements).

Finally, most companies are not on the stock market at all, and the proportion that are has been shrinking. A public company has shares anyone can buy on an exchange and, in exchange for that access to public money, must file audited financial reports with the SEC on a fixed schedule. A private company has neither the access nor the obligation; its shares change hands in negotiated deals between individual parties.

The number of US public companies has roughly halved since the mid-1990s, from around 8,000 to around 4,000, and two forces did it. Disclosure and governance requirements tightened considerably after the accounting scandals of the early 2000s, which raised the fixed cost of being public and made it uneconomic for smaller firms. At the same time an enormous pool of private equity and venture capital money became available, so a company that needs a billion dollars no longer has to ask the public for it.

The consequence matters if you are investing rather than merely studying. Companies now list later in their lives, at much larger valuations, and frequently after the phase of fastest growth has already happened. The returns from a company going from $50 million to $5 billion increasingly accrue to private investors, and the public gets its ticket at the $5 billion mark. Public equity markets are still where most accessible long-term wealth is built, but they show you a later chapter of the story than they did thirty years ago.

Worked example: dilution you can actually measure

Dilution is the quietest way a shareholder loses money, because the share price need never fall for it to happen. Take a company with 100 million shares and $100 million of net income — EPS is exactly $1.00.

Year Shares issued to staff Shares repurchased Share count EPS on $100M
Start — — 100.0M $1.000
Year 1 3.0M 2.0M 101.0M $0.990
Year 3 3.0M 2.0M 103.0M $0.971
Year 5 3.0M 2.0M 105.0M $0.952

Profits never fell, yet earnings per share dropped 4.8% over five years. Your slice of the company shrank from 1.000% to 0.952% without you selling anything. This is why analysts watch the net change in diluted share count, not the buyback headline: a company announcing "$2 billion of repurchases" while issuing $2.2 billion of stock compensation is not returning capital, it is running a payroll through the equity account.

Check it yourself in thirty seconds on any filing: take diluted weighted average shares from the income statement this year and five years ago. If the count is flat or falling while revenue grows, management is being disciplined. If it climbs 3–5% a year, you are funding compensation.
