Real world: when one share is not one vote

Company Structure Effect
Meta Class B carries 10 votes Mark Zuckerberg holds roughly 13% of the economics and about 61% of the votes — an unremovable majority.
Alphabet Class A (1 vote), B (10 votes), C (GOOG, 0 votes) Founders keep control while issuing stock freely. Note that C shares trade at a persistent small discount to A — that gap is the market pricing a vote.
Snap Public shares carry zero votes The 2017 IPO was the first ever of entirely non-voting stock. S&P responded by barring new multi-class companies from its indices.
Berkshire Hathaway Class A ≈ $700k/share, B = 1/1500th Not about control so much as about never splitting the A shares — deliberately deterring short-term traders.

Practical takeaway: when you buy a share, check what you are buying. The ticker on the screen is often the class with the least power, and "activist investors will fix this company" is simply false when the founder controls a voting majority.

Where returns come from: price + dividends = total return

Owning a stock pays you in exactly two ways, and separating them is the first step to measuring anything correctly. The price can rise, which is price appreciation and is only realised when you sell. And the company can send you cash out of its profits, which is a dividend and arrives whether you sell or not, usually quarterly.

Adding the two gives total return, and this is the only return that describes what actually happened to your money. Stated in words, the rule is: take the price at the end minus the price at the start, add every dividend you received along the way, and divide the whole thing by the price you originally paid. The two halves of that numerator are the two ways of being paid, expressed as a percentage of what you put in:

Total return = P1 − P0 + DP0 = price return + dividend yield
P0 = starting price · P1 = ending price · D = dividends received over the period

Dividends look inconsequential next to price moves. A dividend yield of 2–3% is a rounding error beside a stock that moved 20% in a quarter, and most people mentally discard it. Over decades that is a large mistake, and the reason is that reinvested dividends do not add to your return — they multiply it.

Follow the loop. A dividend arrives as cash; you use it to buy more shares of the same company; those additional shares pay dividends of their own next quarter, which buy still more shares. Your wealth is now growing along two independent dimensions at once: the price per share is rising at the price return, and the number of shares you hold is rising at roughly the dividend yield. Since your wealth is price multiplied by share count, and both factors are compounding, the combined growth rate is approximately (1 + g)(1 + d) − 1 rather than g + d — the compounding machine from Section 1 running on two engines.

The practical consequence is that the gap between price return and total return widens with time rather than staying constant, which is why it looks negligible on a one-year chart and enormous on a thirty-year one.

Worked example

$10,000 in a stock returning 5% in price with a 3% yield, dividends reinvested, for 30 years. The compound rate is 1.05 × 1.03 = 1.0815, i.e. 8.15% per year. After 30 years: $10,000 × 1.081530 ≈ $104,900. Price alone: $10,000 × 1.0530 ≈ $43,219. The "small" dividend, reinvested, ends up responsible for more than half of the final wealth — and your share count has grown 1.0330 ≈ 2.43× along the way.

Total return machine

Set a price return and a dividend yield, then flip reinvestment on and off — watch what decades of reinvested dividends do to the gap.

Total return ends at—
Price-only ends at—
Dividends added—
Share count growth—

What has all that risk actually paid? Over the past century, US stocks have delivered roughly 7% a year after inflation. The word "after" is doing real work: nominal returns look larger, but a return you cannot spend more with is not a return, so real is the number to reason with.

The portion of that attributable to bearing equity risk specifically is the equity risk premium: what stocks earned above safe government debt, historically 4 to 6 percentage points a year. This is the compensation for standing at the back of the payment queue described earlier. It is not a law of nature and it is not guaranteed for any given decade; it is what investors have collectively demanded to accept residual claims, measured after the fact.

Seven percent real compounds to something hard to intuit. Using the Rule of 72 from Section 1, purchasing power doubles roughly every ten years, so a working lifetime contains four or five doublings. No other broadly accessible asset class has come close over long horizons, which is the entire reason equities occupy so much of this book.

The catch is not the average, it is the path. Equity volatility runs around 15–20% a year, meaning a typical year lands well away from the average in either direction, and the market experiences a drawdown — a fall from a previous peak — of 30% to 50% or more roughly once a decade. The record is not gentle: about −86% peak to trough in 1929–32, around −50% in 1973–74, again in 2000–02, and again in 2008–09, and −34% in five weeks in March 2020.

The critical point is that the 7% average is earned through those episodes and not around them. There is no version of the historical record in which an investor collected the long-run return while avoiding the crashes, because the crashes are when the shares change hands cheaply and the subsequent recovery is a large part of where the return comes from.

This is why time horizon is the most important variable in equity investing, more important than which stocks you pick. Over a single year, equities have been close to a coin flip — positive slightly more often than not, with a wide distribution. Over twenty to thirty years, the historical odds of beating cash have been overwhelming, because the averages have time to assert themselves and a drawdown that occurs in year four has twenty-six years to recover. The operational rule that follows is simple and rarely followed: money you will need next year does not belong in stocks, however attractive the long-run number looks.

Common pitfall

Past return is not a promise. The ~7% real figure is a century-long US average that includes surviving two world wars and winning the economic lottery; Japan's market spent three decades underwater after 1989. History tells you what equities can do and what they charge in volatility — it does not guarantee your particular 20 years will match the average.

Real world: the half of returns most charts hide

Nearly every stock chart you see — on a news site, on your broker's app — is a price chart. It silently deletes dividends. Over a century that omission is not a rounding error, it is most of the answer.

US large-cap stocks, 1926–2023 Annualised $1 becomes
Price return only ≈ 6.2% ≈ $360
Total return (dividends reinvested) ≈ 10.3% ≈ $14,900

Forty times more money, from a 4-point-a-year difference. And the effect is not only about very long horizons: from the March 2000 peak to the end of 2012 — the "lost decade" — the S&P 500's price return was roughly negative, while its total return was modestly positive. Investors who reinvested dividends made money over a period universally described as a disaster.

Practical rule for anyone building datasets: check whether your series is price or total return before you compute a single statistic. ^GSPC is price; ^SP500TR is total return. Comparing a stock's price series to a total-return benchmark will make almost any strategy look good, and it is one of the most common errors in amateur backtests.

Indices and index funds: buying the haystack

A stock index is a rule-based basket of stocks whose combined value is used as a measure of "the market." The words "rule-based" matter: an index is defined by a written methodology stating which companies qualify, how much of each to include, and when the list is revised. It is a specification, and different specifications measuring the same market can produce noticeably different numbers. These are the ones you will hear quoted daily:

Index What's in it Weighting Holdings
S&P 500 Largest US companies; the default "US market" Market cap ~500
Nasdaq-100 Largest non-financial Nasdaq listings; tech-heavy Market cap (modified) 100
Dow Jones Industrial Average 30 blue-chip names picked by committee Price (a historical oddity) 30
Russell 2000 US small-caps Market cap ~2,000
MSCI World / ACWI Developed (and, for ACWI, emerging) markets globally Market cap 1,400+

Almost every serious index is cap-weighted, meaning each company's influence is its market capitalisation divided by the total market capitalisation of all members. Stated as arithmetic, that is a weighted average in which the weight on company i is its cap divided by the sum of all caps.

Cap weighting has a property worth appreciating: it is self-maintaining. If a company's price doubles, its cap doubles, and its weight in the index rises automatically — which is exactly what a portfolio holding those shares would experience without doing anything. A fund tracking a cap-weighted index therefore almost never needs to trade to stay aligned, which is why such funds can charge almost nothing. Any other weighting scheme requires continuous rebalancing, and rebalancing costs money.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average is the famous exception. It is price-weighted, which means it behaves like a portfolio holding exactly one share of each member, so a company's influence is proportional to its price per share. We established a page ago that price per share is an arbitrary artefact of how many shares a company chose to issue. So in the Dow, a company can have five times the influence of another purely because it never split its stock. The index survives on a century of brand recognition rather than on any methodological merit, and no professional uses it to measure anything.

You cannot buy an index, because an index is a formula rather than a product. What you can buy is a fund that implements the formula: index funds and ETFs, which hold the index's constituents at the index's weights and charge an annual fee called the expense ratio. A single share of such a fund makes you a part-owner of 500 or 8,000 businesses at once, which is instant diversification of the kind formalised in Section 15 (Portfolio Theory).

The fee difference between index and actively managed funds is the part most people underrate. A broad index ETF can charge 0.03% a year — three dollars annually per ten thousand invested — against roughly 1% for a typical actively managed fund. One percent sounds trivial against equity returns of 7%, but it is not deducted once; it is deducted every year, from a balance that would otherwise have compounded. Over thirty years, giving up one point of a seven-point return costs roughly a quarter of your final wealth, and the manager collects it whether they beat the index or not.

That arithmetic explains the trillions of dollars that have moved into index funds over the past two decades. It also sets up the question Section 17 (Market Efficiency) answers: an active manager does not merely need to be good, they need to be good enough to overcome that fee every year, against thousands of competitors trying to do the same thing with the same public information.

Worked example: weight a mini-index three ways

Take five companies. Same five stocks, three weighting rules, three completely different portfolios:

Company Price Shares Market cap Cap weight Equal weight Price weight
MegaTech $300 10M $3,000M 45.5% 20% 42.9%
BigBank $50 40M $2,000M 30.3% 20% 7.1%
MidCo $200 5M $1,000M 15.2% 20% 28.6%
SmallCo $100 5M $500M 7.6% 20% 14.3%
TinyCo $50 2M $100M 1.5% 20% 7.1%

Look at BigBank: 30% of the index by economic size, 7% by price weight. A price-weighted index thinks a company is important because of an arbitrary decision about how many pieces to cut its equity into. That is the Dow, and it is why no serious analyst uses it.

Why this matters right now. The S&P 500 is cap-weighted, and by 2024 its ten largest companies were roughly 35% of the entire index — the highest concentration in decades. When you buy "the market," you are buying a portfolio with about a third of its money in ten correlated technology-adjacent names. Compare SPY (cap-weighted) with RSP (equal-weighted) over 2023–24 and you can measure the effect directly: the gap between them is the concentration effect, stated in return terms.

Valuation shorthand: EPS, P/E, and earnings yield

Is a stock cheap or expensive? The question cannot be answered by the price, for the reason established earlier — price per share is arbitrary. It can only be answered by comparing the price to what you receive for it.

The standard comparison uses profit. Start with EPS, earnings per share, which is the company's net profit divided by the number of shares — the slice of annual profit attributable to each share you own. Then divide the price of the share by that figure. In words: the P/E ratio tells you how many dollars you are paying today for each dollar of annual profit the business currently produces. A P/E of 20 means twenty dollars per dollar of yearly earnings, which is also to say that at current profits it would take twenty years of earnings to equal the purchase price:

P/E = price per shareEPS  ·  earnings yield = EPSprice = 1P/E
A stock at $184.32 with EPS of $7.49 trades at P/E ≈ 24.6, an earnings yield of ≈ 4.1%

Turn that ratio upside down and it becomes far easier to compare against everything else. The earnings yield is simply 1 divided by the P/E, and it states the same fact as a percentage return: a P/E of 25 is an earnings yield of 4%, meaning each dollar you invest is currently backed by four cents of annual profit.

Expressing it that way puts equities into the same units as bonds, which is what makes cross-asset reasoning possible. If a Treasury bond pays 4.5% guaranteed and a stock offers an earnings yield of 4.1%, you can ask a precise question: is 4.1% of corporate profit that may grow, and may also fall, worth less or more than 4.5% of fixed coupons that will not do either? There is no formula that answers it, because the answer depends on how much growth you expect and how much uncertainty you will tolerate. But that comparison — a risky growing yield against a safe fixed one — is genuinely half of what investment analysis consists of.

The most common error with P/E is treating it as a verdict. A high P/E does not mean overpriced and a low one does not mean bargain. A P/E is a statement about the future, expressed as a price.

Paying 45 times current earnings only makes sense if you believe those earnings will grow substantially, because at today's profit level the price is indefensible; the buyer is not paying for this year's earnings but for the much larger earnings they expect in 2032. Paying 11 times says the opposite: the buyer expects profits to stagnate or decline, and is unwilling to pay for growth that they do not think is coming. Both numbers are forecasts wearing the disguise of a measurement.

This is the origin of the growth versus value distinction that organises much of the investment industry. Growth investors pay up for companies whose earnings they expect to expand rapidly. Value investors insist on a low multiple, on the view that the market systematically overpays for excitement. Neither approach is right in general, and framing it as a contest misses the point. The only question that matters for any individual stock is whether the future already embedded in its price is more or less optimistic than the future you actually expect.

P/E explorer

Drag price and earnings for a fast grower and a steady utility — see how the same $1 of profit gets very different price tags.

Zippy P/E—
Zippy earnings yield—
Utility P/E—
Utility earnings yield—

P/E has sharp edges, and three of them will catch you if nobody points them out.

The first is negative earnings. If a company lost money, its P/E is not low, it is undefined — dividing by a negative number produces a negative ratio that means nothing, and screening software that reports it as a small number is lying to you. Many young, fast-growing companies fall in this category, and they must be valued some other way.

The second is cyclical earnings, and it inverts your intuition completely. A steel producer at the peak of a construction boom reports record profits, so its P/E looks strikingly low — right at the moment its earnings are about to collapse. At the bottom of a recession the same company reports minimal profits and its P/E looks absurdly high, which may be precisely when it is cheapest. For cyclical businesses, a low P/E is a late-cycle warning rather than a bargain, which is why analysts often use average earnings across a whole cycle instead of the latest year.

The third is one-off items. A single year's earnings can be inflated by an asset sale or depressed by a legal settlement, and neither tells you anything about what the business normally earns. Sorting out which parts of reported profit are repeatable is a substantial part of the work in Section 11, and the full apparatus of valuation — discounted cash flows, comparable companies, and the adjustments that make them meaningful — is Section 13 (Valuation).

Worked example: four companies, four P/Es, four stories

A P/E in isolation says nothing. Here is the same number carrying four different meanings:

Company type P/E Earnings yield What the market is actually saying
Regulated utility 18 5.6% Earnings are boring and near-certain. Priced like a bond with a small growth kicker.
Enterprise software, 25% growth 45 2.2% Today's earnings are irrelevant; you are buying year 10. Any growth stumble re-rates it violently.
Large bank 9 11.1% Cheap because earnings are leveraged and cyclical, and one credit cycle can erase several years of them.
Homebuilder at a cycle peak 5 20.0% A trap. The E is at a peak that will not repeat. Cyclicals look cheapest right before earnings collapse.

That last row is the single most expensive mistake in beginner value investing, and it has a name: the value trap. For cyclicals — miners, homebuilders, chipmakers, airlines — a low P/E is a warning, and the standard fix is to divide price by average earnings over a full cycle (the Shiller CAPE does exactly this with a 10-year average).

Now use the earnings yield as a cross-asset comparison. If the 10-year Treasury pays 4.5% and the S&P's earnings yield is 4.0% (P/E 25), you are accepting less current yield than a risk-free bond, betting entirely on earnings growth. In 2000 the index's earnings yield fell to about 3% against 6% Treasuries; in 2011 it was 8% against 2% Treasuries. You do not need a model to know which of those was the better entry point.

Corporate actions: dividends, buybacks, splits, and going public

Companies hand cash back to shareholders in two ways, and the second one is less obvious than the first. Dividends you have already met: the company sends you money. A buyback, or share repurchase, is the exact mirror image of dilution — the company spends its cash buying its own shares on the open market and cancels them, so the number of claims on the business falls and every remaining share owns a larger slice.

The arithmetic is worth doing once. A firm earns $1 billion with 500 million shares outstanding, so earnings per share are $2.00. It spends cash buying back 25 million shares and retires them. The business is unchanged and still earns $1 billion, but that profit is now divided among 475 million shares, so EPS becomes $2.11 — a 5.3% increase with nothing whatsoever having happened operationally.

In a frictionless world, dividends and buybacks are equivalent: either way the company's cash leaves and shareholders are better off by the same amount. The differences are practical. Buybacks are more tax-efficient in the US, because a dividend is taxed when received while a buyback raises the share price and is taxed only when you choose to sell. They are also more flexible, and this asymmetry drives real behaviour: cutting a dividend is read as a distress signal and can halve a share price, whereas quietly pausing a buyback is a footnote nobody reports. Given a choice between an obligation that is punishing to reverse and one that is not, management picks the second, which is why buybacks now exceed dividends among large US companies.

A stock split changes nothing real whatsoever, and it is worth being emphatic about that because a great deal of nonsense is written about splits. In a 4-for-1 split, each existing $500 share becomes four $125 shares. The company's market capitalisation is identical, your holding is worth exactly what it was, the P/E is unchanged, and the business is unaffected. The only thing that changed is the unit of account.

Splits happen for presentational and mechanical reasons: a lower price per share is psychologically more approachable to retail buyers, and it makes round lots of 100 shares affordable, which used to matter more than it does now that fractional shares exist. This kills the price myth for the last time: a $500 stock is not more expensive than a $50 stock, and splitting it does not make it cheaper. Markets nevertheless sometimes rise on split announcements, which is a small, well-documented irrationality filed under Section 17 (Behavioral Finance).

How does a company get onto the stock market to begin with? There are three routes, and they differ in who takes the risk and who captures the value.

The classic route is the IPO. Investment banks (Section 6) value the company, market it to institutional investors, set a price, and sell newly created shares to the public, collecting fees of roughly 4–7% of the money raised. IPOs are famously prone to "popping" — closing far above the offer price on the first day, sometimes 50% or more above. That pop is usually described as a success and is closer to the opposite: it is the difference between what investors were willing to pay and what the company actually received, and it is money the company could have raised and did not. Whether that underpricing is an unavoidable cost of getting a deal placed or a structural transfer to the banks' best clients is one of the longest-running arguments in corporate finance.

A direct listing skips the underwriting machinery entirely. No new shares are created and no money is raised; existing shares held by founders, employees and early investors simply become tradable on an exchange, and the opening price is discovered by the market rather than negotiated in advance. Spotify did this in 2018 and Coinbase in 2021.

The trade-off is straightforward. A direct listing avoids most of the fees and all of the deliberate underpricing, so nothing is left on the table. But it raises no capital, which only works for a company that does not need any, and it forgoes the banks' role in lining up committed institutional buyers, which can make the first days of trading considerably more volatile.

A SPAC, or special purpose acquisition company, inverts the usual order. Sponsors list an empty shell company containing nothing but cash raised from investors, and then go looking for a private business to merge with. The private company becomes publicly traded by combining with the shell, without ever running an IPO — which is why it is described as going public through the back door.

The mechanism boomed in 2020 and 2021 because a merger was subject to lighter disclosure requirements than an IPO, particularly around forward projections, and because it was faster. The results for the people who supplied the money were poor: the average investor holding shares through a completed SPAC merger lost heavily, while sponsors typically received around 20% of the shell's equity for a nominal sum regardless of outcome. It is a useful case to keep in mind, because the pattern generalises. When a new structure appears that is faster and less disclosed than the established one, the first question worth asking is who the structure was designed by and what they receive whether or not it works.

Worked example: $50 million back to shareholders, two ways

A company earns $100M, has 100M shares (EPS $1.00) trading at $20 (P/E 20), and decides to return $50M. Same cash, two mechanisms:

Dividend Buyback
Mechanism $0.50 per share paid in cash 2.5M shares bought at $20 and cancelled
Shares after 100.0M 97.5M
EPS after $1.000 $1.026
Your position (100 shares) 100 shares + $50 cash 100 shares, now a bigger slice
Tax (US taxable account) Owed this year on $50 Deferred until you sell

Economically these are near-identical; the differences are tax timing and optionality. The buyback lets each shareholder choose whether to take cash (by selling) or increase ownership (by doing nothing) — which is why buybacks overtook dividends as the dominant US payout method after the SEC provided a safe harbour in 1982.

The catch. A buyback creates value only if the shares are bought below intrinsic value. Buy back at $20 what is worth $30 and continuing holders gain; buy back at $30 what is worth $20 and you have transferred wealth from stayers to sellers. Airlines spent roughly $45 billion on repurchases in the decade to 2019 and then requested government support in 2020. Apple, by contrast, has retired well over a third of its shares since 2012 — anyone who simply held has watched their ownership percentage rise every single year.

Reading a stock screen like an analyst

Open any quote page and you are confronted with a wall of numbers with no explanation. Here is what each one is.

OHLC is the open, high, low and close: the first price of the session, the highest and lowest reached during it, and the last. Four numbers summarise a day of continuous trading, and they are the atomic unit of financial price data — every chart you have ever seen and every model in Section 18 is built from sequences of them.

Volume is how many shares changed hands. It is the measure of how much conviction sits behind a price move: a 5% rise on triple the normal volume means many participants revalued the company, while the same 5% on a trickle may be one buyer moving a thin book, and is far more likely to reverse. The 52-week range gives you the highest and lowest price of the past year, which locates today's price in its recent context in a single glance.

Beta measures how much the stock tends to move when the whole market moves. A beta of 1.2 means that historically, when the market rose or fell 1%, this stock moved about 1.2% in the same direction. It is not a vague characterisation — it is literally the slope coefficient you get from regressing the stock's returns on the market's returns, three lines of Python that you will write in Section 15. What it does not measure is risk specific to the company itself, which by construction does not correlate with the market and therefore does not appear in the slope.

Float is the number of shares actually available to trade, after removing insiders' locked-up stakes, strategic holdings and anything else that is not going to be sold. It matters because price is set by the shares that can change hands, not by the shares that exist. A company with 900 million shares outstanding but only 40 million floating has a small effective supply, so a modest amount of buying pressure has to be satisfied out of a thin pool — which is the mechanical explanation behind the violent price moves in the meme stocks of 2021.

Your edge

Every field on that screen is a column in a dataset. OHLCV time series are freely downloadable, beta is a linear regression, cap weighting is a normalized vector, and total return is a cumulative product. When we hit Section 18 (Quant Finance), you'll compute all of this from raw data — most finance professionals can read the screen; far fewer can rebuild it.

Deep dive: why the share count on a screen can lie to you

"Shares outstanding" comes in flavors. Basic shares count what exists today; diluted shares add everything that could become shares — employee options, restricted stock units, convertible bonds. A company with 100M basic shares and 12M in-the-money options is really a 112M-share company for valuation purposes, and careful analysts always divide by the diluted count. The gap between basic and diluted EPS on an income statement (Section 11) is a quick read on how much of the company is being quietly handed to employees each year.

Float can diverge wildly from shares outstanding. A newly listed company might have 90% of its shares locked up by insiders for six months post-IPO; when the lockup expires, supply floods the market. Checking the float and the lockup calendar is standard diligence before touching a recent IPO.

Worked example: one company, three different EPS numbers

A stock trades at $60. Its investor deck leads with "P/E of 24." Its 10-K implies 50. Both are true, and the gap is where analysis lives.

Measure EPS P/E at $60 What it includes
GAAP, trailing twelve months $1.20 50.0 Everything, audited: stock compensation, restructuring, impairments.
Adjusted / "non-GAAP", ttm $2.10 28.6 Management's number, excluding items it deems non-recurring.
Forward (analyst consensus, next 12m) $2.50 24.0 A forecast — of an adjusted number — by people the company talks to.

The largest single adjustment is almost always stock-based compensation, and excluding it is a real choice with a real defence ("no cash left the building") and a real rebuttal ("it diluted your ownership, which is the same thing"). Note that the exclusion and the dilution are two views of the identical event — see the dilution example above.

Three habits worth forming permanently. One: whenever someone quotes a P/E, ask "on which E?" — GAAP, adjusted, forward, or average-through-cycle. Two: pull the reconciliation table that every US filer must publish between GAAP and non-GAAP, and read what is being excluded; "non-recurring" charges that recur every year are a red flag. Three: when you build a screener, store all three fields. Half of the apparent alpha in naive value screens is really a definition mismatch between data vendors.

Check your understanding

1. Stock A trades at $500 with 20 million shares outstanding; Stock B trades at $50 with 4 billion shares. Which company is bigger?

Size is market cap = price × shares. B: $50 × 4B = $200B. A: $500 × 20M = $10B. Price per share alone tells you nothing — it depends on an arbitrary share count.

2. You invest $10,000 at a 5% annual price return with a 3% dividend yield, reinvesting dividends, for 30 years. Your wealth compounds at approximately…

Reinvested returns compound multiplicatively: (1.05)(1.03) − 1 = 8.15%. The extra 0.15% over the naive 8% seems tiny but adds up — the exact 30-year result is ~$104,900 versus $43,219 from price alone.

3. In a price-weighted index like the Dow, which company has the most influence?

Price weighting is effectively holding one share of each member, so influence scales with per-share price — an arbitrary number. A $500 small company outweighs a $50 giant, which is why serious indices are cap-weighted.

4. A steel producer reports record profits at the peak of a construction boom and trades at a P/E of 6. The most careful interpretation is:

Cyclical companies show their lowest P/Es when earnings peak, right before profits fall. A low P/E on boom-time earnings can be more dangerous than a high P/E on trough earnings.

5. A company does a 4-for-1 stock split. What happens to the value of your holding?

A split changes the unit of account, not the business. Market cap, your ownership percentage, and the P/E are all unchanged. Contrast with a buyback, which does change per-share economics by shrinking the share count.

Key takeaways

  • A share is fractional ownership: a residual claim on profits and assets, with losses capped by limited liability — last in line, but with all the upside.
  • Company size is market cap (price × shares), never price per share; splits and share counts are just slicing choices.
  • Total return = price appreciation + dividends. Reinvested dividends compound your share count and can account for over half of long-run wealth.
  • Equities have paid roughly 7% real per year over the last US century — but through 30–50% drawdowns roughly once a decade. The premium is payment for surviving the ride, and past averages are not promises.
  • Serious indices (S&P 500, Russell 2000, MSCI World) are cap-weighted; the price-weighted Dow is a legacy oddity. Index funds and ETFs are the cheap, practical way to own the whole basket.
  • P/E = price per dollar of earnings; its inverse, the earnings yield, makes stocks comparable to bonds. A high P/E is a bet on growth — and P/E breaks on negative or cyclical earnings.
  • Buybacks and dividends both return cash; buybacks shrink the share count and lift EPS. Dilution does the opposite. IPOs, direct listings, and SPACs are just three doors into the public market.
  • On a stock screen, check internal consistency: price ÷ EPS should equal the P/E, beta is a regression slope, and float — not shares outstanding — is what actually trades.

Part II · Financial Markets & Instruments

8. Fixed Income: Bonds and Interest Rates

The bond market is bigger than the stock market, and it is where interest rates — the price of money itself — actually get set. By the end of this section you will be able to price a bond from scratch, explain why prices and yields move in opposite directions, read a yield curve, and estimate exactly how much a rate move will cost a bondholder.

Bond anatomy: a loan cut into pieces

A bond is a loan that has been cut into standardised, tradable pieces. When you buy one you are the lender, and the issuer is the borrower. The standardisation is what makes it different from an ordinary loan: instead of one lender negotiating unique terms with one borrower, the borrower writes a single set of terms and sells thousands of identical claims against them, so that any of those claims can later be sold to anyone else without renegotiating anything.

Because the payments are fixed by contract in advance — a stated amount on stated dates — the whole asset class is called fixed income. Note the sharp contrast with equity from Section 7. A shareholder owns whatever is left over and has no idea what that will be. A bondholder is owed a specific number of dollars on a specific date and is entitled to nothing more, however well the business does. That single difference — a fixed claim rather than a residual one — generates every other property of the asset class.

Three numbers fully define the contract, and once you have them there is nothing left to know about what the bond will pay.

The face value, also called par value and conventionally $1,000 per bond in the US, is the amount repaid at the end. It is also the base the interest is calculated on, which is why it matters even when the bond is trading at some other price.

The coupon is the interest payment, quoted as an annual percentage of face value. A 5% coupon on $1,000 of face value pays $50 a year, and it pays $50 a year regardless of what the bond subsequently trades for — the percentage is attached to the face value, never to the market price. US bonds actually pay half the amount every six months; this section uses annual payments to keep the arithmetic legible. The word is literal: paper bonds once carried detachable coupons along the edge that you clipped and posted in to claim each interest payment.

The maturity is the date the face value comes back and the bond ceases to exist. Put the three together and a bond is a completely specified schedule of future cash, known on the day it is issued: $50 at the end of each year, plus $1,000 at the end of year ten. Everything difficult about bonds comes from the fact that this schedule never changes while the world around it does.

Who borrows this way? Four families of issuer account for nearly all of it, and they differ mainly in how likely they are to pay you back and in how they are taxed:

  • Treasuries — debt of the US federal government (see Section 5 for why it borrows). T-bills mature within a year, notes run 2–10 years, bonds 20–30. Treated as the closest thing to a risk-free benchmark, so everything else is quoted relative to them.
  • Corporates — companies borrowing for factories, acquisitions, or buybacks. Riskier than Treasuries, so they must pay more (we quantify how much in the credit subsection).
  • Munis — state and local government bonds, often federally tax-exempt, which is why their quoted yields look low.
  • Agencies — government-sponsored entities such as Fannie Mae, mostly issuing bonds backed by pools of home mortgages.

Anyone arriving from the equity world is usually surprised by the relative sizes. Bonds outstanding globally total roughly $140 trillion against perhaps $110–120 trillion for all listed stocks, and the US Treasury market alone is around $27 trillion.

Three structural facts explain the gap. A company has exactly one class of ordinary shares but may have dozens of separate bond issues alive at once, each with its own maturity and coupon, because it borrows repeatedly over decades and each borrowing is a new security. Governments — by far the largest borrowers on earth — issue bonds and no equity at all, since there is no such thing as a share in a country. And consumer debt gets converted into bonds too: mortgages, car loans and credit-card balances are bundled into securities and sold, which turns household borrowing into more tradable paper.

Almost all of it trades over the counter, meaning through a network of dealer banks that quote prices on request, rather than on a central exchange like the NYSE. The reason is the fragmentation just described: with tens of thousands of individual bond issues, most of which trade rarely, there is no continuous two-sided market to run an order book on. That has a practical consequence you will meet again — bond prices are less transparent than stock prices, and the spread between what a dealer will buy and sell at is correspondingly wider. This is the market structure from Section 6 in action.

Worked example: decode four real bond quotes

Bond quoting conventions are archaic and non-negotiable. Here is how to read the four families you just met.

Quote Translation
T 4 1/8 11/15/34   98-14+   4.31% A US Treasury paying a 4.125% coupon, maturing 15 Nov 2034, priced at 98 and 14.5 thirty-seconds = 98.453% of face. Per $1,000 of face you pay $984.53 and earn 4.31% to maturity.
AAPL 3.35 08/08/32   +52bp An Apple corporate bond quoted not by price but by spread: 0.52% above the comparable Treasury. Corporate desks trade the spread, because the Treasury leg moves for reasons that have nothing to do with Apple.
NY State Dorm 3.20 07/01/40 A municipal bond. Its 3.20% is free of federal income tax, so compare it to taxable bonds using the tax-equivalent yield: 3.20% ÷ (1 − 0.35) = 4.92% for a 35%-bracket investor. Munis look cheap until you make that adjustment, and then they often are not.
FNMA 5.5 30yr TBA   99-08 An agency mortgage-backed security: a pool of home loans, guaranteed by Fannie Mae, traded before the specific pool is even identified ("to be announced"). Its cash flows depend on when homeowners refinance — which is why it behaves unlike any other bond.

The pattern worth extracting: each market quotes the thing that actually varies. Treasuries quote price (in 32nds, a hangover from pre-decimal trading), corporates quote spread over Treasuries, munis quote yield you must tax-adjust, and mortgages quote a price on a contract for an unspecified pool. If you ever join a fixed-income desk, learning what is quoted is half the onboarding.

Pricing a bond: it is just discounted cash flows

Here is the good news: you already learned the entire pricing model in Section 1. A bond is a known list of future payments, and the value today of any known list of future payments is the sum of what each one is worth today. There is no new theory here — only a discount rate to apply.

In words, the rule is: take each coupon payment, ask what amount of money today would grow into that payment by the date it arrives, and add all those amounts together; then do the same for the face value repaid at maturity and add that too. The sum is the price. The reason distant payments contribute less is the whole content of Section 1 — money arriving in ten years is worth less than the same money arriving next year, because next year's money could have been invested in the interim. Written with symbols, where the coupon C is discounted once for each year until it arrives and the face value F is discounted across the full n years:

P = Σt=1…n C ÷ (1 + y)t  +  F ÷ (1 + y)n
P = price · C = annual coupon in dollars · F = face value · y = market yield per year · n = years to maturity

The discount rate y in that expression is the yield to maturity, or YTM: the going market rate of return for money lent for this length of time to a borrower of this quality. It is defined as the single rate that makes the calculation above come out equal to the price the bond actually trades at, which means in practice the causality runs backwards from how the formula is written — the market sets a price, and the yield is what you solve for.

Now notice the asymmetry, because it is about to explain everything in this section. Of the four quantities in that formula, three are frozen: the coupon C, the face value F and the number of years n are written into the contract and cannot change. Only y moves, and it moves every minute, because it reflects what lenders currently demand — which shifts with central-bank policy, inflation expectations and the market's appetite for risk. A bond is a fixed object being continuously revalued by a moving number.

Worked example: a 3-year, 5% coupon bond at three different yields

Face value $1,000, so the cash flows are $50, $50, $1,050 at years 1, 2, 3.

Market yield 5% (equal to the coupon): 50÷1.05 + 50÷1.05² + 1,050÷1.05³ = 47.62 + 45.35 + 907.03 = $1,000.00. Exactly par.

Market yield 7%: 50÷1.07 + 50÷1.07² + 1,050÷1.07³ = 46.73 + 43.67 + 857.11 = $947.51. Below par.

Market yield 3%: 48.54 + 47.13 + 960.90 = $1,056.57. Above par.

Same bond, same cash flows — three prices. Only the discount rate moved.

Your edge

Bond pricing is a five-line function: loop over t, accumulate cf / (1+y)**t, done. Every readout in this section's widget — price, duration, the whole price–yield curve — falls out of that one loop. When a finance person says "we ran the bond math," they mean someone vectorized this in NumPy.

Worked example: the price on the screen is not the price you pay

You buy a $1,000 face, 5% semiannual bond on a day 73 days after its last coupon (the period is 181 days). The screen says the price is 98.50. Your broker bills you more than $985, and the difference is not a fee.

Component Amount Why
Clean price (98.50% of $1,000) $985.00 The quoted, headline price
Accrued interest: $25 × 73 ÷ 181 $10.08 Interest the seller earned by holding for 73 days
Dirty (invoice) price $995.08 What actually leaves your account

In four months you will receive the whole $25 coupon, including the $10.08 that was economically the seller's. Quoting clean prices exists so the headline number does not sawtooth up by $25 and drop by $25 twice a year for reasons unrelated to interest rates.

Two practical consequences. If you download bond price history and see a smooth series, it is clean prices — you must add accrued interest to compute an actual return. And a bond fund's daily NAV uses dirty prices, which is part of why fund NAVs and bond prices are not directly comparable.

The seesaw: why price and yield move in opposite directions

This is the single most important fact in fixed income, and once you have seen why it must be true you will never need to memorise it: when market yields rise, the prices of existing bonds fall, and when yields fall, prices rise. Not usually, not on average — always, mechanically, as a matter of arithmetic.

You do not need the formula to see it. Suppose you own the 5% coupon bond from above, paying $50 a year. Interest rates in the economy rise, and newly issued bonds of identical maturity and identical credit quality now come with 7% coupons, paying $70 a year.

Put yourself in a buyer's position. Two bonds sit side by side, equally safe, maturing on the same day; one pays $70 a year and one pays $50. Nobody will pay $1,000 for yours while the other is available at $1,000. Your bond is not unsellable, though — it is just mispriced. Lower its price far enough and the buyer's total return becomes competitive, because they are now paying less than $1,000 for something that will repay $1,000 at maturity, and that built-in gain makes up the difference in coupons. For the 3-year bond above, the price at which the returns match exactly is $947.51.

The general principle is the asymmetry from the previous subsection. The cash flows are bolted down by contract and cannot adjust, so price is the only part of the arrangement that can move. When the return lenders require goes up, price is forced down until the fixed cash flows deliver that return. And it works identically in reverse: when yields fall, an old bond paying above-market coupons becomes something people compete for, and its price is bid above face value.

Key idea: price and yield are one object

It is worth being explicit that price and yield are not two related quantities that happen to move together. They are the same information stated in two units, the way a journey can be described in miles per hour or in minutes per mile. Yield is the price restated as an annualised rate of return; given the fixed cash flows, fixing either one determines the other exactly.

This is why bond market language sounds contradictory until it clicks. "Bonds sold off today" and "yields rose today" are not two events, they are one event reported in the two conventions. When a headline says the ten-year Treasury yield jumped, it is telling you that the price of ten-year Treasuries fell, and anyone holding them lost money. Traders quote yields rather than prices because a yield is comparable across bonds with different coupons, maturities and face values, whereas a price is not — $947.51 tells you nothing on its own.

Comparing a bond's coupon to the current market yield sorts every bond into one of three states, and the vocabulary appears constantly in quotes and research:

State Condition Price 3-year example
Premium coupon > market yield above $1,000 $1,056.57 at 3%
Par coupon = market yield exactly $1,000 $1,000.00 at 5%
Discount coupon < market yield below $1,000 $947.51 at 7%

One trap is worth defusing now, because financial media mix these three terms freely and they mean quite different things.

The coupon rate is frozen at issue: $50 on $1,000 of face value is 5%, permanently, no matter what happens to the price. The current yield divides the same $50 by today's market price instead — $50 ÷ $947.51 = 5.28% — which correctly tells you the cash income rate on money invested today, and stops there.

The yield to maturity, 7% in this example, is the complete figure, and the reason it is larger than the current yield is instructive. Current yield counts only the coupons. YTM counts the coupons and the fact that a bond bought at $947.51 will be repaid at $1,000, so there is a further $52.49 of guaranteed gain arriving at maturity. It is the internal rate of return on the whole cash-flow schedule. Use YTM whenever you are comparing bonds against each other or against anything else; the other two are partial views that will mislead you at exactly the moments a bond is trading far from face value.

Key idea

A bond's cash flows never change; its price does. Yield up ⇒ price down. Buy at a discount and the market yield exceeds the coupon; buy at a premium and it is the reverse. Everything else in fixed income is a footnote to this seesaw.

The bond seesaw

Drag the market yield past the coupon rate and watch the price cross par — then stretch the maturity and see the seesaw get more violent.

Price ($1,000 face)$859.53
Trading atDiscount
Modified duration7.42 yrs
Current yield5.82%

Real world: the century bond that fell 75%

In September 2017 Austria — an AA+ rated, stable European sovereign — issued a 100-year bond maturing in 2117, with a coupon of 2.1%. It was heavily oversubscribed. Here is what happened to a "safe government bond" in five years:

Date Market yield Approx. price
Issued, Sept 2017 2.1% 100
Peak, late 2020 ≈ 0.4% ≈ 234
Late 2022 ≈ 3.5% ≈ 60

An investor who bought at the 2020 peak lost roughly three-quarters of their money in a AA+ rated government bond, without a single missed payment and with zero credit deterioration. Austria will repay every euro it promised — in 2117. That is pure interest-rate risk, and it is why "government bonds are safe" is a statement about credit, never about price.

The mirror-image case: in June 2017 Argentina — a country that had defaulted eight times — sold a 100-year bond at a 7.9% yield. Investors queued up for it. Argentina defaulted again in 2020, three years into the hundred. One bond shows you rate risk with no credit risk; the other shows credit risk priced far too cheaply. Every bond you ever analyse is some mixture of those two.

The yield curve: the market's forecast in one line

Take a single issuer — the US Treasury — and plot the yield on each of its bonds against how long that bond has left to run, from 3-month bills out to 30-year bonds. Holding the issuer constant is the whole point: credit quality is identical along the entire line, so any differences in yield can only be about time.

That plot is the yield curve, and it is arguably the most closely watched chart in finance. It is worth understanding why so much attention goes to what looks like a fairly dull line: it compresses the market's collective forecast of growth, inflation and central-bank policy over the next three decades into a single shape, updated continuously, with real money behind every point.

Why should the shape carry information at all? Because a long bond has to compete with an alternative, and that alternative reveals what people expect.

Consider two ways to lend money for ten years. You can buy a ten-year bond and lock in today's ten-year yield. Or you can buy a three-month bill and keep rolling it over, forty times, at whatever short rate prevails each time. If the market believed the second route would clearly pay more, nobody would take the first, and the ten-year yield would have to rise until the two were competitive. So the ten-year yield must be approximately the market's expected average of short-term rates over the next ten years — and short-term rates are what the Fed controls (Section 4). The long end of the curve is a forecast of monetary policy.

There is one adjustment on top of that. Locking money up for a decade carries risk that rolling bills does not: if yields rise, the long bond holder takes a capital loss, and inflation over ten years is far less predictable than over three months. Investors demand extra compensation for bearing that, called the term premium. So a long yield is expected average short rates plus a term premium — which is why the curve usually slopes upward even when nobody expects rates to rise. Three canonical shapes follow from this:

  • Normal (upward-sloping): long yields above short. The default state — steady growth expected, term premium doing its job.
  • Flat: little difference across maturities. A transition state — the market thinks the rate cycle is near a turning point.
  • Inverted: short yields above long. The market is saying today's policy rate is unusually high and will be cut — and central banks cut aggressively mostly when the economy is heading into trouble.

The inverted shape has a remarkable track record. An inversion of the ten-year minus two-year spread, or the ten-year minus three-month version, has preceded every US recession of the past half century, typically by somewhere between six and twenty-four months. That is the indicator introduced in Section 3, and the mechanism should now be clear: an inverted curve means the market expects short rates to be lower in future than they are today, and the main reason the Fed cuts is a weakening economy. The bond market is pricing in trouble.

Treat it as a strong signal rather than a law. Two limitations matter in practice. The lead time is wildly variable, so the signal tells you a recession has become more likely without telling you when — useless as a trading trigger, useful as a reason to prepare. And the sample is small: perhaps eight or nine independent observations in fifty years, which is not many to draw a statistical conclusion from. The deep inversion of 2022–2024 was followed by an unusually long wait, a reminder that "has preceded every recession" and "is reliably followed by one on a useful timescale" are different claims.

Yield curve explorer

Flip between the three classic shapes and read what each one says about the future (illustrative data).

A normal curve: longer lending earns more. The market expects steady growth and policy roughly where it is, and investors collect a term premium for tying money up.

Worked example: extracting next year's rate from today's curve

The curve is not just a shape — you can read specific predictions out of it. Suppose 1-year Treasuries yield 5.0% and 2-year Treasuries yield 4.6%. Two strategies must produce the same result, or there would be free money:

  • A: buy the 2-year and hold. Growth factor = 1.046² = 1.0941.
  • B: buy the 1-year at 5.0%, then reinvest for a second year at whatever the 1-year rate is then. Growth factor = 1.05 × (1 + f).

Set them equal: 1 + f = 1.0941 ÷ 1.05, so f = 4.20%. The market is implicitly forecasting that the 1-year rate a year from now will be 4.20% — that is the forward rate, and every inverted curve contains a similar forecast of cuts.

Now use it. If you believe rates will actually be higher than 4.20% next year, the 1-year bond is the better buy; if lower, the 2-year is. You are no longer guessing about "rates" in the abstract — you are taking a position against a specific number the market has already committed to.

A second trick from the same curve is rolldown. Buy the 2-year at 4.6% and hold it for one year. If the curve has not moved, your bond is now a 1-year bond, which the curve prices at 5.0% — a higher yield, hence a lower price. On an upward-sloping curve the effect reverses and works in your favour: you earn the coupon plus a price gain as the bond rolls down to a lower yield. Carry-and-rolldown is one of the most reliable return sources in fixed income, and it is invisible if you only look at yield to maturity.

Duration and convexity: how hard does the seesaw swing?

The seesaw tells you which direction a bond's price moves when yields change. It says nothing about how far, and the size varies enormously between bonds. The measure of that sensitivity is duration.

You can see the effect in the widget above without any theory. Set the maturity to 10 years and move the yield; then set it to 30 years and move the yield by the same amount. The 30-year bond's price moves several times as far for an identical change. A long bond and a short bond respond to the same event on completely different scales, and if you hold bonds without knowing which you own, you do not know what you are exposed to.

The cleanest way to understand why longer bonds react more is to ask when the money actually arrives. Macaulay duration is the weighted-average arrival time of a bond's cash flows, where each payment date is weighted by the share of the bond's present value that payment represents. If you have handled physical systems, it is a centre of mass; if you have handled data, it is an expected value over payment dates.

Picture the discounted cash flows as weights placed along a plank marked in years. Each small coupon puts a light weight at its own date, and the face value puts one enormous weight right at maturity. The balance point of that plank is the duration. For the 10-year, 5% bond at a 7% yield, the balance point sits at 7.94 years — earlier than ten, because the coupons pull it in, but not much earlier, because the final $1,000 dominates.

Now the reason this predicts price sensitivity. Discounting is compounding in reverse, so a change in the rate applies once for each year until a payment arrives — it is raised to a power. A payment due in one year is barely affected by a one-point change in the discount rate; a payment due in thirty is affected roughly thirty times over. So the further out a bond's centre of mass sits, the more of its value is exposed to that compounding, and the harder its price reacts. Duration converts "how long until I get paid" directly into "how much do I lose if rates rise."

For daily use, traders quote modified duration, which is Macaulay duration divided by one plus the yield — a small adjustment that converts the balance-point measure into a direct sensitivity. The reason for the adjustment is technical; the reason for the number is that it plugs into the most-used rule of thumb in fixed income.

Stated in words: the percentage change in a bond's price is approximately minus its modified duration multiplied by the change in yield, measured in percentage points. So a bond with a modified duration of 7 loses about 7% of its value if yields rise one point, and gains about 7% if they fall one point. The minus sign is the seesaw. The magnitude is the duration. In symbols:

ΔP ÷ P ≈ −Dmod × Δy
ΔP ÷ P = percent price change · Dmod = modified duration · Δy = change in yield (in percentage points)

Worked example: pricing a rate shock

Our 10-year, 5% bond at a 7% yield: price $859.53, modified duration 7.42 (the widget's default readout). Yields jump one percentage point to 8%. Predicted move: −7.42% × $859.53 ≈ −$63.78, so about $795.75. Exact repricing gives $798.70. The linear rule nailed the damage to within $3 — and note which way it missed: the true price fell less than predicted.

Notice that the linear estimate missed in a consistent direction — it predicted a larger loss than actually occurred. That systematic miss has a name: convexity.

The relationship between price and yield is not a straight line; it is a curve that bows toward the origin. Duration is the slope of that curve at the current yield, which means the duration estimate is a straight line drawn tangent to it. Because the true curve bends upward away from the tangent line in both directions, the straight-line estimate always sits below the truth: when yields rise, prices fall less than duration predicts, and when yields fall, prices rise more.

In calculus terms, duration is the first derivative of price with respect to yield and convexity is the second — this is a two-term Taylor expansion in professional dress. Two consequences follow. The duration rule of thumb is reliable for small moves of a few basis points and progressively optimistic about damage for large ones. And convexity is genuinely a good thing to own: it means the asymmetry runs in the holder's favour, which is why bonds with more of it command slightly higher prices for the same yield.

Real world: 2022, the worst bond year in modern history

Duration stopped being an abstraction in 2022. Bonds had been issued for years at rock-bottom coupons, which makes durations long (small coupons = the plank's weight is almost all at the far end). Then the Fed hiked from near 0% to over 4% in nine months. Run the rule: broad bond-index duration around 6.5 and yields up roughly 2.5 points ⇒ ≈ −16% before coupon income. The Bloomberg US Aggregate index finished 2022 down about 13% — its worst year since records began in 1976 — and long-maturity Treasuries lost around 30%, a stock-crash-sized loss in the "safe" asset.

Silicon Valley Bank was the corporate casualty of the same arithmetic: it parked deposits in long-duration Treasuries and agency mortgage bonds, rates rose, and the mark-to-market hole grew to roughly the size of its entire equity. Depositors noticed and ran. There was no exotic credit bet involved — just unhedged duration. Section 16 dissects the risk-management failure in full.

Common pitfall

Duration measures sensitivity to a small, parallel shift in yields — it is a local linear model, not a crystal ball. For big moves you need the convexity term; for twists in the curve's shape (short yields up, long yields down) a single duration number can badly mislead.

Worked example: what duration means for the fund in your 401(k)

Every bond fund publishes an average effective duration. That single number lets you price a rate move before it happens. Take three common US funds and apply ΔP ÷ P ≈ −D × Δy for a 1-point rise in yields:

Fund type Duration Predicted for +1% Actual 2022 return
Short-term Treasury (1–3y) 1.9 −1.9% ≈ −4%
Total bond market (AGG-like) 6.2 −6.2% ≈ −13%
Long Treasury (20y+, TLT-like) 16.5 −16.5% ≈ −31%

The 2022 column is roughly double the prediction because yields rose by roughly two points, not one — the model worked, the shock was bigger. Note how faithfully the ratios hold: the long fund lost about 2.4× the total-market fund, close to 16.5 ÷ 6.2 = 2.7.

The recovery arithmetic, which almost nobody does. The total-market fund fell 13% but its yield rose from about 1.8% to about 4.7%. Every future year now earns roughly 2.9 points more. Holding for approximately the fund's duration (about six years) recovers the capital loss through higher coupons — which is the deep meaning of duration: it is the holding period at which price loss and reinvestment gain cancel out. A rate rise is terrible for a bond holder who sells and, past that horizon, genuinely good for one who does not.

Credit: getting paid for the risk of not getting paid

Everything up to this point has assumed the promised cash flows actually arrive. For US Treasuries that is close enough to a working assumption, for the reason given in Section 5: the borrower can create the currency it owes. For every other issuer the possibility of default is real, and the market charges for it in the only way it can — by demanding a higher yield.

The assessment of that risk starts with a credit rating, a letter grade published by Moody's, S&P or Fitch expressing an opinion on how likely the borrower is to pay. The scale runs from AAA at the top — an issuer expected to survive almost anything — down through AA, A, BBB, BB, B and CCC to D, which means already in default. Ratings are opinions rather than measurements, they are paid for by the issuer being rated, and their failure to anticipate the 2008 mortgage crisis is a permanent stain on the industry. They nonetheless matter enormously, for a reason that has little to do with their accuracy.

One line on that scale does more work than all the others. BBB− and above is investment grade; BB+ and below is high yield, universally known as junk. That boundary is written into regulation and into the investment mandates of pension funds and insurers, many of which are simply not permitted to hold anything below it.

The consequence is a mechanical cliff. When a company is downgraded from BBB− to BB+ — a "fallen angel" — a large set of institutional holders must sell, not because they have changed their view of the company but because their rules no longer allow the holding. Forced selling into a market that knows the selling is forced produces a price fall far larger than the change in underlying risk justifies. This is why companies manage their ratings so carefully around that specific threshold, and why the biggest cluster of corporate bonds sits just above it.

The market price of credit risk is the credit spread: the bond's yield minus the yield on a Treasury of the same maturity. If a BBB-rated corporate bond yields 5.5% while the ten-year Treasury pays 4%, the spread is 1.5 percentage points, quoted as 150 basis points. Subtracting the Treasury yield is what isolates the compensation for credit — both bonds are exposed to the same interest-rate environment, so whatever is left over is being paid for default risk and for the fact that corporate bonds are harder to sell in a hurry.

Because spreads are a pure measure of what investors demand to take corporate risk, they function as an unusually good gauge of collective fear. US high-yield spreads run around 3 to 4 percentage points in calm periods, widened past 20 points during the 2008 crisis, and spiked above 10 in March 2020 before Fed intervention pulled them back. When spreads gap wider, the bond market is repricing the probability of a wave of defaults — and it often does so before equity markets fully react, because bondholders are specifically in the business of thinking about downside scenarios while equity holders are thinking about growth.

Default is also not the same as total loss, and forgetting that leads to badly overestimating the risk. Bondholders sit ahead of shareholders in bankruptcy — the payment queue from Section 7 — so when a company fails, its remaining assets are used to pay creditors before equity receives anything. The recovery rate on senior unsecured corporate bonds has historically averaged around 40 cents on the dollar, and secured lenders typically do considerably better.

That gives a first-pass model of what a spread ought to be. In words: the expected loss on a bond is the probability that it defaults multiplied by the fraction of your money you would fail to recover if it did. A bond with a 2% annual chance of default and a 40% recovery rate has an expected loss of 2% × 60%, or 1.2 percentage points a year. A fair spread is that expected loss plus an additional margin — investors want more than break-even compensation for taking a risk, and they want paying for the difficulty of selling the bond in a stressed market. It is a one-line expected-value calculation, and the useful discipline is comparing the spread you are offered against the expected loss you computed.

Worked example: is the spread big enough to be worth it?

A credit spread is only attractive if it more than covers expected losses. Expected loss has exactly two inputs:

Expected loss = PD × (1 − Recovery rate)
PD = annual probability of default · recovery ≈ 40% for senior unsecured corporates, historically
Rating Spread Annual PD Expected loss Excess over EL
BBB 130 bp 0.2% 12 bp 118 bp
BB 300 bp 1.0% 60 bp 240 bp
CCC 900 bp 12.0% 720 bp 180 bp

Read the last column carefully. The CCC bond pays three times the spread of the BB — and after expected losses it compensates you less. That excess is not free money either: it pays for illiquidity, for mark-to-market volatility, and for the fact that defaults are not independent. They cluster in recessions, exactly when you also lose your job and your equities fall.

This is the entire analytical core of credit investing, and it is a probability-weighted expected-value calculation you already know how to do. The hard part is not the arithmetic — it is estimating PD, which is where everything from ratings-transition matrices to Merton structural models to gradient-boosted default classifiers lives. That is a genuinely good place for someone with your background to enter the industry.

Money markets: the plumbing where cash lives

Below one year of maturity, fixed income stops behaving like investing and starts behaving like infrastructure. The money market is where corporations, funds and governments park cash they will need soon and borrow cash they need briefly, in amounts measured in trillions and for terms measured from one night to a few months.

The purpose is different from everything above. Nobody is trying to earn a return here; they are trying to hold cash without holding literal cash, which would earn nothing and would have to sit somewhere. A corporation with $5 billion between paying suppliers and receiving customer payments needs that money to be entirely safe, available on a known date, and earning something rather than nothing. Every instrument in this market is designed for that requirement, which is why they are all short, all high quality, and all extremely dull by construction.

The instruments themselves are refreshingly simple. Treasury bills pay no coupon at all. Instead you buy them below face value and receive the full face value at maturity, and the difference is your entire return: pay $980.39 today for $1,000 in six months and you have earned $19.61, which is 2% over the period and roughly 4% annualised. Removing coupons removes all the reinvestment questions and makes the instrument a single, clean cash flow.

Commercial paper is the corporate equivalent: unsecured short-term IOUs, typically maturing within 270 days, that large creditworthy companies issue and roll over continuously to fund payroll, inventory and receivables. The word unsecured is important — there is no collateral behind it, only the issuer's name, which is why only the strongest companies can sell it and why the market for it disappears completely the moment anyone doubts those names.

The strangest-sounding instrument is also the most systemically important. A repo, short for repurchase agreement, is structured as a sale: I sell you a Treasury bond today and simultaneously commit to buying it back tomorrow at a slightly higher price.

Look at what that actually accomplishes. I get cash today and give it back tomorrow with a little extra; you hold a Treasury bond in the meantime as security. That is an overnight loan collateralised by a government bond, with the price difference serving as interest. It is written as a sale rather than a loan for legal reasons — if I fail to buy the bond back, you simply own it already, with no bankruptcy process to sit through, which is what makes lenders willing to do it at very low rates.

Trillions of dollars of repo roll over every night. It is how dealer banks finance the inventories of bonds they hold to make markets, and it underpins SOFR, the benchmark interest rate that replaced LIBOR in most floating-rate contracts. The Fed steers short-term rates partly through its own repo operations (Section 4). And when people describe the financial system's plumbing freezing in 2008, the repo and commercial-paper markets are literally what they mean: lenders stopped being willing to lend overnight even against collateral, and institutions that funded themselves night by night discovered they could not.

Finally, money-market funds package all of this for everyone else. They are mutual funds holding nothing but Treasury bills, repo and commercial paper, and they are engineered to maintain a share price of exactly $1.00, distributing their earnings as a yield rather than letting the price rise. That design is deliberate: a stable $1.00 share makes the fund feel and behave like a bank account, which is what its users want.

It is worth being clear about what that $1.00 is, though. It is an accounting convention supported by holding only very safe, very short assets — not a guarantee, not deposit insurance, and not a law of nature. If the underlying holdings fall in value, the price can fall below a dollar, which is called breaking the buck. It has happened, the consequences were severe, and the callout below describes the occasion.

Real world: breaking the buck

In September 2008, the Reserve Primary Fund — a money-market fund holding Lehman Brothers commercial paper — marked its shares at $0.97 when Lehman failed. "Breaking the buck" by three cents sounds trivial; it triggered a $300+ billion institutional run on money funds within days, froze the commercial-paper market that companies use to make payroll, and forced the US Treasury to guarantee money funds outright. The lesson: the most boring corner of finance is the one nobody can function without.

Deep dive: real-world bond math conventions

Everything above used annual coupons for clarity, but US convention is semiannual: a 5% coupon pays $25 every six months, and quoted YTMs are semiannual rates doubled (a "bond-equivalent yield"). The mechanics are identical — halve the coupon and rate, double the period count. Our 10-year, 5% bond at a 7% quoted yield becomes 20 payments of $25 discounted at 3.5% per half-year, giving $857.88 rather than $859.53. Same seesaw, slightly different arithmetic.

Two other conventions you will hit in practice. First, prices are quoted per $100 of face ("95.75" means 95.75% of par) and clean — excluding interest accrued since the last coupon, which the buyer pays on top (the "dirty" price is what actually changes hands). Second, day-count conventions (30/360 for corporates, actual/actual for Treasuries) decide exactly how that accrued interest is computed. None of this changes the concepts; all of it changes the fourth decimal place, which is precisely the sort of thing an analytics team gets paid to reconcile.

One elegant special case worth knowing: a zero-coupon bond (like a T-bill, or Treasury STRIPS at longer maturities) has its entire cash flow at maturity, so its Macaulay duration equals its maturity — the balance-point picture with one single weight at the far end of the plank. Zeros are therefore the purest, most rate-sensitive bonds you can hold.

Worked example: T-bills and repo, with the actual arithmetic

A T-bill. A 91-day bill is quoted at a price of 98.70 per $100 of face. It pays no coupon; your entire return is the $1.30 pull to par. There are two conventional ways to annualise that, and they disagree:

Convention Formula Result
Discount yield (how bills are quoted) 1.30 ÷ 100 × 360 ÷ 91 5.14%
Bond-equivalent yield (comparable to bonds) 1.30 ÷ 98.70 × 365 ÷ 91 5.28%

The discount convention divides by face rather than by what you actually paid, and uses a 360-day year. It understates your real return by about 14 basis points here. Anyone comparing a quoted bill yield with a bond yield without converting is silently comparing two different quantities — a classic junior-analyst error.

A repo. A hedge fund owns $10,000,000 of Treasuries and needs cash overnight. It repos them at a 2% haircut and a 5.30% repo rate:

  • Cash received today: $10,000,000 × 0.98 = $9,800,000.
  • Interest for one night: $9,800,000 × 0.0530 × 1 ÷ 360 = $1,442.78.
  • Repurchase tomorrow for $9,801,442.78.

Economically it is a secured overnight loan; legally it is a sale and a repurchase, which is exactly why the lender is safe if the fund fails — it already owns the collateral. Note the leverage this creates: with a 2% haircut you can finance a Treasury position roughly 50 times over. That is why the repo market — several trillion dollars a day in the US — is where stress shows up first, and why September 2019 and March 2020 both began there.

Check your understanding

1. Market interest rates rise from 4% to 6%. What happens to the price of an existing fixed-coupon bond?

The cash flows cannot change, so the price must. Nobody pays par for a 4% coupon when new bonds pay 6%; the price drops until the old bond's fixed payments yield 6% from the lower purchase price.

2. A bond with a 6% coupon trades at $1,080 (above its $1,000 face). What do you know about its yield to maturity?

Premium price means coupon > market yield. Paying $1,080 for cash flows built on $1,000 also guarantees a capital loss at maturity, dragging the all-in return (YTM) below the 6% coupon rate.

3. The 2-year Treasury yields 5.0% while the 10-year yields 4.2%. Historically, what has this configuration signaled?

That is an inverted curve. Long yields sit below short ones only when the market expects short rates to be cut a lot — and deep cuts historically arrive with recessions. Inversions have preceded every US recession of the past half-century, with variable lead times.

4. A bond fund has a modified duration of 6. Yields rise by 0.5 percentage points. Approximately what happens to the fund's value?

ΔP ÷ P ≈ −D × Δy = −6 × 0.5% = −3%. Duration converts a yield move into a percent price move — and thanks to convexity the true loss would be slightly smaller than 3%.

5. High-yield credit spreads jump from 350 to 800 basis points in a month. What is the bond market saying?

The spread is the market's charge for default risk over Treasuries. Widening from 3.5 to 8 points means investors demand far more compensation to hold risky corporate debt — a classic fear signal that often precedes trouble showing up in equities.

Key takeaways

  • A bond is a tradable loan with contractually fixed cash flows: coupons plus face value at maturity. Globally, bonds outstanding exceed the value of all stocks.
  • Price = sum of discounted cash flows, exactly as in Section 1. The cash flows are frozen; the market yield — and therefore the price — is not.
  • The seesaw: yields up ⇒ prices down, always. Coupon above market yield ⇒ premium; below ⇒ discount; equal ⇒ par. YTM is the all-in return; the coupon rate never changes.
  • The yield curve plots Treasury yields across maturities and encodes the expected path of Fed policy. Inversions have preceded every US recession in half a century, with 6–24-month (and sometimes longer) lead times.
  • Duration is the center of mass of discounted cash flows and the price-sensitivity dial: ΔP ÷ P ≈ −D × Δy. Convexity makes real losses slightly smaller and gains slightly bigger than that linear estimate.
  • Low coupons and long maturities mean high duration — the arithmetic behind 2022's record bond losses and SVB's collapse (Section 16).
  • Credit spreads price default risk over Treasuries; the BBB−/BB+ line splits investment grade from junk, and widening spreads are one of the market's best fear gauges.
  • Money markets — T-bills, repo, commercial paper, money funds — are the system's cash plumbing; when they seize (2008), everything else stops.

Part II · Financial Markets & Instruments

9. Derivatives: Futures, Options and Swaps

Derivatives are contracts whose value is computed from something else — a stock, a bond, a barrel of oil, an interest rate. Master this section and you will be able to read an option chain, price out a hedge, and explain why the same instrument that saves a farmer's season can vaporize a hedge fund.

A contract about a price, not the thing itself

A derivative is a legal agreement whose payoff is calculated from some other price. That other price — a stock, a barrel of oil, an interest rate, an index — is called the underlying, and the word "derived" is meant literally: the contract has no independent value, only a rule that converts the underlying's price into an amount of money one party owes the other.

The consequence worth absorbing first is that you never need to own the underlying to trade the derivative. Nobody buying an oil futures contract has a barrel, a tanker or an intention to acquire either; the contract references the oil price without touching oil. What is being bought and sold is exposure to a price movement, detached from the thing whose price is moving. That separation is what makes derivatives useful, and it is also what makes their size so misleading — the amount of contracts referencing an asset can be many times the amount of the asset itself.

Key idea: a contract with no substance of its own

It helps to be precise about what a derivative contains, because the mystery usually comes from imagining there is more in it than there is.
