The contract specifies three things: which price it references, on what date or dates the reference is taken, and what formula converts that price into a payment between the two parties. There is nothing else in it. No asset is held, no ownership is transferred, and nothing is produced.

This is why derivative positions can be created without limit while the underlying supply is fixed. Two parties can agree to a contract referencing the price of gold without either of them touching gold, and a third and fourth pair can do the same thing an hour later. The obligations are real and the money that moves is real, but the thing generating the numbers is simply a price observed elsewhere — which is exactly why the total notional value of outstanding derivatives can exceed the value of the world's assets without that fact meaning anything alarming by itself.

Two kinds of participant show up to trade these contracts, and the market needs both.

A hedger arrives already carrying a risk they did not choose. A farmer will have wheat to sell in December and is exposed to whatever wheat costs then. An airline will buy jet fuel every month for years. A European exporter will be paid in dollars. None of them wants that exposure — it is a by-product of the business they are actually in — and a derivative lets them shed it, converting an unknown future price into a known one.

A speculator has no such underlying exposure. They take the other side of the hedger's contract because they expect to profit from the price move, and in doing so they accept a risk they did not previously have.

Speculators attract the bad press, and it is worth seeing why the market needs them anyway. Hedging is a transfer of risk, which means someone must accept it. If only hedgers existed, our farmer wanting to sell wheat forward would have to find a flour mill wanting to buy the identical quantity for the identical date at the same moment — a coincidence that would rarely occur, and when it failed the farmer would be left with the risk. Speculators stand ready to take either side at a price, which is what allows a hedger to transact immediately rather than waiting for a perfect match. In the vocabulary of Section 6, speculators are the liquidity providers of the risk-transfer business.

Two properties separate derivatives from everything in Section 7 (Equities) and Section 8 (Fixed Income), and both need to be understood before anything else in this section will land correctly.

They are zero-sum before costs. Every derivative has exactly two sides, and the contract's rule assigns to one side precisely what it takes from the other. If wheat ends the year at $7 and the contract was struck at $6, the seller's loss and the buyer's gain are the same number. Nothing was produced.

Contrast that with a share. A company can make money for the person who bought it in 2010 and for the person who bought it from them in 2018, because in the intervening years the company built things, sold them, and generated profits that did not previously exist. Equity investors as a group can all gain, because the underlying business creates value. A futures contract creates nothing; it only decides who holds an existing exposure.

Add trading costs and the arithmetic becomes slightly worse than zero-sum: commissions and bid–ask spreads are paid out of the pot, so the average participant finishes marginally behind. For a hedger this is entirely acceptable and is the point — the expected shortfall is an insurance premium, paid willingly in exchange for removing an uncertainty they could not afford. For someone trading derivatives to make money, it means the game is negative-sum against the average participant, and being merely average is not good enough.

They embed enormous leverage. Because no asset changes hands at the outset, the money you must put down is not the value of the exposure but a deposit against possible losses. Thousands of dollars can control a six-figure position.

Work through what that does to your returns. Suppose $6,000 of collateral controls $120,000 of exposure — a ratio of twenty to one. The underlying moves 3% in your favour, which is $3,600, and your account is up 60%. The underlying moves 3% against you, and your account is down 60%. The multiplier is symmetric and it is unforgiving: it does not merely amplify the outcome, it means a move that would be unremarkable in the underlying can eliminate your entire stake.

Keep the ordering of these tools in mind for the rest of the section. Derivatives were built as risk-transfer instruments for people with real exposures to manage, and that remains the overwhelming majority of their use by value. The retail application — buying short-dated options as leveraged directional bets — arrived much later, and the empirical record for it is poor: most retail option buyers lose money, and the mechanism explained under time decay below is a large part of why.

Key idea

Derivatives don't create or destroy risk — they relocate it, from someone who doesn't want it to someone who is paid to hold it. Pricing a derivative is pricing that relocation.

Real world: the derivatives already in your life

Derivatives sound exotic because the famous ones blew things up. Most of them are quietly load-bearing infrastructure, and several are probably in your own paperwork:

Contract What it really is
Your fixed-rate mortgage (US) A loan plus a free option: you may prepay and refinance if rates fall, and the bank cannot force you to. That embedded option is why US mortgage rates sit above Treasuries by more than credit risk alone justifies — you are paying for it.
Home or car insurance A put option on your house. You pay a premium; if value is destroyed, the writer pays the difference.
Employee stock options / RSUs Literally call options on your employer, usually with a multi-year vesting schedule. Their value depends on volatility, so a job at a volatile startup has a genuinely different risk profile from the same paper value at a utility.
Airline jet fuel hedging Southwest Airlines hedged fuel aggressively into 2008 and saved billions while rivals were crushed by $140 oil. It then lost money on the same programme when oil collapsed. A hedge is not a bet that wins; it is a decision to stop having an opinion.
Your grocery bill Food companies hedge wheat, corn, sugar, and packaging with futures a year ahead. That is why supermarket prices lag commodity spikes by many months.
Your pension fund Defined-benefit plans owe inflation-linked payments decades out and use interest-rate swaps to match that duration. This is the largest derivatives use case almost nobody outside the industry knows about — and it caused the UK crisis of 2022.

Forwards and futures: locking a price today

The oldest derivative is simply a promise about a future price. A forward is a private contract between two parties: I agree today to sell you 50,000 bushels of wheat in December at $6.00 a bushel, whatever wheat is actually trading at when December arrives.

Two features of that arrangement matter. No money changes hands now — we have agreed a price, not made a payment, so the contract costs nothing to enter. And the agreement binds both of us: in December I must deliver at $6.00 even if wheat is at $9.00, and you must pay $6.00 even if wheat is at $4.00. Neither of us has an option about it, which is what distinguishes a forward from the instruments in the next subsection.

What the contract has achieved is a conversion of uncertainty into certainty for both sides. Before it, the farmer faced an unknown December revenue and the mill faced an unknown December cost. Afterwards, both know exactly what they will receive and pay. Neither has made money, and one of them will end up wishing they had not signed — but both have removed a risk they could not control from a business plan they had to make in advance.

Worked example: the farmer and the flour mill

A farmer will harvest 50,000 bushels in December and needs $5.20/bu to cover costs. Today's December price is $6.00. She sells forward at $6.00, locking in revenue of 50,000 × $6.00 = $300,000 and a profit of $40,000.

If December spot wheat is $5.00: she sells her crop for $250,000, but her forward position gains ($6.00 − $5.00) × 50,000 = $50,000. Total: $300,000. If spot is $7.00: crop fetches $350,000, forward loses $50,000. Total: $300,000 again. The hedge doesn't make her rich — it makes her predictable. The airline hedging jet fuel runs the same trade in mirror image, buying forward to cap its costs.

Forwards have two problems, and both come from being private agreements between two named parties.

The first is finding a match. Your contract must specify a quantity, a quality, a delivery date and a location, and it only exists if some particular counterparty wants exactly the mirror image of all four. A farmer with 50,000 bushels available on 15 December needs a buyer who wants 50,000 bushels on 15 December. The more specific the contract, the harder that is.

The second is counterparty risk. The value of your hedge in December depends entirely on the other party still existing and still being able to pay. If wheat rises to $9.00 and the buyer who agreed to pay $6.00 goes bankrupt instead, you have no hedge — you have a claim in a bankruptcy proceeding and a crop to sell at whatever the market offers.

A futures contract solves both problems with two structural changes. It is standardised — fixed contract size, fixed delivery months, fixed quality specifications — so that every contract for a given month is interchangeable with every other, which means you need to find someone who wants the standard contract rather than someone who wants your specific one. And it is listed on an exchange such as the CME with a clearinghouse inserted between the two sides, so that you face the clearinghouse rather than a stranger — the novation mechanism from Section 6, applied to contracts that will not settle for months.

Inserting itself between every buyer and seller means the clearinghouse now carries the risk it removed from them, so it protects itself with two mechanisms that you will meet repeatedly.

The first is margin: both sides must deposit collateral before trading, typically 3–12% of the contract's total value. This is not a payment or a down payment on the goods; it is a performance bond that stays yours and is returned when the position closes. Its size is calibrated to cover a bad day's move, not the whole contract.

The second is what makes the first sufficient. Positions are marked to market every single day: each evening the exchange revalues every contract at that day's closing price and physically moves cash between the two margin accounts, so the day's gain is credited to one and debited from the other. Losses are never permitted to accumulate unpaid. A contract held for six months is settled 130 times rather than once, which means the clearinghouse is never exposed to more than a single day of movement — which is precisely why a deposit of a few percent is enough.

If daily losses drag your balance below the maintenance margin, you receive a margin call: deposit more cash immediately or have the position closed out at market. Figure 9.2 walks a week of this through for the farmer.

That Wednesday row exposes the hidden cost of hedging with futures, and it is the detail that catches out people who understand the theory. A hedge that is mathematically guaranteed to work at delivery can still demand large amounts of cash today, because mark-to-market does not wait for December. If wheat prices rise, the farmer's futures position loses money daily and she must fund those losses now, even though the offsetting gain — a more valuable crop — will not be realised for months. Being right eventually is no help if you cannot finance the journey, and hedges that were economically sound have destroyed companies for exactly this reason.

Set the two instruments side by side. Futures are standardised, exchange-traded, guaranteed by a clearinghouse, settled in cash every day, and easy to exit by taking the opposite position. Forwards are custom-built, private, exposed to the other party's survival, settled once at the end, and difficult to unwind early because you must renegotiate with the same counterparty.

One practical note that surprises people: most physical commodity futures never result in delivery. Hedgers close their positions out before the delivery month by taking the offsetting trade, keeping the price protection and skipping the trucks of wheat. The physical delivery mechanism still matters even though it is rarely used, because it is what forces the futures price to converge with the actual spot price at expiry — without the possibility of delivery, nothing would tie the two together. Commodities themselves are Section 10.

Worked example: margin, leverage, and the phone call

The clearinghouse's protection is the trader's danger. Buy one E-mini S&P 500 futures contract with the index at 5,000. The contract multiplier is $50 per index point.

Item Amount
Notional exposure (5,000 × $50) $250,000
Initial margin posted ≈ $12,500
Maintenance margin ≈ $11,400
Effective leverage 20×

Now run three days of ordinary market noise:

Day Index Daily P&L Margin balance Event
Mon 5,000 — $12,500 Position opened
Tue 4,970 −$1,500 $11,000 Below maintenance — margin call
Wed 4,900 −$3,500 $9,000 Top up $3,500 or be liquidated
Thu 5,010 +$5,500 — Right view, wrong survival

The index fell 2% and the trader lost 40% of posted capital. It then recovered fully — but a trader who could not wire cash on Wednesday morning was closed out at the bottom and never saw Thursday. Leverage does not change your expected return; it changes your ability to stay in the game long enough to collect it. That distinction has ended more careers than bad forecasting.

Options: the right, but not the obligation

A futures contract obligates both sides. An option is deliberately asymmetric: the buyer acquires a right and the seller takes on an obligation. That asymmetry is the entire substance of the instrument, and everything else about options follows from it.

A call is the right to buy the underlying at a fixed price. A put is the right to sell at a fixed price. That fixed price is the strike, the deadline by which the right must be used is the expiry, and the amount paid up front for the right is the premium.

Because the buyer is acquiring something with no downside obligation, they must pay for it — unlike a future, which costs nothing to enter. The seller, called the writer, receives that premium immediately and in return must perform if the buyer chooses to exercise. The writer has no choice in the matter; the decision belongs entirely to the buyer, who will obviously only exercise when it is to their advantage.

One mechanical detail that trips up beginners: a US equity option contract covers 100 shares. A premium quoted as $3.02 is per share, so one contract costs $302, and every payoff you compute must be multiplied by 100 as well.

Because the buyer exercises only when it helps them, an option's payoff is not a straight line — it bends. Below the strike, a call is simply not exercised and pays nothing, so the buyer's loss stops at the premium they already paid. Above the strike, every dollar the underlying rises is a dollar the call is worth more. Plot that and you get the kinked shapes in Figure 9.3, universally called hockey sticks.

The writer's position is the exact mirror image, and it is worth stating explicitly because it is where the danger in options lives. The call writer's best possible outcome is keeping the premium — that is the maximum, achieved when the option expires worthless. Their worst outcome is unbounded, because the underlying can keep rising and they are obliged to deliver at the strike however far it goes. Buying options means small certain costs and rare large gains; writing them means small certain gains and rare large losses. Both sides sum to zero, as always.

An option's premium at any moment separates cleanly into two components, and keeping them apart makes option prices far less mysterious.

Intrinsic value is what you would collect by exercising immediately. In words: for a call it is the amount by which the stock price exceeds the strike, or zero if the stock is below it — you would never exercise a right to buy at $100 when the market sells at $95, so the value floors at zero rather than going negative. Written compactly that is max(S − K, 0) for a call and max(K − S, 0) for a put.

Time value is everything the option costs above its intrinsic value, and it is payment for the possibility that things improve before expiry. An option on a stock that is currently below the strike has zero intrinsic value and still trades for real money, because the stock might rise before the deadline. Time value is therefore largest when the outcome is most uncertain and falls to exactly zero at expiry, when there is no more possibility left to pay for.

The related vocabulary is moneyness, which just names where the underlying sits relative to the strike. A call with the stock above the strike is in the money, abbreviated ITM, and has positive intrinsic value. With the stock at the strike it is at the money. With the stock below the strike it is out of the money, or OTM, which means its entire price is time value — you are paying purely for the chance of a move, and if nothing happens you lose all of it.

Here is a realistic option chain for a $100 stock with 30 days to expiry. Read it as a grid: strikes run down the rows, and for each strike the market quotes a call and a put, alongside the sensitivity measures explained in the next subsection.

Strike Call bid/ask Call delta Put bid/ask Impl. vol Call moneyness
95 6.15 / 6.30 0.79 0.85 / 0.95 25% ITM: $5 intrinsic + ~$1.20 time
100 2.95 / 3.10 0.53 2.60 / 2.75 25% ATM: all time value
105 1.10 / 1.20 0.27 5.75 / 5.90 25% OTM: all time value

Worked example: leverage cuts both ways

Buy the 100-strike call at $3.02 ($302 per contract). If the stock closes at $110 at expiry, the call is worth $10.00 — a gain of $6.98 per share, or +231%, versus +10% for the stock. If the stock closes at $100 (unchanged!), the call expires worthless: −100% versus 0% for the stock. The option didn't just lever the direction — it added a deadline. You now need to be right about what, how much, and by when. That triple hurdle is why most retail option buyers lose money even when their directional view is decent.

Worked example: three ways to be right about the stock and still lose

Buy the 30-day, $100-strike call for $3.02 ($302 per contract) with the stock at $100. You are correct — the stock goes up. Here is how you lose anyway:

What happens Option value Your P&L
Stock ends at $103 at expiry $3.00 −$2 (−0.7%)
Stock rises to $106 — but only on day 31 $0.00 −$302 (−100%)
Stock rises to $104 next day, but IV falls 30% → 20% ≈ $2.90 ≈ −$12
Stock flat at $100 for 29 days, then jumps to $104 $4.00 +$98 (+32%)

Row 3 is the one that surprises everyone and has a name: volatility crush. It is why buying options into an earnings announcement so often loses money even when the direction is right: you paid for uncertainty, and the announcement removed the uncertainty.

The underlying point is that a stock buyer needs one thing to be right — direction. An option buyer needs three: direction, magnitude, and timing, plus a fourth if implied volatility moves. Each additional condition multiplies the probability of being wrong. That, not the leverage, is the real reason most retail option buyers lose.

What an option is worth: volatility and the Greeks

Why is the at-the-money call in that chain worth $3.02 rather than $1 or $8? The intuition is a probability-weighted average. The option pays whatever the stock ends up above the strike, and nothing at all when it ends below, so its value is the average payoff across all the outcomes the market thinks are possible, weighted by their likelihood and discounted back to today.

That framing immediately tells you what makes options expensive. Anything that widens the distribution of possible ending prices raises the value of a contract that keeps the good outcomes and discards the bad ones. More time to expiry widens it, because prices wander further over longer periods. More volatility widens it, because the stock moves more per day. Notice the asymmetry that makes this work: widening the distribution adds valuable outcomes on the upside while the downside additions are worthless anyway, since below the strike the payoff is already zero and cannot get worse. Uncertainty is straightforwardly good for an option buyer.

Practitioners summarise how an option's price responds to each of its inputs using a set of measures called the Greeks. If you have done any calculus you already know what these are: each Greek is the partial derivative of the option's price with respect to one input, holding the others fixed. There is no new mathematics, only new names.

Delta is the derivative of the option's value with respect to the stock price — the slope. A call with a delta of 0.53 gains about $0.53 when the stock gains $1. Delta has a second reading that is useful and roughly true: it approximates the probability that the option finishes in the money. Look along the chain above and both interpretations line up — the deep in-the-money call has a delta of 0.79, moving nearly as much as the stock and very likely to be exercised, while the out-of-the-money call has 0.27 and behaves like a fractional, unlikely claim.

Theta is the derivative with respect to time, and it is the one that decides most retail outcomes. An option loses value every day that passes without the stock moving, because time value is payment for remaining possibility and each day removes some. The decay is not linear: it accelerates as expiry approaches, since the last week removes a much larger share of the remaining possibility than a week six months out does (Figure 9.4). An option buyer is therefore fighting a clock that speeds up, which is why being directionally right and slightly late still loses money.

Vega is the derivative with respect to volatility: how much the price changes if the market's estimate of future movement rises by one percentage point. It matters because, as the next paragraph explains, volatility is the one input nobody can observe, so it is the input that actually moves.

Look at what goes into pricing an option: the current stock price, the strike, the time remaining, the interest rate, and the volatility of the underlying. Four of those five are facts you can look up. The fifth — volatility over the life of the option — is in the future and cannot be observed by anybody.

This has a consequence that reorganises how the whole market thinks. Since the only genuinely disputable input is volatility, an option's price is effectively a statement about volatility, and options markets are best understood as markets in volatility rather than in direction. Two traders who agree on where a stock will go can still disagree entirely about what its options are worth.

The mechanism for making that explicit is inversion. Take the option's observed market price, hold the four known inputs fixed, and solve backwards for the volatility figure that would produce that price. The answer is the implied volatility shown in the chain above — the market's collective forecast of how much the stock will move, extracted from what people are actually paying. When a trader says options are "expensive," they are not talking about the dollar premium; they mean implied volatility is high relative to the movement they expect to actually occur.

The model that everyone inverts to get that number is Black-Scholes, published in 1973 and the reason a liquid options market exists at all — before it, there was no agreed method for pricing these contracts.

Stated in words rather than symbols, the formula computes what the option is worth as the difference between two terms. The first is the stock price multiplied by the probability-weighted share of outcomes in which you end up owning the stock. The second is the strike price, discounted back to today because you would not pay it until expiry, multiplied by the probability that you exercise at all. In other words: what you expect to receive, minus the present value of what you expect to pay, each weighted by how likely it is to happen. The two N terms are those probabilities, computed from a standard normal distribution under the model's assumption that returns are normally distributed in logarithms.

You do not need the derivation — it lives in Section 18 (Quant Finance). You need to know that it exists, what its five inputs are, that its output is a price you can compute in a dozen lines of code, and that its assumptions are known to be wrong in specific ways that the market corrects for by quoting different implied volatilities at different strikes.

Deep dive: Black-Scholes in ten lines
C = S·N(d1) − K·e−rT·N(d2)
C = call price · S = stock price · K = strike · r = risk-free rate · T = years to expiry · N = standard normal CDF
d1 = ln(S ÷ K) + (r + σ²/2)·Tσ·√T   d2 = d1 − σ·√T
σ = annualized volatility · put price via put-call parity: P = C − S + K·e−rT

As a CS person you can ship this before lunch: N(x) = 0.5 * (1 + erf(x / sqrt(2))) using the error function in any math library, then the two formulas above — about ten lines of Python. Sanity check: S=100, K=100, T=30/365, r=4%, σ=25% gives C ≈ $3.02 and P ≈ $2.69, matching the option chain earlier. Implied volatility is the inverse problem: given a market price, root-find for σ (bisection or Newton's method — the vega is the derivative you need). Note what the buyer's edge must be: the formula assumes volatility; if you pay 25% implied and the stock only realizes 18%, you overpaid even if the model is perfect.

Black-Scholes also gives closed-form Greeks: the call delta is simply N(d1) — which is where the 0.79 / 0.53 / 0.27 column in the chain came from.

Worked example: reading implied volatility as a forecast you can check

Implied volatility is an annualised standard deviation, so you can convert it into a plain-English range in one line:

Expected 1σ move = S × σ × √(T ÷ 365)
S = stock price · σ = implied volatility · T = days to expiry

For a $100 stock with 30% implied volatility and 30 days to expiry: 100 × 0.30 × √(30 ÷ 365) = $8.60. The market is pricing roughly a 68% chance the stock finishes between $91.40 and $108.60, and about a 95% chance between $82.80 and $117.20.

Now the trick every earnings desk uses. The price of the at-the-money straddle (buy the call and the put) is approximately the market's expected absolute move. If a $100 stock's straddle expiring just after earnings costs $8.00, the market expects a move of roughly ±8%. Compare that with what the stock has actually done on its last twelve earnings dates:

Situation What it means
Implied ±8%, historical average ±5% Options look expensive — the market is paying up for fear. Sellers of volatility are favoured.
Implied ±4%, historical average ±7% Options look cheap. Buyers of volatility are favoured.

That comparison — implied versus subsequently realised volatility — is one of the most studied relationships in finance, and it has a persistent finding: implied usually exceeds realised. Option sellers earn a risk premium, on average, for underwriting other people's fear. They also occasionally lose a decade of it in a week, which is the pitfall the next subsection is about. Building the implied-versus-realised series for a handful of tickers is a compact, genuinely impressive portfolio project.

Strategies: composing hockey sticks

Options compose. Because each individual option is a simple kinked function of the underlying price, combining several of them produces a payoff that is the sum of those kinks — and by choosing strikes, expiries and whether you buy or sell each leg, you can construct almost any shape you want at expiry.

The discipline that follows is a simple one, and it is the single most useful habit in options: before entering any multi-leg position, draw or compute its payoff at expiry across the range of underlying prices. Three numbers define it completely — the breakeven price, the maximum gain and the maximum loss — and most bad options trades are ones where the person entering them had never actually looked at those three numbers together. Three canonical compositions are worth knowing by name.

A covered call is owning the stock and writing a call against it. You collect the premium as income immediately, and in exchange you have sold away every dollar of gain above the strike — if the stock doubles, you deliver it at the strike and keep none of the excess. The position is often marketed as generating income from a portfolio, which is true and incomplete: you have converted uncertain future upside into certain present cash, which is a good trade only if the upside you sold was worth less than the premium you received.

A protective put is owning the stock and buying a put on it, and it is straightforwardly insurance. The strike is the floor below which your losses stop; the premium is what the policy costs. As with any insurance, the premium is a certain cost paid against an uncertain loss, and you should expect to lose money on it most years — that is what insurance is, not a sign it was a bad idea.

A straddle is buying a call and a put at the same strike and expiry. You profit if the stock moves far in either direction and lose if it sits still, so you are not betting on direction at all — you are betting on magnitude. This is the purest expression of a view on volatility rather than on price.

Finally, the mirror of insurance is the cash-secured put: you write a put and hold enough cash to buy the shares if you are assigned. You are selling someone else downside protection and keeping the premium if it turns out not to have been needed. It is frequently described as a way to buy a stock you wanted anyway at a discount, which is accurate in the good case and quietly omits the bad one — you are obliged to buy precisely in the scenarios where the stock has fallen.

Build each of them in the tool below. Watch the readouts rather than only the shape of the line: breakeven, maximum gain and maximum loss are the three numbers that actually define what you have constructed, and a payoff diagram that looks attractive can carry a maximum loss you would never accept if it were stated in dollars.

Option payoff builder

Pick a strategy, drag the strike and premium, and read the P&L-at-expiry line against just holding the stock. Stock legs assume shares bought at $100; all figures are per share (×100 for one contract).

Breakeven(s)—
Max gain—
Max loss—
Net premium—

━ strategy P&L at expiry  ·  ╌ stock only (bought at $100)  ·  ● breakeven. For the straddle, equal strikes is the classic straddle; drag the put strike K2 below the call strike to build a strangle.

Two things are worth deliberately producing in that builder.

Set up a covered call with a strike of 80 while holding stock bought at 100. There are premium levels at which the position cannot break even under any outcome: the call caps your gains at a level below your purchase price while leaving the entire downside with you, so no path leads to profit. It is an extreme case, but it makes the general principle visible — writing calls gives away upside, and if you give away more than the premium compensates for, no amount of the stock behaving well will rescue it.

Then build a straddle and look at how far apart the two breakevens sit. You paid two premiums, so the stock must move by more than their combined cost before you make anything at all — and it must do so before expiry. This is where the earnings-announcement trap lives. If everyone expects a large move around an earnings date, that expectation is already in the option prices through elevated implied volatility, so you are not paid for the move happening; you are paid only if the move is larger than the market had already priced. A stock that jumps 8% when the options implied 10% loses money for the straddle holder, which is why implied volatility typically collapses the moment the announcement is out.

Common pitfall: selling options is not free money

Short option strategies win small amounts very often — the writer keeps the premium in most months — which makes the P&L history look like a beautiful, smooth, upward line. Right up until it isn't. The distribution is extremely skewed: frequent small gains, rare catastrophic losses. Traders call it picking up pennies in front of a steamroller. Funds that sold volatility this way (see the February 2018 "Volmageddon" episode, and Section 17 for the general pattern) lost years of gains in days. If a strategy's backtest never loses, ask what tail it is short — your statistics background is exactly the edge here: always look at the full distribution, not the mean.

Worked example: a covered call, month by month

You own 100 shares at $100. You sell one 30-day call struck at $105 and collect $2.00 per share ($200). Four possible worlds at expiry:

Stock at expiry Stock P&L Option P&L Total vs just holding
$90 −$1,000 +$200 −$800 +$200 better
$100 $0 +$200 +$200 +$200 better
$105 +$500 +$200 +$700 +$200 better
$130 +$3,000 −$2,300 +$700 −$2,300 worse

Three worlds out of four look great, which is exactly the trap. The strategy wins slightly, often — and gives away the one outcome that makes long-run equity returns what they are. Equity returns are heavily positively skewed: a small number of enormous winners carry the index. Systematically selling the right tail is systematically selling the source of the return.

The seductive arithmetic is also worth defusing. $2 on $100 for 30 days looks like "2% a month, 24% a year." It is not, because the months where you keep the full premium are not the months that determine your total return. Compare an actual buy-write index against its plain equity benchmark over a decade: the buy-write typically shows lower volatility and lower total return. Both halves of that sentence are the point — you sold volatility and you were paid for it, but you were paid in reduced upside, not in free money.

Swaps: trading cash-flow streams

A swap is an agreement to exchange one stream of future cash flows for another. Where a future concerns a single date and an option concerns a single right, a swap runs for years and settles repeatedly.

The workhorse is the interest-rate swap. One side agrees to pay a fixed rate, say 4%, for five years. The other pays a floating rate that resets periodically with the market — today usually SOFR, the benchmark that replaced LIBOR. On each payment date the two amounts are compared and only the difference actually moves, from whoever owes more to whoever owes less.

Both legs are calculated on a notional amount — $100 million, say — that is never exchanged by either party. It exists purely as the number the percentages are applied to. That detail matters for interpreting headlines. When you read that hundreds of trillions of dollars of derivatives are outstanding, that figure is the sum of notionals, and the cash genuinely at risk is a small fraction of it: on a $100 million swap where the two rates differ by half a point, the money that actually changes hands is $500,000 a year. The notional measures the size of the reference, not the size of the exposure.

What the instrument accomplishes is converting one kind of interest obligation into another without touching the underlying loan. A company that borrowed at a floating rate and now wants certainty does not have to refinance; it enters a swap that pays it floating and charges it fixed, and the floating leg cancels against its loan, leaving it economically fixed.

Worked example: fixing a floating loan

TechCo borrowed $100M from its bank at SOFR + 1.25%, floating. The CFO can't budget around a rate that resets constantly, so TechCo enters a swap: pay 4.00% fixed, receive SOFR, on a $100M notional. Only the net moves each period:

Year 1, SOFR averages 3.50%: TechCo owes 4.00% and is owed 3.50%, so it pays the dealer the net 0.50% = $500,000. Year 2, SOFR averages 4.50%: now TechCo receives the net 0.50% = $500,000. Combine the swap with the loan and the SOFR terms cancel: TechCo's all-in cost is 4.00% + 1.25% = 5.25% fixed, forever, no matter what the Fed does. Same trick, reversed, is how banks and insurers manage the rate risk in their bond portfolios.

The other swap worth knowing is the credit default swap, or CDS, which is insurance on a bond in everything but legal name. The protection buyer pays a periodic fee — say 1% of the notional per year — and if the referenced borrower defaults, the protection seller compensates them for the loss.

Used in moderation it does something genuinely useful. A bank that has lent to a client and does not want more exposure to that client can buy protection instead of selling the loan, which lets it manage its risk without ending a commercial relationship. And because CDS contracts trade continuously, the price of protection is a live market estimate of default probability — often adjusting faster than the rating agencies from Section 8, whose opinions are updated in discrete steps and after deliberation. When CDS spreads on a company widen sharply, the market is repricing its survival in real time.

The word "insurance" is doing something misleading, though, and the next callout explains why. Ordinary insurance requires you to own the thing insured. A CDS does not, so it is possible to buy protection on debt you have no exposure to — which converts an insurance contract into a directional bet on somebody else's failure, and allows far more protection to exist than there is debt to protect.

Real world: CDS and 2008

Two features made CDS the star of the 2008 crisis. You can buy protection on bonds you don't own — like insuring your neighbor's house — so total CDS notional grew to a multiple of the underlying debt. And because CDS were then private, uncleared contracts with little margin, sellers could write essentially unlimited protection. AIG's financial products unit sold protection on mortgage securities against which it held almost no reserves; when housing cracked, collateral calls arrived it could not meet, and the US government committed roughly $182 billion so AIG's failure wouldn't cascade through every counterparty. Post-crisis reforms pushed standard swaps into clearinghouses with daily margin — futures-style plumbing, precisely because that plumbing worked. The full story is in Section 17 (Crises).

Your edge

A swap is just two projected cash-flow vectors netted against each other, and its fair value is the difference of their present values — discounting you already know from Section 1. Swap desks literally hire people to build and maintain those discount curves in code. If you can write clean numerical Python, this corner of finance is one of the most natural entry points (see Section 20).

Worked example: pricing default insurance

A CDS is quoted in basis points per year on a notional. You buy protection on $10,000,000 of a BB-rated company's debt at a spread of 300bp:

Leg Amount
You pay, per year (3.00% × $10M) $300,000
Quarterly payment $75,000
If it defaults with a 40% recovery, you receive $6,000,000
Payments before you break even 20 years

Invert it and the spread becomes a probability. If the market charges 300bp for a 60% loss given default, it is implying roughly 300 ÷ 60 = 5% cumulative default probability per unit of spread duration — the market's own estimate of how likely this company is to fail, updated continuously, published, and available before the ratings agencies move. Analysts routinely trust CDS spreads over ratings for exactly that reason.

Both directions are useful. A bond investor buys protection to keep the yield and shed the credit risk. A speculator with no bonds at all buys protection as a pure bet — "naked" CDS, and the mechanism behind the trades portrayed in The Big Short: paying a few hundred basis points a year for a payoff of many multiples if subprime mortgage pools failed.

Real world: three times swaps moved history

  • Greece, 2001. Currency swaps arranged with Goldman Sachs at off-market exchange rates converted future payments into cash today, which was recorded as a swap rather than as borrowing. Greece's reported deficit met euro-entry criteria; the real one did not. The technique was legal at the time and is a permanent illustration that a derivative can restate a balance sheet without changing any economics.
  • UK pensions, September 2022. Defined-benefit pension funds used interest-rate swaps and repo — "liability-driven investment" — to match 30-year obligations while keeping money invested elsewhere. When an unfunded budget sent gilt yields up over 100bp in days, the swaps moved against them and collateral calls arrived in hours. Funds sold gilts to raise cash, which pushed yields higher, which triggered more calls. The Bank of England had to buy gilts to break the loop. A hedging programme, correctly designed for its purpose, became a systemic accelerant through collateral mechanics alone.
  • Archegos, March 2021. A family office held enormous equity positions through total return swaps rather than shares. Because the banks were the registered owners, no disclosure of a large stake was required and no single bank could see the total. When the positions fell, the collateral calls could not be met. Losses across prime brokers exceeded $10 billion; Credit Suisse alone lost about $5.5 billion, a wound it never fully recovered from.

A common thread runs through all three: the derivative did not create the underlying exposure so much as it changed who could see it. Whenever you evaluate a firm's risk, the question "what is on the balance sheet?" is strictly weaker than "what is the economic exposure, wherever it is booked?"

Check your understanding

1. A farmer shorts wheat futures at $6.00 to hedge her harvest, and by delivery wheat trades at $6.80. Which statement is right?

The hedge locks the price in both directions: the $0.80 futures loss is offset by an extra $0.80 on the physical crop. She gave up the upside — that is the cost of certainty, not a mistake. And no one is exempt from margin.

2. You are long one crude oil futures contract (1,000 barrels) bought at $80. Today's settlement price is $78. What happens to your margin account today?

Mark-to-market is unconditional: a $2 drop × 1,000 barrels = $2,000 leaves your account this evening. Whether you then get a margin call depends on where that leaves your balance relative to maintenance margin.

3. You paid $6 for a call with a $100 strike. At expiry the stock is at $104. Which is true?

Moneyness and profit are different questions. Intrinsic value at expiry is max(104 − 100, 0) = $4, so you exercise (worthless it is not) — but you paid $6 for it, so P&L = 4 − 6 = −$2. Breakeven was $106.

4. A strategy of selling out-of-the-money puts has been profitable 34 of the last 36 months. What is the most statistically sound reaction?

Short-option P&L is heavily skewed — the mean of the distribution can be negative even with a 94% win rate if the rare losses are large enough. "Picking up pennies in front of a steamroller" is a statement about tails, and hit rate ignores tails.

5. A firm pays 3% fixed and receives SOFR on a $50M notional swap. SOFR averages 2% this year. What cash actually moves?

Swaps settle net: 3% owed minus 2% received = 1% of $50M = $500,000 paid by the firm. The notional is only a reference number. And paying fixed while receiving floating hurts when floating rates are low — the fixed payer wins when rates rise.

Key takeaways

  • A derivative's value is a formula evaluated against an underlying price. It relocates risk from hedgers to speculators — both roles are essential — and it is zero-sum before costs.
  • Futures lock in a price today via a standardized, clearinghouse-guaranteed contract; daily mark-to-market and margin calls mean even a "correct" hedge can demand cash along the way.
  • Options are asymmetric: buyers pay a premium for capped-loss, open-ended-gain payoffs; writers accept the mirror image. Value = intrinsic + time value, and the deadline is half the bet.
  • The Greeks are just partial derivatives: delta is the slope versus the stock, theta the daily time decay (which accelerates near expiry), vega the sensitivity to volatility — the one input the market actually trades, via implied volatility and Black-Scholes.
  • Strategies compose kinked payoffs: covered calls trade upside for income, protective puts buy a floor, straddles bet on magnitude rather than direction. Judge every strategy by breakeven, max gain, max loss.
  • Selling options harvests frequent small gains against rare huge losses — a skewed distribution that a win rate cannot summarize. Most retail option buyers lose money; these are professional hedging tools first.
  • Swaps exchange cash-flow streams on a notional that never moves; an interest-rate swap converts floating debt to fixed. CDS are default insurance whose unmargined excesses helped detonate 2008 — and why swaps now clear like futures.

Part II · Financial Markets & Instruments

10. FX, Commodities and Alternative Investments

Beyond stocks and bonds sits a sprawling world: the currency market that dwarfs every other, commodities you can only sensibly touch through futures, and the "alternatives" — real estate, private equity, hedge funds, crypto — that dominate institutional portfolios and finance-job postings alike. By the end of this section you'll be able to read an FX quote, hedge a currency exposure, compute a cap rate, and decode a 2-and-20 fee structure.

The FX market: the biggest market you've never seen a building for

The foreign exchange (FX) market turns over roughly $7.5 trillion a day, according to the Bank for International Settlements' 2022 survey. To put that in proportion: FX trades more in a week than the world's stock markets trade in a year. The reason is that currency is not only an asset people speculate on; it is the settlement layer under every cross-border transaction, so every import, every foreign investment and every hedge on either passes through this market.

There is no exchange floor and no central venue. FX is a decentralised network of dealer banks quoting prices to each other and to clients, open continuously from Monday morning in Asia to Friday evening in New York — an over-the-counter market with the same structure as the swaps market from Section 9 (Derivatives). One consequence worth noting up front: because there is no single exchange, there is no single official price, only a very tight band of quotes from competing dealers.

Currencies trade in pairs, and this is a genuine conceptual difference from every other market rather than a notational quirk. A share has a price in dollars. A currency has no price except in terms of another currency, so every FX trade is simultaneously a purchase of one thing and a sale of another. There is no way to simply "buy dollars" — you buy them with something.

The quote convention catches out everyone at first, so slow down on it. EUR/USD = 1.10 means one euro costs 1.10 US dollars. The first currency named, EUR, is the base currency: it is the thing being priced, and there is always exactly one unit of it. The second, USD, is the quote currency: it supplies the units on the price tag. Read it as a price label on a euro, written in dollars.

Get that straight and the confusing part resolves. When EUR/USD rises from 1.10 to 1.20, a euro now costs more dollars, so the euro strengthened and the dollar weakened — even though your eye reads a rising number containing "USD" and wants to conclude the dollar went up. The number is the price of the base currency, so the number rising always means the first currency got stronger.

Price moves are measured in pips, conventionally the fourth decimal place, or 0.0001, for most pairs. That sounds absurdly fine-grained until you attach a position size to it. On a standard contract of €100,000, one pip is 0.0001 × 100,000 = $10, and ordinary daily ranges run to a hundred pips or more. Trading sizes in this market are large precisely because the percentage moves are small, and that combination is what makes the fourth decimal worth caring about.

Most volume is spot: exchange at today's rate, settling in two business days. But a very large share is forwards and swaps — the same instruments from Section 9, applied to money itself rather than to wheat or interest rates. That share is large because the dominant users are not speculators but companies and investors with future foreign-currency obligations, and a forward is how you fix the rate on something you will not pay for until November.

What moves currencies is mostly what you already met in Section 5 (Fiscal Policy, Debt & Trade), and the four forces are worth restating here in the terms this section uses.

Interest-rate differentials dominate over days and weeks. Money moves toward higher yields, and moving it requires buying the currency, so a country whose central bank (Section 4) raises rates relative to others tends to see its currency bid up. Inflation differentials dominate over years: a currency losing purchasing power at home eventually loses it abroad too, because holders will not accept a steadily eroding store of value. Trade and capital flows act as the structural undercurrent — a country running a persistent deficit needs continuous financing, and the terms on which it gets that financing show up in the exchange rate.

On top of all three sits risk sentiment, which can override the others entirely for weeks at a time. In a panic, money runs to the dollar, the yen and the Swiss franc regardless of interest rates or trade positions, because what investors want in a crisis is not yield but the deepest, most liquid market they can reach.

Interest-rate differentials also power the most famous strategy in the market, the carry trade. The mechanics are simple: borrow in a currency with low interest rates, convert the proceeds, and invest in a currency with high ones. Borrow yen at 0.5%, convert to Australian dollars, invest at 4.5%, and collect the four-point gap.

As Section 5 pointed out, this looks like free money and is not, because the exchange rate can move against you on the way back. The trade earns its four points only if the yen does not strengthen. If it strengthens 5%, converting back costs you more than a year of carry, and you have lost money on a position that was profitable every single day until it wasn't.

The distribution of outcomes is the thing to understand, because it recurs throughout finance. Carry trades produce small, steady, highly regular gains for long stretches, and then very occasionally an enormous loss when everyone attempts to unwind simultaneously — and everyone unwinds simultaneously precisely because they all put the trade on for the same reason. The exits compress into days. Traders describe it as picking up nickels in front of a steamroller, and the August 2024 unwinding of the yen carry trade, which briefly knocked several percent off global equity markets, is a reminder that the steamroller is not hypothetical.

Currency moves: who wins?

Drag EUR/USD away from the 1.10 baseline and watch who gains and who bleeds — the same move, four opposite experiences.

At the 1.10 baseline — no change yet.

Who Position Dollar amount now vs 1.10 baseline
US importer owes a €1,000,000 invoice $1,100,000 —
US exporter books €1,000,000 of sales $1,100,000 —
US tourist faces a €3,000 hotel bill $3,300 —
US investor holds €100,000 of European stocks (flat in €) $110,000 —

Payers of euros (importer, tourist) want a weak euro; receivers and holders of euro assets (exporter, investor) want a strong one. Same price, opposite rooting interests.

Worked example: the trip that teaches the quote convention

Everyone gets EUR/USD backwards once. Here is the fix that sticks. The number is always units of the second currency per one of the first. EUR/USD = 1.10 is "1.10 dollars per euro."

You are… EUR/USD goes 1.10 → 1.20 Effect on you
An American touring Europe The euro got stronger Worse — your dollars buy fewer euros; the trip costs about 9% more.
A European touring the US Your euro got stronger Better — each euro buys $1.20 instead of $1.10.
A US company selling into Europe — Better — euro revenue converts to more dollars.
A European company selling into the US — Worse — dollar revenue converts to fewer euros (the exporter's classic squeeze).

Now the size of the market in one comparison. FX turns over about $7.5 trillion per day. The entire US stock market trades roughly $500 billion a day. FX does the annual volume of the US equity market in something like two weeks — and it has no exchange, no building, and no closing bell, running 24 hours across Sydney, Tokyo, London, and New York.

How companies live with FX

For a company operating in several countries, currency risk is not an opportunity to be traded but a condition to be managed, and it arrives in two distinct forms that call for different responses.

Transaction exposure is risk attached to real cash flows. You have signed a contract to pay a supplier €2 million in ninety days, or you will receive ¥400 million from a customer next quarter. The amount in the foreign currency is fixed; the amount in your own currency is not, and it will be determined by an exchange rate you cannot predict. Real money is genuinely at stake.

Translation exposure is an accounting effect with no cash consequence at all. A US parent company must restate its German subsidiary's euro results in dollars for its consolidated accounts, so reported figures move with the exchange rate even when nothing about the business changed. A subsidiary earning €50 million appears as $55 million when the rate is 1.10 and $50 million at parity — a reported decline of $5 million produced entirely by a currency quote, with identical sales, identical customers and identical costs underneath.

This is why companies report "constant-currency" growth alongside the headline figures: the constant-currency number strips the translation effect out so you can see whether the business actually grew. When you read filings in Section 11, knowing which of the two numbers you are looking at is the difference between analysing a company and analysing an exchange rate.

Transaction exposure is the one companies actively hedge, normally using the currency forwards from Section 9: agree today the rate at which you will convert in ninety days, and the uncertainty disappears.

The reasoning behind hedging it is worth stating explicitly, because it is not "we think the euro will fall." A hedge gives up the favourable outcome along with the unfavourable one — you have fixed the rate, so a move in your favour now benefits you not at all. A company accepts that trade because its competence and its competitive advantage lie in manufacturing, or software, or logistics, and not in forecasting currencies. Carrying an unhedged currency position means running a second, unrelated business that you have no particular skill in, using money that belongs to shareholders who bought into the first one. Translation exposure, by contrast, is usually left unhedged: spending real money to smooth an accounting presentation that has no cash effect is difficult to justify.

Worked example: a European exporter hedges dollar revenue

A German machine-tool maker signs a contract to receive $5,000,000 in six months. Its costs are in euros, so a weakening dollar (EUR/USD rising) directly shrinks its margin. It sells the dollars forward at today's six-month forward rate of 1.10, locking in $5,000,000 ÷ 1.10 = €4,545,455, guaranteed.

Six months later, suppose spot has moved to 1.20. Unhedged, the $5M would convert to only $5,000,000 ÷ 1.20 = €4,166,667. The hedge preserved €378,788 — likely more than the entire profit margin on the machines. If instead spot had fallen to 1.00, the unhedged value would have been €5,000,000 and the hedge "cost" €454,545 of foregone upside. That's the deal: certainty in both directions.

Your edge

Corporate FX desks and treasury analytics teams are heavy consumers of data skills: forecasting exposures from ERP data, computing hedge ratios, simulating rate scenarios. "Treasury analyst" is one of the most underrated data-adjacent entry points into finance.

Deep dive: where forward FX rates come from

Forward rates are not a forecast — they're arbitrage arithmetic, exactly like the futures pricing in Section 9. If US one-year rates are 4% and euro rates are 2%, the one-year forward must satisfy F = S × (1 + rUSD) ÷ (1 + rEUR) = 1.10 × 1.04 ÷ 1.02 ≈ 1.1216. Why: holding dollars for a year earns 4%; holding euros earns 2% plus whatever the currency does. If the forward sat anywhere else, you could borrow one currency, lend the other, lock the forward, and print riskless profit. This relationship is called covered interest parity, and it's one of the most reliably enforced identities in finance. Note the implication: the higher-yielding currency trades at a forward discount — the forward market "gives back" the carry.

Real world: the same dollar move, four corporate outcomes

In 2022 the dollar rose about 15% against a basket of currencies — its strongest run in two decades. One macro event, read four different ways depending on which side of the currency you sat:

Company Exposure What the strong dollar did
Apple, Microsoft ~50% of sales abroad, costs in USD Foreign revenue shrank in dollars. Both blamed FX for multi-billion-dollar revenue drags in their 2022 reports.
A US importer of European goods Buys in EUR, sells in USD Windfall — European goods got 15% cheaper in dollar terms.
An emerging-market government with dollar debt Owes USD, earns local currency Debt burden jumped in local terms — the mechanism behind repeated EM crises.
A Japanese carmaker exporting to the US Costs in JPY, sells in USD Windfall — dollar revenue converted to far more yen. Toyota's 2022 operating profit got a huge FX tailwind.

This is why any multinational's earnings call separates "constant-currency" growth from reported growth. Constant currency strips out the FX move to show whether the underlying business actually grew. When you analyse a global company, that is the number to trust — reported revenue can fall while the business expands, purely because the dollar moved.

Commodities: futures curves, oil and the strange case of gold

Commodities — oil, natural gas, wheat, copper, gold — are the only asset class you could in principle have delivered to your driveway. That physical reality is exactly why almost no financial investor holds them physically.

Consider what owning a barrel of oil actually entails. You must store it, which costs money and requires a tank somebody owns. You must insure it. You must eventually transport it. And throughout, it generates no income whatsoever — a share pays dividends and a bond pays coupons while you hold them, but a barrel of oil sitting in a tank produces nothing and costs you rent. Every one of those is a reason the physical route is reserved for people who actually use the commodity.

So financial exposure comes through the futures contracts of Section 9: standardised, liquid, cash-settled in practice, and requiring no warehouse. You get the price exposure without the barrel. That substitution is clean in principle and introduces one complication that catches even professionals, which is the subject of the next two paragraphs.

The complication is that a futures contract has an expiry date and a commodity does not, so holding commodity exposure through futures means continuously replacing expiring contracts with later ones — and the price relationship between them determines a large part of your return.

Plot the price of each futures contract against its delivery month and you get a curve. If contracts for later delivery cost more than the current spot price, the curve is in contango. This is the normal condition for a storable commodity, and the reason is arbitrage: anyone could buy oil today, store it and deliver it in six months, so the six-month price cannot exceed today's price by more than what storage, insurance and the interest on the money would cost. Contango is those carrying costs made visible.

If later contracts cost less than spot, the curve is in backwardation, which signals that the physical commodity is scarce right now. Someone who needs oil this month to keep a refinery running will pay a premium over the future price, because a promise of oil in December does not run a refinery in June. Backwardation is the market pricing immediate availability.

Here is why the shape of that curve reaches your returns. Because futures expire, a long-term investor must roll the position: sell the contract that is about to expire and buy the next one out.

In contango, that means repeatedly selling a cheap near-dated contract and buying a more expensive far-dated one. And as each contract you hold ages toward its own expiry, its price converges toward spot — it slides down the curve you paid to climb. You bought at the higher far price and will sell at something nearer the lower spot price, over and over. That systematic drag is called negative roll yield, and its practical effect is startling to people meeting it for the first time: an oil ETF can lose 20% over a year in which the spot price of oil ended exactly where it started, purely from the cost of rolling.

In backwardation the identical mechanics run in your favour — you sell the expensive near contract and buy a cheaper far one, and the convergence works for you. The general lesson is that commodity futures returns have two components, the change in the commodity's price and the roll yield, and over long holding periods the second can dominate the first. If you have built data pipelines with scheduled jobs, the shape is familiar: roll yield is a recurring cost or credit baked into the schedule, entirely independent of what the underlying data does.

Two markets are worth knowing individually. Oil is the macroeconomic commodity, because energy is an input to producing and transporting almost everything, which is why an oil shock propagates into the general price level (the supply-shock mechanism of Section 3). The two benchmarks are WTI, traded on NYMEX and referencing US crude delivered at Cushing, Oklahoma, and Brent, traded on ICE and referencing North Sea crude, which is the global reference. Contracts are 1,000 barrels.

In April 2020, WTI futures settled at negative $37 a barrel, and the episode is worth understanding rather than filing as an oddity. Demand had collapsed with the pandemic while production continued, and storage at Cushing was full. Anyone holding the expiring contract was obliged to take delivery of physical oil they had nowhere to put — so they paid others to take the obligation off their hands. A negative price is impossible for an asset you can costlessly decline; it becomes entirely possible for a contract that obliges you to receive something. It is the cleanest available demonstration that a futures price is about delivery logistics and not only about abstract value.

Gold does not fit the pattern of the others. Its industrial demand is tiny relative to its price, it generates no cash flow, and it costs money to store — yet central banks hold roughly 35,000 tonnes of it and have been net buyers in recent years.

The honest framing is that gold is a monetary asset rather than a commodity: its function is to be a store of value that no government can create more of. That explains its behaviour better than any supply-and-demand story about jewellery. Gold tends to rise when real interest rates fall, because the main cost of holding gold is the interest you gave up by not holding cash or bonds — and when that forgone interest is near zero, or negative after inflation, holding a zero-yielding asset costs you nothing. It also rises when confidence in monetary institutions weakens, for the same structural reason.

What you cannot do is value it with the discounting machinery of Section 1 and Section 13, because there are no cash flows to discount. Any statement that gold is worth $2,000 or $4,000 an ounce is an argument about supply, demand and the behaviour of other holders — not a valuation in the sense the rest of this book uses the word. That is a real analytical limitation and not a reason to dismiss the asset; it simply means the tools that apply to it are different ones.

Worked example: why an oil fund can fall while oil rises

This is the single most counterintuitive fact in commodities, and it costs retail investors real money every year. A commodity ETF does not own oil in a tank; it owns futures and must roll them before expiry. Say oil spot is $80, and the futures curve is in contango:

Contract Price
1-month future (you own this) $80.00
2-month future (you must roll into it) $81.60

Each month you sell at $80.00 and rebuy at $81.60 — a 2% loss on the roll, every month, even if spot oil never moves. Annualised, that is roughly a 27% headwind. Over 2009–2020 the largest oil ETF (USO) lost the overwhelming majority of its value while spot oil was roughly flat to higher, entirely because of this roll cost.

The reverse curve, backwardation, pays you to roll. So the practical rule for any commodity position: your return has three parts — spot change, roll yield (the curve), and interest on the collateral — and for a long-term holder the curve shape often matters more than the spot price. This is exactly the kind of hidden structural cost that separates people who read the contract from people who read the headline.

Real estate and REITs: leverage plus a yield you can compute

Real estate is the largest asset class in the world by value, and its defining financial feature is not the buildings but the leverage used to buy them. Almost nobody purchases a $500,000 property with $500,000 of cash. They put down $100,000 and borrow $400,000.

Work through what that does. The property rises 10%, which is $50,000. Your own money in the deal was $100,000, so your equity has grown by 50%. The property falls 20%, which is $100,000 — and your equity is gone entirely, while the $400,000 mortgage remains exactly $400,000, because debt does not share in losses. The asset moved 20%; you lost 100%.

Nothing about the building changed in either case. The same property produces radically different risk depending purely on how it was financed, and the multiplier is the ratio of the asset's value to your own money in it. Keep this in mind for Section 16 (Risk Management), because it is the engine underneath most property busts including 2008: when prices fall by more than the equity cushion, borrowers owe more than the asset is worth, and the losses land on lenders who assumed the collateral would cover them.

Valuing a property starts with the income it produces. A property's net operating income (NOI) is the rent it collects minus the costs of operating it: maintenance, insurance, property tax, management fees. Crucially it excludes the mortgage. The reason for that exclusion is that NOI is meant to describe what the building itself earns, independent of how a particular owner chose to finance it — two buyers with different loans should compute the same NOI for the same building.

The headline valuation measure follows directly. Stated in words: the capitalisation rate is the annual income the property generates divided by its price, which makes it the yield you would earn if you bought the building outright with no borrowing. A building producing $60,000 a year and costing $1 million has a cap rate of 6%, and that figure is directly comparable to a bond yield or the earnings yield on a stock from Section 7:

Cap rate = NOI ÷ Price
NOI = annual rent − operating costs (excluding mortgage) · Price = purchase price · result = unlevered yield

Worked example

A rental property costs $500,000, brings in $42,000 of annual rent and costs $12,000 a year to run. NOI = 42,000 − 12,000 = $30,000, so the cap rate is 30,000 ÷ 500,000 = 6.0%. Compare that to the 10-year Treasury from Section 8: if Treasuries yield 4%, the property offers a 2-percentage-point spread as compensation for illiquidity, vacancies, leaky roofs and tenant risk. If Treasuries rose to 6%, that spread vanishes — which is exactly why property prices sag when rates climb.

Cap rate calculator

Price a property like an analyst: change the numbers and watch the yield spread against Treasuries.

NOI (rent − costs)$30,000
Cap rate6.00%
Spread vs Treasury+2.0 pp

Individual buildings are large, indivisible and slow to sell, which makes them a poor fit for investors who want to adjust their positions. The market built a liquid wrapper around them: the REIT.

A REIT is a listed company whose business is owning income-producing property — apartment blocks, warehouses, shopping centres, mobile phone towers, data centres. The structure exists because of a specific tax bargain: in exchange for distributing at least 90% of taxable income to shareholders as dividends, the REIT itself pays no corporate tax, so rental income is taxed once in the investor's hands rather than twice. That is why REITs pay unusually high dividends — it is a legal requirement, not generosity.

What you get is diversified property exposure with stock-market liquidity: buying a REIT or a REIT index fund takes seconds and can be reversed in seconds. What you also get, and this is the part investors underestimate, is stock-market behaviour. Because REITs trade on exchanges alongside the equities of Section 7, they are repriced by the same investors reacting to the same fears. In 2008 they fell in lockstep with equities, at the exact moment their holders were relying on real estate to behave differently from stocks. The liquidity is genuinely valuable and it has a price: it imports equity-market volatility into an asset whose underlying buildings did not move nearly as much.

Worked example: how leverage turns 5% into 25%

Real estate's defining feature is not the building — it is the mortgage. Buy a $500,000 property with 20% down and watch what leverage does to an ordinary 5% price move:

All cash 20% down + mortgage
Your equity in $500,000 $100,000
Property rises 5% → gain +$25,000 +$25,000
Return on your equity +5% +25%
Property falls 5% → return on equity −5% −25%
Property falls 20% → return on equity −20% −100% (wiped out)

The 5× leverage from a 20%-down mortgage multiplies every price move by five, in both directions. That is the entire story of both housing wealth and housing crises: in 2006–2011, US home prices fell about 27% nationally, and for millions of buyers with small down payments, a 27% price fall was a 100%-plus loss of equity — the definition of "underwater," and the reason foreclosures cascaded.

Note this is leverage on top of the cap-rate yield from the widget above. A property bought at a 6% cap rate, financed at a 4.5% mortgage, earns the 1.5% spread on the borrowed money too — "positive leverage." When financing costs rise above the cap rate, that flips to negative leverage, which is precisely what froze commercial real estate transactions in 2023–24. The cap rate and the mortgage rate crossing is the whole plot.

Private equity and venture capital: illiquidity as a business model

Private equity buys entire companies rather than slices of them — either taking a listed company off the public market or acquiring one that was never listed. Owning the whole thing is the point: it means control, so the owner can change management, strategy and financing without persuading anybody.

The signature transaction is the leveraged buyout, which applies the property-leverage arithmetic from earlier to an entire business, with one important twist: the debt is borrowed against the company being purchased and sits on its balance sheet, not the buyer's. The acquired company services the loans out of its own cash flow.

Follow a stylised deal through. A firm buys a company generating $125 million of EBITDA at a multiple of 8 times, so the price is $1,000 million. It funds that with $400 million of its investors' money and $600 million of debt loaded onto the company. Over five years it improves operations enough to lift EBITDA to $150 million, and uses the company's cash flow to pay debt down from $600 million to $300 million.

Now the exit. Selling at the same 8 times multiple values the business at $1,200 million; subtract the $300 million of remaining debt and the equity is worth $900 million. Against $400 million invested, that is 2.25 times the money in, roughly 17.6% a year.

It is worth decomposing where that return came from, because the answer is often misunderstood. EBITDA grew 20%, which contributed. But the larger effects were financial: paying down $300 million of debt transferred that value straight to the equity holder, and the leverage meant every dollar of enterprise-value gain landed on a $400 million base instead of a $1,000 million one. Notice also what would happen if the exit multiple were 7 rather than 8 — the equity would be worth $750 million, and half the profit would evaporate. Returns in this business depend heavily on the price paid and the price received, which is why LBO performance correlates so strongly with the interest-rate and valuation environment rather than only with operating skill.

Venture capital plays the opposite statistical game. Leveraged buyouts apply debt to stable, predictable cash flows; venture capital funds companies with no cash flows at all and accepts that most will fail, on the expectation that the distribution of outcomes has an extremely fat right tail.

Take a stylised fund making twenty investments of $1 million each. Thirteen go to zero. Five return roughly what went in, $1 million each. One returns five times, $5 million. One returns thirty times, $30 million. The fund collected $40 million on $20 million invested, which is a respectable doubling — and the single best investment returned more than the other nineteen combined.

If you have worked with data, the shape is immediately recognisable: this is a power law, where the mean is meaningless without the tail and the median outcome — zero — tells you nothing about the fund's return. Two consequences follow that distinguish venture investing from everything else in this section. Being wrong about the thirteen failures costs almost nothing, because the maximum loss on each is the amount invested. Missing the one thirty-bagger costs more than all thirteen failures put together. So the discipline is not estimating an average outcome accurately; it is being sure you have a stake in the extreme outcomes, which is why venture investors will fund things that are probably going to fail and refuse things that are probably going to do modestly well.

Both run on identical fund plumbing, and the vocabulary appears in every job description in the industry. The investors — pension funds, university endowments, sovereign wealth funds, wealthy individuals — are limited partners, or LPs: they supply capital, have no role in running the fund, and cannot lose more than they committed. The firm managing the money is the general partner, or GP.

LPs do not hand over cash at the outset. They commit an amount, and the GP calls it down in instalments over several years as deals are found. That matters practically: an LP who has committed $50 million must keep liquidity available for calls that arrive on the GP's schedule rather than their own.

Fees follow the well-known 2-and-20 pattern: roughly 2% a year of committed or invested capital as a management fee, plus 20% of profits. The profit share is called carried interest, and it usually applies only above a hurdle rate of around 8% — the GP takes nothing until investors have earned that much, which is the mechanism intended to align the two sides.

The resulting cash-flow pattern is the J-curve, and understanding it prevents a common misreading of private fund performance. In the early years there are only outflows — capital calls and fees — while the investments themselves are held at cost or written down, so reported returns are negative. Only later, as companies are sold, does cash come back and the curve turn upward. A private fund three years old showing a negative return is not necessarily doing badly; it is at the bottom of the J, and the number is not informative yet.

Common pitfall: smooth ≠ safe

Private funds report returns from appraised valuations, updated quarterly by the GP itself, not from market prices. Stale, managed marks make the return series look eerily smooth — low "volatility," low "correlation" with stocks. Much of that is measurement artifact, not economics: if you only reprice your house once a year, its price chart is smooth too. Practitioners call this volatility laundering. When you build risk models in Section 16, de-smoothing private-asset returns is a real analytical task.

Worked example: the power law that runs venture capital

VC returns do not look like a bell curve — they look like a lottery with a few enormous winners. A representative $100M fund making 20 equal $5M bets might end up like this:

Outcome # of bets Return each Cash back
Total loss 10 0× $0
Return capital, roughly 6 1× $30M
Solid win 3 5× $75M
The one that matters 1 30× $150M
Total 20 — $255M

Half the investments returned literally nothing, and the fund still turned $100M into $255M — because a single 30× winner produced more than all nineteen others combined. This is the power law, and it inverts normal investing instincts. A VC does not diversify to reduce loss; every loss is capped at 1× anyway. They are hunting the one outcome that returns the whole fund, so the fatal error is not backing a company that fails — it is passing on the one that becomes Google.

The data backs the caricature. Studies of venture portfolios consistently find that a small percentage of deals generate the majority of all returns, and that the best funds are separated from the rest almost entirely by whether they caught one or two of these outliers. If you ever model VC, mean and median are nearly useless — the entire distribution lives in its right tail.

Hedge funds: the strategy zoo and the fee arithmetic

A hedge fund is defined less by what it does than by what it is permitted to do. Because it accepts money only from institutions and wealthy individuals rather than the general public, it operates under much lighter regulation than a mutual fund, and that freedom is the product being sold.

Specifically, it can engage in short selling, borrowing a security and selling it in the hope of buying it back cheaper, which allows it to profit from falling prices. It can borrow to amplify positions. It can use derivatives without restriction. And it can concentrate — putting 30% of the fund into a single idea, which a regulated mutual fund generally cannot.

The name is a historical artefact from the original strategy of holding long and short positions simultaneously so that market direction cancelled out. Many hedge funds today hedge nothing at all; the label now denotes a legal structure and a fee arrangement rather than a technique. The main strategy families are:

Strategy The bet Example
