Long/short equity Stock picking on both sides — long the good, short the bad Long AMD, short a weaker rival; market moves partly cancel
Global macro Big directional calls on rates, currencies, commodities Soros shorting the pound in 1992
Arbitrage / relative value Tiny pricing gaps between related securities, levered up Convertible bond vs the issuer's stock
Quantitative / systematic Statistical signals traded by algorithm at scale Renaissance, Two Sigma — where your skill set aims (Section 18)
Event-driven Mergers, bankruptcies, restructurings Buying a takeover target below the deal price

Now the fee arithmetic, which is brutal, frequently glossed over, and asked about in interviews. Take 2-and-20 under the common convention that the management fee is charged first and the performance fee applies to what remains.

A fund earns 10% gross. Subtract the 2% management fee, leaving 8%. The manager takes 20% of that 8%, which is 1.6%. The investor receives 6.4%. So a 10% gross return became a 6.4% net return, and the manager took 3.6 percentage points of it — 36% of the gross return in a single year.

Compound that for a decade and the gap becomes structural rather than annoying. One hundred dollars growing at 10% gross reaches $259. The same hundred growing at 6.4% net reaches $186. The manager's cumulative take is the $73 difference, which is 46% of the $159 of gross profit the fund generated. Nearly half the value created went to the manager, and the investor carried all of the risk.

The implication is not that hedge funds are a scam; it is that the bar is extremely high. To be worth holding, a fund cannot merely match the market before fees — it must beat it by enough to cover a fee load that consumes around half of the excess, consistently, for years. That is precisely the kind of persistent outperformance that Section 17 (Market Efficiency) shows to be rare and hard to identify in advance.

One more filter is needed to read hedge-fund performance data at all: survivorship bias.

Hedge fund indices are assembled from funds that choose to report their returns to a database, and reporting is voluntary. Consider what that means mechanically. A fund performing badly has no incentive to report, and a fund that collapses stops reporting entirely — and in many databases its history disappears along with it. Meanwhile a new fund joining the database is often permitted to "backfill" its past returns, and a fund only chooses to join after a good stretch worth showing. Failures are removed from the sample and successes are added retroactively.

Studies estimate the resulting overstatement of average industry returns at several percentage points a year, which is roughly the size of the outperformance being advertised. You already know this failure mode from machine learning: it is training on a dataset from which the negative outcomes were silently deleted, then reporting accuracy on it. The habit to build is asking, of any performance figure from any voluntary database, what happened to the entities that are no longer in the sample.

Crypto as an asset class: how an analyst frames it honestly

Blockchain mechanics belong to Section 19 (FinTech); here crypto is treated purely as a portfolio asset, which means asking the same questions asked of everything else in this section. Three facts dominate the answer.

The first is volatility. Bitcoin's annualised volatility has historically run 60–80%, against roughly 15–20% for the S&P 500 — three to four times as much movement per unit of time. Drawdowns of 70–80% have occurred repeatedly, not once. Any position size has to be chosen with that in mind, because a holding that would be uncomfortable at a 30% loss is untenable at 80%.

The second is custody risk, and it is a genuinely different category of risk from anything else in this book. Owning crypto means controlling the cryptographic keys that authorise transfers, so custody failures — a lost key, a compromised wallet, or an exchange that turns out to have been spending customer assets, as FTX did in 2022 — can produce a total loss with no price movement at all. Compare that with the settlement and custody machinery of Section 6: a Treasury bond held at a broker is recorded at a central depository, and if the broker fails the bond still exists and still belongs to you. In crypto, possession of the key is ownership, and there is nobody to appeal to.

The third fact is the analytically deepest: there are no cash flows. A share has earnings, a bond has coupons, a building has rent, so the discounting machinery of Section 1 and Section 13 (Valuation) can produce an intrinsic value to argue over. Two analysts disagreeing about a stock are disagreeing about forecasts, and the disagreement has a structure.

Bitcoin pays nothing to anybody, ever. Its value therefore rests entirely on its fixed supply — a hard-coded cap of 21 million units — and on what the next holder is prepared to pay. That does not make it worthless; gold has traded on exactly that basis for five thousand years, as discussed above. But it changes what analysis can even mean. There is no model that concludes bitcoin is cheap at $40,000, because there is no cash flow to compare the price against. There is only supply, demand and narrative.

There is also a diversification claim to handle carefully. Crypto's correlation with technology stocks was near zero through most of the 2010s, which supported the argument that it behaved independently of everything else. That correlation rose sharply during the 2022 tightening cycle — crypto fell alongside risky equities, driven by the same rising real rates. This is the recurring pattern noted at the end of this section: diversification benefits measured in calm periods have a habit of weakening in exactly the conditions that made you want them.

The honest summary is a description rather than a verdict: a high-volatility, custody-fragile, cash-flow-free asset whose diversification properties are unstable. Sized small enough that a total loss is survivable, it is a defensible position for someone who wants the exposure. Sized on conviction alone, it is a bet whose downside is the entire stake.

Worked example: does Bitcoin actually diversify a portfolio?

Crypto is sold as "digital gold" — an uncorrelated hedge. An analyst tests that claim with a correlation, and the honest answer is "it depends entirely on the regime."

Period BTC–S&P 500 correlation Interpretation
2017–2019 ≈ 0.0 Genuinely uncorrelated — the "digital gold" story looked true.
March 2020 crash ≈ +0.6 Fell with stocks, hard. When investors need cash, they sell what they can.
2022 rate-hike selloff ≈ +0.5 Traded as a high-beta tech stock, down ~65% with the Nasdaq.

The pattern is the cruel one for a diversifier: correlation drifts toward zero in calm markets and jumps toward one in a crisis — exactly the moments diversification is supposed to help. This is a recurring property of risk assets in general, and you will see it again in Section 15 and Section 16: correlations are not constants, and they rise precisely when you were counting on them to be low.

The deeper analytical problem, though, is valuation. A stock has earnings, a bond has coupons, a building has rent — you can discount them (Section 1). A Bitcoin has no cash flow, so there is no discounted-cash-flow anchor at all; its price is entirely what the next buyer will pay. That does not make the price zero — scarcity and adoption are real forces — but it does mean the tools from the rest of this course give you a valuation of exactly nothing to stand on. An honest analyst states that limitation out loud rather than inventing a model to hide it.

Why alternatives at all — and the Part II instrument map

After the fees, the lock-ups and the custody problems, why do pension funds and endowments commit trillions to alternative investments? The answer is one word: correlation.

The reasoning is worth stating carefully because it is genuinely powerful. A portfolio's risk is not the average of its holdings' risks. It depends on how the holdings move relative to each other, because when one falls and another rises the two partially cancel. Combine assets whose correlation is below one and the portfolio's volatility comes out below the weighted average of its parts — you have reduced risk without reducing expected return, which is as close to a free lunch as finance offers. You will derive this properly in Section 15 (Portfolio Theory).

That is what alternatives are bought for. Real assets that track inflation behave differently from bonds, which inflation damages. Macro funds can profit from the volatility that hurts everything else. Farmland's returns have essentially nothing to do with the Nasdaq. Each imperfect correlation is a genuine diversification credit against the fees.

Two caveats keep the pitch honest. Correlations tend to converge toward one during a crisis, because in a panic investors sell whatever they can rather than whatever they should, and 2008 demonstrated this across nearly every asset class at once — diversification weakens exactly when it is needed. And some of the advertised low correlation is a measurement artefact: assets valued by periodic appraisal rather than by continuous trading appear smoother than they are, which understates both their volatility and their correlation with everything else. The case for alternatives is real. It is smaller than the brochure states.

That closes Part II. You've now met every major instrument class — here's the map to keep:

Instrument What it is Who uses it Risk level Where you'll meet it in a job
Common stock (s07) Ownership share of a company's profits Everyone: retail to pensions Medium–high Equity research, any valuation work
Index funds / ETFs (s07) One ticker holding a whole market basket Retail, advisors, institutions Medium Asset management, fund analytics
Treasuries (s08) Loans to the US government; the risk-free benchmark Central banks, funds, banks Low (rate risk only) Every discount rate you'll ever compute
Corporate bonds (s08) Loans to companies, priced by credit spread Insurers, pensions, credit funds Low–medium Credit analysis, ratings, risk teams
Futures / forwards (s09) Locked-in future price for an asset Hedgers and speculators High (levered) Commodities desks, treasury, clearing
Options (s09) The right, not obligation, to buy/sell at a set price Hedgers, traders, employees High (asymmetric) Derivatives pricing, market risk, comp packages
Swaps (s09) Exchanging cash-flow streams (fixed vs floating) Banks, corporates, funds Varies Bank ALM, rates desks, XVA analytics
FX (s10) One currency priced in another Corporates, banks, macro funds Medium (levered: high) Treasury, international anything
Commodities (s10) Physical goods accessed via futures Producers, consumers, CTAs High Energy trading, inflation modeling
REITs (s10) Listed companies owning income property Income investors, allocators Medium–high Real-asset research, dividend models
PE / VC funds (s10) Locked-up funds buying private companies Institutions, the wealthy High + illiquid Deal teams, LP analytics, fund reporting
Hedge funds (s10) Flexible private funds; short, leverage, derivatives Institutions, the wealthy Varies wildly Quant research — the natural home for your skills
Crypto (s10) Digital scarce assets with no cash flows Retail, some institutions Very high FinTech, digital-asset risk teams

Check your understanding

1. EUR/USD rises from 1.10 to 1.25. Who is hurt?

EUR/USD rising means each euro costs more dollars. Anyone who must pay euros — like the importer — now needs more dollars to settle the same invoice. Euro receivers and euro-asset holders gain, and the European tourist finds America cheaper.

2. An oil ETF rolls its long futures position monthly while the curve is in steep contango and spot oil stays flat all year. The ETF most likely…

In contango the next contract is always pricier than the expiring one, and each contract tends to slide down toward spot as it ages. That negative roll yield produces losses even when spot goes nowhere.

3. A hedge fund returns 10% gross. Under 2-and-20 (management fee taken first, then 20% of the remainder), the investor nets about…

(10% − 2%) × 0.80 = 6.4%. The 2% management fee comes off the top, then the manager keeps 20% of the remaining 8%.

4. A building generates $30,000 of NOI and is priced at $600,000. Its cap rate is…

Cap rate = NOI ÷ price = 30,000 ÷ 600,000 = 5.0%. (20% is the inverted ratio — price over NOI gives the "multiple," 20×, not the yield.)

5. The core risk of a carry trade (borrow yen at 0.5%, invest in Australian dollars at 4.5%) is that…

Carry accrues slowly, but the FX loss when the low-rate funding currency rallies can arrive all at once — especially in a crowded unwind, as in August 2024. Steady nickels, occasional steamroller.

Key takeaways

  • FX quotes price the base currency in units of the quote currency: EUR/USD = 1.10 means one euro costs $1.10, and a rising quote means a stronger euro.
  • Currencies move on rate differentials, inflation gaps and capital flows; the carry trade harvests the rate gap and periodically gets crushed when it unwinds.
  • Companies hedge transaction exposure with forwards — trading upside away to lock certainty — while translation exposure is an accounting effect you'll meet in filings.
  • Commodity investors live on the futures curve: contango bleeds negative roll yield, backwardation pays positive roll yield, regardless of what spot does. Gold is the cash-flow-free anti-currency.
  • Real estate = leverage plus a computable yield: cap rate = NOI ÷ price, judged as a spread over Treasuries; REITs make property liquid at the cost of stock-like volatility.
  • PE and VC run on GP/LP fund mechanics, 2-and-20 with carry, and a J-curve; VC returns follow a power law where one winner carries the fund, and smooth private "returns" partly reflect stale appraisals.
  • Fee drag compounds: 10% gross becomes 6.4% net under 2-and-20 — $259 vs $186 on $100 over a decade — and survivorship bias inflates the track records you're shown.
  • Crypto is a high-volatility asset with custody risk and no cash flows to discount; alternatives in general earn their place only through genuine (not appraisal-smoothed) low correlation — the bridge to Section 15.

Part III · Corporate Finance & Accounting

11. Financial Statements: The Language of Business

Every company on Earth describes itself with the same three documents, and every analyst job you might want assumes you can read them fluently. By the end of this section you will be able to walk a single transaction through all three statements and explain why the balance sheet can never, ever fail to balance.

Why statements exist, and where to find them

A company is a machine that takes in money and, if it works, produces more money. Financial statements are the standardised, periodic report of what happened inside that machine — the only structured description of it that outsiders are entitled to.

They exist because of a separation that runs through all of modern finance: the people who supply the capital are usually not the people running the business. A shareholder owns part of a company they have never visited; a bank has lent money to managers it does not supervise. Both need a trustworthy, comparable account of what is being done with their money, and neither can simply walk in and look. Regulators, tax authorities, employees, suppliers and competitors all read the statements too, but the audience they are designed for is investors and creditors, and that shapes what they contain.

There are three statements, and the reason there are three rather than one is that they answer genuinely different questions about the same business.

The income statement asks whether the company made a profit during a period. It covers a stretch of time — a quarter, a year — and everything in it describes activity that happened between two dates.

The balance sheet asks what the company owns and owes right now. It describes a single instant, the last moment of the reporting period, and says nothing about how it got there.

The cash flow statement asks where the cash actually went during the period. It exists because profit and cash are not the same thing, for reasons the next subsection makes precise, and somebody has to reconcile them.

A period report, a snapshot and a reconciliation. If it helps, they are a diff, a database dump and a transaction log describing the same system — and as with those, you cannot understand what happened from any one of them alone.

For any of this to be comparable across companies, everyone has to follow the same rules. US companies use GAAP, set by the Financial Accounting Standards Board; most of the rest of the world uses IFRS. The two differ in character as well as in detail: GAAP is more rules-based, specifying precisely what to do in enumerated situations, while IFRS is more principles-based, stating an objective and expecting judgement. They agree entirely on the big structure and diverge on specifics — how inventory is costed, how leases are treated, when development spending may be recorded as an asset rather than an expense. Cross-border comparison therefore needs care at the line-item level, not wholesale distrust.

An independent accounting firm then performs an audit and signs an opinion that the statements fairly present the company's position in accordance with those rules. It is worth being precise about what that opinion is and is not. The auditor is testing whether the numbers were produced by a sound process and follow the standards; they sample transactions rather than examining all of them, and they are engaged and paid by the company they are auditing. An audit is a meaningful check on sloppiness and a weak check on determined fraud, which is why the large accounting scandals were all signed off by reputable firms.

For US public companies all of this is free and public. The 10-K is the audited annual report and contains far more than the statements — a description of the business, an extended discussion of risks, and management's own narrative account of the year. The 10-Q is the quarterly version, slimmer and reviewed rather than fully audited. Both are filed to EDGAR, the SEC's database at sec.gov/edgar, where anyone can read them within minutes of publication.

One career note before going further, because it changes how much attention this section deserves. For analyst roles this is the most directly job-critical material in the course. Interviews for equity research, investment banking, credit analysis and corporate FP&A test exactly what is on this page, and the single most common technical question in all of them is the three-statement linkage covered later in this section — how a change in one statement propagates through the other two.

The accrual revolution: earned, not received

Here is the idea that unlocks everything else, and it is genuinely counterintuitive the first time. The statements are not built on cash. They are built on accrual accounting, under which revenue is recorded when it is earned — you delivered the goods or performed the service — and expenses are recorded when they are incurred, meaning when the resource was consumed. Neither has anything to do with when money moves.

The purpose is to measure economic performance in the period it actually occurred. Consider the alternative. If you recorded revenue only when customers paid, a company that shipped a record quantity of goods in December on 60-day terms would report a terrible December and a spectacular February, and neither number would describe what the business did in either month. Cash timing is largely an artefact of payment terms, and payment terms are negotiable, seasonal and manipulable. Accrual accounting tries to strip that out so that a period's figures describe the period's activity.

The cost of that choice is what the whole rest of this section deals with. Deciding when revenue is earned and when a resource was consumed requires judgement, and judgement can be wrong, optimistic, or deliberately abused. Accrual accounting buys a truer picture at the price of introducing estimates — which is exactly why the third statement, dealing only in cash, exists as a check.

Meet the running example for this section: Cascade Roasters, Inc., a coffee roaster with $1,000 million of annual revenue. Its full numbers appear shortly; start with one transaction.

In December, Cascade ships $120,000 of beans to a hotel chain that pays 60 days later. Under accrual rules, December's income statement records $120,000 of revenue, because the beans were delivered in December and Cascade has done everything required of it — that timing rule is revenue recognition, set out in the US by the ASC 606 standard.

But no money arrived. So the balance sheet must record something to keep the books consistent, and what it records is a $120,000 account receivable: an asset representing the customer's obligation to pay. The bank account shows nothing until February, at which point the receivable disappears and cash replaces it — a swap of one asset for another, with no effect on profit at all, because the profit was already recognised in December.

That is the general shape of every accrual: profit is recognised at one moment, cash moves at another, and a balance-sheet item holds the difference in between.

Worked example: accrual and cash telling opposite stories

Two gyms open in January. Gym A sells 100 annual memberships at $1,200 each, all paid up front: $120,000 of cash lands in January, but it has only earned one month of service, so January revenue is $10,000 — the other $110,000 sits on the balance sheet as deferred revenue, a liability (it owes 11 months of gym).

Gym B bills companies $10,000 for January corporate memberships, payable in March. January revenue: $10,000. January cash: $0. Same January performance on the income statement; wildly different bank accounts. Accrual profit and cash flow are two different signals about the same business — you need both.

Expenses work the same way in reverse. If Cascade pays for a year of insurance in advance, the cash leaves immediately but the expense is spread across the income statement at one-twelfth per month, because the insurance is being consumed month by month; in between, the unused portion sits on the balance sheet as a prepaid asset. If employees earn wages in December that are paid in January, December's income statement bears the expense, because that is when the work was done, and the balance sheet carries an accrued liability until the payment clears.

Notice the pattern in both directions: whenever recognition and cash payment happen at different times, a balance-sheet account appears to hold the difference, and it unwinds when the cash finally moves. Those holding accounts are what connect the three statements to each other, and the machinery that makes them work is the subject of the next three subsections.

The income statement, line by line

The income statement is a subtraction cascade. It starts at the top with everything the company sold, then removes categories of cost in a fixed order, and each intermediate subtotal has a name and tells you something different about the business.

Here is Cascade Roasters' year in millions of dollars, with the margin shown at each level. A margin is simply that line divided by revenue, and the reason analysts work in margins rather than dollars is comparability: $200 million of profit means nothing until you know whether it came from $1 billion of sales or $50 billion, whereas a 20% margin is directly comparable across companies of any size.

Line $M Margin What it means
Revenue 1,000.0 — value of goods/services delivered this year
− COGS 400.0 — green coffee, roasting labor, packaging
= Gross profit 600.0 60.0% profit on the product itself
− Operating expenses 300.0 — S&M 150, R&D 40, G&A 110
= EBITDA 300.0 30.0% operating profit before D&A
− D&A 50.0 — wear on roasters, trucks, software
= EBIT 250.0 25.0% operating profit
− Interest expense 20.0 — cost of the $300M of debt
= Pre-tax income 230.0 23.0% what the tax authority sees
− Tax (21%) 48.3 — 230 × 0.21
= Net income 181.7 18.2% the bottom line, owned by shareholders

Now the vocabulary of that cascade, in the order the subtractions happen.

COGS, cost of goods sold, is the direct cost of producing the specific things that were sold this period: the coffee beans, the packaging, the wages of the people operating the roasters. The defining test is whether the cost scales with units — one more bag sold means one more bag's worth of beans. Subtracting COGS from revenue leaves gross profit, which measures how much the product itself earns before any of the cost of being a company. Gross margin is the single best indicator of pricing power: a company that can charge far above its production cost has something customers cannot easily substitute.

Operating expenses, or opex, are the costs of running the organisation rather than producing the units. They come in three conventional buckets: sales and marketing, which is what it costs to acquire customers; research and development, which is spending on future products rather than current ones; and general and administrative, meaning executives, finance, legal and HR. These do not scale one-for-one with sales, which is why growing revenue against roughly fixed opex is how companies become profitable.

Subtract opex and you reach EBITDA. The name is an instruction: earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation. Bankers favour it because those four items depend on decisions unrelated to how well the business operates — interest depends on how the company was financed, tax on where it is domiciled, depreciation on accounting policy — so removing them makes two companies more comparable. The same removals are why EBITDA flatters companies that own a lot of equipment, a criticism taken up in Section 12.

Next come the non-cash charges, and they need explaining because they are the clearest example of accrual thinking.

When Cascade buys a $50 million roasting line that will last ten years, charging the whole $50 million against the year of purchase would be misleading — the machine will produce revenue for a decade, so the cost belongs across that decade. Depreciation spreads it, expensing perhaps $5 million a year. Amortisation does the identical thing for intangible assets such as acquired patents or software; together they are written D&A. The crucial property is that no cash moves in those later years — the cash all left when the machine was bought — so D&A reduces reported profit without reducing the bank balance, which is why the cash flow statement adds it straight back.

Subtracting D&A gives EBIT, operating profit. Then interest is deducted, then tax, leaving net income.

That ordering is not arbitrary — it encodes the payment queue from Section 6 and Section 7. Suppliers and employees are paid first, inside COGS and opex. Lenders take their interest next, before any profit is declared. The government takes tax after that. Whatever survives all of it is net income, and it belongs to shareholders, who are last precisely because they are the residual claimants. Reading down the income statement is reading down the seniority of claims.

Real world: the same $100 of sales, five business models

An income statement's shape tells you what kind of business you are looking at before you know its name. Here is roughly where $100 of revenue ends up across five real industries:

Of every $100 in sales… Grocer (Kroger) Automaker (Ford) Apple Enterprise software Pharma
Cost of goods sold $78 $85 $56 $20 $25
Gross profit $22 $15 $44 $80 $75
Operating expenses (SG&A, R&D) $19 $11 $14 $55 $50
Operating profit $3 $4 $30 $25 $25

Read the stories straight off the columns. The grocer keeps $3 of $100 — a razor-thin margin that only works on gigantic volume and fast inventory turnover; a 2% cost slip wipes out most of the profit. Software keeps $80 of gross profit because copying code is nearly free, then spends most of it on salespeople and engineers — its cost is in the operating lines, not COGS. Pharma looks identical at the gross line but its big number is R&D, most of which funds drugs that will never reach market.

The practical lesson: never compare margins across industries. A 3% net margin is excellent for a grocer and catastrophic for a software company. Every ratio in Section 12 is only meaningful against the right peer set — and choosing that peer set is half of real analysis.

The balance sheet: an invariant that never breaks

The balance sheet is a snapshot at a single instant — midnight on the last day of the period — rather than a record of a stretch of time. Everything on it is a stock, not a flow: what exists at that moment, with no information about how it got there.

Its entire structure rests on one identity. Stated in words: everything a company owns was paid for by somebody, and there are only two kinds of somebody — people it must pay back, and people who own the residual. So the total value of what it owns must equal the sum of what it owes to outsiders and what belongs to shareholders. There is nothing else it could be:

Assets = Liabilities + Equity
what the company owns = who financed it (lenders) + who owns the residual (shareholders)

Take the three terms in turn. An asset is a resource expected to produce future economic value — cash, receivables, inventory, machinery, a patent. A liability is an obligation to an outsider: unpaid supplier bills, bank loans, bonds, money taken from customers for goods not yet delivered. And equity is what remains for the owners after every liability is met — defined as a subtraction, exactly as in Section 7.

Why can it never fail to balance? Because of double-entry bookkeeping, a five-hundred-year-old system in which every transaction is recorded in two places chosen so that the identity is preserved. In programming terms, Assets = Liabilities + Equity is an invariant, and every transaction is an atomic commit required to leave the invariant intact.

Work through the cases and you will see there is no way out. Borrow $50: cash rises 50 and debt rises 50, so both sides rise equally. Buy a $30 roaster with cash: one asset rises 30 and another falls 30, so the left side is unchanged and the right side never moved. Earn $10 of profit: assets rise 10, and equity rises 10 because retained profit belongs to the owners. Pay a $20 supplier bill: cash falls 20 and the payable falls 20, shrinking both sides together.

There is no legal sequence of entries that breaks it, which has a practical consequence worth internalising: if a balance sheet does not balance, nobody has discovered an interesting economic fact. Someone made an arithmetic error, and the only question is where.

Both sides of the statement are sorted by time, and knowing the sort order tells you how to read it quickly.

On the asset side, current assets are those expected to turn into cash within a year: cash itself, receivables, and inventory, which is an asset while it sits in the warehouse and becomes COGS the moment it is sold. Non-current assets are the long-lived ones, chiefly PP&E — property, plant and equipment — carried at what was paid for them minus the depreciation charged so far.

The right side splits the same way. Current liabilities are due within a year: accounts payable owed to suppliers, and short-term debt. Non-current liabilities are bonds and long-term loans.

The gap between the two short-term sides is working capital, and it deserves attention now because it drives the cash flow story below. It measures the money trapped in the ordinary gears of operating: cash you have spent on inventory not yet sold, plus cash owed to you by customers, minus cash you are holding because you have not yet paid suppliers. A growing business must fund that gap out of its own pocket before the revenue arrives — which is why working capital is where profitable companies go to run out of money.

Two more balance-sheet residents come up constantly and are widely misunderstood.

Goodwill appears after an acquisition. If a company pays $1 billion for a business whose identifiable net assets are worth $600 million, the accounts must record something for the missing $400 million or they will not balance — and that something is goodwill. It is the accounting placeholder for everything paid for that cannot be pointed at: brand, customer relationships, the acquired team, expected synergies. It is not depreciated, but it must be tested for impairment, so when an acquisition disappoints the company writes goodwill down and books a large non-cash loss. A big goodwill write-off is an admission, in accounting language, that the price paid was too high.

Total equity is often called book value, and the distance between it and market capitalisation from Section 7 can be enormous. The reason is that the two are measuring different things. Book value records historical cost — what assets were paid for, less depreciation — while market value prices expected future cash flows. A software company whose main asset is code its engineers wrote may carry almost nothing on the balance sheet and be worth tens of billions, because the accounting rules expensed the salaries as they were paid and recognised no asset. Book value is not a bad estimate of market value; it is not an estimate of market value at all.

Worked example: three companies, identical assets, opposite risk

The invariant Assets = Liabilities + Equity hides a decision that matters enormously: who financed the assets? Three companies each own exactly $1,000M of assets earning $100M of operating profit. The only difference is the split of the right-hand side.

Conservative Balanced Aggressive
Assets $1,000M $1,000M $1,000M
Debt (at 6%) $100M $500M $800M
Equity $900M $500M $200M
Operating profit $100M $100M $100M
Interest owed −$6M −$30M −$48M
Profit to equity $94M $70M $52M
Return on equity 10.4% 14.0% 26.0%

In good times, leverage is magic: the aggressive company earns 26% on equity versus 10% for the conservative one, from the identical assets. Now let a recession cut operating profit to $40M. The conservative company still clears $34M; the aggressive one owes $48M of interest on $40M of profit — it cannot pay, and equity holders may be wiped out entirely.

That is the whole trade-off the right-hand side of the balance sheet encodes, and it is why "return on equity" means nothing until you know how much debt manufactured it. A 26% ROE built on 80% debt is not four times better than a 10% ROE — it is the same business wearing more risk. The DuPont decomposition in Section 12 exists precisely to separate these two sources of return.

The cash flow statement: profit is an opinion, cash is a fact

Accrual accounting produces a truer picture of a period's activity, and it achieves that using estimates: when revenue is earned, how many years a roasting line will last, which receivables will ultimately be collected, what a warranty will cost. Every one of those is a judgement, and judgements can be optimistic without being fraudulent.

Cash is the one figure containing no judgement whatsoever. Money is either in the account or it is not. Hence the analyst proverb that profit is an opinion and cash is a fact — not a claim that profit is meaningless, but a reminder about which number can be argued with.

The cash flow statement reconciles the two, and it sorts every movement of cash into three buckets according to why the money moved: from running the business, from buying or selling long-term assets, or from dealings with the people who financed the company. The split matters because the three have completely different implications — a company whose cash is rising because it is operating well is in a different position from one whose cash is rising because it borrowed.

CFO — cash flow from operations. This is the cash the core business actually generated, and it is the most important line in the three statements. Almost every company presents it using the indirect method, which starts from net income and then undoes each accrual adjustment to get back to cash.

Two kinds of repair are needed. First, add back the non-cash expenses: D&A reduced profit but no money left the building this year, so it goes straight back in.

Second, adjust for changes in working capital, and this is where the reasoning is worth doing slowly. If receivables grew, it means you recorded revenue for goods you delivered but have not been paid for — profit includes money you do not have, so subtract the increase. If inventory grew, you spent cash buying beans that have not yet been sold, so no expense was recorded but cash did leave — subtract that too. If payables grew, you recorded costs for supplies you have not yet paid for, so your suppliers are effectively financing you — add it back. The rule underneath all three: an increase in an operating asset consumes cash, and an increase in an operating liability provides it.

For Cascade in a steady year: net income of 181.7, plus D&A of 50, with working capital roughly unchanged, gives CFO of 231.7.

CFI — cash flow from investing. This bucket covers cash spent on or received from long-lived assets, and it is dominated by capex, the purchase of equipment and property, alongside acquisitions and purchases or sales of securities. Note the asymmetry with the income statement: buying a roasting line takes cash now and appears here in full, while the income statement will only see it gradually, as depreciation, over ten years. Cascade spends 80 on new roasting lines, so CFI is −80.

CFF — cash flow from financing. This is money moving between the company and the people who fund it: borrowing and repaying debt, issuing shares, buying shares back, and paying dividends. Cascade pays a dividend of 30 and raises nothing, so CFF is −30.

Add the three: 231.7 − 80 − 30 = +121.7, so cash rises from 100 to 221.7. And that ending figure is the identical "cash" line at the top of the balance sheet — the first visible sign that these are not three independent documents but three views of one set of records.

FCF = CFO − capex
free cash flow: cash the business generates after maintaining and growing its asset base — the raw material of valuation (Section 13)

Free cash flow is operating cash flow minus capital expenditure — in words, the cash the business produced after paying for the equipment needed to keep producing it. For Cascade that is 231.7 − 80 = 151.7. It is the figure most valuation work is built on, because it is what is genuinely available to be paid out to lenders and shareholders without shrinking the business.

Why do analysts prefer it to net income? Because growth consumes cash even while it manufactures profit, and the two can point in opposite directions for years.

Consider a company doubling its sales annually. To sell more, it must first buy more inventory — cash out, no expense recorded yet. It sells on credit, so revenue and profit are recorded while the cash arrives months later. It buys more equipment to increase capacity — cash out, recognised only slowly as depreciation. Every one of those is a consequence of succeeding, and every one drains the bank account. The income statement shows a company performing brilliantly while the cash flow statement shows money leaving.

This is not a hypothetical failure mode. Profitable, fast-growing companies run out of cash and fail regularly, and the mechanism is always the same: working capital and capex consumed the money before the profits turned into collections. Net income tells you whether the business model works; free cash flow tells you whether the company survives long enough to prove it.

Common pitfall

"Net income up, so cash must be up" is the classic beginner error — and its mirror image matters too. Amazon ran near-zero accounting profit for years while gushing operating cash; many dot-com era firms showed rising profits while cash bled out through receivables. When profit and CFO diverge for several periods in a row, that gap is the first thing to investigate (Section 12 turns this into formal ratios).

Real world: profitable companies that ran out of cash

"Profit is an opinion, cash is a fact" is not a slogan — it is a coroner's report. Companies reporting healthy accounting profits go bankrupt regularly, because you pay employees and lenders in cash, not in net income.

Case The trap
Fast-growing manufacturer Every sale is profitable, but growth means buying inventory and extending credit to customers before being paid. Profit rises while cash drains into working capital. Grow fast enough and you go bankrupt — profitably. This has a name: overtrading.
Enron, 2001 Reported billions in profit while operating cash flow lagged far behind. The gap between the two — net income sprinting ahead of CFO for years — was visible in the filings before the collapse.
Carillion (UK), 2018 A construction giant reporting profits and paying dividends right up to collapse, while booking revenue on contracts long before the cash arrived and stretching payments to suppliers to flatter its own cash position.
WeWork, 2019 Enormous "community-adjusted EBITDA" — a bespoke profit metric — sat atop cash burn of billions a year. The IPO collapsed once investors read the cash flow statement instead of the invented one.

The single most useful habit this section can give you: whenever you see rising net income, immediately find cash flow from operations on the same filing and compare the two trends. If profit climbs for several periods while CFO stalls or falls, something is being recognised as revenue that has not turned into money — and that gap is where the majority of accounting failures announce themselves in advance, to anyone who bothers to look.

How the three statements connect

The three statements are not three files. They are three views of a single set of records, connected by shared values, and the connections are what make the system self-checking — change one thing and it must propagate correctly through all three or the balance sheet stops balancing.

There are four connections to learn. Once you know them you can reconstruct any one statement from the other two, which is precisely what interviewers are testing when they ask what happens to all three statements if depreciation increases by $10.

  • Net income → equity and CFO. The income statement's bottom line flows into balance-sheet equity as retained earnings (net income minus dividends), and the same number is the first line of the cash flow statement.
  • Capex → PP&E and CFI. Cash spent on equipment leaves through CFI and lands on the balance sheet as PP&E.
  • Borrowing → cash and debt via CFF. Raise debt and CFF brings cash in while the liability side records the obligation.
  • Ending cash closes the loop. The cash flow statement's final number is the balance sheet's cash line.

Worked example: the classic interview question

"Walk me through $10 of extra depreciation" — asked in nearly every banking and research interview. At a 21% tax rate: Income statement: D&A +10, so EBIT −10, tax −2.1, net income −7.9. Cash flow statement: start −7.9, add back the non-cash +10, so CFO +2.1 — cash actually rises because of the tax shield. Balance sheet: cash +2.1 and PP&E −10, so assets −7.9; retained earnings −7.9 on the other side. Assets down 7.9 = equity down 7.9. Balanced. Now try it live below.

Three-statement flow-through: Cascade Roasters

Drag the sliders and watch all three statements recompute ($ millions) — changed lines are shaded. Then press "Trace $100 of extra revenue" and step through the path a dollar of growth takes.

Model assumptions: opex $300M and D&A $50M held flat; operating working capital = 20% of revenue; new debt is raised at year-end, so it adds cash but no interest this year; tax is zero when pre-tax income is negative; dividend fixed at $30M. Negative ending cash means the company would need financing.

Two things are worth watching for deliberately as you use the model.

First, the balance check never moves off zero. That is not the widget quietly forcing it — it is because the model is constructed from balanced entries, exactly as real accounting is. Every input you change writes to two places, so the invariant survives regardless of what you do. If you can build a mental model where that is obviously true, you have understood double-entry.

Second, push revenue growth up and watch operating cash flow fall behind net income. Each additional dollar of sales traps roughly twenty cents in working capital — inventory bought and receivables extended ahead of collection — so the faster the company grows, the wider the gap between the profit it reports and the cash it holds. That is the mechanism from the previous subsection, and Figure 11.5, happening in real time under your hands.

Reading a real 10-K in 15 minutes

A 10-K runs to between 100 and 300 pages, and a large fraction of it is legally required boilerplate that carries no information. Nobody reads it end to end, and reading it in order is a bad strategy anyway, because the most informative sections are not at the front.

What analysts do instead is triage: go directly to the parts where new information is most likely to be, in a fixed order, and read the rest only if something prompts you to. The routine below takes about fifteen minutes and extracts perhaps 80% of what a full read would give you.

  • Minutes 1–3: the three statements. Revenue trend, margins, CFO versus net income, debt level, cash. You now know the shape of the business.
  • Minutes 4–8: MD&A. Management explains, in prose, why the numbers moved. Skim for what changed year over year and how they describe demand, pricing, and costs.
  • Minutes 9–11: segment data. A "cloud company" that earns 70% of profit from legacy licenses is a different investment than its headline suggests. Segments reveal the real mix.
  • Minutes 12–14: footnotes, selectively. Revenue recognition policy, debt maturities, and anything the auditor flagged as a critical audit matter. Footnotes are where inconvenient facts go to hide in plain sight.
  • Minute 15: risk factors, diff only. The section is mostly legal boilerplate — but compare it against last year's filing and read what is new. Companies quietly disclose emerging problems here first. (A CS reflex that serves you well: never read the file, read the diff.)

Red flags preview

Keep a mental alarm list while you skim: net income growing while CFO shrinks for multiple periods; receivables or inventory growing much faster than revenue; frequent "one-time" charges that recur every year; auditor changes; heavy reliance on non-GAAP metrics that always look better than the GAAP ones. Section 12 turns these into quantitative ratio tests.

Your edge

Every filing on EDGAR is machine-readable — modern filings carry XBRL tags, and the SEC publishes bulk financial-statement datasets. While most analysts read one 10-K at a time, you can parse thousands: screen for the receivables-versus-revenue divergence above across the whole market, or diff risk-factor text programmatically. Statement literacy plus data skills is precisely the combination Section 18 builds toward.

Deep dive: why revenue recognition is where fraud lives

Most accounting scandals are, at bottom, revenue-timing scandals, because "earned" involves judgment. Under the ASC 606 standard, a company must identify its contractual performance obligations and recognize revenue as each is satisfied — but multi-year contracts, bundled products, and bill-and-hold arrangements leave room to be aggressive. Classic tricks: channel stuffing (shipping unordered product to distributors at quarter-end and booking it as sales), recognizing multi-year contract value up front, and booking barter or round-trip transactions as revenue.

The tell is almost always on the other statements: fictional revenue creates receivables that never convert to cash, so days sales outstanding stretches and CFO decouples from net income. Enron, one of the largest frauds in history, reported rising profits while operating cash flow told a much uglier story. This is why the linkage matters — a lie on one statement must leave fingerprints on the other two, because the invariant always has to hold.

Worked example: three numbers that expose a problem

You do not need forensic accounting to catch most trouble — you need three ratios computed across a few years, watching for one line growing faster than sales. Here is a company where each is drifting the wrong way:

Signal Year 1 Year 3 What it may mean
Days sales outstanding (receivables ÷ sales × 365) 45 days 78 days Customers are paying slower — or "sales" are being booked that will never be collected.
Inventory days (inventory ÷ COGS × 365) 60 days 110 days Product is not selling. A write-down is coming that will hit future profit.
Net income ÷ CFO 0.9 1.8 Profit is increasingly "paper" — twice as much reported income as cash generated.

Individually each has an innocent explanation. Rising DSO might be a big new customer with 90-day terms; rising inventory might be a deliberate build before a product launch. But all three moving the wrong way at once is the classic fingerprint of revenue being pulled forward: fictional or premature sales create receivables that are never collected and inventory that never moves, and the cash flow statement refuses to corroborate the income statement.

This is exactly the kind of thing you can automate. Pull the standardised XBRL financials the SEC publishes for every filer, compute these three series for a few thousand companies, and flag the ones where all three deteriorate together. You will have built, in an afternoon, a crude version of the earnings-quality screens that quant funds pay for — and a portfolio piece that demonstrates you can turn accounting into code.

Check your understanding

1. Cascade delivers $200k of coffee to a client in December; the client pays in February. Under accrual accounting, when does Cascade record the revenue?

Accrual accounting recognizes revenue when it is earned — at delivery. Until payment arrives, the $200k sits on the balance sheet as an account receivable.

2. Depreciation increases by $10 (tax rate 21%), nothing else changes. What happens to the company's cash?

Net income falls $7.9 (10 less 2.1 of tax saved), but the full $10 is added back on the cash flow statement since no cash left. Net effect: +10 − 7.9 = +$2.1 — the tax shield.

3. Why can a legitimate balance sheet never fail to balance?

The identity is an invariant. Every transaction is a balanced entry — like an atomic commit that must leave the invariant intact — so no sequence of valid entries can break it.

4. A fast-growing retailer reports record net income, but CFO has been negative for four straight quarters. The most likely explanation is:

Working capital consumes cash during growth: inventory is bought and credit extended before revenue is collected. Profit is an opinion; cash is a fact — and this divergence is normal for fast growers but deadly if financing dries up. (Faster depreciation would raise CFO, not lower it.)

5. A company reports CFO of $500M and capex of $180M. Its free cash flow is:

FCF = CFO − capex = 500 − 180 = $320M: the cash left over after operating the business and maintaining its asset base. Capex is very much a cash outflow, just reported in CFI rather than CFO.

Key takeaways

  • Three statements, three questions: the income statement measures period profit, the balance sheet snapshots what is owned and owed, the cash flow statement tracks actual cash. US GAAP and IFRS are the two rulebooks; audited 10-Ks and 10-Qs are free on EDGAR.
  • Accrual accounting records revenue when earned and expenses when incurred — so reported profit and the bank balance can tell opposite stories in any given period.
  • The income statement is a cascade — revenue → gross profit → EBITDA → EBIT → net income — and the margin at each checkpoint tells you where the money leaks.
  • Assets = Liabilities + Equity is an invariant enforced by double-entry bookkeeping: every transaction is a balanced entry, so the sheet cannot fail to balance.
  • Profit is an opinion, cash is a fact: CFO starts from net income, adds back non-cash charges, and subtracts the working capital that growth traps. FCF = CFO − capex.
  • The statements link through shared lines: net income feeds retained earnings and the top of the CFS; capex flows through CFI into PP&E; the CFS's ending cash is the balance sheet's cash.
  • Read 10-Ks by triage — statements, MD&A, segments, footnotes, then the diff of the risk factors — and treat a persistent profit-versus-CFO divergence as the number-one red flag.
  • For analyst interviews, the three-statement walk-through (e.g., $10 of depreciation) is the single most-tested skill in this course. Drill it until it is reflex.

Part III · Corporate Finance & Accounting

12. Ratio Analysis: Reading a Company Like a Pro

In Section 11 you learned to read the three financial statements — the raw tables. Ratios are the queries you run against those tables, and by the end of this section you'll be able to size up a company's profitability, safety, efficiency, and price tag in about ten minutes.

Why ratios: the great normalizer

Raw financial figures carry almost no information on their own. Take a statement like "this company earned $1.25 billion last year." Is that good? For a young company it would be extraordinary; for Walmart it would be a catastrophe, since Walmart earns roughly ten times that. The number alone does not permit any judgement at all.

It becomes information the moment you divide it by something: profit per dollar of sales, profit per dollar of assets, debt per dollar of annual earnings. That division does something specific — it removes scale. Once scale is out of the way, a corner grocer and a global chain become directly comparable, and so do this year's company and the same company a decade ago, even though it has tripled in size since.

This is the whole idea behind ratio analysis, and it is worth naming explicitly because it also explains the limits. A ratio answers "per unit of what?" — and the answer is only as meaningful as the denominator you chose. Most of the skill in this section is knowing which denominator makes a particular question answerable.

Two rules govern every ratio you will ever compute, and violating either one produces confident nonsense.

Always compare against peers. A net margin of 2.5% is alarming for a software company and entirely healthy for a supermarket, because the two businesses have different cost structures, different capital needs and different competitive dynamics. Every industry has its own gravity, set by how much competition there is, how much capital is required to enter, and how much of the final price is bought-in materials. A ratio compared against the wrong industry is worse than no ratio, because it produces a conclusion rather than a shrug.

Always compare against history. A single snapshot cannot tell you which direction anything is moving, and direction is usually where the information is. A company whose gross margin slid from 8% to 5% over three years is telling you something is eroding — competitors, input costs, pricing power — that no single-year figure of 5% could reveal. Conversely a 5% margin that has climbed from 2% is a different company entirely.

A ratio with no peer group and no trend behind it is close to worthless. If you take one operational habit from this section, make it that you never quote a ratio as a single number.

There is a third rule, about what ratios are for. They generate questions, not answers.

Suppose inventory turnover suddenly halves — goods are sitting on the shelf twice as long as they used to. The ratio does not tell you why, and there are several completely different explanations. Demand may have collapsed, which is bad. Management may be deliberately stockpiling ahead of an announced supplier price rise, which is good. A new warehouse may have opened and filled, which is neutral and temporary. An acquisition may have brought in a different kind of inventory, which means the two years are not comparable at all.

The ratio's job is to point your attention at the right paragraph of the 10-K, where the explanation will be. Treating a ratio as a verdict skips the step where you find out which of those four worlds you are in — and the four worlds have opposite implications. Treat ratios as anomaly detectors and the workflow becomes: compute broadly, notice what moved, then read narrowly.

Your edge: this is feature engineering

You already do this for a living. Raw statements are the source tables; ratios are derived features — normalized, scale-invariant, comparable across entities and time, exactly like converting raw counts to per-capita rates or click totals to click-through rates before feeding a model. Quant equity funds literally use these ratios as model inputs (Section 18). The whole section is one big feature_pipeline.py for companies.

Two deliberately opposite companies run through this section, because the fastest way to build intuition about a ratio is to see it applied to businesses that sit at opposite ends of it.

SteadyMart is a grocery chain: $50 billion of revenue, very thin margins on each item, warehouses and shelves full of inventory, and a large physical asset base of stores and distribution centres. CloudNine is a software company: $2 billion of revenue, fat margins because copying software costs almost nothing, no inventory whatsoever, and few physical assets.

Almost every ratio below will place them at opposite extremes, and in several cases the company that looks better on one measure looks worse on another. That is not a defect in the ratios; it is the point. Two viable businesses can succeed through entirely different mechanisms, and the ratios are how you tell which mechanism you are looking at.

Profitability: margins, ROA, ROE, ROIC

Profitability ratios divide profit by one of two things, and the choice produces two families that answer different questions. Dividing by revenue gives margins, which ask how much of each sales dollar survives to a particular line. Dividing by capital gives returns, which ask how much profit each dollar invested in the business produces.

The margins form a ladder running down the income statement from Section 11, with each rung stripping out one more category of cost. Reading them together tells you where a company's profit is won or lost — a firm with a strong gross margin and a weak operating margin has a good product and an expensive organisation, which is a completely different problem from a weak gross margin:

  • Gross margin = (Revenue − COGS) ÷ Revenue. What's left after the direct cost of the product itself. SteadyMart: (50,000 − 37,500) ÷ 50,000 = 25%. CloudNine: (2,000 − 400) ÷ 2,000 = 80% — serving one more customer costs a SaaS firm almost nothing.
  • Operating margin = Operating income ÷ Revenue. After SG&A, R&D, depreciation. SteadyMart: 2,000 ÷ 50,000 = 4%. CloudNine: 400 ÷ 2,000 = 20%.
  • Net margin = Net income ÷ Revenue. The bottom line. SteadyMart: 1,250 ÷ 50,000 = 2.5%. CloudNine: 300 ÷ 2,000 = 15%.

Now the returns family, which asks a different question: not how much of each sale becomes profit, but how much profit each dollar of resources produces.

ROA, net income divided by total assets, measures profit per dollar of stuff the company controls, regardless of who funded it. SteadyMart: 1,250 ÷ 20,000 = 6.25%. CloudNine: 300 ÷ 3,000 = 10%.

ROE, net income divided by shareholders' equity, measures profit per dollar of the owners' money specifically. SteadyMart: 1,250 ÷ 8,000 = 15.6%. CloudNine: 300 ÷ 2,400 = 12.5%.

Look carefully at what just happened. CloudNine beats SteadyMart on every margin and on ROA, and yet SteadyMart's return on equity is meaningfully higher. That is not an error, and it is not a sign that SteadyMart is the better business. The difference between ROA and ROE is entirely a matter of how much of the asset base was funded by borrowing rather than by shareholders — and SteadyMart borrows far more. The DuPont decomposition in the next subsection takes this apart properly.

The most informative return of the three is ROIC, return on invested capital, because it is deliberately constructed to be immune to financing decisions and therefore measures the business engine itself.

Two adjustments do that work. The numerator uses operating profit after tax rather than net income, so the interest paid to lenders is not deducted — the measure counts profit available to all funders rather than only shareholders. The denominator adds debt and equity together and subtracts surplus cash, so it counts every dollar actually deployed in the operations, from whatever source, and ignores money sitting idle. In words: how much after-tax operating profit does each dollar genuinely at work in this business produce?

ROIC = NOPAT ÷ Invested capital = EBIT × (1 − t) ÷ (Equity + Debt − Cash)
NOPAT = net operating profit after tax · t = tax rate · invested capital = all funding actually at work

Run both companies through it. SteadyMart's after-tax operating profit is 2,000 × (1 − 0.23) ≈ 1,540, and its invested capital is 8,000 of equity plus 7,500 of debt minus 1,000 of cash = 14,500, giving ROIC of about 10.6%. CloudNine's after-tax operating profit is about 308, and its invested capital is 2,400 + 200 − 1,200 = 1,400, giving roughly 22%.

This is where CloudNine's quality becomes visible in a way ROE concealed. It produces twice the return per dollar of capital deployed, because it barely needs capital: no warehouses, no fleet, no inventory. And there is a second implication that matters more than the level itself. A company earning 22% on capital can reinvest profits into expansion and compound at something near that rate; a company earning 10.6% cannot grow as fast without raising outside money. ROIC compared against the cost of capital from Section 14 is the single cleanest test of whether growth creates value or destroys it.

Key idea: ROIC vs the cost of capital is THE test

Every dollar a company invests has a price — the cost of capital, the return its lenders and shareholders demand (formalized as WACC in Section 14). A company creates value only when ROIC exceeds that hurdle. ROIC of 10.6% against an 8% cost of capital creates value; ROIC of 7% against 9% destroys value, and growing faster just destroys it faster. This single comparison is the spine of valuation in Section 13.

Worked example: two companies, same ROE, only one creates value

ROE is the number shareholders quote, and it is the easiest one to fake with debt. ROIC against the cost of capital is the number that cannot be faked. Two companies both report a 15% ROE:

Compounder Inc. Leveraged Co.
NOPAT (after-tax operating profit) $150M $150M
Invested capital $1,000M $1,500M
ROIC 15.0% 10.0%
Cost of capital (WACC) 8% 8%
Economic spread (ROIC − WACC) +7.0% +2.0%
Value added per year $70M $30M

Same ROE, and Compounder Inc. is more than twice the business. The ROE gap was closed by leverage — Leveraged Co. borrowed its way to a matching headline while earning far less on each dollar actually deployed.

Now the test that matters most in all of corporate finance: a company creates value only when ROIC exceeds WACC. A firm earning 6% on capital that costs 8% destroys value every time it grows — growth makes it smaller in economic terms, even as revenue rises. This single comparison explains why some fast-growing companies are worthless and some no-growth companies are cash machines, and it is the bridge into the valuation math of Section 13 and the cost-of-capital math of Section 14. If you remember one ratio from this entire section, remember ROIC versus WACC.

DuPont: taking ROE apart like an engineer

ROE is the headline figure shareholders watch, and its weakness is that it compresses three different things into one number, so two companies can report an identical ROE for entirely unrelated reasons.

In the 1910s an analyst at DuPont noticed the number can be factored apart. The trick is pure algebra: multiply the definition by revenue over revenue and by assets over assets — both equal to one, so nothing changes — and then regroup the terms. The result splits ROE into three ratios that each describe a distinct business capability. In words: how much profit you keep from each sale, multiplied by how many sales you generate per dollar of assets, multiplied by how many dollars of assets you control per dollar of your own money.

ROE = Net incomeRevenue × RevenueAssets × AssetsEquity = Margin × Turnover × Leverage
margin = pricing power · asset turnover = asset efficiency · leverage = balance-sheet amplification

The classic illustration is a supermarket against a luxury brand, and it shows the three levers substituting for each other.

A supermarket keeps roughly 2% of each sale as profit, which sounds hopeless. But it sells its entire asset base three times over each year, and it funds those assets with three dollars of total assets per dollar of equity. Multiply: 2% × 3.0 × 3.0 = 18% ROE.

A luxury handbag maker keeps 30% of each sale, fifteen times the supermarket's margin. But it turns its assets only half a time a year — inventory is slow-moving and expensive to hold — and it uses modest borrowing at 1.2 times. Multiply: 30% × 0.5 × 1.2 = 18% ROE.

Identical destination by opposite routes. One is a volume machine that makes almost nothing per item and does it constantly; the other is a pricing machine that makes a great deal per item and does it rarely. Neither is better, and no shareholder looking only at ROE would know which one they owned.

Our two companies replay the same story with real numbers. SteadyMart: 2.5% margin × 2.50 asset turnover × 2.50 leverage = 15.6%. CloudNine: 15% × 0.67 × 1.25 = 12.5%. That resolves the puzzle from earlier — the apparently worse business posted the higher ROE by compensating for razor-thin margins with relentless turnover and a substantially leveraged balance sheet.

The decomposition also exposes a risk that ROE hides completely, and this is the practical payoff. Of the three levers, two are hard and one is easy. Raising margins requires pricing power or cost discipline. Raising asset turnover requires operational improvement. Raising leverage requires a phone call to a bank — management can inflate ROE at will simply by borrowing more and buying back shares, without improving the business by a single percentage point.

And leverage is symmetric, as Section 10 showed with property. It multiplies returns in good years and multiplies losses in bad ones, so an ROE built on the leverage lever is not merely lower quality — it is the one that evaporates fastest in a downturn, precisely when the debt still has to be serviced. Two companies with the same ROE are emphatically not the same investment, and the DuPont split is how you tell them apart in thirty seconds.

Real world: DuPont on a warehouse and a jeweller

The DuPont identity earns its keep the moment you point it at two real businesses that reach similar returns by opposite routes. Approximate figures for a mass-market retailer and a luxury house:

Net margin Asset turnover Leverage ROE
Mass-market retailer 2.4% 2.4× 2.9× 16.7%
Luxury goods house 20% 0.6× 1.8× 21.6%

Broadly similar ROE, engineered from completely different physics. The retailer makes almost nothing per item (2.4%) but sells its entire asset base nearly two and a half times a year — it is a velocity business. The luxury house turns its assets barely half a time but keeps 20 cents on every dollar — it is a margin business. Neither can copy the other: if the retailer tried to charge luxury prices it would lose the volume that is its whole model, and if the luxury house chased volume it would destroy the scarcity that justifies its margin.

This is why DuPont is the first thing a good analyst computes. "ROE went from 15% to 18%" is not an insight; "ROE rose because leverage went from 2× to 3× while margins actually fell" is — and it turns a compliment into a warning. Rising ROE driven by rising leverage is borrowed, and it reverses the moment the cycle turns.

Liquidity and solvency: can it pay its bills, and can it survive?

The next family asks whether the company survives, and it splits into two questions with different time horizons that are easy to confuse.

Liquidity asks whether the company can pay the bills falling due over the next twelve months out of assets that will turn into cash in that window. It is a timing question, and a company can fail it while being fundamentally healthy — owning valuable assets that cannot be sold quickly is exactly how solvent businesses go under.

Solvency asks whether the whole capital structure is sustainable: can the earnings the business generates support the total debt it has taken on, over years rather than months? A company can be perfectly liquid and quietly insolvent, paying its bills on time while carrying a debt load its profits will never retire.

The people who care most about both are the lenders you met in Section 8 (Fixed Income), and they do not merely monitor these ratios — they write them into loan agreements as covenants. A covenant is a promise to keep a specified ratio above or below a threshold, and breaching it typically makes the entire loan immediately repayable. That mechanism turns a ratio from a description into a trigger, and it is why companies approaching a covenant limit start behaving strangely near quarter-end.

The short-term pair starts with the current ratio: current assets divided by current liabilities, or in words, how many dollars of things that will become cash within a year sit behind each dollar of bills due within a year. The quick ratio applies the same test after removing inventory, on the grounds that inventory is the current asset you cannot rely on converting quickly at full price — a company in trouble is precisely the one whose goods nobody wants.

SteadyMart: current ratio 4,700 ÷ 4,500 = 1.04; quick ratio (1,000 + 700) ÷ 4,500 = 0.38. CloudNine: both are 1,600 ÷ 400 = 4.0, because it has no inventory to remove.

On paper SteadyMart looks frightening — a quick ratio of 0.38 says it holds only 38 cents of cash and receivables against each dollar of near-term obligations. Apply the first golden rule before concluding anything. A grocer converts inventory to cash within about a month and collects from customers at the till the same day, so its inventory genuinely is nearly cash. The ratio that would signal distress at a machine-tool manufacturer, whose inventory might take a year to sell, is unremarkable here. Thresholds are industry-relative, always.

The gap between the two ratios is worth reading directly: it is essentially the working capital tied up in inventory, expressed as a liquidity difference. A wide gap tells you the company's short-term safety depends on selling things.

The long-term set answers a different question — not "can it pay this year's bills" but "can these earnings support this debt at all" — and a credit analyst works through them in a standard order:

Ratio Formula Rule-of-thumb thresholds lenders use SteadyMart CloudNine
Debt / equity Total debt ÷ equity < 1.0 conservative; > 2.0 aggressive (varies by industry) 0.94 0.08
Net debt / EBITDA (Net debt) ÷ EBITDA < 2× conservative; 2–3× typical investment grade; > 4–5× leveraged / high-yield territory 2.3× net cash
Interest coverage EBIT ÷ interest expense > 4–5× comfortable; 2–3× on watch; < 1.5× distress 5.3× 40×

Work one through properly. SteadyMart's net debt is its total debt of 7,500 minus its cash of 1,000, which is 6,500 — netting the cash off because cash could be used to repay debt tomorrow. Its EBITDA is operating profit of 2,000 plus D&A of 800, so 2,800. Net debt divided by EBITDA is about 2.3, and the sentence that number stands for is: it would take about 2.3 years of gross operating earnings, before interest, tax and any reinvestment, to repay all borrowings. Anything under roughly 3 is comfortably investment-grade territory for a stable business.

Interest coverage asks a more immediate question: how many times over does operating profit cover the interest bill? SteadyMart's is 2,000 ÷ 375 = 5.3 times, which means operating profit could fall by about four-fifths before interest became unpayable. That is the margin of safety a lender actually cares about, because missing an interest payment is what triggers default — not a high debt ratio.

CloudNine holds more cash than debt: net debt of 200 − 1,200 = −1,000, a negative figure meaning it could repay everything and have $1 billion left. From a lender's perspective this is ideal. From a shareholder's it invites a different question, which Section 14 takes up: a billion dollars sitting in short-term deposits is earning far less than the return shareholders expect from the business, so idle cash quietly drags down return on equity. Safety and efficiency pull in opposite directions here, and neither answer is automatically right.

Common pitfall: liquidity ≠ solvency

A company can be liquid but insolvent (plenty of cash today, hopeless debt load long-term) or solvent but illiquid (valuable assets, no cash this quarter — the classic bank-run shape from Section 6). Firms almost always die of illiquidity first: the cash runs out before the balance sheet formally fails. Check both, always.

Efficiency and the cash conversion cycle

Efficiency ratios measure how fast a company cycles its working capital — how quickly money spent on inventory and extended to customers comes back as cash. Three clocks matter, and each measures a different stage of that journey.

Inventory turnover is cost of goods sold divided by inventory, and it counts how many times a year the entire stock is sold and replaced. SteadyMart: 37,500 ÷ 3,000 = 12.5 turns. Converting that into days is more intuitive — divide 365 by the number of turns to get DIO, days inventory outstanding, which for SteadyMart is about 29 days. Goods sit on the shelf for a month.

DSO, days sales outstanding, is receivables divided by revenue times 365, and it counts how long customers take to pay. The two companies could hardly differ more. SteadyMart's shoppers pay at the till, so its DSO is around 5 days. CloudNine invoices corporate customers on 60- or 90-day terms, so its DSO is 400 ÷ 2,000 × 365 = 73 days — it delivers the software immediately and waits two and a half months for the money.

DPO, days payables outstanding, is payables divided by COGS times 365, and it counts how long the company takes to pay its own suppliers. SteadyMart stretches this to about 39 days. Note that a high DPO is a source of free financing — a supplier waiting 39 days for payment is lending you money at zero interest — which is why large retailers negotiate hard on payment terms and small suppliers dread selling to them.

Chain the three clocks together and you get what is probably the most underrated ratio in finance. Stated in words: start on the day you pay for goods, and count the days until the cash from selling them arrives. Goods sit for DIO days, then customers take DSO days to pay — but you did not actually part with money on day zero, because your supplier let you wait DPO days. So the number of days your own cash is tied up is inventory days plus collection days minus the days your supplier financed you. That is the cash conversion cycle:

CCC = DIO + DSO − DPO
days your cash is trapped = days goods sit + days customers owe you − days you owe suppliers

SteadyMart: 29.2 + 5.1 − 38.9 = −4.6 days, and a negative cash conversion cycle is worth reading slowly because it sounds impossible. Trace the timeline: the grocer receives groceries on day 0, sells them around day 29, collects the money at the till essentially immediately — and does not pay the supplier until day 39. The customers' cash arrives five days before the supplier's bill leaves.

The consequence is that growth funds itself. Every additional dollar of sales generates cash before it consumes any, so SteadyMart can open new stores partly on its suppliers' money. This is not a curiosity of grocery retail — it is how Amazon financed a great deal of its early expansion, and it is one of the strongest structural advantages a business can have.

CloudNine, despite margins SteadyMart could never approach, runs 0 + 73 − 54.8 ≈ +18 days. It holds no inventory, but it waits ten weeks to be paid, so every dollar of new sales temporarily consumes cash while the invoice ages. Faster growth means a bigger hole to fund, and the company must finance that gap from its own balance sheet or from investors. The most profitable business in this section is the one whose growth costs it money — which is exactly the gap between profit and cash that Section 11 was about.

Real world: Amazon's negative-CCC superpower

For most of its history Amazon has run a CCC around minus 20 to 30 days: customers pay by card instantly, inventory turns fast, and suppliers wait two to three months. Every incremental sale therefore generates float — an interest-free loan from suppliers that grows automatically with revenue. That float helped fund Amazon's expansion for decades with less need for outside capital. A negative CCC means growth feeds cash instead of eating it, which is why analysts treat it as a structural superpower.

Worked example: how a growing company drowns in its own success

The cash conversion cycle is not just a diagnostic — it is a cash forecast. A manufacturer has DIO = 80 days, DSO = 60 days, DPO = 40 days, so its CCC = 80 + 60 − 40 = 100 days. Every dollar of sales ties up cash for 100 days before it comes back.

Now it lands a huge contract and doubles sales from $50M to $100M. Sounds triumphant. Watch the cash:

Working-capital line At $50M At $100M Extra cash needed
Inventory (80 days) $11.0M $21.9M $10.9M
Receivables (60 days) $8.2M $16.4M $8.2M
Less: payables (40 days) −$5.5M −$11.0M −$5.5M
Net working capital $13.7M $27.4M $13.7M

Doubling sales demands roughly $13.7M of extra cash — locked in inventory and unpaid invoices — before the profit on the new contract arrives. A company that grows faster than it can finance its working capital runs out of cash while its income statement looks glorious. This is "overtrading," and it kills more small companies than losses do.

Shrinking the CCC frees this cash directly: knock DSO from 60 to 45 days by invoicing faster and you release about $2M with no new sales at all. That is why "cash is trapped in the cycle" is a lever a good operator actively pulls, and why a negative CCC — customers paying before suppliers are paid, as with Amazon or Dell in its heyday — is a genuine competitive weapon: growth funds itself instead of consuming cash.

Market ratios: what the price tag says

Every ratio so far has used only the financial statements, which means it describes the business and says nothing about what you would pay to own it. Market ratios add one ingredient from outside the accounts — the share price from Section 7 — and ask a different question: given all of the above, what are investors currently paying for it?

SteadyMart trades at a market capitalisation of 20,000 and CloudNine at 9,000.
