Note immediately that the smaller-revenue company carries nearly half the larger one's market value, which is the market pricing the differences the previous subsections identified: higher margins, higher ROIC, and presumably faster expected growth.

  • P/E = price ÷ earnings. SteadyMart: 20,000 ÷ 1,250 = 16×. CloudNine: 9,000 ÷ 300 = 30×. The market pays almost twice as much per dollar of CloudNine's profit — it's pricing in growth and that 22% ROIC. Best for stable, profitable firms; meaningless when earnings are negative or temporarily depressed.
  • P/B = price ÷ book value. SteadyMart 2.5×, CloudNine 3.75×. Most useful for banks and insurers, whose assets are financial and marked close to reality; least useful for firms whose real assets (brands, code) never hit the balance sheet.
  • EV/EBITDA = enterprise value ÷ EBITDA. EV adds net debt to market cap, so the ratio is capital-structure-neutral — ideal for comparing firms with different debt loads, and the workhorse of buyout analysis. SteadyMart: (20,000 + 6,500) ÷ 2,800 ≈ 9.5×. CloudNine: (9,000 − 1,000) ÷ 460 ≈ 17.4×.
  • FCF yield = free cash flow ÷ market cap. SteadyMart: 1,150 ÷ 20,000 = 5.75%; CloudNine: 350 ÷ 9,000 ≈ 3.9%. The hardest multiple to fake, because it's built on cash (remember Section 11: cash is the ground truth).
  • Dividend yield = dividends ÷ price. SteadyMart pays 500, so 2.5%; CloudNine pays nothing, reinvesting everything at its 22% ROIC — which, given the ROIC-vs-cost-of-capital test, is exactly what it should do.

One reframe before Section 13, because it is the most common conceptual error in this whole area. A multiple is not a valuation. It is shorthand for one.

Saying a company trades at 30 times earnings states a fact about the price and asserts nothing about whether that price is correct. Thirty times is cheap for a business growing 40% a year at a 25% return on capital, and wildly expensive for one growing 2% with returns below its cost of capital. The multiple compresses growth, returns and risk into a single number and then hides which of them is doing the work.

Valuation, the subject of the next section, is the discipline of unpacking that: building the expected cash flows explicitly and checking whether the multiple the market is quoting is justified by them. Ratios do not answer that question. What they do is tell you which multiples deserve the interrogation, which is a genuinely useful thing for a number to do.

Two-company ratio lab: SteadyMart vs CloudNine

Same two companies, five lenses. Click through the ratio families and watch the DuPont view explain how a 2.5%-margin grocer out-ROEs an 80%-gross-margin SaaS firm. All figures in $ millions.

Mini-financials ($M) SteadyMart (grocery) CloudNine (SaaS)
Revenue 50,000 2,000
COGS 37,500 400
Operating income (EBIT) 2,000 400
EBITDA 2,800 460
Interest expense 375 10
Net income 1,250 300
Cash 1,000 1,200
Receivables 700 400
Inventory 3,000 0
Total assets 20,000 3,000
Current assets / current liabilities 4,700 / 4,500 1,600 / 400
Accounts payable (within CL) 4,000 60
Total debt 7,500 200
Shareholders' equity 8,000 2,400
Market cap 20,000 9,000
Free cash flow / dividends 1,150 / 500 350 / 0

Worked example: the same company, cheap and expensive at once

A crucial habit: a company is never simply "cheap" or "expensive" — it is cheap on some multiples and expensive on others, and the disagreement is the signal. One company, one day, five lenses:

Multiple Value Peer median Verdict
P/E (price ÷ earnings) 25× 18× Looks expensive
EV/EBITDA 8× 11× Looks cheap
P/B (price ÷ book) 1.2× 2.5× Looks very cheap
FCF yield 5.0% 4.0% Looks cheap
Dividend yield 1.0% 3.0% Looks stingy

The P/E screams "expensive" while EV/EBITDA and P/B whisper "bargain." What reconciles them? Usually debt and non-cash charges. P/E is hit by heavy interest expense and big depreciation, both of which sit below EBITDA — so a capital-intensive, indebted company routinely looks dear on P/E and cheap on EV/EBITDA. The low P/B says the market doubts the assets are worth their book value; the healthy FCF yield says the cash is real.

The analyst's move is not to average these into one verdict — it is to ask why they disagree. Each multiple is a ratio with a different numerator and denominator, sensitive to different things: P/E to earnings and leverage, EV/EBITDA to capital structure-neutral operating profit, P/B to asset quality, FCF yield to actual cash. When they point in different directions, you have found the exact question the valuation in Section 13 exists to answer.

Earnings quality and red flags: a forensic mini-checklist

Every ratio in this section trusts the reported figures, and Section 11 established why that trust is conditional. Accounting runs on accruals, which means management makes judgement calls about when revenue is earned and when costs are incurred. Those calls are legitimate and necessary, and they are also where the pressure lands when a quarter is going badly.

Earnings quality is the question of how much of the reported bottom line is real, repeatable cash generation and how much is accounting judgement holding it up. It is not the same question as profitability. A company can have excellent margins and poor earnings quality, and that combination has preceded most of the well-known accounting failures.

The good news is that low earnings quality leaves detectable traces, because the accruals that flatter profit have to sit somewhere on the balance sheet and cannot be reversed indefinitely. A short forensic checklist catches most of the classic games:

  • Net income growing while operating cash flow shrinks. Profits are an opinion; cash is a fact. When the two diverge for several quarters, the "profit" is increasingly made of accruals — book revenue that hasn't been collected, or costs that haven't been recognized. This single check would have flagged Enron years early.
  • Receivables growing faster than revenue. If sales rise 10% but receivables rise 30%, the company is either extending desperate credit terms or channel stuffing — borrowing next quarter's sales to make this quarter's number. Watch DSO trend upward.
  • Serial "one-time" charges. A restructuring charge every single year is not one-time; it's a recurring cost that management wants you to exclude. Compare "adjusted" earnings to plain GAAP earnings — a persistently widening gap is a tell.
  • Aggressive capitalization. When a company chooses to capitalize everyday costs, expenses vanish from the income statement into the balance sheet, inflating today's profit. WorldCom capitalized $3.8 billion of routine network fees this way — for a while, it worked.
  • Inventory outrunning sales. Stock piling up faster than revenue usually precedes markdowns and margin pain — the turnover ratio sniffs it out before management admits it.

Notice what every flag on that list has in common: each is itself a ratio, or a comparison of two growth rates — cash from operations against net income, the growth in receivables against the growth in revenue, adjusted earnings against GAAP earnings. Forensic accounting is not a separate discipline with its own tools. It is ratio analysis conducted with a suspicious mind, comparing two things that ought to move together and asking why they did not.

Be clear about what a flag means, though. None of these proves anything. Receivables growing faster than revenue is consistent with fraud and equally consistent with a deliberate move into enterprise customers who pay on ninety-day terms. What the flag earns is a place on your list of things to read the footnotes about — and the discipline that separates good analysts from confident ones is doing that reading before forming the conclusion rather than after.

Deep dive: when ratios break

Every ratio has failure modes, and knowing them separates users from tourists. Negative equity: a company that has bought back more stock than it ever earned (Home Depot and Starbucks have both been here) can have negative book equity, making ROE and debt/equity mathematically meaningless — the denominators flip sign. Use ROIC and net debt/EBITDA instead. Negative earnings: P/E is undefined for loss-makers; analysts fall back on EV/Sales or forward earnings estimates, each with its own hazards. EBITDA skepticism: EBITDA ignores capital expenditure entirely, which is why Warren Buffett quips that managements touting EBITDA are hoping you'll forget that depreciation is a real cost — a telecom that must replace its network every seven years cannot pay creditors with EBITDA. Point-in-time denominators: balance-sheet items are snapshots, so a retailer's year-end inventory (measured after the holiday sell-down) understates its true average; careful analysts use averages of beginning and ending balances. The pattern: whenever a ratio looks absurd, check whether a denominator is small, negative, or unrepresentative before drawing any conclusion.

Check your understanding

1. Firm A has 10% net margin, 1.5× asset turnover, 1.0× leverage. Firm B has 2% margin, 2.5× turnover, 3.0× leverage. Both show 15% ROE. Which statement is most accurate?

DuPont shows the levers: A earns its 15% with no leverage at all, while B multiplies a thin margin by 3× borrowed money (2% × 2.5 × 3.0 = 15%). B's ROE would collapse fastest in a downturn, when leverage cuts both ways.

2. A company earns 7% ROIC while its cost of capital is 9%, and it's reinvesting heavily to grow revenue 20% a year. What is it doing to shareholder value?

Value is created only when ROIC exceeds the cost of capital. Earning 7% on money that costs 9% loses 2 cents per dollar invested, so pouring more capital in at that spread just scales up the loss.

3. A retailer has a cash conversion cycle of −8 days. What does that mean?

Negative CCC means DPO exceeds DIO + DSO: money comes in before it goes out. Growth then generates interest-free float rather than consuming cash — the Amazon-style superpower.

4. Net income has grown 15% a year for three years, but operating cash flow has fallen each year and DSO keeps climbing. The most likely explanation?

Rising DSO plus profits diverging from cash means revenue is being recognized well ahead of collection — possibly channel stuffing. (Note the third option has it backwards: depreciation lowers net income, not operating cash flow.)

5. You want to compare two similar manufacturers, one debt-free and one financed 60% with debt. Which multiple compares their operating businesses most cleanly?

P/E is distorted by capital structure — the levered firm's earnings are reduced by interest while its equity is smaller. EV/EBITDA prices the whole business (equity plus net debt) against profit measured before financing costs, making the two comparable.

Key takeaways

  • Ratios normalize away size — they are engineered features derived from raw statements. Always compare against peers and against the company's own history, and treat every ratio as a question generator, not a verdict.
  • Margins (gross → operating → net) measure profit per dollar of sales; ROA, ROE, and ROIC measure profit per dollar of capital. ROIC versus the cost of capital is the single test of whether a company creates value.
  • DuPont factors ROE into margin × turnover × leverage: a 2%-margin supermarket and a 30%-margin luxury house can post identical ROE through opposite levers — and ROE built on leverage is the fragile kind.
  • Lenders live on liquidity and solvency ratios: quick ratio near 1, net debt/EBITDA under ~3×, and interest coverage above ~4–5× are the classic comfort zones, all industry-dependent.
  • The cash conversion cycle (DIO + DSO − DPO) counts the days cash is trapped in operations; a negative CCC means suppliers finance the business and growth generates float instead of consuming cash.
  • Market multiples are shorthand valuations: P/E for stable earners, P/B for banks, EV/EBITDA across capital structures, FCF yield when you want the number hardest to fake.
  • Earnings quality checks are ratios too: cash flow diverging from net income, receivables outrunning revenue, serial one-time charges, and aggressive capitalization are the four flags that catch most accounting games.

Part III · Corporate Finance & Accounting

13. Valuation: What Is a Company Worth?

Every price on a stock screen is an opinion; valuation is how you form your own. By the end of this section you will be able to build a discounted cash flow model from scratch, sanity-check it with multiples, and answer the classic interview question "walk me through a DCF" without breaking a sweat.

Price is what you pay, value is what you estimate

Section 7 (Equities) established that a stock's market price is simply the last price at which two strangers agreed to trade. That number is a fact, observable to five decimal places, and it requires no judgement to state.

What the company is worth — its intrinsic value — is not a fact. It is an estimate of something that has not happened yet: the cash the business will produce over the rest of its existence. Two competent analysts with the same data will produce different numbers, because they hold different beliefs about the future, and neither can be shown to be wrong today.

Every serious valuation therefore comes with error bars, whether the analyst states them or not. A spreadsheet that outputs $31.47 is not more precise than one that outputs "somewhere between $26 and $38" — it is less honest about the same underlying uncertainty. Holding that distinction between price and value clearly in mind is what the rest of this section depends on.

There are two families of valuation method, and they attack the problem from opposite directions.

Intrinsic valuation asks what cash the business will hand its owners over its lifetime, and what that stream is worth today. It requires you to forecast the future explicitly and to state a rate at which future money is discounted. That is the discounted cash flow method, and mechanically it is nothing more than the time-value machinery from Section 1 pointed at an entire company instead of a single payment. Its virtue is that every assumption is visible; its weakness is that it requires you to make them.

Relative valuation asks a lazier and often smarter question: what are similar companies selling for right now? Instead of forecasting anything, you observe what the market pays for comparable businesses and apply the same ratio to yours. This is the world of multiples and comparable companies. Its virtue is that it is fast and grounded in real transactions; its weakness is that it inherits whatever the market currently believes, so in a bubble every company looks correctly priced relative to every other one.

Professionals use both, and the disagreement between them is often more informative than either result alone.

Key idea: the same two methods, on a house

The two families are not abstractions peculiar to companies; they are how anyone prices anything that produces income, and a house makes the distinction concrete. The intrinsic route asks what rent the property would earn, subtracts what it costs to own and maintain, and discounts that stream back to today at a rate reflecting how risky the rental income is. The relative route ignores rent entirely and asks what the three nearly identical houses on the same street sold for last quarter.

Notice that the two methods can disagree, and that the disagreement is informative rather than embarrassing. If the rental math says $400,000 and recent sales say $550,000, either buyers on that street are paying for something the rental calculation misses — an expected rezoning, a school catchment, a belief that prices keep rising — or the street is expensive relative to what the properties actually earn. Both are worth knowing, and neither number is "the truth."

A competent estate agent runs both and becomes suspicious when they diverge sharply. That is precisely the professional habit this section is teaching, and the triangulation discussion at the end returns to it.

Here is the mindset shift that separates people who use valuation models from people who operate spreadsheets. A valuation model is not a machine for computing the answer. It is a device for organising your assumptions so that disagreement becomes legible.

Consider what happens when your model says $31.50 and the market says $28. The naive reading is that you have found 12.5% of upside. The professional reading is that you and the market hold different beliefs, and the model tells you precisely which ones: your growth assumption, your margin assumption, or your view of the risk. You can then ask the productive question — what would have to be true for the market's number to be right? Sometimes the answer is a growth rate you consider implausible, and you have found a disagreement worth acting on. Sometimes it is an assumption you had not examined, and the market has taught you something.

That reframing has a practical consequence for how you build models. The goal is not maximum precision in the output but maximum clarity about the inputs, because the inputs are what you are actually arguing about. A model whose assumptions are buried in hardcoded cells cannot do this job however accurate it turns out to be.

Your edge

You already do this. A valuation model is a forward inference with hand-tuned priors: point estimates in, point estimate out, and the honest deliverable is a sensitivity analysis, not a single number. Treat "intrinsic value = $31.50" the way you'd treat a regression prediction with no confidence interval — politely, but skeptically.

A DCF end to end: every single number

Meet Cascade Beverages, the worked example for this section. It generated free cash flow of $100M this year, carries net debt of $200M, has 50M shares outstanding, and trades at $28 a share.

Free cash flow is the input everything else runs on, so be clear about what it is. It comes from the statements built in Section 11: operating profit after tax, plus depreciation and amortisation added back because they consumed no cash, minus capital expenditure and minus any increase in working capital, both of which consume cash without appearing as expenses. What remains is money the business genuinely produced and does not need in order to keep operating — which is exactly the money available to the people who financed it.

Note whose money it is. Free cash flow at this level is available to lenders and shareholders together, before interest has been paid to anyone. That is deliberate, and it is why the calculation below values the whole business first and only subtracts debt at the very end.

A discounted cash flow model has five moves, and the arithmetic in each is simple; the difficulty is entirely in the assumptions.

Move 1 — project the explicit years. Forecast free cash flow year by year for a period short enough that you can reason about it concretely, conventionally five years. The reason for a finite horizon is practical rather than theoretical: forecasting individual years beyond about five is guesswork dressed up as detail, so everything past that gets handled in one lump by Move 2. For Cascade, assume free cash flow grows at 10% a year:

Year FCF ($M) Discount factor (÷1.10t) Present value ($M)
1 110.00 0.9091 100.00
2 121.00 0.8264 100.00
3 133.10 0.7513 100.00
4 146.41 0.6830 100.00
5 161.05 0.6209 100.00
Sum 500.00

Look at what happened in that table: every present value comes out at exactly $100M. That is not a coincidence in the accidental sense — it happens because the growth rate and the discount rate are both 10%, so each year's cash flow is compounding up at precisely the rate it is being discounted back down at, and the two cancel exactly.

It is worth pausing on that, because it makes a point the rest of the model depends on. Growth by itself creates no value. Cash flows growing at 10% discounted at 10% are worth no more per year than flat cash flows discounted at zero growth would be. Value is created only when growth exceeds the rate of return investors require for the risk taken — which is the same proposition, in valuation language, as the ROIC-versus-cost-of-capital test from Section 12.

Move 2 — the terminal value. Cascade does not cease to exist at the end of year 5, so the model needs a value for everything beyond the forecast horizon, computed as of the end of year 5.

The standard tool is the Gordon growth model, which values a perpetuity growing at a constant rate. Stated in words: the value of a stream of cash that grows forever at a steady rate equals next year's cash flow divided by the difference between the discount rate and the growth rate. The intuition is that the discount rate erodes value each year while growth replenishes it, so what matters is the gap between them — and if growth ever equalled or exceeded the discount rate, the sum would be infinite, which is why the terminal growth rate must be modest.

How modest? A company cannot outgrow the economy forever, or it would eventually become the entire economy. So terminal growth is conventionally capped around the long-run rate of nominal GDP growth — something like 2% to 3%. Anyone using 5% is implicitly claiming the business will one day be larger than the country it operates in. With terminal growth of 2% and a discount rate of 10% from the next subsection:

TV = FCF5 × (1 + g) ÷ (WACC − g) = 161.05 × 1.02 ÷ (0.10 − 0.02) = $2,053.4M
TV = terminal value at end of year 5 · g = perpetual growth rate · WACC = discount rate

Move 3 — discount everything back to today. The explicit years are already in present-value terms and total $500M. The terminal value is expressed as of the end of year 5, so it must be brought back five years like any other year-5 amount: 2,053.4 × 0.6209 = $1,275.0M.

Adding the two gives enterprise value: 500 + 1,275 = $1,775M. Enterprise value is the value of the operating business itself, belonging jointly to everyone who financed it.

Now notice something uncomfortable in that arithmetic. The terminal value is $1,275M of a $1,775M total — 72% of the entire valuation. Roughly three-quarters of the answer comes from a single formula applied to a period beyond any horizon you attempted to forecast, using a growth rate you assumed and a discount rate you estimated. The five years of careful year-by-year projection account for barely a quarter of it. This is true of almost every DCF ever built, and it is the honest reason experienced people are sceptical of precise-looking DCF outputs.

Move 4 — from the business to the shareholders. Enterprise value belongs to everyone who financed the company, and the payment queue from Section 7 decides who is paid first. Lenders have the senior claim, so their claim comes out before shareholders see anything: subtract net debt to get equity value, 1,775 − 200 = $1,575M. Net debt rather than gross debt, because the company's cash could be used to repay borrowings tomorrow.

Move 5 — reduce to a per-share figure. Divide equity value by the share count: 1,575 ÷ 50 = $31.50 a share.

Against a market price of $28, the model implies about 12.5% upside. Stated more honestly, and in the framing from earlier: our assumptions are about 12.5% more optimistic than the ones embedded in the market price. Whether that is an opportunity depends entirely on whether our assumptions are better than the market's, which the model cannot tell us.

WACC: the price tag on risk

Everything above was discounted at 10%. That number was asserted rather than derived, and since the previous subsection showed it drives most of the answer, it deserves proper treatment.

The discount rate for an entire company is its WACC, the weighted average cost of capital, and the reasoning behind it is straightforward. A company is funded by two kinds of provider — lenders and shareholders — and each requires a different return, because each bears different risk. Lenders are paid first and require less; shareholders are paid last and require more. The business as a whole must therefore earn enough to satisfy both, which is the average of the two required returns, weighted by how much of the funding each provides.

In words: multiply the shareholders' required return by the share of total funding they supply, multiply the lenders' required return by the share they supply, and add the two. It is a weighted average and nothing more intimidating than that:

WACC = (E ÷ V) × re + (D ÷ V) × rd × (1 − t)
E = market value of equity · D = market value of debt · V = E + D · re = cost of equity · rd = cost of debt · t = tax rate

The two ingredients need estimating separately. The cost of equity is the return shareholders demand for holding this particular stock, and since nobody publishes it, it must be inferred. The standard estimate is the CAPM.

Stated in words, it says: start with what you can earn taking no risk at all, then add compensation for the risk you are taking, scaled by how much of the market's risk this particular stock carries. The first term is the risk-free rate — a long-dated Treasury yield from Section 8. The scaling factor is beta, which measures how much the stock moves when the market moves. And the thing being scaled is the equity risk premium, the extra annual return investors have demanded for holding equities rather than Treasuries. Written compactly: re = rf + β × ERP.

One feature of that formula is worth flagging now even though it is only justified in Section 15 (Portfolio Theory). It prices only the risk that moves with the market, and ignores risk specific to the individual company entirely — on the argument that company-specific risk can be diversified away for free, so nobody should be paid for bearing it. For now, treat CAPM as a pricing formula for risk and note that it is a model with known empirical problems rather than a law.

Put Cascade's numbers through it. With a risk-free rate of 4%, a beta of 1.25 and an equity risk premium of 5.5%, the cost of equity is 4% + 1.25 × 5.5% = 10.9%.

The cost of debt is easier because it is observable: it is roughly the yield on the company's bonds, say 6%. But the figure that enters WACC is lower than that, because interest payments are deducted from taxable income, so borrowing reduces the tax bill. That saving is called the tax shield, and it means the company's true cost of a 6% loan at a 25% tax rate is 6% × (1 − 0.25) = 4.5%. Note that dividends receive no such treatment, which is one reason debt looks cheap and a central theme of Section 14.

Finally the weights, which use market values rather than balance-sheet values because we are asking what investors require on what they actually have at stake today. Equity is 50M shares × $28 = $1,400M. Debt is $300M gross — note that the $200M of net debt used in Move 4 is this $300M less $100M of cash, and WACC weights use the gross figure. So:

WACC = (1,400 ÷ 1,700) × 10.9% + (300 ÷ 1,700) × 4.5% = 8.98% + 0.79% ≈ 9.8%
We round to 10% for clean arithmetic — and because pretending WACC is precise to two decimals is theater.

One conceptual point before moving on, because it is where most misuse of DCF originates: why does riskier mean a higher discount rate?

Because a dollar you might not receive is worth less today than a dollar you certainly will. Discounting is how that difference gets expressed numerically — there is no other place in the model where uncertainty about the cash flows is recorded. The projections themselves are single numbers presented as though they were certain; the discount rate is what converts them back into something honest.

Which means the discount rate is not a technical parameter to be minimised. Discounting a speculative biotech's projected cash flows at 6% quietly asserts that those projections are as dependable as a regulated utility's, and the model will faithfully reward that assertion with an enormous valuation. The most common way to produce a DCF that says whatever you want is to choose a comfortable discount rate. How companies actually choose their debt-and-equity mix, and whether WACC can be deliberately engineered downward, is the subject of Section 14.

Common pitfall

Weighting WACC with book values from the balance sheet instead of market values, or using yesterday's interest rates for rf. WACC is a current market opportunity cost: what investors could earn elsewhere today, not what the company paid historically.

The embarrassing truth: sensitivity

Now the part practitioners discuss quietly. Move WACC from 10% to 9% and terminal growth from 2% to 3% — one percentage point each, in the same direction — and Cascade's value per share jumps from $31.50 to $42.22. Move them the other way, to 11% and 1%, and it falls to $25.04. That is a 69% swing in the answer from adjusting two inputs by one point apiece, and neither input can be estimated to within a point by anybody.

The mechanism is visible in the terminal value formula. Its denominator is WACC minus g — the difference between two uncertain numbers that happen to be close together. At 10% and 2% the denominator is 0.08; at 9% and 3% it is 0.06. A one-point move in each input changed the denominator by 25%, and since the terminal value is that denominator's reciprocal times a cash flow, the terminal value moved by a third. Dividing by a small, shaky number is exactly as unstable as it sounds, and the terminal value is 72% of the answer.

This is not a flaw to be fixed with better inputs. It is a structural property of valuing a perpetuity, and it means any single DCF output is spurious precision. What the model is genuinely good at is telling you how the answer responds to beliefs — which is what the next two techniques are built to display.

Honest analysts respond to that instability in two standard ways, and both are about presenting a range rather than a point.

The sensitivity table is a grid of valuations computed across a span of WACC values and terminal growth rates — typically a five by five matrix. Its purpose is to show the reader the whole distribution of answers the model produces under reasonable assumptions, instead of one number that pretends the assumptions were known. A reader can then locate their own beliefs on the grid and read off the implied value.

The football field chart does the same job across methods rather than across inputs. Each valuation approach — DCF, trading comparables, precedent transactions, 52-week trading range — is drawn as a horizontal bar spanning the range it produces, with the current market price overlaid as a vertical line. Where several independent methods overlap is where your conviction should live, because agreement between approaches that make different assumptions is genuine evidence in a way that a single method's precision is not.

Both are worth trying live. The model below is the identical Cascade DCF built above — same starting free cash flow, same net debt, same share count — with the three major assumptions exposed as sliders, so you can watch the output respond rather than take the previous paragraphs on trust.

Mini DCF model: Cascade Beverages

Base FCF $100M, net debt $200M, 50M shares, market price $28. Move the sliders and watch the value — and the sensitivity grid — react.

Enterprise value—
Equity value—
Value per share—
vs $28 market price—
Per-share value g −1pp g g +1pp
WACC −1pp — — —
WACC — — —
WACC +1pp — — —

Cells are shaded by upside (toward green) or downside (toward red) vs the $28 market price. The grid clamps WACC − g to at least 0.5pp so the perpetuity never divides by zero — watch values explode as the spread shrinks.

Two minutes with that model teaches the lesson better than the paragraphs above can. Move the explicit-year growth slider across its whole range and the answer shifts modestly. Move WACC or terminal growth by a fraction of that and the answer moves far more.

This is why interviewers press hard on how you derived your discount rate and barely engage with your year-three revenue estimate. It is not that the forecast years are unimportant to understanding the business — they are how you demonstrate you understand it. It is that they contribute little to the number, so an analyst who has polished the projections while waving at the discount rate has spent their effort on the part that does not matter.

Worked example: run the DCF backwards to see what's priced in

Because a DCF is so sensitive to assumptions, the smartest way to use it is often in reverse: instead of forecasting growth to derive a value, take the market's value and solve for the growth it implies. Then you only have to answer one question — is that growth believable?

Cascade trades at $28 with 50M shares, so equity is $1,400M and, adding $200M of net debt, enterprise value is $1,600M. Hold WACC at 10% and terminal growth at 2%, and ask: what five-year FCF growth rate makes the DCF equal $1,600M? Solving the model gives about 7.5%.

The market is implicitly assuming… FCF growth Implied value
What today's $28 price requires 7.5% $28.00
Your base case 10.0% $31.50
A cautious case 5.0% ≈ $25.30

Now the analysis is tractable. You are no longer defending a fragile point estimate; you are judging whether 7.5% annual cash-flow growth is easy or hard for this business. If Cascade has grown 12% for a decade in an expanding market, 7.5% looks conservative and the stock looks cheap. If it is a mature brand losing share, 7.5% looks heroic and the stock looks dear.

This "market-implied expectations" approach is how thoughtful investors actually use a DCF, and it neatly sidesteps the sensitivity embarrassment: you never claim to know the true value, only whether the market's embedded assumption is one you would take the other side of. It is also the most honest framing you can bring to an interview.

Relative valuation: comps and precedents

Relative valuation outsources the hard assumptions to the market: instead of forecasting a company's future, you observe what buyers currently pay for similar businesses and apply the same ratio. The comps method runs in five steps.

Step 1: choose the peer set — companies with similar business models, growth rates, margins and size. This step quietly determines the answer, and it is where most of the manipulation in the method lives. Put a slow-growing regional bottler into a peer set of fast-growing energy-drink companies and every number downstream is meaningless, however carefully computed. Because peer selection is a judgement call that moves the result substantially, an analyst who wants a particular answer can usually construct a peer set that produces it — which is why the first question to ask about any comps analysis is who is in it and who was left out.

Step 2: pull each peer's valuation multiples from market data. Step 3: take the median rather than the mean, because a single peer trading at an extreme multiple — often one with temporarily depressed earnings — would drag an average badly. Step 4: apply the median multiple to your own company's corresponding metric. Step 5: convert the result to a per-share value, subtracting net debt first if the multiple you used was an enterprise-value one.

Two multiples do most of the work, and the difference between them is about which claimants they include.

EV/EBITDA compares the value of the whole business to a profit measure taken before interest is paid. Both the numerator and the denominator therefore belong to lenders and shareholders together, which makes the ratio indifferent to how much debt each company carries. That is exactly what you want when the peer set contains companies with very different borrowing levels, and it is why EV/EBITDA is standard in mergers and acquisitions, where the buyer will refinance the debt anyway.

The P/E ratio compares the equity price to earnings after interest has been deducted. Both halves belong to shareholders alone, so the ratio is internally consistent but is affected by leverage — a more indebted company will show a different P/E even with an identical underlying business. That is acceptable when the peers have similar debt loads, and P/E remains the default for quick public-market comparison because earnings per share is universally reported.

Mixing the two is a well-known rookie error and worth stating as a rule: never place an equity-only numerator over a pre-interest denominator, or the reverse. Price divided by EBITDA compares what shareholders pay against profit that partly belongs to lenders, and the resulting number means nothing at all. Keep both halves of any multiple belonging to the same set of claimants.

Worked example

Cascade's EBITDA is $180M. Five peers trade at EV/EBITDA of 9.2×, 10.1×, 10.8×, 11.5×, and 14.0× (median 10.8×). Implied EV = 10.8 × 180 = $1,944M. Subtract $200M net debt → equity $1,744M → ÷ 50M shares → $34.88. Note the same tail-end steps as the DCF: multiples on EV still require the EV → equity → per-share march.

Precedent transactions are comparables built from prices actually paid in past acquisitions rather than from prices at which shares currently trade. They are constructed the same way and read differently, because they come out systematically higher.

The reason is the control premium, typically 20% to 40% above the pre-announcement share price. A buyer acquiring the whole company is purchasing something a shareholder buying 100 shares does not get: the power to replace management, change strategy, sell divisions, and combine operations with its own to eliminate duplicated costs. That control has value, and acquirers pay for it.

Which gives a clean rule for choosing between the two. Use precedent transactions when valuing a company that is actually being sold, because that is the transaction you are pricing. Use trading comparables when valuing shares you would merely hold, because a minority shareholder is not buying control and should not pay for it. Applying takeover multiples to a company nobody is buying is one of the more common ways to talk yourself into overpaying.

Key idea

A multiple is a compressed DCF. EV/EBITDA of 10.8× is shorthand for a whole bundle of growth, margin, and risk assumptions the market is making about the peers. Comps don't avoid assumptions — they borrow the market's, which is great exactly when the market knows more than you and dangerous exactly when it doesn't (see Section 17 on bubbles).

Worked example: building Cascade's football field

No single method is trusted alone; analysts present a range from several, drawn as a "football field" of overlapping bars. Here is Cascade valued five ways — same company, five lenses:

Method How Value per share
DCF — cautious 5% growth, 10% WACC $25
DCF — base 10% growth, 10% WACC $32
Trading comps 10.8× median EV/EBITDA × $180M − net debt $35
52-week trading range where it has actually changed hands $22 – $34
Precedent M&A acquirers paid ~13× EBITDA, with a control premium $41

The methods do not agree, and that is the point — they bracket a range of roughly $25 to $41, with the current $28 price sitting near the low end. Two structural facts fall straight out of the ordering. Precedent deals sit highest because an acquirer pays a control premium — the right to run the whole company — on top of the market price. Trading comps sit above the base DCF because the peer group is currently priced optimistically, which is exactly the assumption a from-scratch DCF refuses to inherit.

A professional would not report "$33.60." They would say: "Intrinsically Cascade is worth the high-$20s to low-$30s; it would fetch around $40 in a takeover; and at $28 it is toward the bottom of every method's range." That sentence is worth more than any single number, because it tells you both the estimate and how much to trust it.

"Walk me through a DCF" — the interview answer

"Walk me through a DCF" is the single most common technical question in finance interviews, and the reason it is asked is that a good answer demonstrates you understand the whole chain — cash flows, discounting, claimants — rather than having memorised a formula.

Here is an answer you can deliver in about sixty seconds. Every clause of it is something the preceding subsections have now justified, which matters because the follow-up questions probe exactly that:

Say this

  1. "A DCF values a company as the present value of its future free cash flows. I'd start by projecting unlevered free cash flow for five to ten years — revenue growth down to operating profit, taxed, plus depreciation, minus capex and the change in working capital."
  2. "Next I'd estimate a terminal value for everything beyond the projection window, either with the Gordon growth method — final-year FCF times one plus g, over WACC minus g — or an exit multiple on terminal-year EBITDA, and I'd cross-check one against the other."
  3. "Then I'd discount the explicit cash flows and the terminal value back to today at the WACC — cost of equity from CAPM, after-tax cost of debt, weighted by market values. That sum is enterprise value."
  4. "To get to what shareholders own, I'd subtract net debt — and any preferred stock or minority interests — to reach equity value, then divide by diluted shares for a per-share value."
  5. "Finally I'd sensitize it — a WACC-versus-terminal-growth grid — because the terminal value usually carries 60 to 80 percent of the total, and I'd triangulate against trading comps and precedent transactions before trusting the number."

Two follow-ups arrive almost every time, and both are checking whether you understand the model or have merely recited it.

"Why do you subtract net debt?" Because a discounted cash flow built on free cash flow before interest values the entire operating business, and that value belongs to everyone who financed it. Lenders have the senior claim and are paid first, so shareholders own only what is left after the debt is settled. Subtracting net rather than gross debt reflects that the company's cash could retire borrowings immediately.

"What drives the output most?" WACC and terminal growth, because the terminal value is usually the majority of the total and its denominator is the small difference between those two numbers. Which is precisely why the right response is a sensitivity table rather than a defended point estimate. Saying that last part is what signals you have actually built one, because it is the thing people learn only from watching a model swing by 60% on inputs they cannot pin down.

Where each method breaks — and why analysts triangulate

Every valuation tool has a domain where it fails, and knowing the failure modes is worth more than knowing the formulas — using the wrong tool confidently is how people arrive at numbers that are not merely imprecise but structurally wrong.

DCF breaks down for pre-revenue companies. With negative cash flows for the entire forecast period, essentially all of the value ends up in the terminal value, which is computed from a growth rate and a discount rate applied to a cash flow that is itself a guess. The result is a number determined almost entirely by assumptions and almost not at all by evidence — a random-number generator in a suit. Venture investors use staged expected-value reasoning and comparables instead, which is an honest response to the fact that the distribution of outcomes, as Section 10 showed, is a power law rather than a forecast.

P/E breaks down for cyclicals. An automaker shows its lowest P/E at the peak of the cycle, precisely when earnings are about to fall, because the multiple is low on account of a temporarily inflated denominator rather than a cheap numerator. The fix is to use normalised mid-cycle earnings — the average across a full cycle — rather than the latest year, which is the same correction Section 7 flagged.

Book value breaks down for asset-light companies. A software firm's real assets are its engineers, its code and its brand, and the accounting rules from Section 11 expensed all three as they were created rather than recording them. Price-to-book compares a market value that includes those assets to an accounting value that excludes them, so the ratio is not high or low — it is measuring two different things.

Banks require an entirely separate playbook, and the reason is structural rather than conventional. For an ordinary company, debt is financing — money raised to fund operations. For a bank, debt is the raw material: deposits come in and loans go out, so borrowing is the business rather than a way of paying for it.

That breaks the enterprise-value framework at its foundation. Enterprise value exists to separate the operating business from how it was financed, and for a bank there is no such separation to make. EV/EBITDA is meaningless when interest income and interest expense are the operating line items.

So banks are valued on equity-side measures: P/E, price-to-book, and dividend-based models. Price-to-book is genuinely informative here, unlike the software case above, because a bank's assets are financial instruments carried at or near market value rather than historical-cost machinery — the book value is a real estimate of net worth. All of it is disciplined by the regulatory capital requirements from Section 6, which set a floor on how much equity the bank must hold against its assets and therefore cap how much it can earn on that equity.

All of which produces the professional habit the football field chart displays: triangulate. Run a DCF for the fundamental logic of the business, trading comparables for what the market currently pays, precedent transactions if a sale is plausible — and then treat the disagreements between them as the output rather than an inconvenience.

If the DCF says $42 and the comparables say $30, one of two things is true. Either your assumptions are more optimistic than those embedded in every peer's price, in which case you should be able to say exactly which assumption and why you believe it. Or the market is mispricing the sector as a whole, which happens and is worth acting on. Both are useful conclusions, and neither is available from a single method run in isolation. The gap is the insight.

Many investors add one more discipline on top: margin of safety, acting only when the price sits well below the entire range rather than merely below the point estimate. The logic follows directly from everything in this section. Your estimate has error bars you cannot eliminate, so requiring a large gap between price and value means that being somewhat wrong still leaves you with an acceptable outcome. It is buying insurance against your own model.

Deep dive: two refinements you'll meet in real models

Exit multiples. Instead of Gordon growth, many bankers set the terminal value as a multiple of terminal-year EBITDA — e.g. TV = 10 × EBITDA5 — borrowing today's comps for the far future. It feels more concrete but smuggles relative valuation into your intrinsic model; best practice computes TV both ways and checks that each implies a sane version of the other (a Gordon TV implies an exit multiple, and vice versa).

Mid-year convention. Our model discounts each year's FCF as if it all arrives on December 31, but cash actually dribbles in through the year. Discounting at t = 0.5, 1.5, 2.5… (dividing by (1+WACC)t−0.5) treats flows as arriving mid-year and raises the valuation by roughly half a year of discounting — about 4–5% at a 10% WACC. Small, but interviewers love asking about it.

Real world: valuing a company that loses money

A DCF needs positive cash flows and a P/E needs positive earnings, so how did anyone value Amazon in 2000, Tesla in 2015, or a pre-profit SaaS company today? By climbing the income statement to find the highest line that is reliable, and valuing that — then imposing discipline with a path to profit.

Situation What you can't use What analysts use instead
Pre-revenue biotech Everything financial Probability-weighted value of the drug pipeline: market size × chance of approval × discount.
Early SaaS, growing 60%, unprofitable P/E, DCF EV/Revenue, plus "Rule of 40" (growth % + margin % should exceed 40) and unit economics (LTV/CAC).
Bank EV/EBITDA (debt is raw material) P/B and P/E, judged against return on equity.
Loss-making marketplace Current earnings Contribution margin per order × a credible future order count — a DCF on the mature business it might become.

The danger is that the further up the income statement you go, the easier the number is to fake. Revenue multiples embed an assumed future margin, so "10× revenue" quietly smuggles in a profitability forecast you never stated. The 1999 dot-com bubble and the 2021 growth-stock bubble were both, at heart, revenue multiples applied to companies whose assumed future margins never arrived.

The professional discipline is to always translate a revenue multiple back into the DCF it implies: "10× revenue only makes sense if this company reaches 25% margins and keeps growing 20% for a decade — is that plausible?" If you cannot write down that sentence, you are not valuing the company, you are hoping. And the honest version of every valuation is a probability distribution, not a point — the same forward-inference-with-priors mindset you brought from data work, applied to a business.

Check your understanding

1. Your DCF gives an enterprise value of $1,775M. The company has $300M of debt, $100M of cash, and 50M shares. What is the per-share value?

EV belongs to debt and equity holders together. Subtract net debt (300 − 100 = 200) to get equity value of $1,575M, then divide by 50M shares: $31.50. Ignoring debt overstates the answer; ignoring the cash understates it.

2. In a typical 5-year DCF, roughly what share of enterprise value comes from the terminal value?

Terminal value usually carries 60–80% of EV (72% in our Cascade model). That is why WACC and terminal growth dominate the output — and why honest analysts always present a sensitivity grid.

3. You're comping five peers whose debt loads range from zero to heavy. Which multiple keeps the comparison fair?

P/E mixes an equity price with post-interest earnings, so leverage distorts it differently for each peer. EV/EBITDA compares whole-business value to pre-interest profit, neutralizing capital-structure differences.

4. WACC is 8% and terminal growth is 3%. An analyst nudges terminal growth to 4%. What happens to the terminal value?

TV = FCF×(1+g)/(WACC−g). The denominator drops from 0.05 to 0.04 (a 25% boost) and the numerator ticks up too — about a 26% jump in total from a one-point tweak. The WACC−g spread is the most explosive input in the model.

5. Why does a DCF fail for a pre-revenue startup?

The mechanics still run — you can always discount numbers — but with negative explicit-year flows, the answer is nearly 100% terminal value built on guesses. The model outputs false precision rather than insight; comparables and staged expected-value approaches work better.

Key takeaways

  • Price is a fact; intrinsic value is an estimate with error bars. A valuation model organizes your assumptions so disagreement with the market becomes legible.
  • DCF in five moves: project FCF for 5–10 years → terminal value via TV = FCF×(1+g)/(WACC−g) → discount everything at WACC → EV − net debt = equity value → ÷ shares. Cascade: $500M + $1,275M = $1,775M EV → $31.50/share.
  • WACC blends the CAPM cost of equity (rf + β×ERP) with the after-tax cost of debt, weighted at market values. Riskier cash flows get higher rates because a dollar you might not receive is worth less.
  • Terminal value is typically 60–80% of EV, and ±1pp on WACC or g swings the answer by double digits — present sensitivity grids and football fields, not point estimates.
  • Comps borrow the market's assumptions: pick honest peers, use median multiples, EV/EBITDA when leverage differs, P/E when it doesn't. Precedent transactions run 20–40% higher because of the control premium.
  • Every method has a failure mode — DCF for pre-revenue startups, P/E for cyclicals, book value for asset-light firms — and banks get equity-side multiples because their debt is raw material. So professionals triangulate.
  • You can now answer "walk me through a DCF" verbatim — and the follow-ups about net debt and sensitivity that prove you mean it.

Part III · Corporate Finance & Accounting

14. Corporate Finance: Decisions Inside the Firm

So far you have watched companies from the outside — reading their statements, computing their ratios, estimating their value. This section walks you through the door: how the people running the firm decide what to build, how to pay for it, and what to hand back to shareholders, using the exact toolkit you have already assembled.

The CFO's three questions

Strip away the org charts, the earnings calls and the job titles, and the work of a CFO reduces to three questions asked repeatedly about every dollar the firm touches. They are separable, they use different tools, and confusing them is the source of most bad corporate finance:

  • What should we invest in? This is capital budgeting — build the factory, fund the R&D, buy the rival, or do nothing.
  • How should we fund it? This is capital structure — borrow money, issue shares, or use retained profits.
  • What should we give back? This is payout policy — dividends, buybacks, or reinvest everything.

Every corporate headline you will ever read is one of those three wearing a press release. "Apple announces a $110 billion buyback" is a payout decision. "Microsoft acquires Activision" is capital budgeting — an acquisition is simply a very large project with a price tag attached. "Tesla raises $5 billion in new shares" is capital structure.

The classification is worth making a habit, because it tells you immediately which questions the announcement should be answering. A capital budgeting decision should be justified by the return on the money spent relative to what that money costs. A capital structure decision should be justified by the trade-off between the tax benefit of debt and the risk it adds. A payout decision should be justified by the absence of anything better to do with the cash. When a company announces one and defends it using the logic of another — for example, justifying a buyback by saying it will raise earnings per share — you have learned something.

Key idea

This section is where the course converges. Section 1 gave you discounting, Section 11 gave you the statements, Section 12 gave you ROE and ROIC, and Section 13 gave you valuation. Corporate finance is those four tools pointed inward: the CFO runs the same math on the firm's own projects that an analyst runs on the firm's stock.

Capital budgeting I: the NPV rule

Suppose the firm can spend $1,000 today on a project that returns cash over the following five years. Should it? The question sounds like it needs judgement and mostly does not: there is a correct method, and it is one you already know.

The gold-standard answer is net present value, or NPV. Stated in words: convert every future cash flow the project produces into what it is worth today, add all of those up, and subtract what the project costs to start. If the total is positive, the project produces more value than the money spent on it could produce elsewhere at similar risk, so do it. If negative, do not.

The word "net" is doing real work in that name. The initial outlay is included as a cash flow, just a negative one occurring at time zero, which is why the rule is simply "accept if the sum is above zero" rather than a comparison against the cost. In symbols, where CFt is the cash flow in year t and the year-zero flow is normally negative:

NPV = Σt=0n CFt ÷ (1 + r)t
CFt = cash flow in year t (CF0 is usually negative) · r = discount rate · accept if NPV > 0

Nothing in that formula is new. It is the time-value machinery from Section 1 pointed at a project rather than a bank deposit, and it is the identical present-value engine that produced the company valuation in Section 13.

The relationship between the two is worth stating explicitly, because it makes the whole of Part III cohere. A firm is a portfolio of projects. A discounted cash flow model values that entire portfolio from the outside, as an investor would. Capital budgeting values one candidate project at a time, from the inside, as a manager must. Same mathematics, different vantage point — and the reason a company with consistently positive-NPV projects is worth more than the sum of its assets is precisely that a DCF capitalises the value those projects will create.

Worked example: two rival projects

Project A ("Steady") costs $1,000 and pays $300 a year for five years. Project B ("Moonshot") costs $1,000, pays nothing for four years, then $2,000 in year 5. At a 10% discount rate:

NPVA = −1,000 + 300×(1 − 1.10−5)÷0.10 = −1,000 + 300×3.7908 = +$137
NPVB = −1,000 + 2,000÷1.105 = −1,000 + 2,000×0.6209 = +$242

Both add value, but if they are mutually exclusive, take B: it adds $105 more in today's dollars. Hold that thought — a popular rival metric is about to disagree.

A useful way to see all of this at once is the NPV profile: plot the project's NPV against the discount rate rather than computing it at one rate.

Read the shape and you learn what the project is. At a discount rate of zero, the curve starts at the raw undiscounted sum of the cash flows, because a zero rate means future money is worth its face value. As the rate rises, distant cash flows get compressed hardest — they are divided by (1 + r) once for each intervening year — so the curve falls, and it falls steeply for projects whose payoff is far away. The rate at which the curve crosses zero is the point where the project exactly breaks even against its cost of capital, and that rate has a famous name, which is the subject of the next subsection.

Your edge

NPV is a fold: cashflows.reduce((s, cf, t) => s + cf / (1 + r) ** t, 0). One line of code, and it is the single most consequential formula in corporate life. When you build financial models, most of the complexity is estimating the inputs (the cash flows), not the math.

Real world: the NPV rule as companies actually apply it

The formula is a fold over cash flows; the hard part is that every input is a forecast, and small changes flip decisions. Here is what capital budgeting looks like for four real project types:

Project The number that decides it
A new chip fab (~$20bn, TSMC/Intel scale) Terminal-year demand and the discount rate. The plant runs for 15+ years, so most of the NPV sits in far-future cash flows — which is why a 2-point move in WACC can turn a "yes" into a "no."
An offshore wind farm The power-purchase price and the interest rate. Costs are almost entirely up front, revenue is a fixed stream for 25 years — economically it is a long bond, and it lives or dies on rates.
A pharma drug program Probability of approval. Multiply each future cash flow by its chance of ever existing (often under 10%), which is just NPV with a probability weight on every term.
A software feature Incremental retention. The cost is a few engineer-years; the benefit is a small, uncertain lift in a subscription renewal rate compounding for years.

Two disciplines separate a real NPV from a spreadsheet fantasy. Use incremental cash flows only — the cash that exists because of the project and would not otherwise. Sunk costs (the market study you already paid for) are excluded; opportunity costs (the factory floor this project occupies, which could have been rented) are included, even though no invoice records them. And ignore accounting profit — NPV runs on cash, so you add back depreciation and subtract the working-capital build from Section 12. Companies that budget on accounting earnings instead of cash systematically overvalue capital-heavy projects.

Capital budgeting II: IRR, payback, and their traps

In practice, executives quote a project's IRR, internal rate of return, far more often than its NPV. The IRR is the discount rate at which the NPV equals exactly zero — that crossing point on the profile above — and it is interpreted as the project's implied annualised return. The decision rule is to accept the project if its IRR exceeds the hurdle rate the firm requires.

The appeal is obvious. "This project yields 15%" is a sentence anybody understands, it compares directly against a cost of capital, and it needs no units — you can quote it without knowing whether the project is worth thousands or billions. That last property is exactly where the trouble starts, because a return percentage deliberately discards the size of the prize, and size is what shareholders actually receive:

  • Scale-blindness. A $1 project returning $2 next year has a 100% IRR and adds about $0.82 of value at r = 10%. A $1,000 project returning $1,300 has a mere 30% IRR and adds $182. IRR picks the first; your bank account prefers the second. Percentages don't pay salaries — dollars do.
  • Multiple IRRs. If cash flows change sign more than once (invest, earn, then pay cleanup costs), the NPV polynomial can have several roots. The flows −100, +230, −132 have IRRs at both 10% and 20% — the number "the" IRR is simply undefined. (Check: at 15%, NPV = −100 + 230/1.15 − 132/1.15² = +0.19, positive between the two roots.)
  • The reinvestment assumption. IRR implicitly assumes every interim cash flow gets reinvested at the IRR itself. A 40% IRR project assumes you can redeploy each payout at 40% — usually fantasy. NPV assumes reinvestment at the discount rate, which is honest.

The third measure you will meet in the wild is the payback period: how long until the accumulated cash flows have covered the initial outlay. Project A recovers $1,000 at $300 a year, so it pays back in about 3.3 years; Project B not until year 5.

Payback is a reasonable quick liquidity check — a firm that cannot afford to wait genuinely does care how soon money returns — and it is a poor investment criterion, for two separate reasons. It ignores the time value of money entirely, treating a dollar in year three as equal to a dollar today. And more damagingly, it ignores everything that happens after the payback date. By payback logic, a project that returns your money in year three and then produces nothing at all beats one that returns it in year four and then pays a fortune for a decade. It is answering "when am I safe?" rather than "how much do I make?", and those are different questions.

Now the main event, and the clearest demonstration of why the choice of criterion matters. Below, Projects A and B are evaluated at every discount rate at once. B has the larger total prize but makes you wait for it; A drip-feeds cash from the start.

That difference in timing produces the shapes you see. B's curve starts higher, because undiscounted its cash flows total more. It falls faster, because its cash flows are further out and therefore more damaged by discounting. Two curves with different starting heights and different slopes cross — and they do so here at about 14.4%.

Which produces the paradox. Project A has the higher IRR, 15.2% against 14.9%, so the IRR rule says choose A. But at any discount rate below 14.4%, B has the higher NPV, so the NPV rule says choose B. At a realistic cost of capital of, say, 10%, the two rules give opposite answers about the same pair of projects.

When they disagree, trust NPV. The reason is what each one measures. NPV reports dollars of value created at the firm's actual cost of capital, which is the quantity shareholders end up owning. IRR reports a rate, and a rate says nothing about how much capital earns it — a 30% return on $10,000 is worth less than a 12% return on $10 million. IRR also implicitly assumes interim cash flows can be reinvested at the IRR itself, which is exactly the assumption that flatters the front-loaded project. Quote IRR to communicate; decide on NPV.

Project duel — NPV vs IRR

Drag the discount rate. Watch the verdict flip as you cross ~14.4% (rankings swap) and ~15.2% (both go negative) — and notice IRR would have picked A the whole time.

NPV A · Steady (IRR 15.2%)—
NPV B · Moonshot (IRR 14.9%)—
Verdict—

Common pitfall

Private equity marketing decks lean hard on IRR because early cash returns inflate it. A fund that returns your money fast at a modest multiple can post a dazzling IRR while creating less wealth than a slower fund with a bigger multiple. Always ask for the dollar multiple alongside the percentage.

Worked example: how IRR flatters a private-equity fund

IRR's reinvestment quirk is not academic — it is a marketing tool. Two funds both turn $100M into $200M, a clean 2× over the life of the fund. Watch how differently they can report:

Fund A (fast flip) Fund B (long hold)
Invest $100M at year 0 $100M at year 0
Return $200M at year 2 at year 8
Multiple (MOIC) 2.0× 2.0×
Reported IRR 41% 9%

Identical money multiple, wildly different IRR — because IRR rewards speed and implicitly assumes you can redeploy the returned cash at the same 41%, which you almost never can. A fund that exits an investment quickly can post a dazzling IRR while returning no more total money than a plodding rival. This is why sophisticated limited partners insist on seeing MOIC alongside IRR, and why a fund quoting only IRR is telling you how fast, not how much.

There is even a technique — "subscription lines" — where funds borrow to delay calling investors' capital, mechanically shrinking the time money is invested and inflating the reported IRR without improving a single deal. The arithmetic that makes this work is exactly the reinvestment assumption above. Whenever a return metric can be improved by changing timing rather than outcomes, treat it with suspicion.

The hurdle rate: WACC and the value-creation test

NPV requires a discount rate, and everything above quietly assumed one. Where does it come from? Not from a market quote — no one publishes the right discount rate for your project — so it has to be built from the cost of the money being spent.

The firm's money comes from two groups with claims on it, and each requires a different return because each bears different risk. The cost of debt is observable: it is roughly the yield on the firm's own bonds, from Section 8, because that is what the market currently demands to lend to it. The cost of equity is not observable and must be estimated, usually with the CAPM from Section 13: it is the return shareholders require for holding a stock of this risk.

Blend the two in proportion to how much of the funding each provides and you get the WACC. In words: the share of funding from equity times what equity costs, plus the share from debt times what debt costs after tax. The after-tax adjustment on the debt leg is there because interest is deducted from taxable profit, so the government pays part of the interest bill:

WACC = (E ÷ V) × rE + (D ÷ V) × rD × (1 − t)
E, D = market value of equity, debt · V = E + D · rE, rD = cost of equity, debt · t = tax rate (interest is tax-deductible)

Work an example. A firm is financed 70% with equity costing 9% and 30% with debt costing 5% before tax, at a 21% tax rate. The debt's after-tax cost is 5% × (1 − 0.21) = 3.95%. So WACC = 0.70 × 9% + 0.30 × 3.95% = 6.3% + 1.185% ≈ 7.5%.

It matters what kind of number that 7.5% is. It is not an accounting cost — nobody writes a cheque for it, and it appears on no financial statement. It is an opportunity cost: the return the firm's investors could earn elsewhere on investments of comparable risk. That framing is what makes the decision rule work. A project earning 6% is not a project that loses money; it is a project that makes its investors poorer than the alternative they gave up to fund it, which is the same thing from their point of view.

It also explains why the discount rate is specific to risk rather than to the firm. If a project is riskier than the company's existing business, its investors' alternatives are riskier investments with higher expected returns, so the correct hurdle is higher — a point the failure mode below turns on.

This closes a loop opened in Section 12. There you computed ROIC, the return a business actually earns on the capital tied up inside it, and the discussion stopped short of saying what counts as a good ROIC — because the benchmark had not been built yet. WACC is that benchmark, and comparing the two is the single most useful test in corporate finance:

Key idea: the value-creation inequality

A firm creates value if and only if ROIC > WACC. Earn 15% on capital that costs 7.5% and every reinvested dollar is worth more than a dollar; earn 6% and growth actively destroys value — the firm is a machine for converting good money into bad projects. Revenue can grow, EPS can grow, the CEO can ring the opening bell, and value still burns. This single inequality explains most of what separates great compounders from value traps in Section 13-style valuations.

In practice firms set a hurdle rate at, or slightly above, their WACC and require anyone proposing a project to clear it. The small buffer exists because project sponsors are optimistic — the person who wants the project approved is also the person forecasting its cash flows — so a hurdle a little above the true cost of capital absorbs some of that optimism.

There is a quiet failure mode in that arrangement, and it is common enough to look for deliberately. A single company-wide WACC gets applied to every division, but WACC is the cost of capital for the firm's average risk. A stable, predictable division evaluated at the company rate is being held to too high a bar and will reject good projects. A speculative division evaluated at the same rate is being held to too low a bar and will approve bad ones, because its true cost of capital is higher than the average.

The result is a systematic transfer: the boring divisions' safe cash flows end up subsidising the exciting divisions' risky projects, and because everything cleared the same official hurdle it looks disciplined the whole way. The correction is to use divisional costs of capital estimated from the betas of comparable standalone companies, which is more work and is why many firms do not.

Capital structure: the debt–equity trade-off

Now the second question: how should the firm pay for all this? Start with an observation that looks like it settles the matter and does not. Debt is cheaper than equity, for two independent reasons. Lenders take less risk because they are paid first, so they require a lower return. And interest is deductible from taxable profit while dividends are not, so the government effectively pays part of the interest bill.

If debt is cheaper, why not fund everything with it? Because cheapness and cost are different things here. Debt is a hard promise: a fixed amount on a fixed date, owed regardless of how the year went. Equity is a soft claim — in a bad year shareholders simply receive nothing and the company carries on. Substituting hard promises for soft claims lowers the average cost of capital and converts bad years into potentially fatal ones.

So the capital structure decision is a genuine trade-off with a prize on one side and a price on the other, and the optimum is somewhere in the middle rather than at either extreme.

The prize: the tax shield. Interest is deducted before tax is computed; dividends are paid out of profit after tax. That asymmetry is a genuine subsidy to borrowing, and it can be valued precisely.

Borrow $100 million at 6% and the annual interest bill is $6 million. That $6 million reduces taxable income by $6 million, so at a 21% tax rate the firm's tax bill falls by $6M × 21% = $1.26 million every year. That saving is real cash the firm keeps solely because of how it financed itself, and it is called the tax shield.

If the debt is permanent — refinanced indefinitely, as large companies generally do — that saving is a perpetuity, so its value is the annual amount divided by the discount rate: 1.26 ÷ 0.06 = $21 million. Notice that $21 million is exactly the tax rate multiplied by the debt, 21% of $100 million, which is not a coincidence: the interest rate cancels between the numerator and the denominator. The value of the shield depends on how much you borrow and the tax rate, not on what the debt costs.

The price: financial distress. As debt rises, so does the probability of a year in which the firm cannot meet a payment. And the costs of approaching that state are far larger than the legal bill, which is what people usually picture.

Financial distress costs begin long before any default. Customers stop buying from a company that might not be around to honour a warranty or support a product — which is devastating for anything sold with a service commitment. Suppliers withdraw credit terms and demand cash up front, which consumes working capital at precisely the wrong moment. The best employees, who have the most options, leave first. And management, hoarding cash to survive, cancels genuinely positive-NPV projects, so the firm's future earning power shrinks.

The important structural point is that all of these destroy value even if the company never actually defaults. The mere elevated probability of distress is enough to trigger them, which is why the cost curve rises smoothly with leverage rather than switching on at bankruptcy. Somewhere along that curve, the marginal tax shield stops being worth the marginal distress cost, and that point is the optimal capital structure — different for every industry, which is why a utility with stable regulated cash flows can carry debt that would destroy a biotech.

Between the prize and the price sits leverage's defining property, which is that it amplifies whatever happens. It is worth seeing the amplification arithmetic directly rather than taking it on trust.

Take a firm with $100 million of assets. Funded entirely by equity, a 12% return on those assets produces $12 million of profit on $100 million of shareholders' money, so ROE is 12% — the same as the asset return, because there is nothing to amplify.

Now fund the identical assets with $50 million of equity and $50 million of debt at 5%, so the interest bill is $2.5 million (ignoring tax for clarity). The assets still earn 12%, or $12 million, but the lenders take $2.5 million of it, leaving $9.5 million for shareholders whose stake is now only $50 million:

Scenario Asset return Profit after interest ROE (on $50M equity)
Good year +12% → $12.0M $12.0M − $2.5M = $9.5M +19.0%
Bad year −4% → −$4.0M −$4.0M − $2.5M = −$6.5M −13.0%

Same business, same swings in what the assets earn, and the shareholder's experience has changed from a range of 12% down to −4% into a range of 19% down to −13%. Leverage did not improve the business; it widened the distribution of outcomes for the equity holder in both directions.

This is precisely the third lever of the DuPont decomposition from Section 12, now seen from the inside — there you observed that ROE could be raised by borrowing, and here is the mechanism that does it. The reason the amplification works is that the debt's cost is fixed at 5% while the assets' return varies. Everything the assets earn above 5% belongs entirely to the shrunken equity base; everything they fall short by is subtracted from it.

The general relationship, with debt costing rD and leverage L defined as assets divided by equity, is: ROE = L × ROA − (L − 1) × rD. In words, the shareholder earns the asset return magnified by the leverage ratio, minus the cost of the borrowed portion. Checking against the example: 2 × 12% − 1 × 5% = 19%, which matches.

Leverage amplifier

Set the asset return and the leverage ratio (debt costs 5%). Watch what leverage does to a bad year.

ROE unlevered (1×)—
ROE at your leverage—

—

One piece of theory frames everything above. In 1958, Modigliani and Miller proved that in a perfectly frictionless world — no taxes, no distress costs, no information gaps between managers and investors — capital structure is irrelevant. The total value of a firm is determined by the cash its assets produce, and how you divide the claims on that cash between lenders and shareholders does not change the total. Cutting a pizza into different pieces does not produce more pizza.

That sounds like a result with no practical content, and it is the opposite. It tells you exactly where the value in capital structure decisions must come from: not from financial engineering itself, but from the frictions the theorem assumed away. Taxes, distress costs and information asymmetry are not footnotes to the theory — after Modigliani and Miller, they are the entire subject.

It functions like a no-free-lunch theorem in that respect. It does not say there is no lunch; it says the lunch cannot be where you were looking, which narrows the search enormously. Whenever someone claims a financing structure creates value, the theorem tells you to ask which specific friction they are exploiting — and if they cannot name one, they are moving pizza slices around.

Worked example: the leverage that saved a company and the leverage that killed one

Leverage multiplies asset returns into equity returns, symmetrically, in both directions. Take a business with $1,000M of assets earning a 10% operating return in a good year and −5% in a bad one, and finance it three ways:

No debt 50% debt 80% debt
Equity $1,000M $500M $200M
Interest (debt at 5%) $0 $25M $40M
Good year (+$100M operating) +10% +15% +30%
Bad year (−$50M operating) −5% −15% −45%

The 80%-debt structure turns a fine 10% year into a spectacular 30% and a survivable −5% year into a −45% bloodbath. It also changes the question in the bad year: at 80% debt the $40M interest bill against a $50M operating loss means the company cannot pay its lenders from operations — it must raise cash, cut, or default, exactly when doing any of those is hardest.

This is the whole plot of the leveraged-buyout industry and of most corporate failures. The same debt that produced private equity's returns for two decades of falling rates became a noose when rates rose in 2022 and interest bills reset upward against unchanged operating profits. Leverage does not change whether a business is good; it changes how little has to go wrong before the equity is gone.

Payout policy: dividends vs buybacks

Suppose the firm generates more cash than its positive-NPV projects can absorb. Simply holding the surplus is not a neutral act — it is itself a capital allocation decision, and usually a poor one. Cash in the bank earns a money-market rate of a few percent, while the shareholders whose money it is require the WACC. Every year the cash sits there, it is earning less than its opportunity cost, which destroys value quietly and continuously.

There is a governance dimension too. Large cash balances remove the discipline that having to justify spending to outside investors imposes, and the historical record on what companies do with unneeded cash — expensive acquisitions at the top of cycles, above all — is not encouraging. Which brings us to the third question: returning the money. There are two pipes for doing it.

A dividend is a direct cash payment, a fixed amount per share, usually quarterly. The crucial feature is not the mechanics but the expectation it creates. Once a company has paid a dividend for several years, the market treats it as a quasi-promise, and cutting it is read as a signal that management expects serious trouble. Dividend cuts routinely knock 10–20% off a share price on the announcement — which means initiating a dividend commits the firm to finding that cash every quarter, in good years and bad.

A buyback, or share repurchase, spends the same cash buying the firm's own shares in the open market and cancelling them.
